en: Victorious is he, for whom compassion— residing within his heart— flowed forth upon seeing this entire world afflicted by the disease of wretchedness, and became manifest in the form of aesthetic rasa.
*Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇādhipati!
Having bowed to him who is skilled in protecting from the fear of worldly existence, [the author] composes the Mugdhāvabodhinī.
I have obtained this commentary, which is well-composed according to the *Rasahṛdaya* and proceeds with straightforward clarity.
In the Kurala family, which is an ocean of virtues, there was Hariharamiśra, whose greatness was renowned;
his son, honored on earth, was famous by the name Maheśa.

Then, in his lineage, there was a lord named Bhāratībhāvasaṃyuta; his son was Prastutavāgbhirīśvara, who possessed four arms and whose mind was purified by devotion, born into a family of his own realm through the power of its ancestral tradition.
In the lineage of Khaṇḍelavāla, there was the elder Pārijātakataru on this earth; his son was indeed Nāthaballavasuda, who was endowed with life, fame, and wealth.
And by his son, Sāvare, the lord of the bound [manuscript] who sought righteousness, effort was constantly made here by him, the son of Uccaja, for the sake of the gods.

At the commencement of this treatise, the venerable teacher Śrī Govindapāda performs an auspicious invocation (maṅgala) in the form of a statement of the subject matter (vastunirdeśa) for the sake of honoring the tradition of the learned, [referring] to the feet of the Blessed One, the Guru, who is teaching the scripture—
beginning with the words "Victorious," and so forth.
The definition of an auspicious opening (maṅgalalakṣaṇa) is as follows: "An auspicious opening consists of a benediction, a salutation, or a statement of the subject matter."
The exposition of the objective entity is fivefold: that which exists, that which appears, the pleasant, form, and name—this is the pentad of parts.
The first three are of the nature of Brahman, and the following two are of the nature of Śakti.
That Hara is victorious; he exists with supreme excellence.
"Behold the entire world"—from this specification of the object, it follows that there must be a seer.
And thus says the Śruti: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper."
He sees though he has no eyes; he hears though he has no ears;
he knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him. Him they call the foremost, the ancient Person (Puruṣa).
In whose very heart compassion, consisting of the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), has arisen—that is, become manifest.
Having become what, having dissolved, and having flowed away—since it is logical that there is a falling away from the place of that which has dissolved. // GRhtCM_1.1:14 //
This very [truth] resides within the heart.
Thus, this indeclinable expresses the negation of [the word] being in any other position.
"Having the form of mercury" (rasarūpiṇī) means she whose essential nature is mercury (rasa), which is quicksilver (pārada).
And thus says the verse:
"Rasa is water; rasa is joy; rasa is that which is preceded by the erotic (śṛṅgāra);
and rasa is found in the sweet and other tastes, in exudations, in mercury, and in poison."
Thus, [the word] has multiple meanings. // GRhtCM_1.1:18 //
In general, its nature is fluidity; specifically, its nature is taste, which is the quality of being beneficial to all.
And so it is said in the *Rasaratnākara*:
"It is the sole fire that burns away the sins committed since birth, and takes the form of a lion to subdue the elephants of the misery of poverty. (GRhtCM 1.1:20)

Of what kind of Hara? Of him who beholds the world—the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)—as agitated by wretchedness and disease; "wretchedness" (dainya) being a state of misery or poverty, and "diseases" (gadāḥ) being ailments. Thus it is filled and pervaded by those. (GRhtCM 1.1:21)
"Akhilam" is a term meaning "all-pervading."
Just as in the *Mañjarī*:
"Whichever formulation corresponds to whichever disease, one should administer it with that very [substance];
thus Rasendra Hara removes the diseases of men, elephants, and horses. (GRhtCM 1.1:23)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.1:24 //
And there is another opinion:
in that [context], the sequence of the compendium (*saṃhitākrama*) is stated even without the ash of mercury (*rasabhasma*).
Even what is not explicitly mentioned there and there should be understood for the sake of pacifying the limbs [of the ritual].
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.1:26 //
Victorious is he who is clothed in yellow garments, the conqueror of Bali, who rides upon Garuḍa— the one whose intense passion destroys the serpent race;
like Hari, this son of Harā has shattered the heavy burden of the misery of worldly existence.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
"Yellow," etc. // GRhtCM_1.2:1 //
By this verse, the poet indicates the equality of Haraja and Hari.
Victorious is that Haraja, described by the ancient poets, who exists in supreme excellence; he is called Haraja because he was born from Hara, the Lord (Īśvara).
He is compared to Hari, that is, to Viṣṇu.

Of what nature is Hari? He is the one clad in yellow garments (*pītāmbara*); that is, he whose two garments (*ambare*) or cloths (*vastra*) are yellow, because of his wearing a pair of fine silk robes (*dukūla*).
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is called "Balijit" because he conquers Bali, a specific Daitya named Bali.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? [The text says] "for the destruction of the nāgas," and so forth: he is that Garuḍa, the lord of birds, who possesses intense passion—that is, great delight—for the destruction or ruin of the nāgas such as Śeṣa and others; thus he is described. Again, how qualified is he? By the epithet beginning with "crushed" (*vidalita*), it means he by whom the burden of suffering of *bhava*—of cyclic existence—has been crushed or removed.
"Wretchedness" (*dainya*) refers to poverty, and "suffering" (*duḥkha*) refers to the form of disease; the "burden" (*bhara*) of these two is their abundance. // GRhtCM_1.2:8 //
Now he qualifies the one born of Hara: "Pītāmbara" (the yellow-robed one); the meaning of "pītāmbara" is as explained previously.
How is it appropriate? This king of sūtras clarifies that very point: four types of garments were worn according to the distinction of castes, beginning with the Brahmins.
As it is stated in the *Rasaratnākara*:
"The mercury of the Brahmins and the other castes has the appearance of white, red, yellow, and black. (GRhtCM_1.2:11)
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are to be known by their wearing white, red, yellow, and black garments respectively, but not by their actual physical form.
As in the *Rasamañjarī*:
"That which is deep blue within and radiant without, possessing a brilliance like the midday sun. (GRhtCM_1.2:13)
The saying goes that his inner nature was one thing, while his outward garments were another.
The word "atha" is used in the sense of conjunction; it signifies clarity of mind.
The word *atha* is used in the senses of auspiciousness, immediately following, commencement, inquiry, time, one's own authority, promise, and conjunction. (GRhtCM 1.2:16)
Furthermore, what are his specific qualities? He is the "conqueror of Bali" (balijit), meaning he conquers the *bali*—that is, the skin produced by old age.
Thus, [the word] has multiple meanings. // GRhtCM_1.2:18 //

Furthermore, what are his specific characteristics? "Nāgakṣaya" and so forth: he is *nā*, meaning one in the form of a male (*puruṣa*). Furthermore, what are his characteristics? That by which one goes is *ga*;

*gakṣaye* means when there is the destruction of the two wings (*pakṣa-nāśe*). He who possesses intense passion (*bahala-rāga*)—that is *rasa*—is carried like Garuḍa by that [passion]. Thus it is said. (GRhtCM 1.2:19)
The intended meaning is: does mercury grant the power of traveling through the sky when its wings have been destroyed?
As it is said in the *Rasaratnākara*:

"When killed, it destroys old age and death; when swooned, it is the destroyer of diseases; and when bound, it grants movement through the sky. Who else besides mercury (sūta) is such a performer of actions? (GRhtCM 1.2:21).
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.2:22 //

Furthermore, what are his specific qualities? The phrase beginning with "vidalita" (shattered) and so forth indicates, through the theme of compassion, his capacity to remove the suffering of those in distress. // GRhtCM_1.2:23 //

Having fainted, it removes pain; having experienced bondage, it becomes the giver of liberation; when well-deadened, it makes one immortal—what other source of compassion is there besides mercury? (GRht 1.3)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Who else besides that previously specified Lord Śiva—who is devoted to compassion and full of mercy—could there be who removes *ruj*, the pain of the body? None at all; for [Śiva] alone removes it. 1.3.1*
Having become what? Having fainted; that is, having become unconscious.

The characteristic of *mūrchita* (coagulated) mercury is described in the *Rasaratnākara*: "When the mercury, having abandoned its intense volatility, appears with the luster of collyrium (*kajjala*), it should then be known as *mūrchita* by the wise. (GRhtCM 1.3:3)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.3:4 //
Having experienced bondage again and having held it fast, he becomes a giver of liberation; that is, he bestows liberation.
Liberation is described as being fourfold, distinguished by the categories of *sālokya*, *sārūpya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sāyujya*.
Bondage is primarily of two kinds, and by way of its intermediate functions, it is of four kinds.
Now follows the enumeration of the two kinds of bondage: bondage without seed and bondage with seed.
Regarding the "seedless" (nirbīja) bound [mercury], as described in the *Rasamañjarī*:
"The mercury, having been digested with gold weighing one-quarter part, is reduced to a paste through the application of sulfur;
then, being repeatedly heated (*puṭita*) with equal parts of sulfur in succession, it is named 'seedless' and removes all diseases. (GRhtCM 1.3:9)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.3:10 //
Furthermore, as for that which is bound by seed (*bījabaddha*):
that which is processed together with mercury, gold, copper, iron, and sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) reduced to the state of seed,
and then joined with sixfold fragrant powders, possesses even greater potency when bound by seed.
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.3:12 //
The intermediate fourfold classification of binding is as follows:
"A *poṭa*, a *khoṭa*, a *jalaukā*, and the state of ash—these four types of binding are to be understood by the best of physicians in the process of extraction. (GRhtCM 1.3:13)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.3:14 //
The definition of *khoṭa* is given in the *Saṃketakalikā*:
"A *poṭa* is a compact mass, while a *piṣṭī* is a solid pillar;
when heated, it becomes a *khoṭa*, but when struck, it turns into powder. (GRhtCM 1.3:15)
When blown again, it melts and becomes *khoṭa*; such is the characteristic of *khoṭa*.
It is like a leech, a binding of cloth, or ash; it becomes like ash.
Thus [it is said]. // GRhtCM_1.3:17 //
Furthermore, being well-remembered, it renders one immortal.

In the *Vidagdhamukhamaṇḍana-bahirlāpikā*, the word "su" is used in the sense of praise (*pūjā*), as in the expression "sumṛtaḥ. What word is declared to mean "praise"? [Answer: *su*]. Who bears a breast that is not a breast? [Answer: *astanam*]. And who is renowned as the weapon of the enemy of the demon Pralamba? [Answer: *uraḥ*]. (GRhtCM 1.3:19)
He is to be honored as Sunāsīra.
The word "dead" (mṛta) is used for the sake of specification. // GRhtCM_1.3:21 //
Just as one who is dead:
"Moisture, density, mobility, and heavy brilliance—if these qualities are not found in someone, one should know him to be a corpse-like initiate (mṛtasūtakam). (GRhtCM 1.3:22)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.3:23 //
"He is to be worshipped," as it says in the *Rasendramaṅgala*:
"If one, through negligence, kills unbound mercury, that powerful mercury causes great suffering. (GRhtCM 1.3:24)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.3:25 //
He who has died through the succession of bonds beginning with the *mūrchanā* is worthy of worship, and not otherwise.
And as it is stated in the *Rasamañjarī*: "O Maheśvarī, he who destroys mercury that is undigested or seedless is a slayer of a Brahmin, a man of evil conduct, and a traitor to me."
Thus, this meaning is logically consistent.
Devotion to compassion is the inherent nature of the virtuous.
As it is said:
"Even when being cut, the sandalwood tree perfumes the blade of the axe. (GRhtCM 1.3:30)

Since it pacifies even that which is considered incurable— arising from the mass of sins committed by harming the preceptor of the gods, cows, or the twice-born— who else is more purifying than it? (GRht 1.4)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: "Surety," etc. // GRhtCM_1.4:1 //
Therefore, what other second thing is heard of that is more pure—indeed, exceedingly pure—than this king of elixirs? None at all.

For this reason, by certainty (*api*), it pacifies even incurable disease; that which is incurable despite being endowed with all forms—even by divine medicines—is nonetheless cured through the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*). And what is that incurable [disease]? It is that which arises from the collection of sins produced by the injury or killing, or the insulting, of gods (*sura*), teachers (*guru*), cows (*go*), and the twice-born (*dvija*).
From this, the chapter on misdeeds arises.
Indeed, that certain manifestation of Śiva vibrates within him spontaneously;
for otherwise, how could it pacify the disease of sin merely by its shining forth?
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
"Of that," and so forth. GRhtCM 1.5:1.
By this inference, the poet brings about what is recognized by the world.
Regarding that aforementioned king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*), there is a certain ineffable manifestation of Śaṅkara that is universal;
it "pacifies" (*śamayati*), meaning it brings about the cessation of suffering. "Śam" is peace or serenity; he who performs this is *Śaṃkara*. This [elixir] belongs to him, hence it is *Śāṃkara*.
The essential meaning is that this [elixir] manifests for the sake of the cessation of suffering. // GRhtCM_1.5:3 //

Suffering is twofold, consisting of that which is mental and that which is physical; furthermore, it is threefold due to the distinctions of the external (ādhibhautika), the celestial (ādhidaivika), and the internal (ādhyātmika).
Furthermore, this king of elixirs vibrates and manifests of its own accord.

Otherwise, in no other way and without the manifestation of Śaṅkara, how could one pacify the disease of sin—leprosy—which arises from the multitude of sins committed by harming the preceptor of the gods, cows, and the twice-born?
Why? Because it is merely a manifestation and because it is within the range of vision.
As it is said in the *Rasendramaṅgala*:

"By the merit gained from performing a hundred horse-sacrifices, or by the gift of ten million cows and ten million lordly elephants, or by the dharma equal to the gift of gold and land—a man may obtain that same merit simply by beholding the birth [of mercury]. (GRhtCM 1.5:8)
And that is the blessed beginning of the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*), in which there is constant compassion from the very start:
"Once the mercury is perfected, I shall make the earth free from old age and death."

*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: The poet praises the threefold binding of the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) through the states of being fainted, bound, and dead, beginning with the words "rasa" and so forth. (GRhtCM 1.6:1)
O people, the binding of mercury—the alchemical fixation of quicksilver—is blessed; for at its commencement, compassion constantly and continuously arises—this is the implied meaning.

"What will my form be when I have attained perfection in the art of alchemy (rasa) and achieved complete mastery over it, such that I shall make this earth free from old age and death?"—thus spoke he who was named Govinda.
Due to extreme proximity, even the present tense is expressed by the suffix *lṛṭ*.
"Free from decay and death" is an adverbial modifier of the action.
Old age, graying hair, death, and the relinquishing of life—just as these are absent from the earth, so too is old age and death not applicable to it.
In this context, by the word "mahī" (earth), those humans and others who dwell upon the earth are intended, because [the term] functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Furthermore, it is logical that through the power of elixirs (rasāyana), the prevention of old age may occur.
As it is said in the *Hitopadeśa*:
"That which destroys old age and disease is an elixir (*rasāyana*);
one whose body is purified should practice it in the first or middle stage of life."
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.6:9 //
How is the prevention of death not logical through ordinary medicine due to the diminution of other medicinal potencies, yet logical through the superior power of *raseśvara*? // GRhtCM_1.6:10 //
As it is said in the *Rasaratnākara*:
"O Vainateya, O King of Elixirs (sūtarāja) praised by the gods, I bow to you, who are like Garuda to the serpent of death and old age.
(GRhtCM 1.6:11)
And those who, without abandoning their bodies, have attained the form born from the creation of Hara and Gaurī—
they are the venerable Rasasiddhas, the hosts of mantras who serve as their attendants.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states "He who... and so forth to explain what the superiority [of this path] consists in by way of its negation of old age and death. GRhtCM_1.7:1 //
Those who have thus attained perfection in the alchemical elixir are worthy of being saluted, fit for respectful greeting, and deserving of praise.
The root *vad* is used in the senses of salutation and praise.

Of what nature are they? They are "not having abandoned the body" (*atyaktaśarīrāḥ*), meaning those by whom the body has not been relinquished; that is to say, they are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
The body is of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle; the gross consists of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, while the subtle consists of the three sheaths.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"This triad of sheaths—consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, and consisting of vital breath—when combined, produces the subtle body."
The subtle body is indeed something else.
And those who have attained perfection while not having abandoned their physical bodies are thus described:
the yogi Manthānabhairava, Siddhabuddha, Kanthaḍī, Koraṇṭaka, Surānanda, Siddhapāda, and Carpaṭī.
Kaṇerī, Pūjyapāda, Nityanātha, Nirañjana, Kapālī, Bindunātha, Kākacaṇḍīśvara, and Gaja.
Āllama, Prabhudeva, Ghoḍācolī, Ṭhiṇṭhinī, Bhālukin, Nāgadeva, Khaṇḍī, and likewise Kāpālika.
These and other great siddhas, by virtue of the grace resulting from the enjoyment of the elixir (*rasa*),
having shattered the staff of Time (*kāladaṇḍa*), wander throughout the three worlds.
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.7:12 //
Furthermore, what are they like? They have attained a body; that is, they are those who have taken up a physical form.

Of what kind was that body? It was "born from the creation of Hara and Gaurī"; Hara is Mahādeva and Gaurī is Pārvatī; their "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) means their procreation through sexual union, and the meaning is that [the sons] were born precisely from that.
Furthermore, for whom the "multitudes of mantras" (*mantragaṇāḥ*) are "servants" (*kiṅkarāḥ*), meaning that the collections of mantras are those who carry out his commands.

First, this birth in a noble family is the fruit of well-performed deeds; moreover, there is intelligence therein, and that too bears the fruit of weighing the entire surface of the earth; furthermore, the world is easily governed. (GRht 1.8)
The fruits of being subject to the earth are objects of desire, and those objects have various enjoyments as their fruit;
yet these enjoyments reside in the body, which is impermanent— alas, everything is in vain!

The word *tāvat* signifies totality; for according to the [grammatical] rule, "the pair *yāvat-tāvat* is used in the senses of totality (*sākalya*), limit (*avadhi*), measure (*māna*), and determination (*avadhāraṇa*). (GRhtCM 1.8–9:1)

This is the fruit of well-performed deeds, the fruit of well-executed actions; how much is this birth within a lineage of auspicious merit? "Independent intellect" (svatantrā dhīḥ) means an intellect that is under one's own control.
The word "api" (even/also) signifies with certainty.
That intellect has as its fruit the weighing of the entire surface of the earth; that which has the weighing of the whole, without exception, of the earth's surface as its fruit, is thus described.
Regarding "weighing" (*tulanam*): by means of a scale in the form of independent cognition, there indeed occurs a weighing of the entire surface of the earth. It is logical [to ask]:

"What is its shape? What is its measure? By whom is it inhabited? And by whom is it supported? Thus, according to the prescriptions of the astronomical Siddhāntas, the earth—which is beyond direct perception—is apprehended through the intellect.
Furthermore, by means of birth in a noble family and independent intelligence, the surface of the earth is easily governed, honored, and known.

By grasping one part, the whole is grasped; whether great or small, the ground is vast. That place where such great beings reside is worthy of worship, for it is impossible to know [it as anything else]; thus, it is "the whole. The connection with birth in a noble family is explained by the words beginning with "the ground" (*bhūtala*).
Regarding "subjection to the earth": the subjection (*vidheyatā*) on the earth—that is, within the terrestrial sphere (*pṛthivīmaṇḍala*)—is proficiency in all actions;

its "purposes" (*arthāḥ*) are the tasks to be accomplished. Of what nature are they? They are "having various enjoyments as their fruit" (*vividhabhogaphalāḥ*): those various things are enjoyments, thus "various enjoyments" (*vividhabhogāḥ*), meaning manifold pleasures; those for which these are the fruit are so described.
They are fruits, having the nature of fruit.
Enjoyments exist within the body; they come into being there.
Why? Because the Vedānta Sūtra states that the body is the locus for experiencing the fruits of *prārabdha* karma.
Therefore, the body is the substratum of enjoyments.
"Aho" is used in the sense of either "alas" (in distress) or "wonderful" (in amazement).
The intended meaning is that this body, however, is the most excellent of all.
That is liberation, because of the statement: "in the casting away of the body."

"Thus, having considered wealth, the body, and enjoyments to be impermanent, one should always strive [for liberation]. And that liberation comes from knowledge; that [knowledge] comes from practice; and that [practice] is possible when the body is stable. (GRhT 1.10)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Considering the body to be the means for achieving all goals, [the author] instructs what is desired: "O people, one must always exert effort at all times, day and night. Having done what? Having considered wealth, the body, and enjoyments to be impermanent and perishable—thus one must exert effort. 1.10.1*
What is the meaning? It means that just as the body might be eternally stable, if the body were eternal, then everything would be eternal.

Through the knowledge of that eternal body—by the realization that through this very [knowledge] which is most excellent, the body itself becomes eternal—and through the practice of that very [knowledge], liberation occurs.
When what exists? When the body is stable.
Through the qualities of the mind supported by the body, there is the sixfold action; the instability of the body and its cessation constitute the stability of the body, which is liberation.
He states that very thing in the words of the Guru to Rāma:
"Liberation is not on the back of the sky, nor in the netherworld, nor on the surface of the earth;
the complete cessation of all desires and the tranquility of the mind—this is what one perceives as liberation. (GRhtCM 1.10:6)
No elixir whatsoever, such as mercury or base metals, is capable of stabilizing that [mind],
for it is itself unstable by nature, combustible, subject to dissolution, and subject to drying. (GRht 1.11)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

By means of the stability—that is, the state of steadiness—of that body, it becomes a more effective agent (*kārakatarām*) for alchemy (*rasāyanam*), which is capable of destroying old age and disease. GRhtCM_1.11:1 //
The word "api" means "certainly."

What are "mercury, metals, and so forth"? Mercury (*sūta*) is *pārada*; "metals" (*lohāḥ*) refers to the nine types, including gold and others, which are distinguished as artificial (*kṛtrima*) and natural (*akṛtrima*).

The artificial ones are rājarīti, kharparī, and ghoṣa; the natural ones are gold, silver, copper, lead, and tin. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the major minerals (*mahārasa*) and minor minerals (*uparasa*) are to be understood.
What are these "descents of mercury" (rasāvatāra)?
For instance, realgar, orpiment, vimala, acala, sasyaka, kānta, vaikrānta, and pakṣipati are the great mercurial substances (mahārasa).
Sulphate of iron, sulphur, mica, alum, cinnabar, zinc, and copperas are declared by the experts in mercury to be the secondary substances (uparasa). Thus [ends verse 1.11].
Or rather, with regard to that body which is capable through stability, what is the elixir (*rasāyana*)—is it mercury, metals, and so forth?
That which is pervaded by the devouring [agent], such as iron and so forth, when it is produced, is thus described; "it produces" refers to the pervader.
The locative case is used in the sense of location (adhikaraṇa).

That body is itself unstable, having the nature of instability; furthermore, it is combustible, capable of being burnt; it is moistenable, capable of being made wet and decayed; and it is purifiable, capable of being dried up by fire, water, and wind—the meaning is that the body is combustible, moistenable, and capable of being dried.
The essential meaning is this: by means of mercury, iron, and so forth, the impermanent body may become permanent; this alone is the effort [to be made].
START GRhT 1.12–13 (Dissolution of Plants – Immortality)
Wooden herbs dissolve into lead; lead dissolves into tin, and tin into copper;
copper dissolves into silver, and silver into gold; and gold dissolves into mercury.

That alone is the king of essences (*rasarāja*), in which all living beings inevitably dissolve as in the Supreme Self; it makes the body free from old age and death. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* Just as all beings ultimately merge into the Supreme Self, so too do they find their dissolution in this [mercury]. This singular sovereign of fluids renders the body undecaying and immortal.

In the preceding verse, mercury, metals, and so forth were mentioned; therein, he demonstrates the sequence of the pervasive substratum (*adhivyāpakādhikaraṇa*) with the words "wood and herbs," and so on.

Wooden plants, such as the *kumārikā* and others, dissolve into lead (*nāga*); that lead dissolves into tin (*vaṅga*); that tin also dissolves into copper (*śulba*); that copper dissolves into silver (*tāra*); that silver dissolves into gold (*kanaka*); and that gold dissolves into mercury (*sūta*, *pārada*). Thus it is said.
How is it dissolved according to the prescribed method—both individually and as a collective whole?
Because the [base] elements constitute a group of enemies, there is even the conjunction of the great rasas and the uparasas; and the word "even" (api) [indicates this].
He describes [the state] as a totality with the words "in the supreme self," and so forth.
This unique king of essences, included within the beginning and end of the elements, makes the body ageless and immortal, free from old age and death.

*Rasarāja* means that which shines, glitters, or manifests itself, being encompassed by the *rasas*, *mahārasas*, and *uparasas*; or, as for the specific meaning, it is that which reigns (*rājate*) when the *rasas*, *mahārasas*, and *uparasas* have been rendered indifferent.

And thus says the Sūtra: "The sixth and seventh [case endings] are used in the sense of disregard. Alternatively, it is the king of the *rasas*—that is, the major *rasas*, minor *rasas*, and metallic ores (*dhātus*)—and is taught as being preeminent among them; its mention by way of preeminence is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), through which alone the inclusion of everything else is to be understood.
The particle *iva* is used in the sense of similarity.

In the Self, which is Brahman, there occurs the constant and certain dissolution—meaning the merging or absorption—of all beings, that is, of all living creatures; within Him, everything comes to rest.
"Sentient beings remain indeed in a state of despondency"—thus these two characteristics have been stated with respect to the nature of the Self as a detached witness.

Likewise, regarding the King of Mercury (rasarāja), one should understand the dissolution (*laya*) of wood, herbs, minerals, great minerals (*mahārasa*), minor minerals (*uparasa*), and so forth. The sequence of dissolution has been taught by means of its "external definition" (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*).

By means of its "essential definition" (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), it should be known that although herbs, minerals, great minerals, minor minerals, and the rest exist separately, they are indeed subsumed within its qualities; for since the Elixir (*sūta*) is subsumed within the qualities of all things, it is described by the teachers as possessing infinite qualities.
The secret is that there is equality between the two due to a particular state of absorption.
Just as yogins, when dissolved into the form of Hara, attain immortality,
so too do gold, iron, and other metals [attain it] when the sky is swallowed by the king of essences (rasarāja).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
To harmonize everything, he says "amṛtatvam" and so forth. GRhtCM_1.14:1.

Those yogins, who perform yoga together with their own selves, having become absorbed in the form of Hara—that is, in the body of Mahādeva—attain immortality; they reach the state of liberation (*muktatva*). According to Amara: "Liberation (*mukti*), isolation (*kaivalya*), nirvāṇa, the highest good (*śreyas*), the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*), and immortality (*amṛta*) [are synonyms]."

In the same manner, when the mercury— the king of essences— has swallowed the sky, that is, when it has consumed the mica (abhraka), then gold, iron, and other metals, having become dissolved, attain the state of nectar (amṛtatva), the condition of ambrosia, and thus become fit for the transformation into immortality.
Gold and iron are "hemalohau"; those for whom these two are the first are called "hemalohādyāḥ," or alternatively, those for whom the metal named gold is the first are so described.
When the mica has been swallowed, the process of *cāraṇā* occurs; it does not happen otherwise.
Having attained a stable body through the power of practice and having acquired knowledge endowed with the eight qualities,
he reaches the state of Brahman, no longer subject to the suffering of dwelling in rebirth.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now, [the author] reveals the fruit of having a stable body with the verse beginning "sthirā" and so forth. GRhtCM_1.15:1.
By means of the practice and consumption of that very king of elixirs mentioned previously, a person of stable body attains the state of Brahman.
The state of Brahman is the very nature of supreme bliss.
Having done what? Having attained knowledge.
What kind of knowledge is it that is endowed with the eight qualities and possessed of the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*?
How does one attain the state of Brahmā?
Furthermore, the meaning is that one does not fall again into the suffering of dwelling in existence—the hardship consisting of the three types of heat inherent in residing in saṃsāra.
Having attained knowledge, one reaches the state of Brahman.
How is it that there is no liberation without knowledge? // GRhtCM_1.15:9 //
Furthermore, in the *Praśnottararatnamālā*, it is asked: "What is the seed of the tree of liberation? It is right knowledge accompanied by action."
The supreme light stands pervading the worlds with one quarter;
that immortal state is easily attained through three quarters, not by mere dispassion alone.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
[The author] describes Brahman, which is accessible through knowledge, by means of a single aspect, and so forth. (GRhtCM 1.16:1)

What is that Brahman like? It is the supreme light, whose very nature is illumination. That supreme light stands pervading and supporting the worlds—the realms of saṃsāra such as heaven, earth, and the netherworld (pātāla). By what means? By a single portion (*ekāṃśena*), because it is the leader of many universes (*brahmāṇḍa*); since within each individual universe there exist many worlds, it is said "by a single portion. Furthermore, that supreme...

The meaning is that the immortal form of light is easily obtained— that is, attained with ease— by means of the three quarters known as practice (abhyāsa), steadiness of body (sthiradeha), and knowledge (jñāna).
First, practice regarding the ease with which the nectar is obtained.
The first cause is a stable body, the second cause is knowledge, and the third cause for liberation is according to the scriptural word, not mere dispassion alone.
Indeed, it is not possible by any means to worship that subtle Brahman with a body that is afflicted by the sufferings of disease, old age, and death, and which perishes in an instant.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Indicating that the cause for a stable body is more significant than the two aforementioned types of knowledge—namely, practice and theoretical knowledge—he says "no," and so forth. (GRhtCM 1.17:1)
The meaning is that, because both [the body and the self] are established as the means of proof, nothing whatsoever distinct from such a body is established in any way at all.

By what kind [of world]? "Afflicted by the suffering of disease, old age, and death. Disease (*vyādhi*) is illness; old age (*jarā*) is grey hair; death (*maraṇa*) is the abandonment of life; and suffering (*duḥkha*) consists of delusion, grief, and so forth. Afflicted (*vidhura*) means struck or tormented by these. This is the form of the root *vyadh* meaning "to strike," with the suffix *-ura* added to the stem *vidhura*.

Furthermore, by what kind of body—characterized as momentary and perishing in an instant—is it possible, and in what manner, to worship or serve that Brahman whose nature is a mass of consciousness and bliss? For how could it be so, since it is subtle, being ungraspable by the senses?
Who could grasp even the name of the perfection of yoga without a body— that reality which is attainable through yoga, stainless, and beyond the range of even the mind? (GRht 1.18)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states "nāma" and so forth, meaning that by every possible means the body must be made stable. GRhtCM_1.18:1.
"Who would take up even the name, that is, even the designation, of the perfection of the body (dehasiddhi), which is the mastery over the physical form? The meaning is: no one at all."
Without what [is there success]? Without a body, how can there be accomplishment? Yet that supreme name is not grasped by anyone as the "name of a body"—this is the intended meaning.
If that body becomes imperishable, stainless, and untainted, then the reality of Brahman will certainly be attained.
That reality is not even within the range of the mind; the meaning is that it cannot be reached even by the intellect.
In that case, by what is the meeting and unification of the two understood? It means: by that very unification of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*). This is the meaning.
From sacrifice, from charity, from austerity, from the study of the Vedas, from self-restraint, and from virtuous conduct— indeed,
through the power of yoga, self-realization is the ultimate good.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Now, [the author] demonstrates that yoga is superior to all ritual acts with the verse beginning "yajñāt" (1.19).
"Extremely beneficial" means that there would be a greater welfare consisting of the warding off of all calamities; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Why? Not merely from sacrifice, such as the Aśvamedha and others; nor from giving, that is, the bestowing of wealth upon worthy recipients (*pātra*); nor again from austerity, such as the *Kṛcchra*, *Atikṛcchra*, *Cāndrāyaṇa*, and *Agnitapana* penances; nor again from the study of the Vedas—the sequential recitation of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas; nor again from self-restraint (*dama*)—for restraint, according to the Vedānta, consists in the control of the external senses.

The withdrawal of the mind from objects other than that [Self]—that which is "other than that," meaning other than hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—and furthermore, from "right conduct" (*sadācāra*): the injunctions revealed by the Vedas, beginning from the *brāhmamuhūrta* and extending through the morning, midday, afternoon, evening, and so on, up until sleep; this collection [of practices] is conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskara*), but it does not produce self-realization (*ātmasaṃvitti*). On the contrary, self-realization [is produced by something else].
The realization of Brahman occurs only through the power of yoga; yoga has been explained previously.
The bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda*), which is free from all objects and the manifold of numerous discursive thoughts (*vikalpa*) that have dissolved away—
even though it vibrates within one whose body is non-vibrating— what can it do for the multitude of living beings?
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He explains what kind of person that living being (*jīva*) is who has attained consciousness through the power of yoga, beginning with the words "galita" and so forth. GRhtCM_1.20:1.
"Galitānalpavikalpa" means one for whom "analpa"—that is, extensive—"vikalpa," meaning false cognition, has "galita," that is, disappeared or become distant; such a person would be one like this.

Furthermore, of what nature is he? "Devoid of all objects" (*sarvārthavivarjita*): he is devoid of all those objects; the meaning is that there is an absence of both the recollection and the performance of tasks, as they are not properly maintained.
Furthermore, how is he characterized? "Bliss of consciousness" (*cidānanda*): he is so called because his bliss, the perfection of happiness, arises from consciousness, which is luminosity.
Through the cause of luminosity, there is bliss; through the cause of insentience, its opposite occurs.

"What does he do?"—that is, he asks—regarding that host of living beings (*jīva-samūha*) whose bodies are unmanifest and whose forms do not vibrate, even though He Himself has thus vibrated and is manifesting?
[The commentary *Prasāda* states: "The word *kim* is used in the senses of questioning and contempt. (GRhtCM 1.20:6–7)
And the man, though absorbed in that, asks and laughs and weeps like one who is intoxicated. // GRhtCM_1.20:8 //
That light consisting of consciousness, situated between the pair of eyebrows, pure as a peacock’s crest or lightning, which illuminates the world—
this dawns for some who have performed meritorious deeds.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Indicating the rarity of self-awareness, he says "the pair of eyebrows," and so forth. GRhtCM_1.21:1.
When that which is situated between the pair of eyebrows shines forth within the two brows, yogis fix their gaze there and perceive it through the *khecarīmudrā*. As stated in the *Haṭhapradīpikā*:
"The tongue enters the cavity of the skull and moves in reverse;
the gaze is fixed between the two brows—this is the *khecarīmudrā*. (GRhtCM 1.21:2)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.21:3 //
Furthermore, that which shines forth as pure amidst the crests of fire and lightning— that is, within the flames and flashes of the thunderbolt— and which again illuminates the world,

meaning it illumines the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), that light consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*) and abounding in radiance manifests, or appears, only for certain meritorious ones who have performed well-ordained deeds; it does not appear to all, because it is a stainless radiance.
Having meditated with vast merit, one is born for the sake of purity; therefore, illumination is appropriate.
One should know that which consists solely of supreme bliss, whose nature is the highest light, free from conceptual construction,
with all afflictions dissolved, peaceful, and self-cognizable.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Elucidating the nature of consciousness as previously described, he says "consisting solely of supreme bliss," and so forth. (GRhtCM 1.22:1)

That Brahman is to be known as consisting solely of supreme bliss; "supreme bliss" (*paramānanda*) means that this bliss is supreme and most excellent, and it is "solely" (*eka*) that is, non-dual—abounding in that [bliss] is what is thus described. Furthermore, how qualified is it? It has the nature of the supreme light (*parama-jyotiḥ-svabhāvam*);
that which is the supreme light is its nature, its very essence. Moreover, because it is bodiless and self-luminous, it is... [further].

It is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), devoid of false knowledge (*mithyājñānaśūnya*), and furthermore, from which all afflictions (*sarvakleśa*) have dissolved—that is, all afflictions and sufferings have been specifically dissolved and removed because it is its very nature. Furthermore, it is peaceful (*śānta*), consisting of tranquility (*śamamaya*), and moreover, it is to be known by oneself (*svayaṃvedya*);
it cannot be known by another, for the realization arises from the thought that "there is no other [knower] than myself. (GRhtCM 1.22:2)
Having fixed the mind upon that [Self], perceiving the entire world as vibrating [with consciousness],
one whose bonds of karma are destroyed attains the state of Brahman even here in this life.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the instruction regarding that which is to be known, beginning with "In that," etc. (GRhtCM 1.23:1).

Having fixed the mind—having established the mind—in that very Self previously described, a person becomes one whose bonds of karma are destroyed; he becomes one who has cast off the fetters of action.
The distinction is that he attains the state of Brahman in this very life, according to the Vedic revelation: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
That man applies his mind [to it].

Doing what? Beholding—perceiving with the eye of the mind—the entire world, that is, the whole of saṃsāra, as consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), whose nature is light, and as a transformation of consciousness; how characterized is the world? It is "throbbing," meaning it is shining intensely by way of superimposition (*adhyāropa*).
And so says the word of the Blessed One:
"He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions. (Gītā 4.18)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.23:7 //
O Pārtha, that man among men is truly wise.
By this, its status as a generality has been stated.

Furthermore, just as there is the delusion of a snake in a rope, the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl, a city of Gandharvas, or water in a desert, so too this saṃsāra has not existed, does not exist, and will not exist; according to the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda), it is purely illusory.
For objects indeed cease when there is a conjunction of the vital breaths and the internal organ;
there is no longer a vibration of the senses or of darkness, and consequently, neither suffering nor pleasure vibrates.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
For one whose karmic bonds have been destroyed, the objects of the senses pass away. (GRhtCM 1.24:1)
Due to the conjunction of the vital breaths and the internal organ, there would be no vibration of the sense faculties.

And likewise, in the Nyāya-śāstra, it is stated that the self (ātman) is conjoined with the mind (manas), the mind with the sense organ (indriya), and the sense organ with the object; thus, because of the rule that the sense organs function by reaching their objects, for this reason, suffering and pleasure do not manifest [directly].

From the illumination of the Self comes the illumination of the vital breaths and the internal organs; having attained that very illumination, the vital breaths and the internal organs cause the sense organs to shine forth.
Therefore, both [subject and object] are illuminated by another.
In the same way, the most profound darkness that is ungraspable becomes illuminated by light when it is pierced by consciousness. // GRhtCM_1.24:7 //
Because both non-existence and darkness are categories of non-being (abhāva), and because both the sense organ and darkness are insentient (jaḍa), there is a similarity between them.
Freed from attachment and aversion, men who act truthfully and are devoid of falsehood become indistinguishable in all respects through contact with the Consciousness-Brahman.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Now, [the author] demonstrates the activity of the internal organs with the verse beginning "rāga... and so forth. "From contact with the Consciousness-Brahman" (*cidbrahmasaṃsparśāt*) means from that contact which occurs within the Self, whose nature is light, in the form of the Consciousness-Brahman; by reason of being established therein, persons are "free from attachment and aversion" (*rāgadveṣaviyuktāḥ*), that is, devoid of affection and enmity.
They would be. // GRhtCM_1.25:1 //

Furthermore, those whose conduct is truthful are followers of the *pravṛtti-dharma*; moreover, they are free from falsehood, meaning they are devoid of improper conduct and untruth. Furthermore, they are without distinction in all things, being equal toward both honor and dishonor in everything;
and thus says the word of the Blessed One:
"Equal toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor. (GRhtCM 1.25:2)
And so forth. // GRhtCM_1.25:3 //

Those who have attained the immortal state of Brahman and have fulfilled their purpose remain forever joyful and blissful, their bodies radiant, endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest. (GRht 1.26)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Demonstrating the attainment of liberation through the state of touch within the Self, he says "tiṣṭhanti" and so forth. (GRhtCM_1.26:1)

Those who have attained the state of Brahman—the immortal, the identity with liberation—are those who have accomplished their purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*), meaning they have performed all duties and reached perfection. Furthermore, they remain here in this world endowed with *aṇimā* and the other powers;
as for these powers, *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, and likewise *garimā*.
Attainment, omnipotence, lordship, and mastery are the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi).
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.26:3 //

Furthermore, they possess radiant bodies, their forms consisting primarily of light; moreover, they are eternally blissful—meaning those whose joy and delight exist at all times—because they are immersed in supreme bliss.
One should know the body to be the abode of sciences and the root of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;
what else could be a higher good than this, were it not for its being subject to old age and death?
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
[The author] says "the abode" (*āyatana*) and so forth, stating that everything must be known as having the body as its root. GRhtCM_1.27:1.

Having abandoned—that is, having cast off—one body that is singular, undecaying, immortal, and devoid of old age and death, what other [body] is there? It means: none whatsoever. Of what nature is that body? It is the "abode" (*āyatana*) of the sciences (*vidyā*), meaning the dwelling place of the fourteen branches of knowledge beginning with grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is the "root" (*mūla*), meaning the cause, of the four goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*): dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; for dharma and the others...
The four [elements] are indeed well known.
START GRht 1.28:

Even by means of the instruments of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, he who does not know the *sūtaka* (the birth-impurity), how shall he know the God whose form is unseen and who consists of pure consciousness? GRht_1.28 // @------------------
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Indicating that [the work] is easy to understand for those who examine themselves, he says "by means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇataḥ*), and so forth. 1.28:1.

That person who does not know *sūtaka*, the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), from what source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—whether as the instrument of knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*) or as the means for achieving valid cognition (*pramiti*)—from what kind of source of valid cognition? From perception (*pratyakṣa*), which consists of form graspable by the sense of sight; how will that man know the self, which is composed of consciousness and is exceedingly subtle? The meaning is: "not at all," because it is beyond the range of the senses.

Of what nature is it? It is "without beginning and without body" (*anādivigraham*); that in which both a beginning (*ādi*) and a body (*vigraha*) do not exist is such. The intended meaning is that because of the absence of an origin and a physical form, there is an absence of gross cognition.
[It is] that which has been worn out by old age and has fallen under the power of sufferings such as coughing and asthma.
That is suitable for meditative concentration, as it restrains the outward flow of the intellect and the senses.

How can a mortal man—first a child of sixteen years, addicted to the tasting of sensual pleasures, and later, having developed discernment, grown old—attain liberation? *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* A young man of sixteen is obsessed with relishing the flavors of the sense objects; subsequently, having become aware of the distinction between reality and illusion, he grows old. How, then, can such a mortal attain liberation?
Showing the instability of the body through the divisions of its stages of life, he says "the child," and so forth.
"Sixteen years old" means a boy whose age consists of sixteen years; that is to say, he is a youth of sixteen.
In another treatise, it is stated that even in childhood, there exist distinctions of age.
As in the verse:
"Up to the fifth year it is *kaumāra* (childhood); up to nine years it is *paugaṇḍa*; up to sixteen it is *kiśora*; and beyond that is youth (*yauvana*). (GRhtCM 1.29–30:4)
Thus. // GRhtCM_1.29-30:5 //
The fool is incapable of knowing reality.

Furthermore, after sixteen years, one becomes addicted to the tasting of the flavors of sense objects (*viṣaya-rasa*). The sense objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; the "flavors" (*rasa*) are the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrifying, the loathsome, the marvelous, and the peaceful (*śānta*).

Some do not mention the peaceful flavor because it is free from emotional transformation (*nirvikāratva*). One is "addicted" (*lampaṭa*)—that is, intensely attached—to the tasting of these. Alternatively, following the sense objects, there is affection (*sneha*) therein. From that point onward, one develops discernment (*viveka*), meaning that inquiry (*vicāra*) arises.
Then, how could an old man who is incapable attain liberation or isolation (*kaivalya*)? The meaning is "not at all," because of the state of being afflicted by old age.
For those who have no realization of the Supreme Self within this very body,
that Brahman becomes even more remote for them after the abandonment of the body. (GRht 1.31)

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī): Having reflected upon the intention of the preceding verse, [the author], being questioned regarding the attainment of liberation, says "In this... and so forth. (GRhtCM_1.31:1)

While this body, which is of the nature of the field (*kṣetra*), persists, for those men in whom self-realization has not arisen— that is, in whom knowledge of Brahman has not arisen— for those very men, after the abandonment of the body, following the casting off of the physical frame, that Brahman is "farther away," meaning far, far away.
Brahmā and the other gods worship Him, having taken recourse to His divine body;
so too do other sages who are liberated while living and who endure until the end of the kalpa.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now, he confirms the previously stated view with the words "Brahmā and others," etc. (GRhtCM_1.32:1).

In whom Brahmā and others—Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and the rest who are knowers of Brahman—sacrifice; that is to say, they perform *saṅgati* (association) or attain [union]. The root *yaja* is used in the senses of worshiping a deity, performing *saṅgati*, and giving; here, the sense of performing *saṅgati* is indicated.

Having done what do they attain the divine, supreme body? Having resorted to and attained it, other sages besides those beginning with Brahmā—namely Nārada and others who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta)—worship it; that is, they cultivate union with it.
What is their specific quality? They endure until the end of the eon; the sense is that they remain even at the time of universal dissolution.
Brahmā and the others remain standing.
Therefore, by the yogi desiring liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), a divine body must first be fashioned through the union of the creation of Hara and Gaurī.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Having thus reflected in many ways, he speaks the praise of the desired object, beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), and so forth. (GRhtCM_1.33:1)

Since Brahmā and others, as well as other *jīvanmuktas*, attained liberation after assuming a divine body, for that reason a yogi engaged in yoga must first assume a divine body; the meaning is that he must make his body firm.
By what kind of yogi? By a yogi desiring liberation while living (jīvanmukti), a divine body (divyā tanuḥ) should be fashioned.
Why? Because of the union of the creation of Hara and Gaurī.
The meaning is that the mercury was created by Umā’s lord, and [the result follows] from its consumption.
What is desired is accomplished by one with a firm body, but not otherwise.

Furthermore, in the procedure for its accomplishment, the wise person must first understand with great effort the eighteen refinements (*saṃskāra*) which are purified by each respective ritual action.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Because it is the cause of the divine body, the eighteen purifications (*saṃskāra*) must first be diligently understood by a wise person—one of venerable intellect—in the procedure for the accomplishment of mercury, that is, in the instruction on its preparation. (GRhtCM 1.34:1) They are called "purifications" because they are purified (*saṃskriyante*). (GRhtCM 1.34:2)

In the case of males as well, the sixteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), beginning with *garbhādhāna*, take place; therefore, by means of these rites, there is equality between the two [genders] in terms of being free from defects and possessing virtues.
Therefore, there should be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Of what nature are these formations? They are pure with respect to each action; that is, they are faultless in relation to every individual deed.
START GRH 2.1–2 (18 saṃskāras):
Sweating, rubbing, fainting, raising, throwing down, stopping, and restraining; and...
Then, the measure of the lamp’s consumption of the sky and the procedure for its movement.

Internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*), external liquefaction (*bāhyadruti*), digestion (*jāraṇa*), coloring (*rasarāga*), transmutation (*sāraṇa*), penetration (*krāmaṇa*), piercing (*vedha*), and consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*): thus the alchemical operation (*rasakarma*) consists of eighteen types. (GRht 2.2) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [The commentary explains each of these technical terms in detail.]
He whose fame is lived upon even by the gods at their assemblies—
that illustrious one caused this commentary, *Mugdhabodhinī*, to be composed.
With two noble verses, the summary of the eighteen refinements of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) has been provided.
START GRH 2.3 (1. Svedana):
With *āsurī*, *paṭu*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *citra*, fresh ginger, and radish, each taken in one-sixteenth part;
The sudation of the processed mercury (*sūta*) with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) over three days by means of a mild fire.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now he states the definition for the accomplishment of the purificatory processes (*saṃskāra*).*
In this regard, clarifying the method for the first-mentioned refinement, which is steaming (*svedana*), he says "Āsurī," and so forth.

The sudation, that is, the process of heating, of the mercury (sūta) should be performed with a mild fire—that is, a very small flame—for a duration of three days, so that it lasts for a period of three days.
By what sour gruel? By sauvīra.
Along with what? Together with asurī, paṭu, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), citra, fresh ginger (ārdraka), and radish (mūlaka).
*Āsurī* is black mustard; *rājikā* is the same; *paṭu* is a specific type of salt, namely *saindhava*, though some explain the word *paṭu* as referring to alkali (*kṣāra*) as well.
The "three pungents" (*kaṭukatraya*) are ginger, black pepper, and long pepper. *Citraka* is well known. *Ārdraka* is a specific type of bulbous root that is the cause of *nāgara*.
*Mūlaka* is a well-known specific type of bulbous root.
By what kind of parts? By these sixteen parts; each [element] is joined with one sixteenth part.
This is the explanation accepted by all.
In this regard, there is a distinction: one should prepare all types of fermented grain liquids (*dhānyāmla*) in *kāñjika*, provided they are made without the husks.
Uragā, triphalā, krāntā, laghuparṇī, and śatāvarī.
It should be processed with that [substance] and steamed with the medicinal juices for three days over a mild fire.
Having ground it repeatedly with a vigorous swinging apparatus (dolāyantra),
according to the *Rasendramaṅgala*.

Indeed, for a substance placed in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus), the process of digestion (*pācana*) using alkaline or acidic medicinal herbs is called "sweating" (*svedana*), which causes the loosening of impurities;
such is the technical definition. GRhtCM_2.3:13.
Having filled half the belly of the vessel with a liquid substance,
one should carefully fashion two openings on both sides of its mouth.

One should place a staff over it and, having tied a *rasa-poṭalī* (mercury-pouch) in its middle, one should heat it; this is known as the *dolā-yantra* (swing apparatus). Thus ends the description of the *dolā-yantra*.
START GRHT 2.4 (2. Mardana):
With burnt jaggery, wool, salt, temple soot, brick-dust, and *surī* [liquor], [one should perform the rubbing].
One should perform a rubbing for three days using [the substances] measured at one-sixteenth part of the mercury, along with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states "guḍa... etc., clarifying the method for the rubbing (*mardana*), which was the second subject introduced.
*Commentary (GRhtCM 2.4:1)*: He states "guḍa... etc., clarifying the method for the rubbing (*mardana*), which was the second subject introduced.
The mercury should be rubbed with these medicinal herbs for a period of three days.
By these [substances]: *guḍa* (molasses), *dagdhorṇā* (burnt wool), and *lavaṇa* (salt). *Guḍa* is well known as a product of sugarcane.
*Dagdhorṇā* is a compound meaning "that which is both burnt and wool"; *ūrṇā* is understood here as a mass of sheep's wool. *Lavaṇa* refers specifically to *saindhava* (rock salt).
Alternatively, there is a reading *guḍadagdhorṇārajanī*, in which case *haridrā* (turmeric) is to be taken, not *saindhava*. 2.4.3.
Measured by a sixteenth part of mercury, that is, having the dimension of a sixteenth part of mercury.
The word "part" (aṃśa) is to be connected with each [of the preceding terms].
And here is the distinction: on an auspicious day, the mercury should be bound with fourfold cloths and placed [in the crucible].
One should grind [the ingredients] in a mortar made of iron, copper, or stone while they are indeed heated.

Grinding with the aforementioned medicinal herbs, along with all sour substances and fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika), is called "rubbing" (mardana); it destroys external impurities—such is the technical definition.
In this context, the yantra should indeed be known as the "Khalu" (the True).
As for the characteristics of that [stone]: an unsuitable stone is blue, dark, glossy, hard, and heavy.
It is sixteen finger-breadths in height and nine finger-breadths in width.
Thus, the characteristics of an unsuitable stone have been explained as a digression.
It is indeed nine finger-breadths in height, equal to one *kalā* (one-sixteenth) in length, ten finger-breadths in width, and likewise [nine] finger-breadths in depth according to the sages.
For on the rim, it should be one finger-breadth wide, very smooth, shaped like a half-moon, and twelve fingers long; this indeed is considered the mortar for grinding.
START GRht 2.5–6 (3. *mūrcchanā*):
Impurity (*mala*), fire (*śikhi*), and poison (*viṣa*) are the three natural defects of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
It causes fainting through impurity, burning through fire, and death through poison.

The house-maid (*gṛhakanyā*) removes impurity, while *triphalā*, fire, and *citraka* remove poison. Therefore, one should repeatedly saturate [the powder] seven times with these mixed together. (GRht 2.6) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* The house-maid removes impurity; *triphalā*, fire, and *citraka* remove poison. Therefore, one should repeatedly saturate [the powder] seven times with these mixed together. (GRht 2.6)
There are three defects of mercury, which is the essence.
Of what nature are they? They are designated as "impurity, fire, and poison"; that is to say, those whose names (abhidhāna) are precisely these—impurity, fire, and poison—are so described.
Furthermore, what are their specific characteristics? They are *naisargika*, meaning they are innate (*sahaja*), pertaining to *nisarga*, which is birth or origin.
And here the distinction is that there are five impurities (mala) and so forth as defects, and seven coverings (kañcuka) beginning with earth (bhū).
"The eight types of leprosy reside within the *rasa*; they bestow infinite defects upon that *rasa*," so it is said in the *Rasasaṃketakalikā*.
Although five natural defects (doṣas), beginning with impurity (mala), are mentioned in the *Rasendramaṅgala*, here only three are [explicitly] stated.

Why are the other two—heaviness (*gurutva*) and volatility (*capalatva*)—not included as natural defects? Because they are not removed by the three purificatory processes (*saṃskāras*) consisting of sweating (*svedana*), rubbing (*mardana*), and tempering (*mūrchana*).
By the inclusion of the term "natural," there would also be the inclusion of those that are "accidental."
In this context, the innate [dispositions] have been stated; why have the acquired ones not been stated? Because there is neither existence nor non-existence of acquired dispositions.

The *rasa*, when consumed while enveloped by the three *doṣas*, what does it do? By means of impurity (*mala*), it produces fainting (*mūrchā*), that is, the delusion of the senses; by means of the fault of fire (*śikhin*), it produces burning; and by means of poison (*viṣa*), it produces death (*mṛtyu*). The sense is that the removal of these [obstacles] must be accomplished. (GRhtCM 2.5–6:10)

That which consists of the destruction of the mercury's own nature and its reduction to a paste is called "lost-paste" (*naṣṭapiṣṭa*) by the learned, even though it is [technically] conquered mercury.
That which causes the state of being "destroyed and ground" by means of the medicinal substances prescribed for *mardana* is called *mūrchana*; it is the destroyer of the three *doṣas*.
The instrument here is indeed the mortar previously mentioned.
He states that *gṛhakanyā* and so forth remove the three *doṣas* and cause fainting (*mūrchana*).
The house-girl and the house-maid remove the first impurity, the primary defect.

Furthermore, *triphalā* is the combination of three fruits; it removes the second [of the three] humors, fire (*agni*). As for the combination: "One *harītakī* should be used, two *vibhītaka*s should be used, and four *āmalaka*s—this is proclaimed as *triphalā*.
Furthermore, the fire of *citraka* removes—that is, it drives away—the third *doṣa*, which is poison (*viṣa*). // GRhtCM_2.5-6:17 //

Therefore, for this reason, one should cause the mercury to coagulate seven times with these three—gṛhakanyā, triphalā, and citraka—mixed and combined together; one should perform the coagulation according to the prescribed rule. Furthermore, there is a specific instruction here:
the masters of speech should always perform the coagulation of the king of mercury.
First, among the poisons, there is *triphalā*, and likewise *bṛhatī* and *upaviṣa*.
Mercury should then be ground for one *yāma* with either *karkoṭī*, *kṣārakanda*, *citraka*, or *gṛhakanyā*.
Taking a *kiṃnara* machine, one should smear its surface with medicinal herbs;
one should place mercury combined with nine times its weight [of gold] in the middle of the machine.
One should place a shallow bowl over the mercury, seal the joint firmly with clay,
fill it with salt, and carefully block the opening.
Having placed it upon a cauldron, the wise one should ignite a blazing fire;
after one watch (three hours), having removed it from the heat, the mercury should be allowed to cool.
Having carefully extracted the mercury from the apparatus and revived the swooning substance,
one should then add the mercury— provided it has not become inert— in a proportion of one-sixteenth part to that which was previously swooned.

One should grind mercury together with borax and *ṭaṅkaṇa* (sal ammoniac) mixed with honey; then it should be subjected to sudation in a *dolāyantra* along with alkaline substances, acids, and salts. After raising [the mercury], one should cause the Lord of Mercury (*raseśvara*) to undergo the process of fainting (*mūrchana*) repeatedly, twenty-one times in total, each time after it has been raised again.
Thus, in the *Rasasāra*. (GRhtCM 2.5–6:26)
START GRht 2.7 (Saṃskāra:
Utthāpana)
Indeed, by this rubbing, the mercury (sūta), being thoroughly purified and freed from lead and tin, rises up from the decoction of sour gruel in the *pātanayantra*.

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* By means of this grinding, the mercury— completely cleansed and liberated from lead and tin— is brought forth from the boiling of *kāñjika* (sour gruel) in the *pātanayantra* (a vessel for sublimation).
The meaning is that mercury becomes free from lead and tin; it means that mercury becomes devoid of the two defects of lead and tin. Being of what nature? Being "well-arisen" (samutthita).
Having been properly raised within the *pātana* apparatus, which consists of a pair of vessels joined together as a seal.
Why [is it called] *kāñjika* or *sauvīra*? The meaning is that it is so named because of its combination with the decoction previously described.
For "hi" means certainly.
By this purgative, which is the aforementioned cleansing, the mercury (sūta) becomes thoroughly purified; it becomes specifically purified—this is the "arousing" (utthāpana).
By this procedure, the resurrection of mercury even when situated in vermilion occurs.
Furthermore, by means of the yoga of sweating and so forth, one brings about the restoration of the natural form.
This is called "arousing that," which destroys the calamity of fainting.
The act of placing [the image] upright is "raising. // GRhtCM_2.7:9 //
In this regard, the diagram (yantra) has a circumference of eight finger-breadths and a width of ten finger-breadths;
its height is four finger-breadths, and below it is a water-reservoir one finger-breadth deep.
One should insert the mouth of the lower vessel into the opening of the upper vessel,
which has a back measuring sixteen finger-breadths in width.
On both sides, with buffalo milk, flour, *maṇḍūra*, and molasses.
Having smeared it, one should dry the joint and pour water into the water-reservoir;
this should then be placed upon the hearth—this is described as the *pātanāyantra*.
Thus. // GRhtCM_2.7:14 //
START GRH 2.8 (Saṃskāra: Casting Down)
Having performed *ūrdhvapātana* (upward sublimation),
the mercury-paste is precipitated to remove any suspicion of lead or tin;
having been freed from those defects, the mercury thus falls down pure.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Clarifying the process of *pātana* (precipitation), which was indicated in the fifth [chapter], he says "having done," etc. (GRhtCM_2.8:1).

Furthermore, having made the risen mercury into a paste with lead (śulba), and having performed the grinding so that there may be a fusion of those two along with copper (tāmra), it is precipitated in a *pātana* apparatus by one who knows the ritual—
this is the remainder [of the instruction].
Why? Because of the fear of lead and tin, and because of the exhaustion caused by the defects of lead and tin.
Likewise, when it falls according to the prescribed method and the act of causing it to fall has been performed, the mercury (sūta) becomes pure.

The meaning is that, although "times" (*vāram*) is not explicitly stated here, according to another text, when the process of precipitation (*pātanakarma*) is performed twenty-one times—specifically three times seven times—the suspicion regarding lead and tin (*nāgavaṅga*) is completely destroyed. // GRhtCM_2.8:5 //
And here is the specific procedure for the *pātana* apparatus:
two parts of purified mercury combined with one part of copper,
to which a twentieth part of salt has been added, should be ground into a fine paste.
The lower vessel should be eight finger-breadths wide and ten finger-breadths in length;
below the neck, it should have a water-holding cavity measuring four finger-breadths all around.
With its mouth like the interior of a vessel submerged in water, its own edge immersed in the liquid,
a *ciṇṭighaṭī* should be placed above, with a belly sixteen finger-breadths in width.

Dropped into that vessel [consisting of] lower and upper parts, the mercury (rasendra), being freed from all defects, becomes exceedingly potent; even when its digestion is complete, it must be cast down again.
Downward, upward, and likewise sideways—the fall is said to be threefold;
wherever the lord of mercury (sūtendra) stays, there is fire, otherwise water.

The extraction of mercury, which has been rubbed with prescribed medicinal herbs and placed within a *yantra*, upwards, downwards, or sideways, is called *pātana*; it destroys the impurities (*kañcuka*) produced by contact with tin and lead.
Thus. // GRhtCM_2.8:12 //

In the case of upward distillation (*ūrdhvapāta*), the liquid (*rasa*) moves upward; there, fire is in the lower vessel and water is in the upper vessel. In downward distillation (*adhaḥpāta*), however, the liquid moves downward; that machine is the same, but with the reversal of fire and water—here, water is in the lower vessel and fire is in the upper vessel. In horizontal distillation (*tiryakpāta*), the liquid falls horizontally; there, on the back of one vessel...
Water [is placed] beneath another vessel, and fire [is placed] below that.
START GRHT 2.9–16 (The *pātanayantra*):
The lower vessel shall have a width of eight *aṅgulas* and a length of ten *aṅgulas*.
Four finger-breadths below the throat, it is elevated and forms a reservoir for water.
Its mouth is like the opening of a vessel placed inside [another], its own lip submerged in water;
above, it is flattened like a jar, with a belly sixteen finger-breadths wide that should be provided.
When cast into that upper vessel, the mercury (rasendra), being freed from all defects,
becomes exceedingly fit for medicinal substances and for the practice of alchemy (rasāyana).
Having performed the "downward-dropping" (*adhaḥpātana*) and reduced the powder to a fine paste with *triphalā*, *śikhi*, *śigru*, *rājikā*, and *paṭu*,
one should smear it onto the upper vessel and subject it to downward-dropping using one *palā* of ignited [substance] below.
Alternatively, having been cast into a lamp-furnace and freed from all defects,
the king of mercury (sūtarāja) should be precipitated by the method of transverse precipitation (tiryakpātana). GRht 2.13.
Having placed finely ground mica-leaf mixed with mercury and lemon juice into a mortar,
one should grind it until it reaches the state of a vanished paste (naṣṭapiṣṭa).
One should gradually cause the mercury, which has been cast down by the transverse-dropping method, to fall into a steady fire;
having been thoroughly heated, it is made to fall until it no longer falls, provided the fire remains firm.
Afflicted by suppression, crushing, and the falling [of the vital breath], it becomes weak due to its feeble power; yet,
through nourishment obtained from the lotuses of emanation during the state of suppression, it would not become impotent.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Clarifying the process of purification known as "obstruction" (*nirodhana*), which was indicated in the sixth [chapter], he says "mardana," etc. (GRhtCM_2.9-16:1).
Having undergone a specific refinement through these processes of rubbing, blending, and casting, it becomes debased due to its weak potency.

The meaning is that it becomes afflicted by a contemptible process. Furthermore, after being rubbed together with the "lotuses of creation" (sṛṣṭyambuja), through confinement—either within a pair of crucibles (*mūṣā*) or in a small flask (*kūpikā*)—the mercury, having attained nourishment and regained its strength, shall not be impotent; it does not become devoid of semen (*śukra*).
The ignorant claim that "creation" consists of urine, semen, and blood; that "ambuja" means salt; and that "saindhava" means a lotus.
As for the ritual of creation (*sṛṣṭi*):
the urine, semen, and blood of cows, goats, sheep, men, and women—
this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭi*, which destroys the defect of impotence.
Thus, from the descent of power.
As for the *yantra*:
one should prepare a pair of crucibles using a lump of red rock salt (*saindhava*). Having placed mercury along with *navasāra* and *nimbuka* within that crucible-cup (*sampuṭa*), [one proceeds].
One should carefully apply an excellent seal to the junction of the *sampuṭa* vessel;
having taken the "diamond-clay" (*vajramṛtsnā*), one should wrap it around that [junction] with great effort.
Having dried it in the shade, one should then place it in a hole in the ground;
there, the filling above the crucible should be eight finger-breadths in measure.
For a period of twenty-one days, one should maintain a fire of dried cow-dung;
every day, a new crucible containing rock salt must be prepared.
One should then cause it to sweat with effort and place it within the interior of the earth;
or else, one should place the mercury (sūta) mixed with rock salt (saindhava) inside a small crucible (kūpikā).
Then it should be placed within the earth for a period of twenty-one days;
this is known by the name Nirodhaka, which produces a great mouth in the mercury.
Thus. // GRhtCM_2.9-16:12 //
START GRht 2.17 (7. niyamana):
Having thus acquired vigor, that fickle mind is subsequently properly restrained.
[This is] from the sweat of the cobra’s lotus-eye, the *mārkava*, the *karkoṭī*, and the *ciñcikā*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He explains the seventh prescribed refinement, beginning with the words "iti" and so forth.

Thus, by means of the previously described method involving restraint and so forth, and following that period of confinement, this volatile and flickering mercury is controlled; that is, its regulation is performed by one who knows the ritual procedure.

Why? Because of the sweating [of the mercury] with snake, garlic, lotus, *mārkava*, and *karkoṭī*—where "snake" refers to betel nut (*tāmbūla*), "garlic" to *rasona*, "lotus" to salt, "*mārkava*" to *bhṛṅgarāja*, and "*karkoṭī*" to the well-known *vandhyā*; and with *ciñcikā*, which is the sour *amlikā*. By these [substances], [the mercury is processed].
That which is sweat produced together with the heating by fire in a press. // GRhtCM_2.17:3 //

Of what nature is he? He is one who has correctly acquired vigor (*vīrya*), one who has attained strength, and is thus possessed of heroism; the meaning is that the "taste" (*rasa*) is restrained for the sake of eliminating fickleness.
And here is the specific detail: having coated a glass flask with clay, the mercury is released inside;
after adding one-sixteenth part of borax, a small amount is placed in the middle.
A firm door-seal should be fashioned from adamantine clay;
having placed a small pit in the center of the ground, the interior should be filled with white [clay].
A fire of dried cow-dung should be maintained for a period of twenty-one days;
this is called the "Restrictive" fire, which brings about the final end of the [internal] fire.

The practice of "rasasveda" (the sweating of the vital essence) which is performed to prevent the fickleness of the *vīrya* (vital energy) once it has been obtained through retention is indeed called "niyamana" (restraint).
Thus. // GRhtCM_2.17:9 //
As for the characteristics of the machine:
"A water-receptacle holding four *prasthas*, with a mouth four finger-breadths wide—this is called the jar-machine (*ghaṭayantra*), and it is known as that which provides irrigation. (GRhtCM 2.17:10)

These medicinal herbs consist of earth, mica, borax, and black pepper, and not only these, but furthermore salt, *asurī*, ginger, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
With earth, *tuvarī*, *khaga*, iron sulfate (*kāsīsa*), borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), *saubhāgya*, black pepper (*marica*), and pungent salt (*ūṣaṇa*)—with these [it is prepared].

Furthermore, with salt (saindhava), black mustard (āsurī rājikā), drumstick tree (śigru), the saubhāñjana—a specific type of tree—and the previously mentioned sour gruel (kāñjika) that has turned acidic; with these [one should proceed]. GRhtCM_2.18:5 //
And here is the specific procedure:
the mercury (rasarāja) should be subjected to sweating with alkaline substances, acids, poisons, and liquors.
Having taken a citron (bījapūra), one should remove its stalk and prepare [the vessel].
