having carefully closed the opening, one should bind it within a cloth.
The swinging-sweat therapy (dolāsveda) should be performed for a period of twenty-one days;
every day, a fresh citron fruit should be used.
For one who is licking the elements and is oppressed by hunger,
the stimulation of the king of essences (rasarāja) must be performed by this very means.
The purification of the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) should be performed for three days, or seven days, or fourteen, or twenty-one; each successive stage is progressively better.
Thus. // GRhtCM_2.18:11 //
Thus illuminated as a *cāraṇa*, it is pure, possessing the brilliance of thousands of flickering streaks of lightning.
When the noble king of essences (*rasarāja*) becomes [united with] the *sattva* and other qualities, then it is the seed (*bīja*).

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states the examination of mercury, which has undergone the eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), as established by further refinements, beginning with the words "Thus," etc. (GRhtCM_2.19:1).
In the manner previously described, the king of essences (rasarāja), being thus ignited and afflicted by hunger, becomes purified.
When the king of essences (rasarāja) is of such a nature, then the master should perform the work of extraction (cāraṇakarma).

Of what nature is it? It is said to be "having a luster like a thousand flickering lightning-garlands," meaning its radiance is like that of a thousand lightnings which are intensely moving and characterized by a nature of constant motion.

Having done what? Having given—that is, having added—this certain thing about to be mentioned hereafter, known as a mineral, an ore, a great elixir, or a jewel, which is the second [ingredient] related to the King of Elixirs (Rasarāja).

In the rites of yellow, the yellow [color] comes first; in the rites of white, the face [the white color] comes first.

Gold, silver, and so forth, when placed in the mortar, cause the mercury to become "mouthed" (kṛtamukha) and flow.
Furthermore, the mercury that is "faceless" (punarnirmukha)—that is, mercury whose face has not been prepared—when rubbed and ground in a mortar, consumes and devours what was mentioned previously.

Just as with the verse:

The measure of food consisting of edible substances for a person of this size,

Thus is the technical definition. GRhtCM_2.20:12.

Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the purification of mercury (*rasa-śodhana*), in the *Mugdhabodhinī*, a commentary on the *Rasahṛdaya*, composed by Caturbhuja Miśra, the son of Maheśa Miśra, who is like a moon to the ocean of the illustrious Kurala lineage.
Those who have accomplished their purpose by obtaining the leaves and other ingredients through the transmutation of seed-mercury devoid of density (*ghanarahita-bīja-cāraṇa*).
The wretched, having reached the ocean, are satisfied with the gain of a single cowrie shell.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
[He is] the being who swallows the moon, who brings happiness to the source of lotuses.*

By means of this verse, describing the excellence of the qualities and the esteemed nature of the work, he says "ghanetyādi" (beginning with *ghana*). 3.1:2.
Those persons who are of such a kind are indeed pitiable.

Of what nature are they? They are those who have accomplished their purpose through the substances such as leaves obtained by means of seed-transmutation devoid of *ghana* (mica). "Devoid of *ghana*" means free from or excluded from mica; that which is obtained through "seed-transmutation"—the swallowing of seeds consisting of other metals and so forth—namely, the substances such as leaves, including leaf-dyeing, color-increase, star-formation, extraction (*tārakṛṣṭī*), compounding (*melāpaka*), and other such things; by means of these, they are those who have fulfilled their purpose and perfected themselves.
The word "they think" (*manyante*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

What kind of wretches are they? Having reached the ocean, the mine of jewels, they are satisfied with the acquisition of a mere cowrie shell; that is to say, they have attained contentment with the gain of a single kapardika due to their state of poverty. This is the intended meaning.

In the same way, such wretched people, having obtained this treatise which is like a jewel-mine containing many gems, consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose with mere trifles such as leaves and the like.

The similarity between the ocean of scriptures and the sea lies in their jewels of virtue; the similarity between the two substances, the cowrie shell and the leaf, lies in their worthlessness, since both are indeed base.

For this treatise bestows much, because it provides the piercing by means of a seal (*mudrikā-vedha*), the piercing by touch (*sparśa-vedha*), the piercing by fumes (*dhūma-vedha*), the piercing by sound (*śabda-vedha*), the piercing of base metals (*dhāmya-vedha*), the piercing of non-base metals (*adhāmya-vedha*), and the piercing of minerals (*dhātu-vedha*).
Furthermore, others who were great— having disregarded Lakṣmī, the king of elephants, the Kaustubha gem, and so forth—

Furthermore, describing the hundredfold excellence of qualities in this treatise, he says "others," and so forth. GRhtCM_3.2:1.

Others, greater than those who came before, exist.

This indeed is the nature of the virtuous, as it was before, toward those who are poor and wretched.
Therefore, this treatise serves as a touchstone for distinguishing between the base and the great.
Through alkaline substances, medicinal herbs, pungents, and acids, there is an awakening of hunger and attachment by means of sweating;
however, there can be no cutting of the wings nor any state of fluidity without the sky (space).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the means for swallowing the sky (*gaganagrāsa*) by virtue of its supreme excellence, beginning with the words "in alkaline [substance]," etc. (GRhtCM 3.3:1).
The sense of hunger for the king of essences arises; this is the completion of the sentence.

By what means? By alkaline herbs, pungent substances, and acids; "alkaline herbs" refers to *ahimāra* and so forth, "pungent" refers to rock salt (*saindhava*), and "acid" refers to *amlavetasa* and the like. The meaning is that by these, the production of hunger occurs.
As for the alkaline herbs:
*ahimāra*, *apāmārga*, combined with *taṇḍulīyaka*.
Snuhī, arka, karavīra, lāṅgalī, and kṣīrakanda.
Karkoṭī, kañcukī, tumbā, palāśa, agnimanthaka,
karīra, citraka, śigru, varuṇa, vetasa, and vaṭa.
One should burn the tubers of *paṭola*, *arjuna*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *kadalī*, *vajrakanda*, *aśvattha*, *sūraṇa*, and *jālī* many times over.
One should likewise burn all [substances] with smokeless fire and *devadālī*;
this group is proclaimed by the name "Medicinal Alkali" (*auṣadhikṣāra*).
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.3:8 //

Ambaṣṭhā, karamarda, kapittha, and karaṇā,
combined with the five acids (pañcāmla), are proclaimed as the group of sour substances (amlavarga).

or else, sour vetiver (amlavetasa) alone is the most excellent of all.
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.3:12 //

Through these—alkalis, medicinal herbs, pungents, and acids—there arises an awakening of hunger; and there arise passion and bondage. Passion is *rañjana* (coloring/dyeing), and bondage has been described previously.
For what reason? Because of sweat produced by these aforementioned instruments.
The word "again" (punar) is used as an intensifier.

"Cutting the wings" (pakṣaccheda) means the excision of the wings of the mercury; the sense is that its stability, whether as a substance (dravyatva) or as possessing qualities (guṇavattva), does not exist without the mica (abhraka). // GRhtCM_3.3:16 //
When processed with mica (*abhraka*), mercury becomes powerful; for its transmutation (*cāraṇa*),
the great yogas known as *saṃdhāna*, *vāsana*, *auṣadhi*, *nirmukha*, and *samukha* have been taught.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states "the state of being a substance" [in the verse] with the words "digested by abhraka," and so forth. GRhtCM_3.4:1.
In one devoid of strength and with excessive hunger, there arises impotence.
Just as [impure] metal, due to its coldness, lack of malleability, and through the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*),
consumes [the impurities] by means of the abundant application of *viḍ* salts, so too does one who has attained the digested state consume [the elements] while remaining in the undigested state.
From excessive fire, from fasting, and from being devoid of the *krāmaṇa* [fluid], these transformations are to be known; through these eight, one becomes impotent.
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.4:5 //
Therefore, after the eight purificatory processes (saṃskāra), the mercury must be made to digest mica (abhraka), because by digesting mica it becomes powerful.
That in which [the mercury] has not been processed according to the method of "swallowing" (grāsanyāya) after being digested by mica (abhraka) is so described.
These [preparations] are prescribed for the swallowing and the mere consumption of that mercury which is fit for the process of *abhrajāraṇā*.
These very great yogas, which are the faces of the medicinal herbs of the *saṃdhāna* [fermentation] process and which bring about the state of being a great substance,
involve the fermentation of all grains and the eight medicinal herbs and so forth; for example, having placed all the grains inside, one should prepare *āranāla*.
One should place there medicinal herbs together with their leaves and roots.
One should prepare that [mixture] combined with earth, green vitriol, sea salt, rock salt, the three pungents, and black mustard; it should remain for seven days in a warm place.
One should then combine that, joined with the fluxing agent (*cāraṇāla*), in a copper vessel;
this is the "digestion" (*saṃdhāna*) for the purpose of fluxing mica (*abhraka*).
Just as there are medicinal herbs,

so too should one understand the category of medicinal plants as it has been described in the scriptures; having correctly identified those born of water and those born of land, one should then employ them.
The water-born *utpalī*, the *padmā*, and the land-born *prasāriṇī*;
the *jālinī*, the *abhracandrā*, the *citraparṇī*, and the *triparṇikā*;
as well as the *rasacandraukasa* and the *jalamūlaka*.
The samaṅgā is water-born, as is the apāmārga that arises from water.

"Reconnection" (*saṃdhāna*) refers to the medicinal herbs of latent impressions (*vāsanauṣadhi*); by means of these, those yogas which are "without face and with face" are produced—meaning they are "faceless and then possessed of a face."

Those previously mentioned.

and with the juice of the "three creations" (sṛṣṭitraya), water-pepper (nīrakaṇā)—known in the world as *paṭu*—and *tumburu* (known as *jalakaṇā* and *tumbaru*), which are both well-known in the world as *tumburu*; that is, the rubbing should be done with these three creations and the juice of water-pepper and *tumburu*. // GRhtCM_3.5:11 //

cloud-essence (abhra) that is devoid of luster and "dead" is an elixir for an aged body.
"It destroys the intoxication and pride of women, and it is recommended for those whose virility has been impaired.

Abhraka processed with the juices of ghanarava, śigru, and punarnavā undergoes digestion.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method beginning with "yava" and so forth.*

Furthermore, the mica (*abhraka*) should be enclosed within *yavaciñcikā* juice; *yavaciñcikā* is well known as *yavaciñcikā* in common parlance, and its juice is its liquid extract. It should be "enclosed" by that, meaning it has been processed through exposure to the sun. Furthermore, it should be combined with its root, *śatāvarī*, and *gada*; "its root" refers to the root of that *yavaciñcikā*, while *śatāvarī* means "having a hundred [parts]," and *gada* means *kuṣṭha*. It should be "filled" with these, meaning pervaded or saturated by them.
When there is an absence of fresh medicinal herbs, then this procedure is as follows:
having taken dried substances when fresh juices are unavailable,
they should be cooked in eight times their weight of water and the decoction should be taken when reduced to one-fourth.
Thus [it is said]. // GRhtCM_3.6:5 //
Furthermore, it should be processed with the juice of *ghanarava*, *śigru*, and *punarnavā*. *Ghanarava* is *taṇḍulīyaka*;

*śigru* is *saubhāñjana*, known in the world as *suhijana*; and *punarnavā* is commonly known as *varṣābhū*. The meaning is that [the substance] should be saturated with the juice of these, and then dried by exposure to the sun.
In this manner, the mercury moves within the cloud.
It should be understood that the word "meditation" (bhāvanā) is used here without the prefix *nir-*, because it is consistent with other texts. // GRhtCM_3.6:8 //
In this regard, there is a specific distinction: // GRhtCM_3.6:9 //
Having ground [the substance] in the juice of *somavallī*, one should administer it for three *puṭa*s;
then, one should saturate it seven times with the juice of *somavallī* alone.
One should cause [the mercury] to be placed in an earthen vessel together with the juice;
one should rub the root of the *śarapuṅkhā* with cow’s milk and mix it as a paste with the mercury, causing the mica (*gagana*) to move above and below it.
One should place it in the heat of the sun with its face turned away; it swallows [the substance] in an instant, and a paste is quickly produced—of this there is no need for doubt.
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.6:13 //
Furthermore:
Having taken the juice of *tilaparṇī*, one should saturate *gagana* with it;
through rubbing, a *piṣṭī* is produced—of this there is no need for doubt.
Thus [it is said]. GRhtCM 3.6:15.
Furthermore:
One should repeatedly saturate *nāga* with the exudation of *muṇḍī*;
having combined that with *abhraka*, one should burn it again and again on a plate.
The powder of sulphur and mica should be diligently washed seven times with each of the following: citraka, fresh ginger, and roots [of the aforementioned plants].
The mercury, impregnated with *nāgamuṇḍīra* and processed with the acid of *luṅga*, should be administered in a sixteenth part [of the total]; thus the mercury should be processed in a *dolāyantra*.
Thus ends the practice of the faceless movement.
Mix Sarjikṣāra, kṣiti, khaga, ṭaṅkaṇa, and salt, and keep it in a vessel of *arka* wood for three days for the purpose of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
Fermented rice-gruel that has stood overnight is recommended for meditation in the sky and other such states.
Having melted pure silver in that [liquid], one should pour it [into it] a hundred times;
or else tin may be used in the process of whitening, but it should never be employed for the sake of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
The powders of mercury, the secondary minerals (uparasa), nectar-like substances, metals, and metallic elixirs— all these,
as well as whatever else is a substance for processing (cāraṇa), must be processed by means of this [elixir].
He speaks of the practice performed in the presence [of the deity] with the words beginning "sarji," and so forth.
Regarding *āranāla* mentioned in the context of the preparation for steaming (*svedana*), that is *kāñjika*.
In an *arkabhājana*, that is, a copper vessel.
For up to three days, one should perform the process of reconstitution using that which has been kept overnight.

What kind of *āranāla* (fermented rice water) is used? It is combined with *sarjī*, *kṣiti*, *khaga*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and salt. *Sarjī* is well known; it is called *sājī* in common parlance. *Kṣiti* is *sphaṭikā*; *khaga* is *kāsīsa*; *ṭaṅkaṇa* is *saubhāgya*, which is called *sohāgā* in common parlance.
Regarding salt, *saindhava* is used; in its absence, whichever is available among the eight types of salts should be employed—this is the rule for salt.
Saindhava, rucaka, kṛṣṇa, viḍa, sāmudra,
audbhida, romaka, and pāṃśuja— these are called the eight salts.
Thus, one should perform [the rite] endowed with and combined with these.

Then, that *āranāla* is recommended as the primary substance for the visualization of space and so forth, and for the saturation of mica and so forth; mica and the other substances will be described further on.
Cāraṇā is considered to be of two kinds: *nirmukhā* (faceless) and *samukhā* (with face). *Nirmukhā* cāraṇā is said to occur through the implantation of the seed (*bījādhāna*).
Pure gold and silver are designated as "seed."
The casting of seed by sixty-four parts is called the "mouth."
When this is done, the mercury becomes possessed of a mouth and greedy for morsels;
it becomes capable of devouring even hard metals.
For this practice of *cāraṇā* has been explained in its direct form by the excellent commentators.
Thus.

The distinction should be understood as follows: the "mouthless" processing (*nirmukhacāraṇa*) applies to secondary minerals such as mica (*abhraka*), while the "mouthed" processing (*samukhacāraṇa*) applies to primary metals such as gold (*hema*).

The meaning is that in the practice of *rasāyana* for the purpose of bodily transformation, lead (*nāga*) and tin (*vaṅga*) are not to be ingested; rather, seeds such as gold (*svarṇa*) and the like are to be ingested.
By the word "etc. (ādi), he indicates the specific application for *nāga* and *vaṅga*, beginning with the words "in that" (*tasmin*) and so forth.

In that aforementioned *saṃdhāna*, one should melt pure, purified lead (*nāga*)— that is, tin (*sīsaka*)— and, by means of the application of fire (as is understood), pour it out after it has been reduced to the state of water; or else, in that very same *saṃdhāna*, one should melt tin (*vaṅga*) or mercury (*raṅga*) and pour it out.
"Kativārān" means a hundred times; that is to say, for every hundred.
That tin (vaṅga) should be employed in the procedure for mercury (tāra) when preparing silver; the meaning is that it should be made combined with the mercury.
In this Āryā, regarding the section on gold, the specific meaning is that although the *nāga* has not been mentioned, it should be added from another text. // GRhtCM_3.7-9:19 //

That lead (nāga) and tin (vaṅga) should not be employed for the purpose of alchemical elixirs (*rasāyana*) or for the attainment of bodily perfection (*śarīrasiddhi*), because it is stated that lead and tin give rise to two adventitious defects (*aupādhika-doṣa*), namely throat-obstruction (*galabandha*) and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). However, it is appropriate to employ this lead and tin for the purpose of "swallowing" (*grāsa*),
because the sense is that by means of this [lead and tin] being internalized, it swallows other substances as well.
Regarding tin (*vaṅga*), there is a distinction:
tin is said to be of two kinds, namely *khuraka* and *miśraka*.
*Khuraka* is superior in terms of its qualities, while *miśraka* is not beneficial for the mercury.
Thus, that which is suitable for the work of silver should be taken.
Clarifying the sequence beginning with space, he says "space," and so forth.
By means of this aforementioned unification (*saṃdhāna*), one should bring everything—everything without exception—to its state of being meditated upon; that is, one should effect its meditation.
What is meant by "everything"? It refers to the powders of mercury, secondary minerals, elixirs, iron, and metallic salts, and so forth.

Gaganam (sky-metal), abhraka (mica), and that which is known as vajra; rasas and mahārasas, namely hiṅgula, svarṇamākṣika, rūpyamākṣika, śilājatu, capala, cumbaka, vaikrānta, kharpara, gairika, sphaṭika, and kāsīsa;

amṛta (nectar) or viṣa (poison); the amṛtalohas (immortal metals)—they are called *amṛta* because they do not die (*na mṛtāḥ*), and they are called *lohāḥ* because they flow (*dhāvanti*); these are the rasas mentioned previously.
The metallic ores (*āyasā lohāḥ*) are those from which powders and pastes (*cūrṇāni kalkāni*) are produced through their combination, such as copper, mica, and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the secondary minerals (*uparasa*) is also intended.

Not only these [metals] alone are to be processed by means of this amalgamation (*saṃdhāna*), but whatever else is a substance for *cāraṇa*— such as precious materials or gems suitable for *cāraṇa*— that too is to be processed by this amalgamation for the purpose of *cāraṇa*.
First, indeed, the mercury (*rasa*) flows into that mass of gold which has been softened and ground into a paste.
Having added [the ingredients] for the act of transmutation (*tārakarma*) to silver (*tāra*), one then produces the sky (gold).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific procedure for gold and silver at the beginning with the words "ādau" and so forth.*
Immediately after that, [one should take] a paste of gold—that is, of refined gold—which has been rubbed in a mortar; the phrase "by the method to be described" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The vital essence flows through that paste.
Having done what should one give the paste? First, at the very beginning, having added *gagana* (mica) to the Lord of Mercury (*sūteśvara*).
The qualification for gold has been shown. // GRhtCM_3.10:5 //
In the work of gold, one should give only gold; in the work of silver, one should give only silver.
There is a distinction regarding gold:
gold is said to be of five kinds—natural, produced from fire, and born together [with it].
These three types of gold should be joined to make it sixteen-carat (ṣoḍaśavarṇaka).
Mineral [mercury] derived from alchemical discourse, purified and processed with excellent leaves,
enriched with fourteen colors, removes the diseases of human beings.
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.10:9 //
There is also a distinction regarding silver (*tāra*): on Mount Kailāsa, there is native silver, as well as that produced from mines and that which is artificial;
in reverse order of these qualities, it is superior, and it is beneficial for mercury extracted from lead.
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.10:11 //
One should also recite the preceding syllable as *tāra*.

Having added [the ingredients] bit by bit and rubbed mercury, mica, gold, iron, and so forth in a mortar with the essence, the Lord of Mercury (rasendra) undergoes digestion (*carati*) with earth, birds, cane, and the acid of *bījapūra*. GRht 3.11
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Regarding the grinding of the paste, he states the vessels and medicinal substances [to be used] starting with "truṭiśaḥ" and so forth. GRhtCM_3.11:1.

"Cloud, gold, iron, and so forth": "cloud" (abhra) is understood to be *abhraka* (mica); "gold" (*hema*) is *kanaka*, which is itself a metal (*loha*); thus, "cloud-metal" (*abhrakaloha*) refers to mica and gold, and that which has these as its beginning is [the compound]. GRhtCM_3.11:2.

Such a substance, when rubbed and ground with the acids of earth (kṣiti), sky (khaga), cane (vetasa), and citron (bījapūra)— where "earth, sky, cane, and citron" refers to the three aforementioned acids— mercury (rasendra) flows.
Having done what? Having crushed it and given away even a tiny fragment, bit by bit.
In what essence, indeed, does it reside? // GRhtCM_3.11:5 //
This is the essence of that which is of a sharp nature; such is the essence within that very thing.
In its entirety, there are distinctions; blunt (*muṇḍa*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), and likewise attractive (*kānta*)—these are its thirteen varieties.
Blunt is said to be of three kinds: dull (*mṛdu*), blunted (*kuṇṭha*), and reddish-brown (*kaḍāra*).
Kharasāra, hannāla, tārāvarta,
viḍa, kālaloha, and that which is called gaja— these six are said to be the types of *tīkṣṇa* (steel).
Loha is said to be of four kinds: romaka, bhrāmaka, cumbaka, and drāvaka; their qualities increase progressively.
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.11:10 //
Regarding the mortar: the mortar, made of stone or other materials, should be without a spout and have a bowl two finger-breadths deep;
a groove eight finger-breadths wide should be made, and it may be either long or circular.
The roller should be twelve finger-breadths long and four finger-breadths wide;
its surface should be made circular, resembling the belly of a mirror.
Thus it is said. (GRhtCM 3.11:13)
The phrase "beginning with stone" (aśmādi) is to be understood as referring to stone, iron, and copper.
Whether with a face or without a face, it may be equal, or twice, four times,
eight times, sixteen times, or even thirty-two times [the size] of the original. (GRht 3.12)
Thus is leaf-abhraka described; by that procedure one should cause the mercury to move.
(Cāraṇa) The swallow, the paste, and the womb—these three characteristics constitute the process of moving [the mercury]. (GRht 3.13)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the measure for the transmutation (*cāraṇā*) of the metals and so forth, beginning with "with the face" (*samukham*), etc. (GRhtCM_3.12-13:1).
Thus, "the aforementioned leaf-abhraka" means the process of digesting leaf-abhraka as previously described.

Whether the process of circulation (*cāraṇa*) is "with face" (*samukha*), meaning accompanied by the mouth, or "without face" (*nirmukha*), meaning devoid of the mouth—it is equal and the same in both cases that one should cause the mercury (*sūta*) to circulate; the remaining sense is that it refers to the metals and so forth. Here there is an option: one may cause it to circulate doubled [in weight] relative to the mercury, or quadrupled relative to the mercury, or eightfold relative to the mercury, or sixteenfold relative to the mercury, or thirty-two-fold.
One should cause [the mercury] to circulate, multiplied thirty-two times from the amount of the *sūta*.
By that previously mentioned procedure, beginning with the words "having given in minute portions" and so forth.
The *cāraṇā* is characterized by three marks; that which possesses these three marks or signs is thus described.

How is the "swallowing" (grāsa) of mica (abhraka) effected? Is it by being mouthless (nirmukha) or by having a mouth (samukha)? Furthermore, there is the "pasting" (piṣṭī), which is the mixing of mercury with mica and other substances; then there is the "impregnation" (garbha), wherein the sky in the form of mercury remains within the womb of the mercury.
A *yugma* consists of two verses connected by a syntactical relation (*anvaya*). (GRhtCM 3.12–13)
START GRht 3.14-15 (Wrong views regarding *jāraṇa*):
Even by those who [claim that] the sky (*gagana*) is processed through various methods of breaking [the substance] by means of the procedure of shaking (*dolana*).
It was seen by them being prescribed for the practice of movement, yet not being shaken.
Others of empty intellect think that the powder produced by grinding perfumes with a pestle and mortar, when raised by the method of swinging, is "digested mercury.

(GRht 3.15) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [This refers to those who believe that] the dust resulting from the pulverization of fragrant substances with a metal pestle, when stirred up by the process of oscillation, constitutes "digested" (jīrṇa) mercury.
Thus, the measure for swallowing the sky and so forth has been explained; now he describes the procedure for *cāraṇā*, beginning with "by the method of swinging," and so on.

The remainder [of the meaning] is as follows: with those very same medicinal substances by which the "sky-stone" (*gaganamabhraka*) has been ground or pounded, one should prepare it refined through various types of *bhaṅga* (breaks or waves); this applies whether the substances are used in small or large quantities.
Various kinds—that is, many types—of *bhaṅgas*, which are like waves born from the ocean of the scriptures, have been used to refine or embellish it.
What kind of sky is indicated—that is, pointed out—by the procedure of killing, which is the enactment of the state of the five elements?
The sense is that even such a sky as this is to be employed in the practice of movement (*cāraṇā*) by means of the procedure of swinging (*dolana*).
Now, he states the opinion of those of small intellect with the words "others," and so forth.

Others than the great are those of meager intellect; that is to say, those whose intellect (*mati*) or understanding (*buddhi*) is meager (*tuccha*), i.e., small (*stoka*), are thus described as being of small intellect.
They consider mercury to be "digested" when it has been subjected to the process of *jāraṇā* (digestion).

What is "the powder of sulphur-paste and copper-paste"? It means the paste of sulphur that has been ground into a fine powder, and the paste of copper—that is, the copper-paste—that has been ground into a fine powder; the dust or powder resulting from both that sulphur-paste and that copper-paste, just like the sulphur-paste itself.
One should saturate the powder of sulphur seven times with the juice of chickpeas,
and likewise seven times with female blood.
Then, one should place one *pala* of pure mercury in an iron pan (*kharpara*),
and add sulphur that has been processed (*bhāvita*), combined with a human bone-mass (*narapiṇḍa*).
Even in a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra), the paste becomes [liquefied] in an instant by means of heat.
In this very way, even a rope or a clod of earth becomes [the deity].

Of what nature is it? It is the powder produced from the grinding of fragrant substances and metals, brought forth by the method of swinging—that is, generated by means of a swinging apparatus (*dolikāyantra*).
The sense is that what was stated [previously] is inconsistent.
START GRht 3.16 (golakamukha):
[The extraction] of mercury and other substances heated with oil and so forth, by means of a globule-mouthed vessel made of gold, silver, and the like.
The king of essences (mercury) moves through the thick [substances] and attains a solid state by means of gold and other [metals].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
While demonstrating the "manifestation of latent impressions" (*vāsanāmukhacāraṇa*), which is included within the "manifest movement" (*samukhacāraṇa*), he says "in oil," etc.*

The king of essences, mercury (pārada), consumes—that is, it assimilates—the nine types of metallic substances previously mentioned, consisting of both artificial and natural varieties, such as gold, silver, and so forth.
By which opening of the skull?
And *golaka* is a specific type of mouth; thus, the meaning is "with the *golaka*-mouth of the *viḍa*."
When what exists? When the oil and other substances have been heated.

Those things of which oil is the first are the "oil-based substances," namely oil, fat, urine, semen, and menstrual blood. When the mercury—which has been heated and brought to a state of heat—exists together with these, the lord of elixirs (*rasendra*) assimilates the dense *abhraka* mica.
Furthermore, by being swallowed as fresh morsels of gold and other materials, it attains the state of a solid mass; that is, it reaches density.
As for the oils:
those derived from *kaṅguṇī*, *tumbinī*, *ghoṣā*, *karañja*, and *śrīphala*;
and those produced from *kaṭu*, *vātāri*, *siddhārtha*, *somarājī*, and *vibhītaka*.
Likewise, [the seeds] of *atasī*, *mahākālī*, *nimba*, and sesame;
as well as *apāmārga*, *devadālī*, *dantī*, and the form of *tumbaru*.
Oil is produced from the fruits of the aṅkola, unmatta, and bhallātaka. Thus [it is said].
Just as [one avoids] fat,
so too one should avoid the fat of goats, camels, donkeys, sheep, and buffaloes.
Thus it is said.
Just as with urine, flowers, and semen:
one should employ the urine of elephants, young camels, female buffaloes, donkeys, and horses;
likewise, the urine, menstrual flow, and semen of women and men.
Thus [it is said]. GRhtCM_3.16:12.
START GRht 3.17 (mukha:: śukapicchamukha) Others, having made it clear, administer the thick [substance] using a peacock-feather tip.
According to the procedure for the instruction of the Siddhas, [the practice] is performed with a morsel of food that is not dry.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Regarding that intention, he states another opinion, beginning with "others," and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_3.17:1): Regarding that intention, he states another opinion, beginning with "others," and so forth.*

Some perform the *cāraṇā* (digestion) according to the method described; others, having purified mercury (*rasa*) by making it clear and subjecting it to the eight purificatory processes (*saṃskāra*) beginning with sweating (*svedana*), or having prepared dense mica (*ghanābhraka*) derived from cinnabar (*hiṅgula*), perform the *cāraṇā* of that mica.
By what [means]? By that which has a parrot-feather-like face; that is, by those joints whose faces have the particularity of being like a parrot's plumage.
"And when what does one cause [the food] to move? It means: when the morsel has been swallowed, when the mouthful has been consumed, it is then moved again.

By what method of the instructions of the Siddhas? By that method of instruction belonging to those previously mentioned—such as Rasasiddha, Nityanātha, Vīranātha, and others—by means of which they became accomplished.
It is not by means of a dry union that there can be a re-activation, because once moisture has been attained, it would have reached a state of being sapless.
Like a parrot’s feather:
having thoroughly dried up ashes, alkalis, salts, and salts,
one should stir them with the group of sour substances (amlavarga) and place them in a copper vessel.
One should saturate the mica, which has the luster of a parrot’s plumage, with that [fluid];
at that very moment, the mercury swallows it and is formed into a pill (*golaka*).
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.17:9 //
Alternatively, mercury and mica in equal parts, combined with salt, should be heated until cooked.
Having cast it into an iron vessel, it moves like a black cloud at the end of its heating (*sveda*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
With the words "Or else" (*athavā*) and so forth, he states another method according to the intention of another school.*
One should perform the previously mentioned procedure, or else, according to another alternative, one should perform this which is about to be described.

Regarding "mākṣikagaganam": *gagana* (abhraka) combined with *mākṣika* (cinnabar), these two in equal parts—that is, in identical proportions—should be subjected to *puṭa* (roasting). This is joined with *paṭu*, which is rock salt (*saindhava*); because it is consistent with other treatises, it should be roasted with the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*).
Being thus mixed and combined, one should cook it by subjecting it to fire-roasting (*vahnipuṭita*)—this is the remainder of the sense.
Having done what? Having placed it in a vessel of iron, such as a bowl made from a skull, and having set it in the center.
The meaning is that such a black cloud-like mercury (rasa), amidst the heat of the fire within the sweat, moves and swallows [the ore] quickly through its union with sulfur (mākṣika).
I shall now declare that instruction for the introduction of sulphur and mica (*gandhābhraka*),
by which the mercury, its wings severed, becomes fit for both alchemy (*rasa*) and elixirs (*rasāyana*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the method of instruction with the words "that" (*tam*) and so forth.

By which instruction the entry of sulphur-mercury (*gandhābhraka*) occurs—that is, that entry of the mica (*abhra*) which arises from the conjunction with sulphur (*gandhapāṣāṇa*), whereby the mica enters into the interior of the mercury—I, the poet, [shall explain] that instruction.
I shall speak; I will tell.
Due to extreme proximity, even the present tense is expressed by the suffix *laṭ*.
But furthermore: // GRhtCM_3.19:3 //

And mercury with its wings clipped is fit for both *rasa* and *rasāyana*: it is fit and capable for use in *rasa*, which destroys diseases such as fever (as in the *Jvarāṅkuśa* and other formulations), and in *rasāyana*, which destroys old age and disease.
As it says in the *Mañjarī*:
"Killed [mercury] is for the purification of the body; swooned [mercury] is the destroyer of disease."
In some diseases, mercury ash is used for the sake of the body; in others, it is used in a state of being "mūrchita" (rendered inert).
One should employ the bound [mantra] by means of the rite seen in the scriptures through the two [methods].
Thus. // GRhtCM_3.19:7 //
The meaning is that by the entry of the "scent-cloud" (gandhābhra), one becomes immovable with severed wings.
Sulfur bestows color upon the king of mercury and is capable of digesting and transforming the seed-mantras.
Sulfur is said to be the cutter of the wings of *sūtaka* (mercury) for the purpose of binding mercury.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states "the king of mercury," etc., while qualifying sulfur. *Commentary (GRhtCM 3.20:1).*
In the binding of mercury—that is, in the fixation of *pārada*—the *lelinaka* sulphur is the most excellent of all.
For what reason? Because sulphur (gandhaka) cuts through the wings of mercury (sūta), that is, it cuts through the two wings of quicksilver (pārada).

Furthermore, from where does it derive its name? It is the "king of essences" (rasarāja), mercury (pārada); it is so called because it bestows "coloration" (rāga), that is, the process of tinting, upon that king of essences.
Furthermore, from what source do seeds possess the capacity for ripening and digestion? "Ripening and digestion" (pākajāraṇe) refers to both the process of ripening and the process of digestion.

START Gṛhya-sūtra 3.21–25 (Mercury: *māraṇa*, *pakṣaccheda*) 21. When Mercury is in conjunction with the moon, one should perform the rite of *māraṇa* (the killing of the enemy). 22. One should draw the figure of the enemy on a piece of birch-bark (*bhūrja-patra*) using the blood of a crow and a cat. 23. Having written his name and lineage there, one should wrap it in a cloth made from the skin of a black goat. 24. Then, having fasted for three nights and being pure, one should bury it at the foot of a *śamī* tree or under a crossroads. 25. By this act, the enemy’s power is destroyed; this is known as *pakṣaccheda* (the cutting off of wings or support).
Having first added sulphur in minute portions (truṭiśas) to the mortar, and mercury also in minute portions,
it should be rubbed until it becomes a paste.
Thereafter,
having added equal parts of melted buffalo fat and lac, and having added mercury drop by drop, one should prepare the desired paste.
And she too is cast down by glowing stones into the *dīpikā* machine;
thereafter, he—freed from impurity and with his wings clipped by *abhra* and *gandha*.
The mercury in the form of ash is joined with gold, and that [mercury] is in a state of *dvandva* (union).
He says "having given," etc., so that the cutting away of the wings of the mercury may occur by means of sulphur (*gandhaka*) and mica (*abhraka*).

First, at the outset, one should place sulphur in small quantities—piece by piece or in minute portions—into a mortar made of iron, copper, or stone; having added the sulphur and mercury repeatedly, it should be rubbed until that paste attains a single consistency, which is known as *kajjalī*.
This is the explicit meaning.
Thereafter, following that—that is, after the mercury and sulphur have been ground into a paste—one should add *gagana* (mica) to that mercury-sulphur paste;
the meaning is that the mica should be mixed in equal proportions with the mercury and sulphur.

"With what? With the fat of frogs, fish, crabs, and porpoises; that is, with the melted fat—melted meaning liquefied—that has been produced from the bodies of frogs, fish, crabs, and porpoises, which has taken the form of oil."
The essential meaning is that after the addition of equal parts of mica (abhraka), it should be rubbed with the fat of a rat.
Just as with ox-tail fat,
so too with that derived from frogs or fish, or the fat of a crab;
one should likewise expect the respective odors of these, or even the fat of a porpoise, in their proper order.
Among these, the fat of a buffalo alone properly binds the well-melted [mercury] and effects its coloring through the procedure of the *maṇimūṣā* crucible.
This is called *balivasā*; it binds the *sūtaka* (the flow) in an instant.
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that one should perform the grinding of mercury, sulfur, and mica together.

That aforementioned paste of mercury, sulphur, and mica, when subsequently processed in a *dīpikā* apparatus by downward sublimation (*adhaḥpātana*), becomes mercury that is free from impurities and has abandoned its defects.
When that [defilement] has been freed from impurity, he becomes one whose wings have been clipped—that is, his wings are severed.

Regarding the phrase *kābhyām abhragandhābhyām*: "cloud" (*abhra*) and "sulfur" (*gandha*) together form *abhragandhau*; by means of these two, through their conjunction, there arises the pleasure of grinding mercury with sulfur and mica. Since sulfur alone is capable of effecting a dual fusion (*dvandvamelana*), how much more so when combined with the fat of a *balī* (bull) [as stated in the third verse]—this is the meaning of the third verse.
This is a *kulaka*. (GRhtCM 3.21–23:13)
He describes the appearance of the previously processed mercury and its attainment of another state of action with the verse beginning "ashes," etc. (GRhtCM 3.21–23:14).
And furthermore: // GRhtCM_3.21-23:15 //
Then, due to being cast downwards, the mercury takes the form of ash, becoming like ashes.
And that mercury in the form of ash is to be joined with gold—that is, with *svarṇa*—in the union of both, by one who knows the ritual; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Alternatively, the indeclinable [particle] is used in the sense of conjunction because of the connection of a single meaning, and also in the sense of an alternative position.
START GRht 3.24–25 (Mercury: *māraṇa*, compounding with gold)
Alternatively, having cooked a paste of sulfur, one should place it in the midst of molten sulfur.
And that gold-dust is again processed with sulphur;
in this way, mercury unites with gold in a binary compound (*dvandva*) and likewise dies in an instant.

Alternatively, one should prepare a *gandhapiṣṭi* (mercury-sulphur paste) together with gold according to the previously described method. Or else, having cooked it within liquefied sulphur—meaning having made it well-cooked through the application of fire—one should make a *rasahemagandhapiṣṭi* (a paste of mercury, gold, and sulphur), just like a regular paste; this is the meaning.
He states the procedure for the previously mentioned union of the couple with the words beginning with "set" (that), etc. (GRhtCM 3.24–25:2).
And furthermore: // GRhtCM_3.24-25:3 //
That aforementioned gold-paste is the eternal union of mercury-gold and the seminal fluid of sulphur.
That which has been mixed with gold is the gold-paste (*hemapiṣṭī*); it is then cooked again in sulfur. The cooking should be performed skillfully in the sulfur as previously described.
In this manner, by the prescribed method, mercury (pārada) unites with gold; it reaches a state of fusion when there is a union, that is, when the two are joined together.
Thus, when a couple unites according to the prescribed method, one dies after a short time from that moment and attains the state of the five elements.
The meaning is that one dies because of performing only a small amount of further ritual action.
Thus ends the procedure for cutting off the wings.
Others do not desire the cutting off of their wings in a duel, nor the destruction of their vital essence; they rejoice at the ripening of seeds, yet thereafter they suffer.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "the others," etc., because merely cutting away the side of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) would not be sufficient. GRhtCM_3.26:1
Those persons who, according to the aforementioned method, desire the "cutting of the wings"— that is, the excision of the wings of mercury— or who,

by means of the aforementioned *dvandva* (mercury, gold, and sulphur), do not desire the killing of mercury through that *dvandva*; and furthermore, who do not desire the "cooking" (*pāka*)— the thorough maturation by means of the application of fire— even of the "seeds" (*bīja*), such as red mica, mercury-gold, and so forth.

Those men, having previously learned of the cutting off of their wings, rejoice and become filled with joy; the meaning is that they do so upon learning of the accomplishment of another task instead of the wing-cutting. Subsequently, when the task fails, they suffer and become filled with distress.
Having thus considered that traveling through the sky involves many faults and great exertion, a method is now set forth which is consistent even with the *Karmaśāstra*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Having pointed out the movement through the sky, he says "in this way" (*ittham*) and so forth, praising another refinement (*saṃskāra*). GRhtCM_3.27:1.

In this treatise, I, the author of the work, shall indicate—that is, provide an exposition of—a method that is highly consistent with the practice, consisting of the extraction of the essence (*sattva-niṣkāsa*), in the subsequent chapter. It is called "consistent" (*saṃvādī*) because it is experienced and refined by those who are experts in the process of refinement (*saṃskāra*).

Having done what? Having understood that traveling through the sky—traveling through the clouds—is achieved in the manner thus described by means of many defects, many hardships, much exertion, and great toil.
The meaning is that immediately after the practice of moving through the sky (gaganacāraṇa), another superior method is now being described.
The individual soul (jīva) is ungraspable, untainted, subtle in its movement, all-pervading, and imperishable;
as long as it does not enter a womb, how could it experience bondage? (GRht 3.28)

Thus ends the third awakening, consisting of the face-to-face instruction on the mica-footed [preparation] which is included within the face of the purification of latent impressions (*nirmukhavāsanā*), in the tantra named *Rasahṛdaya*, composed by the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants who are supreme swans (*paramahaṃsaparivrājaka*).
*Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
Showing another method, he says "ungraspable," and so forth.

Such is Hara (Śiva) as long as he does not enter—that is, does not unite with—the *abhraka* (mercurial substance) in the womb (*yoni*). As long as there is no union, how could he undergo bondage? He attains it from nowhere; the meaning is that while he has not entered the womb, he does not incur bondage. What is this Hara like? He is "ungraspable" (*agrāhya*); Hara cannot be grasped in any way because he is without parts (*niravayava*), for Hara is of the same nature as his [the mercury's] qualities, according to the principle that "the effect conforms to its cause.

Furthermore, what is he like? He is "untainted" (*nirlepa*); he is not smeared by the various defects and qualities (*doṣaguṇa*) of transformation, because those defects and qualities have ceased to exist.
Furthermore, "subtle movement" refers to that which has a subtle course, a subtle motion, or a subtle progression, because it is observed in the form of smoke.
Furthermore, it is pervasive, because it pervades the body, metals, and so forth.
Furthermore, it is "inexhaustible" (akṣaya), meaning that which has no exhaustion; this is because it is always of the nature of existence.

Furthermore, the meaning of the intent is this: the living self (jīva) lacks luminosity when in the non-living (ajīva); having abandoned its own nature, it possesses adventitious adjuncts (upādhi) due to being characterized by impure adjuncts, whereas in the unconditioned (nirupādhi), there is the perfection of the [true] adjunct.
"Because of the Vedāntic statement: 'Ignorance, which has no beginning, has that [Self] as its locus and that [Self] as its object.'"

Thus ends the third awakening (avabodha), consisting of the movement of the leaf-stalks (*samukhapattrādhrakacāraṇa*) included within the face of the *nirmukhavāsanā*, in the *Mugdhāvabodhinī*, a commentary on the *Rasahṛdaya* composed by Caturbhuja, the son of Maheśa, who is like a drop of nectar from the ocean of the illustrious Kuralava lineage.
START GRht 4.1:

That cloud which is black, red, or yellow, devoid of thick stars, and from which living beings have fallen, is a "Vajrin" (thunderbolt-bearing) cloud; it should be employed for the rite of yellow [subjugation]. GRht_4.1 // @------------------

*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:* Now, regarding the transmutation of the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), he describes the various colors of the sky (*gagana*) for that process of coloring (*pītakarman*) in the verse beginning with "black" (*kṛṣṇa*). 4.1.1.
The cloud is threefold—black, red, and yellow; "one by whom a being has been struck down" (*pātitasattva*) is a compound meaning one for whom a being has been caused to fall.
A Vajrin of this kind should be employed in yellow rites and in works involving gold.

The characteristic of the Vajrin is that which, even when heated in the fire of *haṭha* and joined [with mercury], becomes free from "gross stars" (*sthūlatārakārahitah*). These "gross stars" consist of a collection of petals;
being free from them, and although not explicitly stated, it is dense and white in color, to be employed in white rituals. This is the intended meaning, as it accords with other texts.
As it is stated in another treatise: "Red, yellow, black, and sky-colored [gems] are recommended for goldsmithing."
In rites of transference, the white variety is used; however, for the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*), all varieties are indeed excellent.
Even regarding the clouds, the author of the commentary mentions a distinction: "Once, having seen Hara, the captivating Goddess Girijā... (GRhtCM 4.1:8).
Then that vigor was released, and from it white mica (śvetābhraka) was born.
White, red, yellow, and black—due to contact with those respective grounds, there are four kinds:
the Pināka, the Dardura, the Nāga, and the Vajrābhra.
When its mass of petals is scorched in the fire, the *pināka* flower emits nothing but a puffing sound;
the serpent may hiss, like the croaking of a frog.
The fourth, the sky-going vajra, shall never undergo transformation in fire;
therefore, the vajra-iron is supreme, as it conquers disease, old age, and death.
For the sky here is devoid of moonlight, even though it is perfumed a hundredfold with various fragrances;
yet the mercury (rasendra) does not move within it— how, then, could it prevail over the *sattva* element despite all effort?
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:

Indicating that there is difficulty regarding the mica-leaf (*abhrapattra*) during the process of *cāraṇā*, whereas there is ease regarding the *sattva*, he says "devoid of moonlight" (*niścandrikam*), and so forth. (GRhtCM_4.2:1)

In this case, regarding this processing (*cāraṇa-saṃskāra*), even if the moonless sky— devoid of stars— is perfumed in a hundred ways by means of the aforementioned perfumes that serve as medicinal herbs (*vāsanauṣadhi*), and even if the "king of essences" (*rasendra*), namely mercury, is processed with great effort, it does not "move through" (*carati*) or swallow the mineral *abhra*. (GRhtCM 4.2:2)

And here, as for the statement "how might the *sattva* arise through effort": the meaning is how the *sattva* might somehow become capable through exertion; that is, how the *sattva* might become capable through diligent effort.
Apart from the single essence of the cloud (the mind), there is nothing else capable of clipping its wings; therefore,
with its range obstructed by that, it is restrained and easily bound.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Because it is easy to understand and because its qualities are superior, he praises *sattva* with the words beginning "having abandoned," etc. (GRhtCM 4.3:1).

Except for the single essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), no other [substance] is capable of cutting away the wings of mercury; it is not a cutter of the wings of *pārada*. By means of that essence, mercury (*rasa*, *pārada*) is restrained in such a way that there may be ease;
the meaning is that the restraint of mercury comes to pass. And it is bound: it attains bondage, meaning that the mercury becomes bound.

Being of what nature does one undergo restraint and bondage? Being one whose movement is obstructed—that is, one whose *prasara* (movement), which is a proceeding or a superior going, has been obstructed or checked. (This is the "cutting off of the wings" [pakṣaccheda]).

He who seeks to effect the binding of mercury (*rasabandha*) without first performing the "cutting of the wings" (*pakṣaccheda*) is like a dull-witted man who, having failed to conquer his senses, desires liberation through mere seeds alone. (GRht 4.4) *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* The "cutting of the wings" refers to the stabilization of mercury through the application of various medicinal substances (*uparasas*, *lohakas*, etc.). Without this preliminary process, the mercury remains volatile and cannot be bound. To attempt the fixation of mercury without such preparation is as futile as a person with uncontrolled senses hoping for liberation by merely sowing seeds. Just as a seed requires cultivation, irrigation, and protection from pests to yield fruit, so too does mercury require specific alchemical processing to achieve its transformative power. One who neglects these essential steps is compared to a fool who expects immediate results without laying the necessary groundwork. Thus, the verse emphasizes that mastery over the senses and the prior refinement of the mercury are indispensable prerequisites for any spiritual or alchemical success.
Demonstrating the qualification for the binding of mercury (*rasabandhana*), he says: "The cutting of the wings," and so forth.

The sense is that the disputant who, without swallowing the essence of the cloud (mercury), attempts—that is, exerts himself—to effect the binding of the *rasa*, to perform the fixation of mercury, by cutting his own wings and failing to provide the means for sustaining them, is not a disputant at all, but rather a fool; he is unwise. // GRhtCM_4.4:2 //
Who, having performed the binding of mercury, would desire to perform [it] with seeds such as red clouds, gold, mercury, and so forth? // GRhtCM_4.4:3 //
Thus, an indeclinable (avyaya) excludes other substances.
Having severed the wings, the binding should be performed; this is the correct procedure, whereas otherwise it is not the procedure.
He states an example of what is not a valid method: "Just as a man who has not conquered his senses and is a libertine might desire liberation."
There is a similarity between one whose senses are uncontrolled and one who is dull-witted. // GRhtCM_4.4:7 //
When the mercury processed with mica does not fall downward nor remain upward in the apparatus, and there is no belching [of vapors],
it should be known as "severed of its wings. (GRht 4.5)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the characteristics of mercury whose wings have been clipped with the words "not," and so forth. GRhtCM_4.5:1.
Such is the mercury (pārada) or elixir (sūta); "with wings cut" (pakṣacchinna) is a compound meaning that its two wings have been severed or clipped.

Who is he? He is one who does not fall downward even when subjected to a downward pull; nor does his lower part go upward when subjected to an upward pull from below. Being "non-eructing" (anudgārī) means he is motionless and remains perfectly steady within the machine—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, what is its specific characteristic? It is "abhrajīrṇa," which is a compound meaning that mercury (rasa) in which the mica (abhraka) has been digested, having reached a state of complete exhaustion.
The implied meaning is that the cutting of the wings does not occur by a mere mouthful [of abhraka] until the mica has been digested through practice.
"He is a charioteer whose wings have been clipped," he said. // GRhtCM_4.5:6 //
Those clouds are said to be of four colors, beginning with white, and they are devoid of coarse stars.
Others, when heated, release their essence as *vajrasattva* and turn into glass.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Having set aside "vajra-mercury" (*vajrābhra*), [the author] says "white," etc., showing that the Pināka, Nāga, and Bheka types are incapable of liberating living beings. GRhtCM_4.6:1.

Those which have been blown [upon], which are devoid of large stars, free from a mass of leaves, and described previously as being red, yellow, and black—those are said to be of the four colors, beginning with white.
The meaning is that if, among the three clouds of red, yellow, and black color, the white color is joined at the beginning, then they become four colors.
Among those four castes, he who is the Vajrin, known as Vajra, and is solid—he, when heated, emits *satva*; being heated, he relinquishes *satva*, and no others do.
Others, called pināka, nāga, and bheka, when blown, attain the state of glass; they assume the form of glass, yet there is no emergence of a sentient being.
START GRht 4.7:
Whatever clouds are described in the world as white, red, black, or yellow— [these are the subtypes of clouds according to their potency].
"Of little strength and devoid of essence, [other clouds are inferior]; however, the vajra-cloud is the best of all.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Because it is superior by virtue of possessing both essence and strength, he praises the vajra-cloud once more with the words beginning "white" (sitetyādi).*
In the world of saṃsāra, whatever clouds have been described or spoken of are said to be of little strength; that is, those in which there is little power are so designated.
"Devoid of sentient beings" means they are free from sentient beings; the meaning is that when those [elements] have been incinerated, there is an absence of sentient beings.
What are those "dense" ones? They are white, red, black, and yellow; the meaning is that there are no other colors besides these—white, red, black, and yellow.
Among all four castes, the Vajrin, known as Vajra, is the most excellent and preeminent.
Even when it is produced, the supreme essence is proclaimed as fit to be employed by those practicing alchemy (*rasāyana*).
The three kinds of *gagana* (mica) that are inedible are glass (*kāca*), slag (*kiṭṭa*), and leaf-dust (*pattrarajas*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* Regarding the statement "it is to be given even with mercury" (*sūte'pi*), etc., he speaks of the mica (*abhra*) that is to be offered. (GRhtCM_4.8:1)

Rasāyana is the elixir for those practitioners of Rasāyana, a medicine that destroys old age and disease; those who possess it or in whom it resides are called "rasāyanins. Among them, the supreme or primary essence is proclaimed and described as the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), as stated in another treatise: "A wise person who has undergone purification and practices with this essence shall attain the stabilization of youth."
Thus. // GRhtCM_4.8:2 //
It produces an excellent and most superior essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) within both mercury and *pārada*, which is capable of "cutting the wings" [of base metals] and bestows strength.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of sky: that which is inedible, that which is unfit for consumption, and that which [is found] even in the elixir of alchemists.
What are those three types? First is *kāca*, which is brought to the form of glass by smelting in fire; second is *kiṭṭa*, which attains the nature of dross through smelting;
and third is *pattrarajas*, which is the dust collected from leaves. These three kinds are unfit for consumption because they are inherently defective.
When heated by the transformations of grass and wood, the cloud releases its essence as it perspires.
Having discarded the dross of glass, the essence should be grasped with effort.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Demonstrating the procedure for precipitating the sattva, he says "muñcati" and so forth.*

When the *ghana* (mass) has been heated (*svinna*) by means of medicinal preparations made from the specific transformations of "grass-essence" (*tṛṇasāra*)— those whose essence is grass— and by substances such as *sūryāvartaka* and others, it, being blown in the fire, releases its essence (*sattva*) and effects the precipitation of that essence (*sattvapāta*).
Furthermore, having again discarded the glass and the dross, when the essence becomes associated with fallen glass and dross, then it should be taken with effort; this is the meaning.
START GRht 4.10 (Abhra:: Sattva:: Pātana):
Having bound the mineral to be sweated into a ball with buffalo curd, milk, urine, dung, and ghee;
Now, combined with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), it causes a being to fall, appearing like iron.
(GRht 4.10) *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now he states another specific method, beginning with "it should be sweated" (*svedya*).*

The thick [mercury] is to be sweated; the procedure for sweating the aforementioned mercury using modifications of grass-wood has been described. Furthermore, having bound the mass of the thick [mercury], with what [should it be done]? Together with buffalo curd, milk, urine, dung, and clarified butter—*māhiṣa* means belonging to a buffalo;
thus, having bound the mass with these, namely curd, milk, urine, *śakṛt* (dung), and *ājya* (clarified butter).
The word "atha" is used here as a conjunction.
"With the five products of the cow"—meaning it should be prepared by binding a ball [of clay] mixed with the milk, curd, urine, dung, and clarified butter of cows.
This mass, resembling iron and possessing the luster of a shaven head, causes the being to fall due to its prior connection; "of the cloud" is the word to be supplied.
START GRht 4.11:
Minerals whose juices have been dried by the heat of the sun release only a small amount of *sattva*.
Remaining in their own places, those very [elements] release the greatest amount [of essence].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

"Those whose fluids have been drunk by the sun's heat" means those elements whose fluids—i.e., liquid essences—have been drunk, that is, dried up, by the sun's heat, i.e., the solar warmth; being thus smelted, they release only a small amount, merely a slight measure, of *sattva*.
They abandon it.

Furthermore, those very elements (dhātus), whose essences have been dried up by the sun's heat, remaining in their own locations— that is, abiding in their respective places as liquid masses or forms— being of such a nature, release their abundance, meaning they flow out in great quantity. // GRhtCM_4.11:2 //
"Those whose juices turn yellow in the sun's heat" refers to certain liquefying medicinal herbs, such as *sūryāvarta*, plantain (*kadalī*), and *vandhyākarkoṭakī*.
When one has blown [the breath] deeply and profoundly, the cloud rains down in streams of gold;
one should know that the stainless being has fallen like a drop from the mouth of a god.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the characteristics of one who has fallen [from his practice] with the words "very deep," and so forth. (GRhtCM_4.12:1)

Just as a dense cloud, having been blown up with great depth, rains down with streams of gold— that is, with streams of beautiful color— or rather, with those whose color is like gold (suvarṇa) due to their purity and luminosity, it produces a downpour of rain. // GRhtCM_4.12:2 //

Of what nature is it? It is equal to the face of a god, equal to fire, and pure—meaning stainless—because it is free from smoke such as green, yellow, red, and so forth. One should perceive the *sattva* fallen in that manner; this is the meaning of "of the cloud" (*ghanasya*).
Likewise, it is stated in another text:
"In the great-flaming fire by means of the intense bellows-fire..."
When it is excessively blazing, the Buddhas become embers that have reached exhaustion.
If it does not happen again, the wise one should repeat it two or three times until the fire becomes blazing, with pure flames and great power.
One should know that the essence has then fallen; there is no doubt about this.
Once fallen, it should be separated from the dross and charcoal.
Having characterized it as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), it should then be blown [upon] correctly;
thus blown twice or thrice, it completely releases its essence.
START GRht 4.13–14 (abhra:: sattva: “eaten” without a mukha)
If that which resembles iron has fallen and become [one with] the sky, its essence flows;
it unites even in all dualities and moves by means of medicinal herbs even without mouths.
When gaganam (mica) together with mākṣika (pyrite) is smelted, it yields sattvam that provides a mukham (mouth).
And thereafter, the essence (sattva) combined with lead (nāga) and tin (vaṅga) bestows a beautiful face.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Demonstrating the superiority of the qualities of the essence through its combination with the internal essence of honey (mākṣika), he says "mākṣika" and so forth.*
That which exists in the sky is "gagana"; ending with the suffix *aṇ*, there is no *vṛddhi* substitution according to the rule *ṇito vā*. "Gagana" is the essence of the clouds (*abhrasattva*).

That which is derived from honey is *mākṣika*; when that *mākṣika-sattva* is combined with the previously mentioned *sattva* and both are smelted, that dual *sattva* becomes "mouth-bestowing" (*mukhaprada*) for the mercury—this is the remainder [of the sense].
The compound *mukhaprada* is analyzed as "that which gives (*pradadāti*) the mouth (*mukham*) excellently (*prakṛṣṭena*)."
And thereafter, following that, "together with the *nāgas* and *vaṅgas*" refers to the previously mentioned sky, which is the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), meaning it bestows a beautiful face.
Alternatively, there is the reading "sukhapradaṃ" (bestowing happiness); the meaning of this option is that in this yoga, having abandoned many afflictions, movement occurs with ease.
START GRhT 4.15 (abhra:: sattva:: induction of garbhadruti)
Through the application of *mākṣika-sattva* and *rañjana-bandhana*, the mercury (*sūtaka*) moves entirely into the state of *ghana-sattva*.
It certainly liquefies the interior (*garbhadrāvī*), and thus it is both colored (*rajyate*) and bound (*badhyate*). (GRht 4.15)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states "mākṣika" and so forth, indicating that the essence of mākṣika is primary. GRhtCM_4.15:1.
Sūtaka (mercury), pārada (mercury), ghanasattva (the essence of mica), and abhrasattva (the essence of mica)—all these, without exception, move.
Why? Because of its application to the essence of *mākṣika*; *mākṣika* is *svarṇamākṣika*, and it is because of its application to that essence.
"Niyaṭaṃ" means certain and settled.

Through the application of the essence of *mākṣika*, the mercury moves as the essence of *ghana*; it is called "womb-dissolving" (*garbhadrāvī*) because it dissolves the essence within the womb and renders that essence into a liquid form.
The meaning is that the essence of mica and iron remains in the form of a liquid within the belly of the *sūta* (mercury).
In this manner, by means of this procedure, mercury (pārada) together with the *sūtaka* becomes colored—that is, it becomes possessed of color—and it is bound; the meaning is that it becomes fixed.
START GRht 4.16 (Abhra:: Sattva::
for the binding of mercury)
The essence (satva) of the ore, which is beautiful, combined with *tālaka*, and repeatedly smelted three times, becomes here a supreme binder of mercury (*rasendra*).
*Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
Immediately after the application of honey, another [application] is described, beginning with the words "the essence" (sattva) and so forth.

The essence (*sattva*) of thick clouds, as well as *kānta*— a specific type of iron— when combined with *tālaka* (orpiment), being thoroughly processed and smelted, all three likewise take on the form of an essence. If the essence is not obtained by smelting once, then one should smelt it again two or three times.

When the essence (sattva) of *ghanasatva* and *ākṣikasatva* is melted through the application of a flux (*yoga*) and blown with intense heat, that essence becomes a binder for mercury (*rasa*, *pārada*), being most excellent and providing supreme fixation.
The meaning is that through the movement of that being, the *rasa* attains bondage.
The characteristics of *kāntaloha* (magnetite):
when it is placed in a vessel, a drop of oil does not spread upon the water; asafoetida does not release its own fragrance; and the paste of neem does not retain its bitterness.
When cooked, milk maintains its peak-like shape rather than spreading on the ground. They know that iron possessing these characteristics is *kāntaloha*, and nothing else.
Thus [it is said]. (GRhtCM 4.16:5)
START GRHT 4.17 (Abhra:: Sattva:: Induction of Garbhadruti)
Iron and the essence of mica (abhrakasattva), when combined with an equal portion of orpiment (tālaka),
undergoes digestion; and through the application of pressure and being rubbed with the fingers, it melts within the crucible.
He states the method for preparing an alloy of the essence of *kāntaloha* and mica in the verse beginning with "loham" (iron), etc. (GRhtCM 4.17:1).
And *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). // GRhtCM_4.17:2 //

The iron (loha) possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, such as muṇḍa and the like, and the essence of mica (abhrasattva), when processed with an equal portion of orpiment (tālaka)— meaning that which has been brought to a state of single-bodiedness by being processed through the mouth and other parts according to the previous procedure, the root *sṛ* meaning "to go" taking the form *sārita*, which signifies "merged"— in such a manner, mercury moves through the essence of magnetite and mica.

Furthermore, that which is rubbed by the fingers—that is, massaged with the fingers—melts within the womb of the essence (*rasa*) inside the beautiful cloud-like being, and merges into its very nature.
Why? Because of its connection with pressing; "pressing" (abhiṣava) means crushing, and it is so called because of that connection.
The word "metal" (loha) implies that a combination with one of the thirteen varieties of metal must be performed.
START GRht 4.18 (abhra:: sattva: induction of cāraṇa)
Then, tin and realgar, combined with one-sixth part of orpiment, circulate;
through the application of pressure, the mercury flows and moves—of this there is no doubt.
(GRht 4.18) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [The commentary explains that by adding these substances, the mercury becomes mobile and flows under the influence of the processing technique.]
Having explained the formulation with iron, he states the formulation with tin, beginning with the words "tin" and so forth.

Now, after the discussion of iron, tin—known as *khura*—and mica (*abhraka*): these two, when combined with one-sixth part of *tālaka* (realgar), having been brought into a single substance by means of that sixth part of *tālaka*, the mercury (*rasa*) courses through their very nature.

Why? Because of its connection with pressing (*abhiṣava*). Pressing is crushing; because of that connection, the form *abhiṣavaḥ* is derived from the verbal root *ṣuñ* in the sense of "pressing. // GRhtCM_4.18:3 //
Furthermore, the taste circulates and mingles.
That which has been transmuted flows; that which flows becomes liquefied in the mercury. Due to its distinctness, it merges [with it]; of this there is no doubt, as if it were beyond all doubt.
Because tin is light and melts easily, the addition of one-sixth part of orpiment is appropriate; because iron is hard, an equal proportion is prescribed.
START GRHT 4.19–20 (Abhra:: Sattva::
Induction of Cāraṇa)
Thick and golden-colored, the essence falls in five layers with the folds of the Nicula plant;
it renders the sky like a small ball, stainless and free from dross.

Having reduced that to powder, it is then repeatedly saturated with alkaline acids and made into a thick mass; when rubbed with the juice of the three creations (*sṛṣṭitraya*), water-cress (*nīrakaṇā*), and *tumburu*, it becomes active. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* The "three creations" refers to the three types of mercury: *rasa* (liquid), *baddha* (bound), and *mūrchita* (coagulated). The "water-cress" is *nīlakaṇṭhī*. The *tumburu* is the *tumburu* plant. By rubbing [the powder] with these, it attains its medicinal efficacy.
He states the procedure for the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) beginning with the words "thick" (*bahala*), and so forth.

And that "dead sky" (mṛtagagana), having been made into pills (vaṭakīkṛta), is so described because it is not [already] a pill but is being made into a pill; here, the suffix *cvi* is used in the sense of a transformation from one state to another (*abhūtatadbhāve*). When the dead sky—that is, dead mica (*mṛtābhra*)—which has been processed with five pouches of *nicula* (the juice of the *vetasa* tree) and thus made into pills, falls as a sattva, it is due to the blowing [of the flame] by fire after applying a combination of liquefying medicinal herbs.
The remainder.
To what extent does the being fall—dense, vast, and exceeding other methods?
Of what nature is it? It is gold-colored, yellowish-white, known as "light" (prakāśa), and furthermore stainless, pure, and free from dross.
When this exists, there is an absence of the dross of glass.
This is the most excellent procedure; the meaning is that it is superior to the previously mentioned [method] which involves the slaughter of many sentient beings.
He states the procedure for causing the movement of pure beings with the words beginning with "that" (tad), etc. (GRhtCM 4.19–20).

Then, immediately after that procedure for precipitating the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), one should reduce that very same mica-essence to powder, prepare it as a paste, and saturate it with alkaline substances (*kṣāra*) and acids (*amla*). The alkaline substances are *svarjikā* and so forth; the acids are *jambīra* and so forth. The meaning is that one should subject it to heating in a closed crucible (*gharmapuṭita*) many times, i.e., repeatedly.
Furthermore, one should grind it with the juice of the three creations, water-pepper (*nīrakaṇā*), and *tumburu*. "The three creations" refers to those previously mentioned: urine, semen, and blood.
*Nīrakaṇā* is water-pepper (*jalapippalī*), and *tumburu* is well known. One should perform the grinding with the juice of these.
When the essence of mica has been prepared in this manner, the mercury moves toward and devours it; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
