When equal parts of ghanasatva, copper (śulba), and mākṣika are combined and thus united, that is called śulvābhra;
the mercury moves within it and is quickly digested.

Thus, the dense essence (ghanasattva), together with tāpya and śulba, having been rubbed in an iron mortar, the lord of mercury (rasendra) flows [when processed] with sour gruel (kāñjika) and the acids of vetasa, jambīra, and bījapūra. *GRht 4.22* *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī*
Now, he states the calculation for the area of a rhombus (śulba) with the verse beginning "ghana," and so forth.
When the essence of mica (*ghanasattva*), copper (*śulba*), and pyrite (*mākṣika*) are combined in equal proportions— that is, when the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), copper,
and golden pyrite are employed in equal parts— these, once mixed together, are called *śulvābhra*.
Regarding this, he explains what kind of mercury (*śulba*) should be employed:
"There are two types of mercury, that from Mleccha and that from Nepal; among these, the Nepalese is superior.
It withstands repeated hammering, is glossy, has red leaves, is stainless, and is soft."
But the *mleccha* iron, when washed, is black, rough yet oily, and unable to withstand being beaten; mixed with *nāga* (lead) and *loha* (iron), it is not excellent for alchemical work (*rasakarma*).
Therefore, the meaning is that Nepalese iron (*nepālaka*) should be taken.
That mercury quickly penetrates the copper; furthermore, that copper quickly—that is, rapidly—digests, meaning it undergoes the process of *jāraṇā*.
In this context, the application of honey is for the purpose of fusing copper with the essence of mica, so that the mercury may become pleased; such is the meaning.
He states the procedure for the movement of the cord and the clouds, beginning with "iti" and so forth.

Thus, as previously stated, the "tāpya-śulba-sahita" [mixture]—consisting of *tāpya* (gold-macerating mineral) and *śulba* (copper known as Nepalese)—along with *ghana-sattva* (essence of iron), should be rubbed in a heated iron mortar (*taptaloha-khalvaka*). With what should it be rubbed? It should be ground using *kāñjika*, *vetasa*, and the acidic juices of *jambīra* and *bījapūra*. *Kāñjika* is prepared according to the aforementioned method; it is *sauvīra* (sour gruel), and *vetasa* is the rattan cane.
Cukra is well-known as *jambīra*, and *bījapūra* is *mātuluṅga*; [these are used] with their sour liquids.
Then the lord of mercury, the quicksilver, moves through and swallows the sulphur-cloud.
By the mention of an iron mortar, the intended meaning is that one should perform the rubbing in a heated mortar.
START GRHT 4.23 (Bhasman [of various metals]: Rañjana):
Thus, a *khoṭa* is prepared from *tīkṣṇa*, copper, and lead, combined with *mākṣika*.
And that ash, when processed by the method of encapsulation (*puṭavidhi*), becomes a quick colorant.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method with the words "iti" and so forth.*

Thus, one should prepare an equal portion—meaning parts of identical weight—of the previously described *tīkṣṇa-śulba-nāga*, which consists of these three: *tīkṣṇa* (steel), copper (*tāmra*), and lead (*nāga*), combined with *mākṣika* (pyrite), that is, joined with gold-pyrite (*svarṇamākṣika*).
The resulting *khoṭa* (solidified mass) should be reduced to ash by means of the stabilization of the paste (*piṣṭī-stambha*) using all those aforementioned ingredients.

By means of the *puṭa* method—that is, by the procedure of heating in a crucible—that *khoṭa* is to be reduced to ash. Furthermore, when that ash is processed (*nirvyūḍha*) into a *satva*, it becomes a coloring agent for *satva*; when processed into an *abhrasatva* (mercury of mica), it bestows color upon it. Once colored, that *satva* becomes a colorant for mercury (*rasa*).

One should diligently practice the conduct (*cārya*) regarding the *rasa* which possesses a dense essence; having combined that kind of dense [substance] with all the seeds (*sarvabīja*), one should extract it from the mixture of dualities (*dvandvasaṃkara*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states "the practice (*cārya*) for one whose dense essence has been colored" in the verse beginning with "the practice," etc. (GRhtCM_4.24:1).

That kind of previously colored, dense *satva*, as well as uncolored *satva* produced from dense clouds (*ghanasatva*) or arising solely from dense clouds, should be processed in mercury (*rasa*, i.e., *pārada*) by means of the measure of swallowing the morsel (*grāsagrahaṇa*), and this cloud-*satva* should then be joined with the mercury.
Or else, having combined all seeds and every substance that produces passion within a sentient being, one should cause it to be carried away and indeed carry it away.
Why? Because of the confusion of pairs (*dvandva-saṃkara*). "Confusion" (*saṃkara*) means a mixture (*melāpa*) of pairs; according to Amarasimha, *saṃkara* also means a heap of refuse (*avakara*).
The form *nirvāhyam* is derived from the root *vah* in the sense of "to carry" or "to lead," as explained previously.
"‘Nir’ signifies ‘undecaying’ (niravyaya) and ‘certainty’ (niścaya), while [the same prefix] signifies ‘negation’ (niṣedha) and ‘absence of certainty’ (nirniścaya); thus says Amara.

He who does not know first the processing of mica and then the processing of internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) of gold, is no speaker at all; he merely causes the ruin of his wealth in vain. (GRht 4.25)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Now, he states what is to be known regarding the transmutation of mercury, beginning with the words "abhraka" and so forth. GRhtCM_4.25:1.
That proponent who is a formulator of mercury first does not know the "movement" (*cāraṇa*) of mica— that is, how the mercury moves through and devours the mica—

and subsequently does not know the "movement" of internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*), wherein mica and other minerals remain in a molten, liquid state within the womb of the mercury; and finally, he does not know the "movement" or devouring of gold— that is, of *suvarṇa*— then his effort is indeed in vain.
It causes the false loss of purpose and the destruction of wealth due to the failure to accomplish one's objective.
The intended meaning is that only an omniscient being could engage in the practice of alchemy (*rasakriyā*).
START GRht 4.26 (Cloud: Sattva:
Grāsa)
I shall now declare the secret of the "swallowing of the sky" (gaganagrāsa), which occurs through the conjunction of the clouds and the sun:
it is the essence of *abhra* alone that is swallowed with effort, not its entire body. (GRht 4.26)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the secret of the morsel (*grāsarahasya*) beginning with "the sky," etc. (GRhtCM 4.26).

I, the venerable teacher Śrī Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, shall speak—that is, I declare—the secret of swallowing the sky, which is one and without a second: the curiosity of swallowing the *abhraka* [mica]. Why? Because of the conjunction of the cloud (*ghana*) and the sun (*arka*); "cloud" refers to the essence of *abhraka*, and "sun" refers to copper (*tāmra*). From their conjunction, the dross (*khoṭa*) produced from the essences of both should be taken.
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates an alternative position.
When a mineral of a particular sattva-ore comes into contact with another mineral due to their dual nature or through admixture, the name becomes a compound of those two;
for example, *śulvābhra*, *nāgābhra*, *vaṅgābhra*, *mākṣikābhra*, and *hemābhra*. In this way, the formation of names occurs everywhere through conjunction.

The liquefaction of that which has been swallowed within the womb is called *garbhadruti*; whereas having indeed liquefied dense substances (*ghanasattva*) and so forth externally for the sake of the digestion (*jāraṇā*) by the Lord of Mercury (*rasendra*), that is called *bāhyadruti*.

START GRht 5.1 If the solid essence does not fall into the womb, or if the seeds do not flow, and there is no conjunction with external fluidity, then how is the mercury (sūta) bound here? GRht_5.1 // @------------------
With the rays of your speech, satisfy Janaka’s son, who has been scorched by the rays of [Rāvaṇa’s] words;
and with your long-lasting radiance, cause the night-lotuses blooming on the lake to shine.
Now, he speaks in praise of the internal alchemy (*garbhadruti*) and external alchemy (*bāhyadruti*), beginning with the words "If," and so forth.
If indeed the essence of mica (*ghanasattva*) or the essence of cloud-stone (*abhrasattva*) does not fall into the interior of mercury (*pārada*), or if it does not attain fluidity;

or if seeds such as *śulbābhra* and others do not melt within the belly of mercury and do not become liquid in nature; and if external liquefaction (*bāhyadruti*) is likewise not possible—then, when this [process] has been undertaken here, how could this mercury (*sūta-rasa*) exist?
Otherwise, one is bound; there is no other means whatsoever.
Even if the morsel of food is consumed, it does not attain oneness if it is devoid of the *garbhadruti* (inner melting).
Without that state of oneness, it is not digested; therefore, that [melting] must be performed.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Showing the superiority of the "impregnation" (*garbhadruti*), he says "garbha... and so forth. GRhtCM_5.2:1.

Even if a morsel has been consumed and even if it has reached the state of being circulated, if it is devoid of *garbhadruti*—if it remains in the stomach lacking the transformation into the form of *rasa*—then it does not attain unity;
it does not become the nature of *rasa*.
Furthermore, without becoming one with it, the morsel is not digested; it does not attain the state of being assimilated (*jāraṇatva*).

For that reason, the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) preceded by the melting of the embryo (*garbhadruti*) should be performed; the meaning is that digestion is the cause for the binding of the mercury (*rasabandha*).
First, some kind of processing of the seeds must be performed such that they dissolve within the womb by means of the "king of juices" (mercury) along with the group of sour substances.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states what must first be done in the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) with the words "of the seeds," and so forth. GRhtCM_5.3:1.

For seeds such as *śulba* and *abhraka*, a certain indefinable refinement (*saṃskāra*) that causes liquefaction within the womb must first be performed; it is called *saṃskāra* because it is refined (*saṃskriyate*). 5.3.2.
Of what nature is it? It is "of such a kind," meaning similar to those seeds; the sense is that just as seeds possess potency, so too must the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) be rendered potent.
By what should the purification be performed? By the group of acidic substances, such as the jambīra fruit and others.

The meaning is that by which chemical process (*saṃskāra*) the seeds produced from the primary and secondary metals (*dhātu-upadhātu*), such as base metals and mica, melt within the womb of the king of mercury (*rasarāja*), that is, inside the mercury.
START GRHT 5.4 (Seed suitable for *garbhadruti* [1]):
Gold that has been sown with an equal amount of honey and combined with an equal amount of honey-essence (*mākṣikasattva*).
It flows within the womb and, once matured, it binds the molten [metal]; otherwise, it does not.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
This passage beginning with "sametya" etc., praises the seed of gold.*

Having performed the *vāpa* (repeated casting) of equal parts— that is, the repeated addition (*ākṣepa*) of equal portions of *mākṣika* [copper pyrite] to the gold by means of fire— one should then make that gold into a *khoṭa* (solidified mass), joined with an equal amount of *mākṣika-sattva* (the essence of *mākṣika*), which is itself equal in measure to the gold.
That gold in the form of a crucible melts within the mercury in its interior.
Furthermore, that melted gold undergoes digestion; it reaches a state of being fully digested.
That gold, being thus heated and processed with the lord of mercury (raseśvara), binds [it].
Otherwise, in another manner, the charioteer does not incur bondage.
The meaning is that the sowing of honey-beeswax bestows an enhancement of color upon gold.
START GRHT 5.5 (Tārāriṣṭa):
The essence of copper, when melted and processed with one-quarter part of gold and so forth, produces silver.
It turns base metal into excellent gold by means of a leaf-coating.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Regarding the verse beginning with "mākṣikasattva," it describes the excellence of qualities [attained] in the mercury through the processing of the essence of honey-ore.* *Commentary (GRhtCM 5.5:1): [Same as above]*

The essence of *mākṣika* (copper pyrite), which has been melted through the application of fire and medicinal herbs— that quintessence of *mākṣika* gold which was previously dissolved into mercury along with gold (*kanaka*), and which has again been processed (*jārita*) in portions starting from one-quarter (*pāda*) and so on, until it reaches complete exhaustion by means of the quarter-portion essence—
this mercury (*sūta*) transforms base silver (*tārāriṣṭa*)— that is, silver and the like— into excellent gold of full color; this is the meaning.
By what method? By means of a leaf-ointment; that is, by that ointment which [is applied] there to the leaf for piercing the thorn, through the application of fire—this is the ellipsis.
The explicit meaning is that gold will be produced by applying a coating of silver leaf to [mercury] that has been processed with the essence of *hemamākṣika*.
START GRht 5.6 (garbhadruti:: test for ~):
If it has attained a state of uniform consistency and, when released from the cloth, it exceeds [the original weight] upon weighing;
That morsel is "swift" (*druta*); having melted within the womb, it is digested quickly.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the definition of "melting within the womb" (*garbhadruti*) with the words beginning "sametya," etc.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_5.6:1): [The same]*

If the *grāsa* has attained a state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*), meaning it has reached a form identical to the mercury, and furthermore, if it falls from the cloth— meaning it has emerged from a white cloth four times its size— and if it should even be found in excess during weighing (*tulanā*) or the act of weighing, then the *grāsa* must be known as "melted within" (*garbhadruta*); that is, the mercury should be understood as being in a state of internal melting.
The meaning is clear.
Furthermore, that mercury, having melted and quickly attained a liquid state, digests even the bodily constituents (dhātus) according to the prescribed method; this is the remainder of the sense.
Neither by fermented liquids (*biḍa*), nor by alkalis (*kṣāra*), nor by fats (*sneha*) does gold or silver dissolve. START GRht 5.7 (The role of *tāpyasattva*)
[This is] by means of blood kept for three days together with the essence of honey (*mākṣika-sattva*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
[The author] states the excellence of the essence of honey with the words "not," and so forth.*
Without the essence of *mākṣika*, that is, without the core of *svarṇamākṣika*, neither gold (*hema* or *kanaka*) nor silver (*tāra* or *rūpya*) will liquefy.
By what means? By means of *viḍa* salts; by means of balls (*piṇḍa*) made from conch powder, solar alkali (*arkakṣāra*), and so forth;
and according to another text: "Salt, alkali, and *uparasa*—these, together with acids, are considered *viḍa*.
When the [metal] is placed in an equal [quantity of] *garbha*, it indeed becomes liquefied by this very [mixture]."
Thus. GRhtCM_5.7:3.
Not only with acids, but even with alkalis—such as svarjikā, yavakṣāra, ṭaṅkaṇa, and so forth—it does not [dissolve].

Not only with alkaline substances, but also with oils— provided they are not oils such as those derived from *kaṅguṇikā*, *vināda*, *doṣā*, *karajja*, and *śrīphala*; nor those produced from *kaṭu*, *vātāri*, *siddhārtha*, *somarājī*, and *vibhītaka*.

The oil is produced from linseed, from the seeds of the great black neem, and likewise from sesame; it is also derived from apāmārga, devadālī, dantī, tumbara, aṅkola, unmatta, and the fruits of bhallātaka.
Thus. // GRhtCM_5.7:5 //
It does not liquefy even with oils;
furthermore, liquefaction occurs within the crucible through the presence of *mākṣika* (pyrite).
By what specific [ingredient]? By the presence of honey, by blood, and by the group of red substances.
For three days—that is, for a period of three days—by means of that which has been placed within the group of red substances.
The red group (*raktavarga*) is as follows:
pomegranate, *kiṃśuka*, *bandhūka*, safflower, along with madder,
turmeric and its like, combined with lac-resin.
Combined with red sandalwood, it is proclaimed as the "red group" (raktavarga).
Thus [ends the section].

START GRHT 5.8–12 (Mercury: *cāraṇa*, *garbhadruti*) 8. Mercury is the best among all the metals for the purpose of *cāraṇa* [dissolving] and *garbhadruti* [internal liquefaction]. It is said that mercury is the foremost among all the metals. 9. Mercury, when combined with sulfur, dissolves all the metals; it is the most excellent among all the metals for the purpose of *cāraṇa*. 10. Mercury, having been purified by means of *mūrchana* [solidification], becomes fit for use; it is the best among all the metals for the purpose of *garbhadruti*. 11. Mercury, when combined with the juices of *arka*, *kumārikā*, and *viṣṇukrāntā*, dissolves all the metals; it is the most excellent among all the metals for the purpose of *cāraṇa*. 12.
Mercury, having been combined with the juices of *arkapuṣpī*, *kumārī*, and *viṣṇukrāntā*, dissolves all the metals; it is the most excellent among all the metals for the purpose of *garbhadruti*.
Salt saturated with the juice of *devī*, along with powdered *ahipatra* ground on a stone—
this, having been properly calcined through three *puṭa* cycles, should be stored in an iron vessel.
The mouth-base should be fashioned with a hollow half-finger-breadth deep and a clearly defined, wide rim;
upon that, another bowl should be placed, one finger-breadth in height.
Three apertures having been made, it is recommended that iron rods be inserted into the four-finger-high openings; there too, gold plates should be joined.
Having placed them beneath the apparatus and fumigated them, one should kindle a fire;
by the mere application of smoke, the gold leaves become black.
Once these have been heated by fire and subsequently killed by smoke in the apparatus (*yantra*),

the mercury (*rasendra*) circulates due to the process of cooking gold and liquefies within the womb (*garbha*). *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [The commentary explains that the mercury, having been processed through heating and fumigation, undergoes a transformation where it flows and dissolves within the crucible during the alchemical operation.]
He describes the procedure for the apparatus for the digestion of gold with the verse beginning "salt" (lavaṇam), etc. (GRhtCM 5.8–12).
First, one should take rock salt (*saindhava*) saturated with the juice of the goddess (*devī*), and then mix it with the juice of *brāhmī* itself.
Furthermore, one should soak salt and *ahipatra* with the juice of *brāhmī*, and then grind and pulverize those two together with a stone on a broad grinding slab.
Furthermore, one should place this in an iron vessel, that is, a metal container.
This established substance, by being subjected to three layers [of processing] and the application of fire through the *tripuṭaka* method, becomes well-matured (*sumṛta*).

For that [iron vessel] which has been flooded with the juice of *devī* and well-mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*), a bowl (*kaṭorikā*) should be made as a support for its mouth; that is, one whose mouth itself serves as the base. Such a bowl—clearly manifest, vast, and inverted (meaning turned face-down)—is to be fashioned from iron.
This bowl should be taken and placed upon the upper part, on top of that bowl.
Of what specific quality is it? It is "finger-high" (*aṅgulotsedhā*); that whose height or measure (*utsedhaḥ parimāṇam*) is one finger is so described.
Furthermore, what are its specific characteristics? It is half-a-finger deep—that is, it has a depth of the measure of half a finger—at its center.

Furthermore, what are its specific characteristics? It is one in which "the three apertures have been made"—that is, the three apertures (*chidratritaya*) have been fashioned; such a vessel is praised as having "three well-proportioned apertures" (*saṃtulavihitachidratritayā*).
The meaning is that above that [main body], there is a bowl-like lid (*kaṭorikā*) on the upper part, four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) in height.

Furthermore, rods should be joined to the three holes; iron rods are to be inserted there again, and into those holes as well, gold leaves—thin golden plates pierced by thorns—are to be placed. When such a machine has been previously constructed, the gold leaves are placed within it and heated.

Then one should kindle the fire; one should ignite the fire beneath the apparatus, at the lower part of the apparatus. At that time, those gold leaves become black, that is, of a dark color. Why? "Merely from the coating of smoke"—smoke and the act of smearing are "smoke-coating" (dhūmopalepa); "merely from that" means by that measure alone.
With whatever medicinal herb the incense was described as being made, an anointing with that same medicinal herb should be performed upon the leaves.
Furthermore, what kind of gold leaves does the lord of mercury digest? They are heated by fire; that is, they have been made hot through contact with fire.
This is declared to be the alchemy of gold.
Thus ends the *kulaka* consisting of five verses.
START GRht 5.13 (silver:: garbhadruti [in mercury]):
By that very [mercury], having subjected a silver leaf to sweating according to the prescribed method through the application of a mechanical device, [one should proceed].
That silver becomes black in color and melts within the crucible.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now, he describes the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of silver with the words "tena" and so forth.*
By that very same procedure, using the aforementioned covering, the tāra-leaf becomes a silver plate of black color and dark luster.

By what means? By means of a mechanical device for heating; "saṃsveda" refers to a powerful fire, and "yantrayogena" means by whichever machine is connected to that [fire] and by whatever application thereof.
Furthermore, that silver leaf melts within the interior of the mercury, reaching the state of liquid water.
Furthermore, when that mercury flows in that apparatus—indicated by the word "and"—it digests that leaf, turning it black like silver.
START GRhyasūtra 5.14 (Gold and Silver:
*garbhadruti*)
Alternatively, by means of the application of a mechanical device (*yantra-yoga*) using mercury known as *nāga* which is powerful,
gold or silver melts within the crucible; of this there is no doubt.
Now he states another yoga, beginning with "Alternatively" (athavā) and so forth.
Alternatively, the word "or" (*athavā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because they both aim at the same purpose.
By means of a mechanical device, tin together with the substance *balin* becomes black.
Furthermore, it is clear that not only tin (vaṅga), but also lead (nāga) by its name, would follow this same procedure for the preparation of lead.
"By the name 'Nāga'" means by the name Nāga; for Amarasimha states: "ākhyā, hve, abhidhāna, nāmadheya, and nāma [are synonyms]."

Whether it be tin (*vaṅga*) or lead (*nāga*), gold-termed (*hemāhvam*) or gold-leafed (*hemapatram*), silver (*tāra*) or silver-leafed (*tārapatram*)—all of this, when treated with *balī*, becomes black; and once dead, all of it dissolves within the womb of the mercury (*rasāntara*). There is no doubt here; this has been stated without ambiguity.
And by the word "ca" (and), one attains complete exhaustion [of suffering].
START GRHT 5.15 (Rasaka: Internal Melting):
Rasaka, combined with bali, according to the application of the previously mentioned procedure.
When it is cooked until it becomes a powder and flows excessively within the crucible.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another application beginning with "rasakam" and so forth.*
Rasaka (calomel) and kharparika (black salt), when combined with an equal portion of sulphur and mercury— this being the remainder of the sense—

and by means of the previously mentioned method of application, that is, by employing the aforementioned procedure involving the apparatus and so forth, it should be cooked intensely and thoroughly until it attains a bodiless state; that powder [is then placed] within the womb, that is, inside the mercury.
By means of the "ca" (and) word, there is the melting of the embryo (*garbhadruti*) and it also ages (*jarati*).
Then,
when mercury is combined with sulphur and mica in a hundredfold proportion, it likewise [dissolves] in the finest gold.
She gives birth and becomes a grinder; for the fetus dissolves—no wonder should be felt at this.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method beginning with "vyūḍha" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM 5.16:1): [He states] another procedure, beginning with "vyūḍha" etc.*
The word "atha" (then) signifies immediately following.

Gandhakāśmā (sulphur) is "gandhapāṣāṇaḥ" (fragrant stone); when it is processed (*vyūḍha*) in excellent gold of full color in a manner that results in a hundredfold increase, that gold infused with its fragrance produces a paste (*piṣṭi*) in mercury—this is indeed certain. It melts within the womb [of the mercury], and thus it becomes *garbhadruti*; there is no wonder in this.
START GRHT 5.17 (Gold:: Seed for Garbhadruti):
Alternatively, excellent mercury processed a hundred times is the superior seed for pure gold.
The seed digests in the mercury (rasendra) and dissolves within the womb; of this there is no doubt.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method with the words "Or else" (*athavā*) and so forth.*

Alternatively, the word "atha vā" (or) is used in a conjunctive sense; one should perform a hundred-fold extraction (*śatanirvyūḍha*) of the best *kharparika*—the most excellent mercury—into pure gold of full color.

A hundred-fold extraction must be performed; that is to say, a hundred-fold extraction into gold of a single unit [of purity] is indeed appropriate. When this is done, it becomes the "excellent seed" (*varabīja*), the supreme seed. That seed melts within the womb, that is, in the interior of the mercury; it undergoes liquefaction within the womb.
In the king of liquids, mercury, it is digested quickly—that is, without delay—and attains complete digestion according to the prescribed method;
there is no doubt regarding this liquefaction and digestion.
START GRHT 5.18 (Gold: Seed for Garbhadruti):
Alternatively, the essence of orpiment or realgar, when processed within gold, [serves as the seed].
Then, the mercury (rasendra) digests a hundredfold in the crucible and melts within the womb.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
In the first part [of the verse], he states another injunction beginning with "athavā" (or else).*

The essence of *tālaka* (mica), which is the core of *haritāla*, when processed a hundredfold—that is, multiplied a hundred times—in gold (*kanaka*), [is done] by means of fire, either in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) or in an open crucible (*prakāśamūṣā*); this is the implied meaning. The clarification is that the extraction of the essence of *tālaka* into gold must be performed; and that essence, whether alone or together with *manaḥśilā* (realgar), should be extracted into that gold.
Then, within the womb of the mercury-essence, the king of mercuries (rasendra) flows; by means of the prescribed method, it is quickly digested.
Mercury, cinnabar, mica, orpiment, vimala, mercury-amrita, tin, iron, and parpaṭī; START GRHT 5.19–21 (lead, tin: combined *māraṇa*).
Snuhi and arka milk ground together with kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar, and lead [is used for application].
Tin, when repeatedly subjected to heating in a closed crucible (puṭa) together with mica, realgar, conch-shell, and mercury,
and mixed with the alkali of tamarind, attains the state of being lifeless (nirjīvatā).
Encased by this procedure, even lead that has reached the state of being devoid of essence dies;
and that [lead], having its life-force departed, may be employed in all ritual operations.
Now he states another method, beginning with "rasa" and so forth.
Regarding "mercury, cinnabar, mica, and pyrite": mercury (*rasa*) is *pārada*; cinnabar (*darada*) is *hiṅgula*; mica (*abhraka*) is well-known; pyrite (*tāpya*) is gold-pyrite (*svarṇamākṣika*);

*vimalā* is copper-pyrite (*rukmamākṣika*); "dead copper" (*mṛtaṃ yacchulbaṃ*) is copper (*tāmra*); and "iron" (*loha*) refers to *muṇḍa* and other varieties. From these—mercury and the others—a *parpaṭikā* (tablet) should be prepared in the same manner as the *rasaparpaṭī*.

That lead (nāga) combined with it [the aforementioned substance], and further combined with kaṅkuṣṭha and śilā—where *kaṅkuṣṭha* is a stone-type mineral of greenish-yellow color that destroys poison, and *śilā* is *manohvā*—that lead (*nāga*) which is a type of tin (*sīsaka*), should be ground with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*.
*Snuhī* is *sehuṇḍa*, and *arka* is the well-known tree; ground with the milks of these two, the lead becomes like dust and is thereby "dead" (*mṛta*).
The phrase "by means of the cock-bag method" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. This seed, once perfected, enters the womb due to its prior connection.
Now, he states the procedure for the seed-syllable of Vaṅga, beginning with "abhraka" and so forth.

Lead that is mixed with the alkali of *ciñcā* (tamarind) and lead joined with the alkali of *amlikā* (sour gruel), along with mica (*abhraka*), yellow orpiment (*tālaka*), conch-shell (*śaṅkha*), and mercury (*rasa*)—these four being well-known; one should repeatedly subject it to *puṭa*-firing until it becomes "non-reverting" (*niruttha*). Thus, one should perform the firing again and again, time after time.

By means of a portion of this medicinal substance, through the process of *puṭana* (roasting in a closed crucible), tin (*vaṅga*) becomes lifeless and reaches its dissolution (*pañcatva*). This seed-substance (*bīja*) is also perfected for the purpose of causing the melting of the core (*garbhadrāvaṇa*) and for the process of assimilation (*jāraṇa*), because of its prior connection with lead (*nāga*) and tin; thus he says "by the method," etc., stating that this medicine is the cause for both lead and tin.
By this method, according to the prescribed procedure, lead (nāga) or tin (sīsaka), when subjected to *puṭa* (encapsulation), dies—that is, it becomes dead.

By this very same procedure, tin (*vaṅga*) that has attained a state of dissolution (*nirutthatā*) or reached bodilessness (*aśarīratā*) is employed by experts in mercury (*rasajña*) in all operations, such as *cāraṇa*, *jāraṇa*, and *bhakṣaṇa*. This is the remainder [of the meaning].

The killing (*māraṇa*) of lead (*nāga*) and mercury (*vaṅga*) is said to be of only one kind; therefore, they are mutually suitable for qualities such as consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*), but not for processes such as digestion (*jāraṇa*).
START GRHT 5.22 (Gold:: Seed for *garbhadruti*):
Dead lead, dead tin, dead excellent copper, and likewise dead iron;
Each one [of these] flows when placed within the womb of excellent gold that has been processed a hundred times.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He explains the method for the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of lead, tin, copper, and iron, beginning with the words "dead lead" (*mṛtanāga*), etc.*

"Dead lead" refers to lead (*nāga*) that has become dead, i.e., devoid of life; likewise, by this same procedure, "dead tin" (*vaṅga*), as well as "dead excellent copper" (*varaśulba*), i.e., copper that has become dead, and likewise "dead steel" (*tīkṣṇa*)— the phrase "by the group of enemies" being understood as the remainder— among these, each one individually, whether lead, tin, copper, or steel, [is to be processed] separately in excellent gold.
One should prepare gold of perfect color by processing it a hundred times; once perfected, it dissolves within the interior of mercury, and by the force of the word "and," it also ages [mercury].
START GRHT 5.23 (Gold:: Mahābīja):
I shall describe the supreme yoga for the liquefaction of gold within a *samagarbha* [crucible].
The powder of *bhrāmaka* and *sasyaka*, processed a hundred times with *mahābīja*, [is effective].
[Commentary, *Mugdhāvabodhinī*:
Demonstrating the power of *mahābīja*, he says "having an equal embryo," and so forth.]

In this treatise, the sense is that those *bījas* which have been taught according to the prescribed method should be employed in a general manner; however, this "Lord of Vārttikas" (*vārttikendra*) yoga is specifically for the purpose of *garbhadruti*. The term *vārttika* refers to those who are skilled in worldly news (*vārtā*), meaning those devoid of instruction in the scriptures; here, the suffix *ik* is used in the sense of "those who are so. Among such *vārttikas*, this is the preeminent yoga, and likewise by this very [method].
The meaning is that in this manner, this [position] is accepted both by those who follow the instructions of the Teacher and by those who are devoid of the instructions of the Teacher.
START GRHT 5.24–26 (Garbhadruti):
Alternatively, [one may use] the fumes of sulfur, the fumes of orpiment, or the juice of realgar and rasaka.
Having placed a very long crucible upside down over half of a shallow bowl, [one should proceed].
The plastering should be applied upwards and made very firm;
having applied it to the back of the crucible, one should then set the Lord of the Daityas on fire.
Having added [the powder] little by little, one should blow it into the crucible fire after it has been smeared with clay;
for the seed melts within the womb, yet it dies if the heating is excessive.
Regarding the method for liquefying the seed within the belly of mercury, he says "Alternatively," and so forth.
The word "or" (*athavā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).

Above the bottom part of the *dīrghatamā* crucible, a paste (*piṣṭī*) made from mercury and the seed-substance (*bīja*) should be applied; furthermore, this paste must be joined so that it becomes very firm.

Having done what? Having placed a *dīrghatamā* [crucible]—meaning one whose mouth is directed toward the lower part—in the half of a clay vessel, that is, in one portion of a broken earthenware pot. Thus it is said.
Having given that [paste].
Furthermore, having done what? Having given the smoke of *gandhaka* (sulphur), or having given the smoke of *tālaka* (orpiment) very little by little, that is, in small amounts;
or having given the smoke of *śilāhvā-rasaka*, where *śilāhvā* is realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and *rasaka* is *kharpara* (alum)—the compound being a *bhāva-samāsa*—having given its smoke.
Again, one should turn that crucible upside down, coat its opening with clay, enclose it in clay, and heat it in a fire of dried cow-dung; "in a fire of dried cow-dung" is the meaning.
Having thus placed the skull-cup face downwards, one should subsequently burn the lord of the Daityas named Bala—by context, this refers to sulphur—following that procedure.
When this has been done, whatever seed is combined with the lord of mercury (rasendra) dissolves within the interior of that lord of mercury inside its womb.
Furthermore, the meaning is that the mercury (rasendra), even when accompanied by its seed (bīja), dies when excessive heating occurs.
This is a *viśeṣaka* because it consists of a connection of three verses.
START GRht 5.27 (viḍa:: production):
Sulphur, talaka, śaila, sauvīraka, rasaka, gairika, and darada;
Alkali, sour substances, salt, and *viḍa* [salt], along with equal parts of *mākṣika*, *vaikrānta*, and *vimala*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Now, for the purpose of digesting gold (*suvarṇajāraṇa*), he describes the *biḍa* [salt] starting with "gandhaka" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM 5.27:1): Now, for the purpose of digesting gold, he states the *biḍa* [salt] beginning with "gandhaka," etc.*

"Gandhakatālakaśailāḥ" refers to sulphur (gandhaka), which is well known; yellow orpiment (tālaka); and "śaila," meaning bitumen (śilājatu). This is a dvandva compound, and thus they are so described; these should be made in equal parts.

Furthermore, "sauvīraka," white antimony (śuklāñjana), "rasaka" (kalium bichromate), "kharparika" (copper pyrite), "gairika" (mineral red ochre), "darada" (mercuric oxide, cinnabar), and "hiṅgula"—here it is a singular collective compound—and all that has been so described should be made in equal parts.

Furthermore, the alkaline, acidic, and saline substances: the alkalines such as *yavakṣāra* and others; the acid such as *jambīra* and others; and the salts such as *saindhava* and others—these also [should be taken] in equal proportions.

"With what? Together with equal parts of *mākṣika*, *vaikrānta*, and *vimala*. *Mākṣika* is gold pyrite (*svarṇamākṣika*); *vaikrānta* is the powder produced from diamond-earth; *vimala* is golden pyrite. These are in equal parts. By these, *biḍa* is called; the meaning is that *biḍa* should be prepared by thoroughly grinding all [the ingredients] in equal parts."
Having prepared a gold paste, rubbed and well-wrapped with this very [substance], one should proceed as follows.
When rubbed in a mortar heated by the *tripuṭa* [method], it likewise melts within the womb.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Just as a seed melts within the womb through the application of *biḍa* [salt-paste] and so forth, he says "having done thus" (*kṛtvā*) and so on.*

The aforementioned paste (piṣṭī) should be rubbed and ground in a heated mortar made of iron—due to its connection with heat—using the previously mentioned *biḍa* formulation consisting of *karīṣa* fire; it should then be wrapped with that very same [substance].
Having done what? Having made a gold-powder—or a golden-powder, or even the powder of another mineral—that is a beautiful-colored powder.
Having been ground in a mortar, it remains in that very manner and not otherwise, dissolving within the womb—the interior of the mercury—and staying there in the form of water.
START GRHT 5.29 (viḍa:: for garbhadruti):
Then, there is the ash of vaikrāntaka, processed one hundred times in blood, which is beneficial for the eyes.
It swallows the pure [substance] refined a hundred times, and melts together with it within the crucible.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now, he describes the internal liquefaction (*garbhaduti*) of *vaikrānta*, beginning with the words "rakta" and so forth.*

One should prepare the ash of vaikrānta, the dust produced from diamond-earth, and the ash arising therefrom, processed a hundred times—that is, purified a hundred times—within the red [substances] of the red group.
Of what specific quality? "Beneficial to the eyes" (*netrahita*); by the term *netrahita*, the nature of a jewel is indicated, for jewels are beneficial to the eyes.
Pure *mākṣika* silver is white in color; that *mākṣika* which has been processed a hundred times in the red group [of minerals] should be used.

When both of those—vaikrānta and vimala—are processed through one hundred red [transmutations], they swallow and devour the mercury equally, setting aside the formal procedure for the "swallowing" (grāsa); the meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that what has been swallowed thus dissolves within the womb of the mercury and undergoes digestion.
Begin at 5:30 PM (Viḍa:
for *garbhadruti*;
always with the *śatanirvāhaṇa*).
Whatever viḍ-yogas there may be, as well as alkalis, acids, salts, and the group of fiery substances—
all these, when processed through a hundred [fusions], are said to effect the liquefaction of the embryo (garbhadruti).
Showing the predominance of the red class (*raktagaṇa*), he says "He who," and so forth.

Whatever *viḍa*-yogas have been described here and in other texts, as well as the alkaline, sour, and salty substances— where "alkaline" refers to *yavakṣāra* and the like, and those derived from trees and herbs; "sour" refers to *jambīra* and the like, as well as those produced from sour trees and vegetables— and furthermore, whatever *dīpta*-groups have been mentioned, namely the *yogas* declared to be stimulating— all of these [should be used].

The groups of salts, alkalis, acids, and pungent substances, when processed a hundred times, effect internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*); that is to say, they cause metals, gems, jewels, and so forth to become liquefied into a liquid state within the interior of the mercury (*rasodara*).
START GRhT 5.31–32 (The quantity of *nirvāhaṇa* = the morsel that is assimilated)
In a formation of one hundred, it is equal; in a formation of seventy-five, it is three-quarters;
in a formation of fifty, it is half; and in a formation of twenty-five, it is one-quarter.

One-eighth [of the width] is for the half-[height]; one-sixteenth is for the half-[width] of the *nirvyūha*; and one-thirty-second is for the half-[width] of that; one-sixty-fourth is for the half-[width] of the half-*nirvyūha*. (GRht 5.32) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [This verse describes the proportional dimensions of the various architectural elements. The half-height of the wall (*bhitti*) is one-eighth of its width. The half-width of the *nirvyūha* (a projecting porch or balcony) is one-sixteenth of the wall's width. The half-width of the *nirvyūha* itself is one-thirty-second of the wall's width. And the half-width of the half-*nirvyūha* is one-sixty-fourth of the wall's width. Thus, the measurement of the half-*nirvyūha* is one-sixty-fourth part of the total width of the wall. This concludes the description of the proportions of the *nirvyūha*. (5.32)
Regarding the performance of one hundred [recitations] and so forth, he states the rule for the equal number and so on, beginning with "one hundred," etc. (GRhtCM 5.31–32).

"Śatanirvyūḍha" means that which has been processed a hundred times; the remainder [of the sentence] is "in the red group [of minerals]. "Sama" means equally; the remainder [of the sentence] is "the mercury swallows. GRhtCM_5.31-32:2.
Furthermore, when [the number] is arranged as seventy-five, it swallows the whole minus one-quarter—that is, excluding the fourth part.
Furthermore, when fifty have been subtracted, half of that is the "half-sum" (ardhārdha).
Furthermore, when there are twenty-five [units], a quarter is one-fourth part.
The specific meaning is that when a deficiency or a surplus has been carried through [the calculation], the deficient or surplus portion is to be understood [as the result]. // GRhtCM_5.31-32:6 //
He states the sequence for the abbreviated performance, beginning with "one-eighth part" and so forth.

Furthermore, when half of that—twelve and a half [units]—has been extracted, it swallows an eighth part; when half of that—six [units]—has been extracted through six cycles, it swallows a sixteenth part; again, when half of that—three [units]—has been extracted through three cycles, it swallows a thirty-second part; and when half of that has been extracted through one or two cycles, the meaning is that the mercury swallows a sixty-fourth part.
Thus has been described the *garbhadruti* [alchemical extraction from the womb] by means of the application of distillation and the group of acidic substances (*amlavarga*).
Having recognized [the substance] by means of the procedure of sweating, it is rubbed upon the surface of a heated mortar.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Regarding the statement beginning with "iti" and so forth, he describes what is to be done when the internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) has occurred.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_5.33:1): [As above]*

Having understood the *garbhadruti* (internal liquefaction) as described by the aforementioned method, one should grind it when it has been heated to a state of high temperature on the surface of a red-hot iron pan using a fire of dried cow-dung (*karīṣāgni*).

By what method of processing (*abhiṣavayoga*)? "Processing" (*abhiṣava*) means crushing; by that method. Not only by this [method], but also by the group of sour substances such as the *jambīra* and so forth; nor only by this, but also by the procedure of sweating (*svedanavidhi*). Since the procedure of sweating has already been described as a refinement (*saṃskāra*), it is not mentioned here;
the remainder [of the sense] is that it is for the purpose of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
START GRHT 5.34 (The performance of *saṃskāra* according to the strength and weakness of the employed *bīja*s, etc.):
Having understood the strength and weakness of the *bīja*s, and having performed the process of crushing (*mardana*) with the king of juices (*rasarāja*).
And the procedure for sweating, as well as the *puṭa* or *yantra* [methods], once the processing of the mercury has been performed.

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* Showing the preliminary equipment for the processes of rubbing (*mardana*) and sweating (*svedana*), he says "having known," etc. (*jñātvetyādi*). *Commentary (GRhtCM 5.34:1):* [Same as above].

Having understood the application of the crushing process regarding the strength and weakness of the seeds— that is, having known that very crushing process performed according to the greater or lesser strength and weakness of the seeds produced through the combination of the primary and secondary minerals— one should perform the procedure for sweating (*sveda*) upon the king of mercury (*rasarāja*),
or perform the *puṭa* [roasting], or perform the application of fire (*vahniyoga*), or perform the mechanical operation (*yantra*) on the prepared mercury; "vihita" means performed.
The meaning is that the "instrument for the embryo" (*garbhayantra*) and so forth are so called because they possess the function of rasa in the form of refinement (*saṃskāra*).
Just as one should not neglect the excellent seed that is being observed by the Sūta,
so too should the task prescribed by the feet of the Guru be performed according to the rule.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Because the process of working with mercury (*sūtaka*) is difficult to understand, he speaks the verse beginning with "mercury" (*sūta*) while praising the feet of the Guru. (GRhtCM 5.35:1)

Just as mercury recognizes— that is, knows— the excellent ore as being fit for its work (this is the ellipsis), and just as the seed does not remain indifferent but perfectly unites [with the soil], in that very same manner, one should perform the rite pointed out by the feet of the Guru— the venerable, purificatory ritual shown by the best of teachers— according to the rule, namely, according to the procedure taught by the teacher.
The characteristics of the Guru:
One who is an expert in all the specialized treatises and skilled in the work of alchemy—
one endowed with such characteristics shall be the teacher of the science of mercury (rasavidyā).
Thus. // GRhtCM_5.35:3 //
Thus ends the section on the liquefaction and digestion [of mercury] within the womb.
START GRht 5.36 (External Alchemy):
Indeed, the stainless external alchemical elixir manifests only for certain perfected beings (*siddhas*).
Having correctly understood from them the reckonings (*kalanā*) as well as the liquefactions (*druti*), [one should act accordingly].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Praising the external liquefaction, he says "the external liquefaction," and so forth.*
Meltedness (druti) is said to be twofold: internal meltedness (garbhadruti) and external meltedness (bāhyadruti).
The internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) has been explained previously; now the external liquefaction (*bāhyadruti*) is being described.
Of what nature is it? It is exceedingly pure, that is, more stainless than the stainless.

Furthermore, this [knowledge] manifests only to certain perfected ones (*siddha*) who have reached the further shore of the science of alchemy (*rasavidyā*), such as Nityanātha and others; it is they who know it.
Because it is difficult to attain, external flow is rare in this world.
Having correctly understood from them that very method of instruction for accomplishment, the *drutis* are the external *drutis*.
START GRHT 5.37-38 (Digestion of Lead):
Lead, the king of mercury, and likewise the excellent seed— these three are processed.
Combined with sulphur, realgar, and orpiment, it becomes a lamp-wick that is free from snakes.
Having tied a lamp made of *śikhī* (a wick) inside a very firm cloth bag,
and having submerged it in oil, it quickly becomes free of snakes.
Now, he describes the digestion of the best snake with the words beginning "the best snake" (varanāgam).

The excellent species of *varanāga* (lead), *sīsaka* (tin) fit for the process of *jāraṇā*, and *rasarāja* (mercury)—that is, mercury purified by the aforementioned refinements; and the best of seeds, the seed of gold (*hemabīja*): these three, having been processed, should be combined. Furthermore, they should be joined with sulfur, realgar, and yellow arsenic—where "sulfur" (*gandhaka*) is well-known, "realgar" (*śilā*) is *manaḥśilā*, and "yellow arsenic" (*āla*) is *haritāla*—and together with these pairs, they should be prepared.
This entire group of six, through the application of a lamp-wick—that is, by means of a lit lamp-wick—becomes "nirnāga," meaning devoid of *nāga*;
the sense is that it consumes (*jarati*) the *nāga*.
He states the procedure so that it may be without a tail, beginning with the words "having bound," and so forth.

That aforementioned group of six [mantras] should be tied in a small packet within a very firm, new cloth—here the locative case indicates the locus of contact—and then submerged in oil derived from sesame seeds. Beneath that, a lamp with a flame (*śikhīkṛta*) should be maintained; "with a flame" (*śikhīkṛta*) means it has been made possessed of a flame (*śikhā*), that is, it possesses a flame.
By this method, it will quickly and swiftly become free of snakes.
Having prepared a long and very firm crucible here, [the lead] is to be blown [with a bellows] into a pit of ashes.
Having first cast in the powder of mica and alum, one should afterwards add mercury, and then again the powder of mica.

Having thus established [the crucible] with ash, it should be heated until it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body; then, having drawn out the mercury therein and ascertained that the lead (nāga) has been entirely well-digested—*GRht 5.40*. *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [The commentary explains: "Having established" means having placed [the crucible] upon the ash. "Heated" means blown with a bellows. "Until it has cooled to the temperature of one's own body" means until it has reached a state of coolness equal to the body's heat. Then, having drawn out the mercury from there and known that the lead has been completely and properly consumed, [one proceeds].
He states the procedure for making [the snake] devoid of its hood in the passage beginning with "having performed," and so forth.

Furthermore, having fashioned a crucible that is long, shaped like a cow’s teat, very firm, and free of flaws like a diamond, one should place powdered *śilā* and *āla*— that is, powdered *manohvā* (realgar) and *haritāla* (orpiment)— into that crucible; thereafter, having added the previously mentioned *sūta* (mercury), and immediately after that, having added more *śilā* powder, one should place that very crucible, now containing the mercury, into a pit of ashes.

One should place [the substance] to be smelted in a pit filled with ashes; then, having covered it again with ashes, one should wait until it has become cool to the touch, that is, until it has cooled down by itself.

In that case, having ascertained that all the mercury (*nāga*) has been well-digested—that is, entirely consumed and reached a state of digestion—within that crucible, one should extract and remove the mercury; this is the procedure for making it free of *nāga*.
[This is] the seed [mantra] for mercury digested by *nāga* (GRht 5.41).
Having recognized that the nāga has been severed, one should again apply it so that it becomes threefold;

thereafter, having purified it, one should subsequently join the excellent seed-syllable (bīja). *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [The commentary explains that once the nāga is known to be broken, it must be restored to its original state and then multiplied by three before being purified and joined with the supreme seed-mantra.]
He states what is to be done immediately after the Nirnāga [yoga] in the verse beginning with "Having known," and so forth.
Having ascertained that the lead has become brittle, one should again burn the lead with mercury according to the previously stated procedure; this is the remainder [of the instruction].
One should act in such a way that the serpent [coil] becomes tripled.

Afterwards, having purified the *sūta* (mercury) and rendered the mercury free of lead (*nirnāga*), one should then add the excellent seed (*bījavara*) previously mentioned, following the digestion of the lead (*nāgajāraṇa*).
Alternatively, having processed silver or tin with mercury until it is free of tin; START GRht 5.42 (mercury:: jāraṇa of tin).
Likewise, [it becomes] free of joints through the application of lacquer (*tālaka*), and by means of mechanical contrivances (*yantra*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now he explains the application of mercury (*tārayoga*) with the words "Alternatively," and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_5.42:1): [The commentary on the verse follows]*
Alternatively, "athavā" indicates another method.

*Tāra* (silver), *vaṅga* (tin), and *sūta* (mercury)— where *tāra* is silver, *vaṅga* is *khuraka* tin, and *sūta* is processed mercury— having circulated these three together and performed their union, one should eliminate the tin (*vaṅga*). Likewise, by that same procedure, through the application of *tāla* (mica) and by means of the *yantra* (apparatus) and the long crucible (*dīrghamūṣā*), one should render it free from tin (*nirvaṅga*), devoid of tin.
Alternatively, [the mercury] bound in a cloth, together with mica and well-wrapped in black gram (*māṣa*), [should be processed].
The *vaṭaka* cooked in oil certainly becomes free of its husk.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states another method with the words "Alternatively," and so forth.

Alternatively, one should cook tin (tāra) in oil produced from sesame seeds until it takes the form of a ball (vaṭaka); indeed, one must certainly cook that ball in such a way that, through the application of fire, it becomes free of tin (nirvaṅga). This is the remainder [of the instruction].
Having performed the stabilization of the paste (*piṣṭīstambha*) by means of the excellent seed (*bījavara*), it should then be processed (*sārita*).
Alternatively, having well-colored the seed with bound mercury, [one should proceed]. GRht 5.44.
Mercury deposited with sulphur, whether placed within or not placed within a chain,
certainly effects internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) when its essence has been joined and extracted.
Having made the seed within the womb of mercury by means of the excellent ash of *sūtaka*, the *piṣṭī* is rubbed according to the rule;

indeed, through the application of pressing (*abhiṣava*), it dissolves within the womb. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* By means of the excellent ash of *sūtaka* (the "birth-fluid" or *rasabandha*), one should prepare the seed (*bīja*) within the womb of mercury (*rasendra*). When the *piṣṭī* (the ground paste) is rubbed according to the prescribed method, it dissolves within the womb due to the application of pressing.
He states another procedure, beginning with the words "piṣṭi" and so forth.

When that [mercury] has been infused—that is, mixed—with the excellent seed, namely the aforementioned golden seed (*kanakabīja*), it forms a solidified paste (*piṣṭīstambha*) or a fixed bolus (*khoṭastambha*).

Thereafter, or subsequently, he shows another method: furthermore, one should combine the seed—the golden seed—which has been well-colored, meaning its hue has been increased by an excellent procedure, with mercury that is bound, that is, mercury fixed as a bolus (*khoṭabaddharasa*).
It has been stated that there are two [types of practitioners] for whom yoga alone must be practiced.
Furthermore, he says "gandhaka" and so forth.

"Placed in sulphur" means the mercury has been deposited—that is, placed—within sulphur; the meaning is that one should place the sulphur above and below so as to make the mercury situated in the middle.

Furthermore, when such a flux (sūta) is placed within a chain in the yoga of "chain-making" (*śṛṅkhalīkaraṇa*), that which is placed is as if not placed; it is unrefined (*ajārita*) and must be processed through the conjunction of the placed and the unplaced. This is certainly a "chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*).
In a flux where the mercury has first been joined and subsequently carried out—that is, "extracted" (*nirvyūḍha*)—therein occurs "embryo-dissolution" (*garbhadruti*).
Seeds dissolve within the belly of mercury.
He describes the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) by means of the *piṣṭī* method, beginning with the words "sūtaka" and so forth.
Furthermore, having placed the seed within that womb which is formed by the mercury (rasendra) inside the mercury-vessel, one should prepare the paste (piṣṭī) according to the prescribed method;
that paste must be rubbed and kneaded because of the application of pressing and the application of friction. With what?
Together with the excellent ash of mercury (sūtaka). By means of that excellent ash of mercury, that paste dissolves in the womb; and by the word "ca" (and), it is digested.
Take mica-leaf (*patrābhraka*) and its essence (*satva*), or *kāṅkṣī*, or magnetite (*kānta*) and pyrite (*mākṣika*), which have been subjected to *puṭa* firing.
With *nirguṇḍī*, house-mallow (*gṛhakanyā*), *cāṅgerī*, and the leaves of the *palāśa* tree.
Having folded it that many times until it takes on the luster of vermilion,
one should cook that remaining portion of salt with its foot-measure [of liquid] in a pot over a fire until it is thoroughly hardened.
One should cause each excellent seed, arranged in groups of a hundred, to be digested by the lord of mercury;
it quickly dissolves within the womb when rubbed with a finger through the application of pressing.
(GRht 5.49) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
He states the procedure for the excellent seed (*bījavaravidhāna*) beginning with "patrābhraka" and so forth.

"Patrābhrakam" refers to either the leaves of mica (*abhraka*) or the essence (*sattva*) of mica. Furthermore, "kāñcī," "saurāṣṭrī," "kānta," and "mākṣika" are mentioned; "kānta" means magnetite, and "mākṣika" refers to gold pyrite (*svarṇamākṣika*). These form a copulative compound (*dvandva*) in the singular. Moreover, this [preparation] is enclosed by *nirguṇḍī*, *gṛhakanyā*, *cāṅgerī*, *palāśa*, and *śāka*. *Nirguṇḍī* is the *sephālikā*; *gṛhakanyā* is the *kumārī*; *cāṅgerī* is an acid vegetable; *palāśa* is the *brahmavṛkṣa*.

*Śāka* is a specific type of tree; this is a *dvandva* compound. Having extracted the juice of these, one should mix it with the previously mentioned medicinal herbs during the heat of the sun—this is the implied meaning.
Then, having encapsulated that medicine, one should again give a quarter-part— that is, a fourth part—

of rock salt (*saindhava*) to that encapsulated medicine and cook it by means of *haṇḍikā-pāka* (cooking in a clay vessel); one should continue cooking it over the fire until it attains the color of vermilion, possessing a hue identical to that of *sindūra*.
How should one cook it so that it becomes very firm? Each [portion] should be arranged in a hundred-fold array.

From below each of the aforementioned secondary minerals (uparasa) that have been made vermilion-colored, a superior seed (bījavara) is produced when processed one hundred times individually; this occurs in gold—this is the remainder of the sense. That seed dissolves within the womb of mercury (rasendra), and by the word "ca" (and), it is digested quickly and rapidly.
"How? By that specific method of pressing and rubbing which is performed with the ring finger. This is the qualification.
START GRht 5.50 (Gold:: Seed with Lead):
Even when the process has been reversed, one should again reverse it and add lead into the bright, excellent gold.
Indeed, that is designated as "serpent-seed" (*ahibīja*), which consists of a mixture of three parts of lead (*nāga*) with excellent, bright gold that has been properly melted and stirred.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He describes the preparation of the seed using lead: when excellent, bright gold—the best of metals—is being thoroughly melted and stirred, one adds pure lead.*

Having caused it to revolve and having caused it to flow away, what should be done? Having added an equal portion of gold, one should again perform the pouring of threefold *śilā* over the lead—that is, one should effect the quenching with *śilā* that is triple the amount.
Śilā is realgar (manaḥśilā).
Thus it is established that the seed-syllable *ahi* is designated as the "nāga-yoga" seed-syllable by those who know the science of mercury; this is the remainder [of the statement].
START GRht 5.51 (Gold and silver: [alloyed with] tin as the seed).
According to that procedure, tin should be cast into excellent gold using a coating of palmyra;
or, having been refined in silver, it becomes an excellent seed through the combination with *truṭita*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):*
Now, he states the seed-mantra through the application of tin and so forth, beginning with the words "tin" (vaṅga).

Furthermore, by that aforementioned method and procedure, one should cast tin into the excellent gold previously described; having been refined by the addition of *tāla* (orpiment), it becomes excellent seed (*sadbījavara*). Or, when the silver is being melted, one should cast tin into it, and once it has been refined and poured out, it likewise becomes excellent seed.
Why? Because from the breaking of the conjunction, it becomes broken; likewise, the excellent seed—that is, the seed of tin—melts and digests as before.
START GRht 5.52 (rasāṅkuśa):
That thunderbolt-cage with a mane of nectar, which issued forth from the serpent, has appeared once again.
It is crooked due to its serpent-like golden coils and is renowned by the name Rasāṅkuśa (the "Taste-Goad").
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He speaks in praise of the seed known as Suvarṇa with the words "yaḥ" and so forth.*

That which has emerged from *bhujaṅga* (lead) and *sīsaka* (tin), having been reduced to exhaustion by the application of *bhujaṅgaśilā*, and which has become distinct, is called *rasakesarīvajrapañjara*.

*Rasa* itself is the *kesarī* (lion); for its sake, there is a *vajrapañjara*—a cage fashioned with *vajra* (diamond/iron) because of its extreme firmness, meaning it is capable of protecting the lion. // GRhtCM_5.52:2 //

Furthermore, it is stated specifically that this is not merely the Vajrapañjara, but rather the Rasāṅkuśa; "rasa" refers to the elephant-form [of the deity], and its "aṅkuśa" (goad) is capable of bringing him under control.
The word *nāma* is used in the sense of "possibility" (*saṃbhāvanā*).
"Renowned" means well-proclaimed.
Why is it that from the crooked act of stealing some object one becomes crooked—that is, devious—and possesses a wicked nature? By means of this gold, the seizing of the serpent was accomplished.

From what kind of curved object? From that which possesses the qualities (*guṇa*) of both *phaṇin*—meaning a serpent (*bhujaṅga*)—and *hema*—meaning gold. Such a curved thing is appropriate; for even a goad (*aṅkuśa*) is curved.
Here, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *bhrāntimān* (the presence of error), because an error arises from seeing a seed of gold as a cage of diamonds, an elephant, and a goad.
