In this manner, having processed the excellent seed and the king of mercury with acid according to the prescribed method,
they should be subjected to sweating until a smooth paste is formed.
By that oil and according to that procedure, the entire mass should be steamed;
or else, the seed, finely ground on a stone, should become a paste.
The cooking should be performed according to the method for *vaṭaka* cakes using oil;
by adding it to the *krāmaṇa* paste along with black gram (*māṣa*), the paste will attain a state of great firmness.
It should be well-cooked over a mild fire until it becomes a solid mass;
then, having extracted the mercury from the mass, the remainder should likewise be cooked again.
Alternatively, when the medicinal mass has been heated in a pan over a brazier according to the prescribed method,
it should be cast back into the mass within the crucible until liquefaction occurs.
Thus, indeed, the excellent seed quickly digests within the womb when in the presence of the king of fluids (rasarāja); yet,
devoid of internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*), it digests within the womb through the application of fluxing agents (*biḍayoga*).
He states the grinding of this seed with the words beginning "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth.

In this manner, by such a method—that is, by means of the instruction implied by the sense—one should perform the procedure called *sveda* (perspiration), whereby the excellent seed [of mercury] is ripened; likewise, the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*), mercury (*pārada*), which has been previously prepared, should be subjected to sweating with an acid such as *jambīra* and the like. This is the procedure known as *sveda*.

In this regard, what is the limit for that which must be performed? It is until the *piṣṭī*—the essence of the mercury and the seed (*rasabīja*)—becomes smooth, clear, and a single unified body; this is the remainder [of the sense].
He states another method with the words beginning "with oil" (tailena), etc.
By that previously mentioned method and procedure for killing, once it has been steamed—that is, heated—with sesame oil, it becomes a powder; "in the fire" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The word "or else" indicates another method.

By means of a stone—that is, a stone-made slab—the seed called *nāga* is rubbed; that which has been rubbed or ground, namely the *nāga* seed, is completely reduced to a powder by the mercury (the remainder of the sentence).
Just as a medicinal pill (*vaṭaka*) is to be cooked, he describes the cooking process and so forth.

The cooking should be performed according to the method for *vaṭaka* (balls), specifically the method for *māṣavaṭaka*, using an application of oil; the meaning is that the cooking on the fire must be carried out in this manner.

Having done what? Having cast it into the *krāmaṇa* ball and placed it in the middle of a *biḍa* ball, it will again attain the state of a firm ball by means of *māṣa* beans, which are a specific type of food; the explicit meaning is that the *krāmaṇa* ball, when wrapped in *māṣa* powder, becomes solid.
He states the procedure for that [practice] beginning with "mṛdu" and so forth.
The *krāmaṇapiṇḍa* produced from powdered black gram (*māṣa*) should be thoroughly cooked until it is completely burnt.

By what means? It is well-cooked by a mild fire, a gentle flame. From that mass, having extracted and taken the remainder—the residue—which is pure mercury, one should cook that [mercury] in another mass in the same manner as before.
Furthermore, he says "Alternatively," and so forth.
The word "or" (*athavā*) indicates an alternative method.

Furthermore, the pastes should again be placed upon a medicinal bolus that has been heated by swinging [in a crucible], brought to a state of heat, and cast into the bolus of the *krāmaṇa* (penetrating) medicines; having positioned them in the middle, over what [substance]—over an earthen vessel (*kharpara*)—and by what method—as previously stated—with oil or with acid?

The essential meaning is that for as long as the *piṣṭī* dissolves within the liquid of the womb, for that long it should be cast into the interior of the *biḍa* and into the interior of the mass (*piṇḍa*).
Furthermore, he says "evam" and so forth.

In this manner, by such a process, [the seed] reaches a state of complete digestion within the interior of the mercury (rasodara) while in the womb; furthermore, being devoid of the womb-fluid (garbhadruti) and free from liquid, the excellent seed is digested by *biḍa*—meaning that *biḍa* is capable of digesting and killing the liquefied seed.
The process of *jāraṇā* (digestion) consists of the quantity of the molten mass through the application of the *biḍa* (flux) machine and other such devices;
its varieties are said to be in the tens of millions.
The phrase "varieties" refers to the types of machines (*yantra*).
As for the varieties of digestion (*jāraṇa*): "The feeding of the morsel (*grāsa*), the liquefaction of the embryo (*garbhadrāvaṇa*), and likewise digestion (*jāraṇa*)—
thus has the threefold digestion been described by the excellent commentators."
Having caused [the mercury] to swallow the morsel (*grāsa*) according to the method of *jāraṇa*, one should then perform the internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) upon birch bark.
When a plaster has been applied with urine that is salty, alkaline, sour, and fragrant with sudhā.
One should digest the morsel by means of the heat from a swing, bound externally with a firm cloth,
in a jar half-filled with *sauvīra* or else with alkaline urine.
In this sequence, one should digest the morsel (*grāsa*) every three days.
Regarding the digestion of the *garbhadruti*, he says "the morsel," and so forth.

Having administered the morsels or mouthfuls in the previously mentioned manner according to their respective numbers, and having again performed the "melting within the womb" (*garbhadruti*), one should thereafter place that mercury, thus melted within the womb, upon a birch leaf—that is, within a pouch made from the bark of the birch tree. This is the meaning.
On what kind of birch bark? On that which has been smeared with a paste made from salt, alkali, acid, lime, and fragrant urine.

"Salts" refers to rock salt (*saindhava*) and others; "alkalis" refers to *svarjikā* and others; "acid" refers to the citron (*jambīra*) and others; "lime" is powdered oyster shell; and "fragrant" refers to a cow, whose urine [is used].
It is on that [bark] upon which a smear has been made by means of this combination.
The meaning is that the mercury (sūta), joined with digestive juices (udaradruti), should be kept [in the crucible].
He states the procedure for digestion (*jāraṇa*) with the verse beginning "dṛḍha" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "bound externally with firm cloth": having performed the sweating by means of the previously mentioned swinging-sweat (*dolāsveda*), which is the method of the swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*), using a cloth that is firm, new, and thick, bound and secured on the outside on all sides, one should digest the morsel— the bolus melted within the mercury.

In what jar? In which vessel? In one that is half-filled with *sauvīra*—that is, with *kāñjika* (sour gruel) produced by the process of fermentation (*svedana*). It is half-filled by means of this *sauvīra*.
The word "or" (*athavā*) indicates an alternative injunction (*vidhyantara*).

Together with alkaline urine and alkalis such as *svarjikā* and others—[the remaining] urines being those of the cow, goat, sheep, and woman—the meaning is that one should cause [the mercury] to digest within a jar half-filled with these.
Now, he states the duration for the digestion of mercury, beginning with the words "by this" (*amunā*) and so forth.

"In this sequence" means by the method already described; when a "bite" (grāsa) has occurred every three days—that is, after a period of three days—another bite is performed, namely a "womb-fluid bite" (garbhadrutagrāsa). The sense is that [the substance] becomes digested (jarati) over the course of three days.
Now, the characteristic of a worn-out [spear] should be known after it has been extracted from the machine. GRht_6.3 //
(Investigation as to whether *jāraṇa* has occurred):
Immediately after it has been removed, one should wash it in a vessel with *kāñjika*.
And therefore, one should remove the impurities from the sour gruel by means of a cloth.
Thereafter, it should be ground in a vessel with lukewarm water so that nothing is lost,
until all the *kāñjika* clinging to it has dried up.
And thus, once the water has been strained and purified by rubbing with the hands,
it should be pressed through a fourfold cloth over a vessel.
If everything has fallen away from the cloth and has become one with the morsel,
and if the wielder of the staff does not exist, then it should be known as the "worn-out morsel" (*jīrṇagrāsa*).
The word "atha" (then) means that after three days of sweating, the signs of the digested *rasa* (elixir) are to be known; one must ascertain whether the dose has been digested or not.
Having done what? Having extracted [it] from the machine called the swing (dolikā), that is, having taken it out from the machine.
He states [the method for] the removal of the impurity of the fluids, beginning with "having extracted," and so forth.
"Merely extracted" means having just been taken out from the press; it should be washed with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) in a vessel or bowl made of clay.
Furthermore, from this liquid, the impure portion containing dregs should be removed and cast outside.
By means of what application of cloth does that very substance remain when placed in a cloth, and not the sour gruel?
And he states the procedure for that very [rite] in the passage beginning with "tadanu" (following that), and so forth.
Thereafter, following the application of the cloth, that liquid is to be stirred in a vessel that is pleasantly warm.

How so? It is so that it does not diminish nor meet with destruction; for if [the mercury] were in a vessel made of bell-metal, copper, lead, tin, gold, or silver, it would indeed be diminished by excessive heat or by the impact of a firm hammer. Therefore, this *pārada* (mercury) should be rubbed until the *kāñjika* adhered to it—the *sauvīra* (sour gruel) resulting from contact with the mercury—dries up and reaches total exhaustion. This is the meaning.
And he states the procedure for that very [practice] beginning with "In this way," and so forth.

In this manner, by rubbing with the hands— that is, by rubbing with the palms of the hands— the juice, having become perfectly pure and free from impurities, and having its water evaporated, should be pressed over a vessel using a fourfold cloth for the purpose of drinking.
He states the characteristics of the "digested consumption" (jīrṇagrāsa) with the words beginning "yadi," and so forth.

Then mercury is to be known as "having digested the morsel" (*jīrṇagrāsa*); that is, it is so called because the morsel within it has been digested, having reached the state of being completely exhausted.
If it is "entire," meaning all of it has fallen from the cloth—that is, dropped from a fourfold-folded cloth—into the bowl; this is the remainder of the sense.

Furthermore, if the *rasa*, having attained oneness with the morsel (*grāsa*) and being joined with it, does not become a wielder of the staff—that is, if it does not assume a stable form—then it should be understood that the morsel is undigested (*jīrṇagrāsa*). This is the meaning. (GRht 6.8: On the Undigestion of the Morsel)
Having extracted the undigested paste from the morsel by means of mercury, one should cause it to fall into the apparatus;
thus the king of mercury becomes healthy, and the digested morsel is further assimilated.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the symptoms of the improper digestion of mercury (*rasājīrṇa*) with the verse beginning "grāsāt" and so forth. GRhtCM_6.8:1.

From the morsel—that is, from contact with the mouthful—one should cause that "unripe paste" (ajīrṇapiṣṭī), which is unripened and possesses the previously described characteristics, to fall from the mercury (sūta) into a vessel suitable for the process of precipitation (pātana).
Thus, having been separated from the morsel, the fallen [mercury] becomes healthy and pure.
The second dose is cooked by placing it on the surface of the fire; once cooked, that mercury (rasendra) digests it.
In the swinging vessel (dolā), four morsels (grāsa) are to be digested in their proper sequence;
the remaining [morsels] are digested in the tortoise-press (kacchapayantra) until they have doubled and so forth.

*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: Regarding the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) by means of consumption (*grāsa*), he describes the use of apparatuses and so forth, beginning with "in a swing" (*dolāyām*). GRhtCM_6.9:1.

In due order, exactly sixty-four days and so forth, four morsels (*grāsa*) are to be digested in the swing (*dolāyantra*); the remaining four morsels, or an incalculable number, are to be digested in the tortoise machine (*kacchapayantra*) and the water machine (*jalayantra*).
Why are there only four remaining? Because in other treatises, there are exactly eight morsels.

What is the limit for *jāraṇa*? It lasts as long as [the substance] digests up to twice the amount of mercury; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), it means that one should not use less than double, while more than double is permissible.
In the *Bṛhacchāstra*, regarding the descent of power (*śaktyavatāra*), eight morsels (*grāsa*) are mentioned in some places, while in others twenty morsels are mentioned.
START GRHT 6.10–12:
(The external characteristics of mercury after the *jāraṇa* of a specific quantity of *abhra*) / In this case,
it is not possible to establish a fixed rule regarding the size of the *grāsa* (bolus).
For it does not grasp the sky in its entirety; therefore, it is to be known by means of its characteristics.
If the mercury swallows sixty-four parts, then one should hold it with a staff;
from the entry of forty parts, it takes on the appearance of milk-porridge.
It becomes the shape of a leech at thirty parts, and at twenty it is without dripping;
at sixteen parts it is like a cutter; beyond that, the morsel is difficult to digest.
Demonstrating that there is no specified number regarding the morsels (*grāsa*), he says "no," and so forth.
In this treatise, it is not possible to establish the rule regarding the measure of the morsel at the very beginning, that is, first.
For this reason, the mercury (*rasa*) does not swallow the sky-like cloud in its entirety; this is the remainder of the sense.
The meaning is that the cloud which has swallowed the sky with all its parts must be recognized by its very characteristics.
Regarding the form of the *rasa* when the lunar phase (*grāsa*) consists of sixty-four parts and so forth, he says "if" (*yadīti*) and so on.
If the mercury indeed swallows sixty-four parts by measure as its morsel, then it certainly maintains its staff; the meaning is that the cloth does not leak [the mercury].

Furthermore, upon entering forty parts [of the circumference], the remainder—namely, within the belly of the mercury—then takes the form of *pāyasa*, having the appearance of boiled milk due to its density.
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "bhavati" and so forth.
By digesting thirty parts from twenty parts, the mercury (rasa) takes on the form of a leech; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Furthermore, by digesting [the mercury] twenty times with a twentieth part [of the additive], it becomes free from spattering and does not move from its seat.
Furthermore, by digesting [the substance] through sixteen parts at a time, it becomes "cuttable" (chedī) by means of razors and other such tools; once cut, it attains separability.
Therefore, above sixteen parts, the morsel becomes difficult to digest.
Having first dissolved the dense sattva with these five morsels,
one who is skilled in the liquefaction of the womb (garbhadrāva) causes the seed to be digested by means of a sixteenth part (kalāṃśa).
The commentary *Mugdhāvabodhinī* states:
"And he says that [point] with the words beginning 'by five,' etc. (GRhtCM_6.13:1).

In this manner, as previously described, a person who is skilled in causing the dissolution of the embryo (*garbhadrāva*) and proficient in liquefying mercury (*rasa*) with ores such as mica (*abhradhātu*) and the like, should apply the *grāsa* (digestible morsel) by means of a sixteenth part (*kalāṃśa*).

Having first caused the essence of mica (*ghanasattva*) to be digested in a beautiful manner by means of the five aforementioned *grāsas*, the meaning is that after the digestion of the mica-essence by those five *grāsas*, one should cause the seed (*bīja*) to be digested by means of the sixteenth part.
SMELLING SMOKE, MAKING A *ciṭiciṭi* SOUND, MOVING LIKE A FROG, AND TREMBLING; these are the changes in the physical qualities of mercury following *jāraṇā*.
When the mercury becomes motionless, it should be understood that the mineral has been fully digested by the mica.
Then, when the mercury (sūta) is smokeless, emits sparks, is motionless, and devoid of movement, it should be known as "matured like a cloud" (*abhrajīrṇa*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [The mercury] becomes smokeless, emits sparks, is motionless, and devoid of movement; this is to be understood as the state of being "matured like a cloud."
He states the characteristics of mercury digested by mica (abhraka) with the verse beginning "smoky" (dhūmra), etc.
The mercury in which the mica has been digested (*jīrṇa*) is of such a nature; it is so described because the mica has been digested within it.
Through contact with fire, it first becomes smoky and takes on a smoky luster; then it makes a crackling sound (*ciṭiciṭi*); thereafter it moves like a frog.
Then, when held in that same manner, it becomes trembling; finally, when in the fire, it becomes motionless and stable.
This is the characteristic of the mercury (*druta*) of the essence of mica (*abhra-sattva*).
He states that very point in the verse beginning with "Kapila," and so forth.
Furthermore, such a rasa that has been digested by the *abhra* (mica) is to be understood as follows.
Of what kind is Kapila in terms of color? He is one who does not belch and whose state is steady; furthermore, that essence abandons its state of scattering and its instability.
Furthermore, being motionless, self-composed, devoid of movement, and with its wings severed—these are the characteristics of a cloud that has become old.
Begin GRHT 6.16–18 (The Tortoise Apparatus): Having placed a very wide jar-neck (ghaṭakharpara) in the middle of a vessel filled with water.
Above that, the charioteer (Sūta) situated in the center should then be placed upon the wall.
Having covered it with a small iron bowl whose seams have been sealed with a paste of cloth and clay,
fill that jar-like vessel with charcoal mixed with dried cow dung and husks.
Through sweating and through massaging, the mercury situated in the tortoise-press (*kacchapayantra*) undergoes digestion;
then, by the power of fire alone, there occurs the internal liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) of all metals.
(GRht 6.18) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
He describes the tortoise-machine with the words beginning "In water," and so forth.

"In the middle of a vessel filled with water" means: having placed a very wide and beautiful elongated jar-fragment (kumbhakharpara) in the center of that vessel which is full of water, one should place the mercury situated in the middle of the *biḍa* salt upon that fragment.

On which wall made of clay, having covered the mercury filled with *viḍa* by means of a small iron bowl— a specific vessel for very small iron filings and the like— and having completely sealed it all around.
With what qualification? "By her who had applied a plaster of cloth and clay to the joints"—that is, she by whom the sealing, the blocking, of the joints was performed with cloth and clay.

Furthermore, regarding that jar or potsherd situated within the wall, filled with charcoal—of what specific kind? Mixed with *karīṣa* and husks; *karīṣa* is the powder of dried cow dung, and *tuṣāḥ* are the husks of rice and other grains—it is said that what is performed in the tortoise-press (*kacchapayantra*) is described by the words "from sweating," and so forth.
The mercury situated within the tortoise apparatus digests the morsel; this is the remainder [of the sense].
Whence [is this]? From sweating, that is, from being heated by fire.
It is not only by means of sweating and massaging, but also by means of feces and so forth; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Then, by the power of fire alone, the state of *garbhadruti* occurs for all metals, such as gold and others, within this interval; here, the power of fire alone is primary.
Having given [the medicine] in this way, it digests and does not decay; the essence (*rasa*) should be prepared accordingly.
However, through alkaline salts (*kṣāra*) and *viḍa* salts, it undergoes decay and vomits up the morsel (*grāsa*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states two methods for the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*) in the verse beginning with "evam" and so forth. (GRhtCM_6.19:1)
In this manner, having placed it in the tortoise-press (*kacchapayantra*), the mercury digests the morsel; "it digests" is the remainder of the sense.
The ritual procedure should be performed in such a way that the *rasa* does not perish—that is, it does not undergo depletion; this is the remaining sense of the statement.
The meaning is: "for the sake of protecting the basis of the task."
Furthermore, by means of alkaline substances and *viḍa* salt, the morsel (*grāsa*) undergoes depletion; that is, it reaches destruction—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Furthermore, that mercury (rasa) intensely swallows—that is, it devours—the "morsel" (grāsa) along with the secondary minerals (uparasa), sulphur (gandha), and so forth.
"With alkalies, acids, fragrances and the like, and pungent urines, for the purpose of digesting the morsel of mercury—that is proclaimed as *biḍa*. Thus is the technical definition. (GRhtCM 6.19:7)
By the word *biḍa*, a lump (*piṇḍa*) is meant.
START GRHT 7.1 (viḍa:: positive effects):
It neither releases the morsel nor desires it again; rather, from the mere act of eating it, it acquires certain qualities.
That which is digested through contact with an abundant amount of pure fire—that shall be the digestion (*jāraṇā*) together with well-compacted *biḍa* salts.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states that digestion by means of *biḍa* salts is easy to accomplish, beginning with the words "the morsel" (*grāsam*). *Commentary (GRhtCM 7.1):* [The same].

It does not release that very morsel, nor does it desire another morsel again and again; rather, from the mere act of eating, it constantly partakes of certain qualities and maintains them—the meaning is that it produces a quality simply from the swallowing of the morsel.
The meaning is that because of the "biḍas," which will have their characteristics described later, the morsel is digested.
Why? Because of the application of abundant, pure fire; that is, because of the application of pure fire (*śuddhāgni*) which is abundant and intense.
By what kind? By those that are very dense and thick.
Since *biḍas* are the best, the digestion (*jāraṇā*) should therefore be performed with *biḍas* alone; the sense is that this is because it is easy to accomplish.
START GRHT 7.2 (viḍa:: for the digestion [jāraṇa] of copper leaves):
With *sauvarcala* salt, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *kākṣī*, *kāsīsa*, *gandhaka*, and *viḍa* salts;
Śigru, when processed a hundred times with its own juice, also digests copper leaves.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He describes the method for preparing biḍa salt with the words "sauvarcala" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_7.2:1): [This is the commentary on verse 7.2]*
The wise man even digests copper leaves—this is the ellipsis; the implication is: "What need is there to mention gold-seeds and the like? // GRhtCM_7.2:2 //
By what means? By means of the *biḍas*.
By what kind of *viḍa* salts? By those containing rock salt (*sauvarcala*), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *kākṣī*, *kāsīsa*, and sulphur (*gandhaka*).
Rock salt is *rucaka*; the three pungents consist of ginger, black pepper, and long pepper; *kākṣī* is *saurāṣṭrī*; *kāsīsa* is *puṣpakāsīsa*; and *gandhaka* is *lelitaka*.
Those *viḍa* salts in which these medicinal substances are present are described as such. 7.2.4.

Furthermore, by what kind [of substances]? By *biḍas* processed a hundred times with the juice of *śigru* (the *saubhāñjana* plant); the sense is that the digestion (*jāraṇā*) will certainly occur by means of the *biḍas* thus prepared.
START GRHT 7.3 (viḍa:: for the digestion [jāraṇa] of gold):
Ash of radish burnt with all its parts, filtered through cow’s urine.
Gold that has been processed a hundred times is instantly consumed by the fat of a rat.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method for subduing [the metal] with the words "all," etc.*

"Root-ash, burnt with all its parts, strained"— this means that the ash of the radish tuber (*mūlakakanda*) which has been burnt along with all its parts, namely the root-bark, leaves, flowers, and fruit, and thus reduced to ashes, should be strained with fragrant urine or cow's water; the meaning is that the lye (*kṣāra*) is to be extracted.

Furthermore, one should prepare the scent with the fat of a bull or a leading bull, or the fat of leeches, frogs, and so forth; likewise, the fat of a frog or a fish, or the fat of a cock, or even the fat of a crocodile, according to the sequence.
A single dose of buffalo fat is the supreme binder for mercury that has been properly processed;
it also effects its coloring through the procedure of the gem-crucible (*maṇimūṣā*).
Thus [it is said]. (GRhtCM 7.3:4)

The ash, having been processed into an alkaline state one hundred times with beef fat, should again be infused one hundred times with that medicinal herb; at that very moment, at that time, gold is digested—the mercury consumes the gold as its "food" through the application of *biḍa* salt; this is the intended meaning.
START GRHT 7.4–7 (viḍa:: for jāraṇa):
Plantain, palāśa, sesame, nicula, kanaka, suradālī, vāstuka, and eraṇḍa;
To these should be added the frog, the bull, and the mokṣaka plant, along with alkali, as available.

Having brought trees that yield alkaline juice—endowed with flowers, fruits, roots, bark, and sprouts—and having cut them into pieces, he should dry their limbs until they are thoroughly parched by being ground on large stones.

Then, having burned them with stalks of sesame, drenched them with the urine of elephants, fragrant horses, and cows, and strained the liquid through cloths, he should discard the ash and boil that water again over a gentle fire using bamboo as fuel.
When that [mixture], while drying, produces many tear-like bubbles that are momentary and fragile,
then one should add the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), asafoetida (hiṅgu), sulphur (gandhaka), the three alkalis (kṣāratraya), the six salts (ṣaḍlavaṇa), and mercury and sulfur (bhūkhagau).
Having mixed the substances and returned, one should place them in a vessel made of iron or a small box resting upon the ground;
having kept them there for seven days, they should be employed for the digestion of mercury (*rasajāraṇa*) and other such purposes when contained within grain.
Now, he describes the specific varieties of alkaline trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, beginning with the word "kadalī" (banana).
The alkaline solution (kṣāra) for these should be prepared according to what is available, without exceeding the prescribed proportions.

These are the plantain (*kadalī*), the *palāśa* (the Brahma-tree), sesame (*tila*), the *nicula* (the reed-tree), the *kanaka* (thorn-apple), the *suradālī* (Devadālī), the *vāstuka* (alkaline herb), and the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*). Here, *kadalī* is the plantain; *palāśa* is the Brahma-tree; *tila* is well known; *nicula* is the reed-tree; *kanaka* is the thorn-apple; *suradālī* is Devadālī; *vāstuka* is the alkaline herb; and *eraṇḍa* is the castor-oil plant. These are the substances produced from alkaline sources.

What are these [plants] characterized by? They are accompanied by *varṣābhū*, *vṛṣa*, and *mokṣaka*. *Varṣābhū* is *punarnavā*; *vṿṣa* is *vāsaka*; and *mokṣaka* is well known as the *mokhāvṛkṣa*. This is the enumeration of those with which they are combined.
Regarding the method for preparing the alkali, he says "to be brought" (*ānīya*), and so forth.
First, having brought the aforementioned alkaline trees from another forest and taken them [there].

Of what specific qualities were they? They were endowed with flowers, fruits, roots, bark, and leaves. "Flowers" (kusumāni) refers to blossoms; "roots" (śiphā) means the root system; "bark" (tvak) refers to the rind; and "sprouts" (pravāla) refers to fresh shoots. These are known as the five limbs (pañcāṅga), and they were possessed of—that is, provided with—these.
Having cut it into many pieces, fragment by fragment.

Not only [those] whose limbs were made into pieces, but even those whose limbs—though ground upon a vast, exceedingly wide stone—were not yet dried up or deprived of their essence; having reduced them to such a state...
Furthermore, having burned those very sesame seeds together with their stalks and stems.

Furthermore, having sprinkled it with the urine of elephants, cows, and horses—which are fragrant like ichor—and having bathed [the site], one should discard that ash; the remainder is that water should be taken up with cloths. This is the implied meaning.
One should cook that water over a mild fire, a gentle flame; for bamboo is cooked by means of bamboo itself, because they share the same nature of fire.
He states the characteristics of the cooking of alkaline water with the words beginning with "tad" (that), etc. (GRhtCM_7.4-7:13).

When that alkaline water, while drying, certainly produces bubbles along with steam— those bubbles which exist together with the steam and the smoke from the evaporation of the water— then it should be known that the alkali has been produced.
Furthermore, at that time, one should add the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa)—ginger, black pepper, and long pepper; asafoetida (hiṅgu or rāmaṭha); sulfur (gandhaka) and lelitaka;

the three alkalis (kṣāratraya) known as sarjikā, yavakṣāra, and ṭaṅkaṇa; the six salts beginning with saindhava; bhuḥ (bhuṅga), turmeric (tuvarī), borax (khaga), and green vitriol (kāsīsa). The meaning is that these should be mixed together with the aforementioned alkaline liquid while it is still moist.

Likewise, having mixed substances such as the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and others, having combined them into one, and having processed them by grinding, one should place them in a pair of iron vessels (*lohamaya-pātra-sampuṭa*), specifically in a metal casket (*śastrakaṭorikāpuṭa*), and keep it for seven days amidst grain— that is, placed in the midst of some kind of grain— on the ground, in a location on the earth; immediately after that, [one may employ] that perfected substance for the digestion of mercury (*rasajāraṇa*) and other purposes.
This form of biḍa is to be employed in the digestion of mercury (*rasajāraṇa*) and other such processes; the meaning is that it is highly recommended for these purposes.
START GRht 7.8 (viḍa:: for garbhadruti): Through the combination of jambīra, bījapūraka, cāṅgerī, and vetasāmla;
Alkalis become extremely effective for the liquefaction (*garbhadruti*) and digestion (*jāraṇa*) [of mercury]; they are highly recommended for these purposes.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Regarding the procedure for alkalis in the process of digestion, he says "jambīra" and so forth.*

The alkalis derived from the aforementioned trees are exceedingly—meaning to a superlative degree—recommended and excellent for the digestion of *garbhadruti* (internal liquefaction) and for the digestion of the "swallowing" (*grāsa*) within the mercury.
Why? Because of the combination of the juices of the *jambīra*, *bījapūraka*, *cāṅgerī*, and *vetasāmla*. The *jambīra* is well-known; the *bījapūraka* is the citron (*mātuluṅga*);

the *cāṅgerī* is the *amlapatrīkā*; and the *vetasāmla* is the *cukraka*. The point is that alkaline substances (*kṣāra*) infused with the juice of these [fruits] perform their function like *biḍa* salt.
START GRHT 7.9 (viḍa:: how to use):
Having first given the viḍa-salt above and below in an eighth part of the mercury (sūta),...
One should perform the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) in this manner; one should increase the fire gradually, step by step.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Regarding the addition of *viḍa* to the mercury, he says "viḍam" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_7.9:1): [The author] states the application of *viḍa* in the mercury with the words beginning with "viḍam."*

First, at the outset, having applied the previously prepared *viḍa* salt—both below and above (i.e., in the lower and upper portions)—in an amount equal to one-eighth part of the mercury (*rasa*), one should perform the digestion (*jāraṇa*) in this manner. Furthermore, "krama" refers to that which proceeds by this sequence; it is the form of the *viḍa*. From that sequence, one should gradually increase the fire; the word "the practitioner" (*karmakṛt*) is to be supplied. Through repeated application of the *viḍa*, the fire increases.
START GRHT 8.1–2 (rañjana: coloring according to abhra):
The mercury of digested abhra displays a luster corresponding to the density [of the mineral].
Black, red, yellow, white, as well as those mixed with combinations [of these colors].

The mercury (rasendra) becomes strongly endowed with a dark-blue color by means of black mica (kṛṣṇābhraka); indeed, it should be known by its color as white, red, yellow, or like fire. (GRht 8.2) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* The mercury becomes intensely colored with a dark-blue hue through the application of black mica; furthermore, it should be understood according to its color as being white, red, yellow, or like fire. (GRht 8.2)
Just as that moon shines in the sky with its loveliness when the clouds have worn away,
so too does he shine among men by resorting to her here.

"Indeed, the production of colors such as yellow and so forth in mercury through the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of well-perfected *biḍa* salts, minerals, and the like, is proclaimed as *rañjana* (coloring).
This is the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). GRhtCM_8.1-2:2.
He describes a specific type of cloud-shade with the words "jīrṇābhraka" and so forth.
When the king of mercury has digested the mica, it then displays a luster corresponding to the density [of the mica], having a color identical to that of the digested mica.

When a black cloud has dissipated, it shows a black shadow; when a red one has dissipated, a red one; likewise, when a yellow one, a yellow one; and when a white, bright one, a white one. Thus, it displays a fourfold variety of shadows.
Furthermore, when there is a mixture or combination of two, three, or four [qualities], it means that it displays a reflection corresponding to those two, three, or four.
Regarding the specific color resulting from the application of mica, he says "black," and so forth.
When the black mica (kṛṣṇābhra) has been fully digested, the mercury shall indeed become powerful; furthermore, it becomes joined with dark dyes and black dyes.

Likewise, that which is white is joined with white dyes, the red with red, and the yellow with yellow; even for the divine fire of Kapila, which causes the destruction of all things by its power in the form of invisibility, such a color of substances is to be known by those skilled in colors according to their taste and appearance.
START GRHT 8.3 (Mercury transmits its own color to other substances): Now, when it does not abandon its own color in its natural state, it is colored by dyes.
For, gradually purified by the methods to be described, it brings about coloration.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He speaks in praise of the colored mercury with the words "atha" and so forth.*

Immediately thereafter, when mercury (rasa), the king of metals, is colored by the dyes such as white and others that will be described hereafter, it does not abandon its own work— that is, its own natural color or inherent form; rather, having been cleansed by those very same dyes and becoming red,
it effects a coloring, acting as a giver of color.
Likewise, one who is not attached does not perform an act of attachment; because it does not exist, there is a negation [of such an act].
Strength resides in the essence of iron; digestion and coloring are established in steel.
And the binding [of mercury] occurs with base metals, and then with the essence (*sāra*) [of mercury] by means of lead (*nāga*) and tin (*vaṅga*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

He states the condition for mercury (*rasa*) when it is joined with the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) and other substances, beginning with the words "strength" (*bala*).* *Commentary (GRhtCM 8.4:1): [He states the condition for mercury when it is joined with the essence of mica and other substances, beginning with the words "strength".]*
"Power resides in the substratum of the essence of mica (abhrakasattva)"; the meaning is that through union with the essence of mica, the mercury (rasa) attains power.

Furthermore, regarding "dyeing in the sharp variety of iron" (*tīkṣṇe lohabhede jāraṇarāgā*): the meaning is that through the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*), the dyes residing within the sharp iron become firmly established.
Regarding the phrase "then the extraction by means of lead and mercury," it means that the substance to be extracted flows out with difficulty due to lead and mercury.
START GRHT 8.5 (The potency of *tīkṣṇaloha*):
By means of *tīkṣṇa*, the mercury penetrates; and by *tīkṣṇa*, the morsel is digested in an instant.
Gold takes up the sharpness from the red [mineral] by means of the sharp [reagent].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that the sharp [reagent] is the cause of all [transmutations], beginning with the words "it permeates" (krāmati).*

By means of sharp iron (*tīkṣṇa*), the mercury (*rasa*) penetrates; it performs the process of *krāmaṇa* (transmigration). Furthermore, having employed sharp iron, the "bite" (*grāsa*) is digested in a moment—that is, in a short time—and undergoes *jāraṇa* (digestion). Moreover, sharp iron is the source—the place of origin—of gold (*suvarṇa*). Furthermore, by employing sharp iron, the mercury takes up the "coloring agents" (*rāga*, i.e., the coloring substances); the meaning is that it places the colors within itself.
START GRHT 8.6 (Sharp Metals:
Transmutation and Digestion)
And that too, having been killed with cinnabar and combined with honey and mercury,
should be perfumed with perfumes, and then it is to be processed like a cloud— both as a *cārya* and as a *jārya*.
Regarding the superior quality of sharp iron through its application with cinnabar, he says "that too" and so forth.

Furthermore, that sharp iron (tīkṣṇa) must certainly be killed or slain with cinnabar (darada) or vermilion (hiṅgula), or with gold pyrite (mākṣika); this sharp iron, combined with copper and killed or slain, should then be perfumed and saturated by means of perfuming herbs (vāsanauṣadha). Only then can it be processed (cārya) and digested (jārya) like a dense cloud (ghanavat) or like mica (abhravat), just as with the essence of mica (sattvābhra); otherwise, it will not be so.
One should use either magnetite, or iron, or gold, or diamonds, emeralds, and so forth.
In the process of coloring with mercury, either one [of these] or all of them together is desired as a mixture.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

He speaks of these starting with "kāntam" (iron), just like [the description of] *tīkṣṇa* (sharp iron).* *Commentary (GRhtCM 8.7:1)*: "He speaks of these starting with 'kāntam', just like [the description of] *tīkṣṇa*."

In the coloring of mercury (*rasarañjana*), for the purpose of dyeing the lord of liquids (*rasendra*), one should use either the lovely iron (*loha*) produced from magnet stone (*cumbakapāṣāṇa*), which is excellent in this context, or *tīkṣṇa*—meaning a specific type of iron—or *kāñcī*, which is gold pyrite (*svarṇamākṣika*).

Or else, among those beginning with diamond (*vajra*) and *sasyaka*—that is, diamond, *capala*, and so forth—one may use any one of them, or all of them; here, the word "any" (*ekata-ma*) refers to whichever is desired.
The connection is with each [term] individually: diamonds and so forth are gems (*ratna*), while sasyaka and so forth are secondary minerals (*upadhātu*).
Or rather, in the coloring by rasa, this very *saṃkara*—the blending of all [types of heroes] such as the *kānta* and others—is desired everywhere.
In mercury (kuṭila), strength is predominant; in the sharp (tīkṣṇa) substance, passion (rāga); but in the serpent (pannaga), there is oiliness (sneha).
Those who know the elements declare that passion, affection, and strength reside in the lotus.
When all these metals, having been killed by *mākṣika* and melted within the crucible (*garbha*),
are digested by means of the application of *viḍa*, the king of mercury attains coloration (*rāga*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Regarding each respective transformation, he states "strength" and so forth, as will be explained. GRhtCM_8.8-9:1/1.
Those who know the elements are called physicians of taste; so they praise them.

Thus, what is the strength in the crooked (kuṭila)? It is excessive. Furthermore, in the sharp (tīkṣṇa), passion (rāga) is excessive; moreover, in the serpent (pannaga), coloring (rañjana) is excessive;

and furthermore, in the elephant (nāga), affection (sneha) is excessive. Moreover, oiliness (snigdhatva) is [excessive]. Thus, these three—passion, affection, and strength—are said to reside in the copper (tāmra).
Just as strength, passion, and affection arise in mercury (rasa) through the digestion (jāraṇā) of the crooked, the sharp, and the serpent, so too do they arise from the digestion of copper alone.
The meaning is that there are three.
He states the method for binding the mercury with the words beginning "by all," and so forth.
By means of the previously mentioned *biḍa* process, once the king of mercury has been digested—that is, has undergone *jāraṇa*—it attains *bandha*, meaning it takes on a state of fixation.
With what [is it] digested? With all these aforementioned metals and minerals.
By what [means]? By those killed by *mākṣika*, that is, slain by *svarṇamākṣika*.
Furthermore, by what characteristics [is it so]? It is said: "melted and flowed within the interior of the essence in the womb."
START GRHT 8.10–11 (Mercury::
Rañjana with a Kṛṣṭi):
With orpiment, cinnabar, and realgar, combined with fats, alkalis, acids, and salts;
The crucible should carry equal, double, or triple quantities of tin, iron, and other such materials.
By means of sprinklings of red oils, one should perform the remainder; this is the extraction of mercury.
Through mere stirring and digestion, it makes the mercury resemble an *indragopa* insect.
He states the method for slaying the elements that are about to be described, beginning with "tālaka" and so forth.
"Vaṅga, weapons, and so forth": vaṅga is tin, śastra is steel; those for which these are the first [members] are "those [things]."

With what should one carry the vessel? With realgar, vermilion, and arsenic; that is, with *tālaka* (realgar), *haritāla* (yellow orpiment), *darada* (vermilion), and *śilā* (arsenic, i.e., *manaḥśilā*).

With what kind [of substances]? Accompanied by oil (*sneha*), alkali (*kṣāra*), acid (*amla*), and salt (*lavaṇa*). Oil refers to sesame oil, castor oil, and so forth; alkali refers to *svarjikā* and the like; acid refers to *jambīra* (citron) and the like; salts refer to rock salt (*saindhava*) and the like—[these are] accompanied by these.
The explicit teaching is that the flow proceeds through the *puṭa* as long as it begins from one part out of twelve and concludes with equal, double, and triple parts respectively.
He states the function of the encapsulated elements (puṭitadhātu) with the words beginning "raktā" and so forth.

One should treat the mercury containing the aforementioned *dhātu* with sprinklings (*niṣeka*) of blood, oil, and the red group of substances; "blood" refers to the red category, "oil" refers to that of *kaṅguṇī* and so forth, and by these sprinklings—meaning the act of pouring—one should render it free from the remaining *dhātus*.

This is the extraction (*kṛṣṭi*) of mercury, the drawing out of its qualities; furthermore, this extraction makes the lord of mercury resemble an *indragopa* insect, making its color exceedingly brilliant.

And why? Because from the mere *cāraṇa* and *jāraṇa* of the metals that have been subjected to *puṭa*, there is both *cāraṇa* and *jāraṇa*, which is to say, the act of making them fully digested (*jīrṇakaraṇa*).
Or rather, it is simply the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of the substance through *cāraṇa*; thus, in both cases, the meaning is exactly the same, with only the phrasing being different.
Alternatively, a pure lotus alone, when sown with cinnabar, produces [the same effect].
Indeed, the mercury (sūta), having been processed three times and digested, becomes similar in appearance to lac juice.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states "Alternatively" (*athavā*) and so forth to praise copper as the primary [substance].*

Alternatively, according to another method, one should make the copper—pure (*kevala*), that is, free from association with other substances, stainless (*amala*), having undergone previous purification (*jātapūrvaśodhana*), tripled (*triguṇa*), and processed (*cīrṇajīrṇa*)—meaning it has first been subjected to *cāraṇa* (calcination/dissolution) and subsequently attained *jāraṇa* (digestion/assimilation). Such copper makes the mercury resemble the juice of lac (*lākṣārasasannibha*), possessing the luster of red resin (*alaktaka*). // GRhtCM_8.12:2 //
START GRht 8.13 (Mercury:: Rañjana):
Of tāpya, sulphur, and mica, which have been infused with the liquid of sacrificial animals dripping from a red-colored group [of plants].
A single drop of mercury, when applied, dyes the lotus white with red.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method, beginning with "rakta" and so forth.*

With the previously mentioned red group of substances—such as pomegranate, *kiṃśuka*, *bandhūka*, and so forth—the *paśujala* (animal-liquid), which is cow’s urine, is processed (*bhāvita*). From among the *tāpya* (cinnabar), sulphur (*gandhaka*), and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) that have been thus processed, by means of one of them—either *tāpya* (gold-magnet ore), sulphur, or realgar—the dead copper is sown (*vāpita*). This causes the lotus-like copper to become colored; the meaning is that it imparts a hue (*rāga*). // GRhtCM_8.13:2 //
START GRht 8.14 (Duration of coloring according to substance):
External fragrance-coloring [is used] when realgar and yellow orpiment have lost their color.
Indeed, only these two—the essence of copper (mākṣika-sattva) and mercury (rasaka)—are recommended for the process of coloring (rañjana).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
This verse mentions sulfur and other substances that are subject to the process of coloring.*
Regarding that, he explains the nature of what kind of passion (*rāga*) sulphur (*gandhaka*) imparts, beginning with the words "externally" (*bāhya*) and so forth.

Regarding external coloring agents (*gandhakarāga*) that exist externally: among realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and yellow orpiment (*tāla*), "realgar" refers to *manaḥśilā* and "yellow orpiment" refers to *haritāla*; both of these are "of agitated color" (*vilulitarāga*), meaning they are of unstable color. Furthermore, regarding the two—copper pyrite essence (*mākṣikasatva*) and *rasaka* (i.e., *svarṇamākṣikasatva* and *kharparika*)—these two alone are excellent for coloring the mercury (*rasa-rāge*), being superior and more effective than realgar, realgar, and yellow orpiment; this is the meaning.
START GRht 8.15 (rasarañjaka [15]) In the sequential process, the sun and mercury, once purified and blown into a silent crucible, [are joined].
Having been processed three times, the mercury becomes aged and acquires a golden luster.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He describes the function of the two primary substances, copper and the crucible, in the verse beginning with "kramavṛttau," etc.*

In the process of gradual transformation (*kramavṛtti*), mercury and copper, having been thoroughly purified or refined by specific methods, should be of the highest quality; they are to be blown with a silent crucible (*mūkamūṣikā*) or heated in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) until they are subjected to fire. When the mercury has thus been processed and digested three times in this manner, it becomes gold-colored. Having undergone *cāraṇa* (dissolution) by means of this [gold-like substance], the mercury subsequently undergoes *jāraṇā* (digestion) by that very same means and acquires the luster of gold.
The meaning is "it would be."
START GRHT 8.16 (rasarañjaka 16):
Now, when the powder of black abhraka is subjected to *puṭa* firing, it likewise becomes entirely red.
The mercury, having been processed three times and digested, becomes similar to the liquefaction of gold.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the application of mica with the words "atha" and so forth.*

Then, following the preparation of the mercury (rasaka), the black-colored powder of mica (abhraka-cūrṇa)— that is, the dark-colored mica dust— being fused with a crucible (kharparaka) according to the procedure for solar mercury (ravirasaka), becomes entirely red; that mica, having thus become red, is consumed (cīrṇa) three times over, and then, having undergone digestion (jīrṇa), the mercury (sūta) [attains its full potency].
The meaning is that it becomes similar to the melting of mercury, resembling liquid gold.
START GRHT 8.17–18 (Mercury:: Rañjana):
Gold that has been calcined, combined with mercury and tāla, [is processed] with three parts of mākṣika.
That [substance], cooked together with salt in a pot until it resembles an indragopa insect, [is prepared].
That powder, when consumed three times the amount of the excellent mercury and fully digested, causes the mercury—
resembling molten gold— to color all metals.
Now, he describes the killing of gold with the verse beginning "triguṇena" (GRhtCM 8.17–18).

Furthermore, when gold has been processed with three parts of *mākṣika* (sulphur) and three parts of *tāpya* (calamine), that dead gold becomes "resembling an *indragopaka*"; the remainder of the sentence implies that its luster is like that of an *indragopaka*, which is a red-colored insect appearing during the rainy season.

What kind of gold? It is "dead" (mṛta), meaning it has reached the state of being reduced to ashes; it is "joined with rasaka and tāla," where *rasaka* is *kharpara* and *tāla* is *haritāla*, and it is "mixed" (*yuta*) with those two. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, combined with sugar and mixed with salt, it is again cooked in a vessel or pot and fired in the fire; that too is as described before.

When the powder of dead gold (mṛtakanaka-cūrṇa) is consumed three times the amount of the excellent mercury (sūtavarapārada), and having been thoroughly processed, transmuted, and melted, the mercury becomes like molten gold; that is to say, it acquires the luster of flowing gold.
Thus, the mercury, when so colored, colors all metals and ores—both artificial and natural, of nine kinds—and turns them into the form of gold.
START GRht 8.19 (The Greatness of Bījāraṇ):
The essence is eight times superior to the leaf; the liquefaction is eight times superior to the essence.
The seed is eight times more potent than the flux; therefore, one should cause the seed to digest [the metal].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that among all metallic juices (dhāturasas), each subsequent one is superior to the preceding, beginning with "from the leaf," etc.*

The essence (*sattva*) in the leaf is eight times superior to the [mercury] in the leaf; when the mica-leaf has been digested, the quality present in that mercury is such that the quality in the essence is eight times greater than that.

Furthermore, the liquefaction (*druti*) resulting from that essence—which takes the form of a liquid—is eight times superior; and the seed (*bīja*), produced by the union of minerals and medicinal juices as previously described, is eight times superior to that liquefaction. Therefore, because of its supreme excellence, one should digest the seed and nothing else.
START GRht 9.1 (Seed [Definition]):
Thus, even though mercury is red, it does not perform its function without the seed (*bīja*).
That [elixir] is employed as two kinds—yellow and white—and this is indeed proven.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He is like the moon in brilliance and like the sun in splendor.*
And he who dwells with the wicked is like one who makes night and day into a single entity.
When, through a specific process of quenching (*nirvāpaṇa*), it becomes of such a color, soft, and possessed of various refinements (*saṃskāra*), that is called the seed (*bīja*). (GRhtCM 9.1:2)
Thus ends the technical rules (paribhāṣā).
He speaks in praise of the seed with the words "Thus," and so forth.

According to the method thus described, even mercury that has been colored does not become a performer of action without the seed; the meaning is that it becomes a performer of action only by means of the seed.
That seed is of two kinds, of two types: yellow and white; one is yellow and the other is white or pale, meaning it is suitable for the manufacture of gold and silver.
That seed, perfected and endowed with all characteristics, should be applied to mercury (pārada), for it must not be unperfected.
START GRHT 9.2 (Purification of the Seed is Necessary):
Its purification is manifold, by means of powdered mercury, minor metals, and metallic ores.
Even by those who are not yet pure, that seed—which is of two kinds—is indeed purified.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
"Of that," and so forth.*
The purification—that is, the cleansing—of that seed is performed in many ways and by numerous methods, because the minerals, secondary minerals, and ores are of many kinds.

By what means? By the powders of the sky, mercury, and metals: "the sky" refers to *abhra* (mica); "mercury" refers to the eight [minerals] such as *vaikrānta* which will be mentioned later; "uparasas" refers to sulphur and others; and "metals" refers to the ores—their powders are by those [means].

Furthermore, by those impure powders of mercury, secondary minerals, and metals—devoid of purity—that seed is not purified; it would remain devoid of purity, according to the principle that "the effect conforms to its cause. Moreover, for one who performs the rite with these impure substances, the mercury itself would become impure.
The *pataṅgī* [creeper] is not pervasive; it is not suitable for the elixir (*rasāyana*) of mercury.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states "he who," etc., to explain the power of the impure seed. *Commentary (GRhtCM 9.3:1):* [Same as above].

Furthermore, specifically, for that person who performs the processing of mercury (rasa) using these impure substances such as gaganādi, the mercury—meaning pārada—becomes non-pervasive and lacks the quality of flowing; it becomes "pataṅgī," meaning it moves upwards and does not remain at the lower part of the apparatus. This is the meaning.
START GRHT 9.4 (Mahārasa):
Vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, adri, darada, and rasa;
Thus, these eight [substances] are the "flavors" (rasas), and their essences (sattvas) shall serve as elixirs (rasāyana).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
These eight flavors to be described hereafter are designated as "rasas."*

These—vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, adri, darada, and rasaka—are known by the name *rasa*. Among them: *vaikrānta* is the powder produced from diamond-earth; *kānta* arises from a magnet; *sasyaka* is capala; *mākṣika* is tāpya; *vimala* is silver pyrite (*raupyamākṣika*);
*adri* is *śilājatu*; *darada* is *hiṅgula*; and *rasaka* is *kharparika*. These are to be understood as the substances designated as *rasa*.
Likewise, may their essences become potent elixirs that destroy old age and disease.
START GRHT 9.5–6 (uparasa):
Sulphur, red ochre, realgar, orpiment, yellow ochre, antimony, and kaṅkuṣṭha;
He states the substances known as *uparasa* [minor minerals] beginning with "gandhaka" and so forth.
This which is about to be described shall be known by the name *uparasa*.

"What is this 'mercury, realgar, mica, alum, earth, and sky'? [The answer is: "Mercury" is well-known; "realgar" is mineral realgar (*dhātugairika*); "mica" is *manohvā*; "alum" is yellow orpiment (*haritāla*); "earth" is rock crystal (*sphaṭikā*); "sky" is green vitriol (*kāsīsa*). All these, furthermore, along with "collyrium" (*añjana*), which is blue collyrium (*nīlāñjana*), and "kaṅkuṣṭha," which is *viraṅga*—these eight are what is meant by the term "minor minerals" (*uparasa*). This is the meaning.
This [group] is known as the secondary minerals (uparasa); the two called śikhi and śaśin are termed sāraloha. (GRht 9.5)
Copper, brass, iron,
steel, magnetite, mica-essence, iron, tin, and lead—
these are declared to be known as "corrupt" (pūti); their purification must be performed.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī): "The peacock and the moon" refer to gold and silver; that is to say, they are known as "essential metal" (*sāraloha*). GRhtCM_9.5-6:1.
He speaks of the designation "corroded metal" in the passage beginning with "tāmra," and so forth.
Copper, brass, steel, magnetite, mica-essence, and iron— namely, copper from Nepal (*nepālaka*), brass (*āra* or *rājarīti*), steel (*tīkṣṇa* or *sāra*),
magnetite (*kānta*) produced from a lodestone, mica-essence (*abhrasattva* or *gaganasāra*), and iron (*loha* or *muṇḍa*)— these, along with tin (*vaṅga*) and lead (*nāga*),
are declared to be known by the name "corrupt" (*pūti*).
The purification of those items known as "corroded metals" (pūtiloha)—that is, the complete removal of their impurities—must be performed.
START GRH 9.7 (The Six Salts): Sauvarcala, saindhava, kacūlika, sāmudra, romaka, and biḍa.
Regarding the term "lavaṇakṣāra," he says "sauvarcala" and so forth.
The teachers say that these [substances] which are about to be described are designated as "salt"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Regarding the salts—sauvarcala, saindhava, cūlika, sāmudra, romaka, and biḍa: *sauvarcala* is *rucaka*;
*saindhava* is called *maṇika* or *manthāhvaya*; *cūlika* is *kācalavaṇa*; *sāmudra* is produced from the salt ocean; *romaka* is well known; and *biḍa* is a specific type of salt. These are they.
START GRht 9.7 (The three alkalis): These six salts are indeed [the five types of salt] together with svarjikā, ṭaṅkaṇa, and yavakṣāra. // GRht_9.7 // @------------------

*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:* Furthermore, svarjī is sarjikā, ṭaṅkaṇa is saubhāgya, and yavakṣāra is well known; these are the alkalis (kṣāra) designated as such for the purpose of alchemical operations on mercury (*rasakarmaṇi*). This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
START GRHT 9.8–9 (Purification of uparasa; extraction of sattva)
Sūryāvarta, kadalī, vandhyā, kośātakī,
suradālī, śigru, vajrakanda, nīrakaṇā, and kākamācī.
When repeatedly treated with salt, alkali, and sour substances using a single essence of these [liquids],
the primary and secondary minerals (rasoparasa) become purified upon being smelted and release their essences (sattva).
He states the group of purifiers along with the solvent, beginning with "sūryāvarta" and so forth.

That which revolves toward the sun— that is, that which rotates [in that direction]— is the plantain (kadalī), the rambhā, the barren one (vandhyā), the fruitless one, the karkoṭī, the kośātakī, the jālinī, the suradālī, the devadālī, the śigru, the saubhāñjana, the vajrakanda, the vadara-sūraṇa-kanda, the nīrakaṇā, the jalapippalī, and the kākamācī; this group is suitable for purification and liquefaction.
Regarding the purification and liquefaction of the purifying agents, he states "of these" and so forth.

From among these aforementioned medicinal herbs, one should repeatedly saturate (bhāvita) the eight metals (rasa), such as vaikrānta and others, and the eight minor metals (uparasa), such as sulphur and others, with the juice of a single herb—that is, with the juice of one of them—and then subject them to heating in a closed crucible (gharmapuṭita). Furthermore, they should be saturated many times with salts, alkalies, and acids;

the salts are the six types beginning with sauvarcala, the alkalies are those beginning with svarjika, and the acids are those beginning with jambīra. With these, [the process] should be performed many times.

When mercury and the secondary minerals (uparasa) have been processed and subjected to intense heat, they become purified and free from defects; furthermore, when they are blown with a bellows, they release—that is, relinquish—their own essential qualities (satva).
Vaikrānta, having been steamed with alkaline substances and acids and then blown [into a flame], melts forcibly.
He describes the purification of the tastes in their proper order, beginning with the words "sweated," and so forth.

One should steam vaikrānta with alkaline and sour substances using the method called *dolā* (swinging). When that steamed vaikrānta is forcibly—meaning with intensity—heated, it melts; it releases its essence and, as soon as it has melted, it is purified merely by the emergence of its *sattva*.
It melts due to its prior connection [with the fluxing agents].

START GRHṚ 9.14 (Purification of lead, tin, bronze, and copper)
The *nāga*, *vaṅga*, and *ghoṣa* are purified by the sun and by the sages [on their respective] days, through the sprinkling of *nirguṇḍī* juice and by the application of the dust from its roots.

*Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* The *nāga* (lead), *vaṅga* (tin), and *ghoṣa* (iron) are purified on Sunday and on the days of the week assigned to the sages (the seven weekdays). This purification is achieved by sprinkling the juice of the *nirguṇḍī* plant and by applying the powder of its roots.
Regarding the purification of iron, he says "it is purified," and so forth.
Lead (nāga) is purified and becomes free from defects by being sprinkled with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and the juice of *śephālī*; tin (*vaṅga*) is likewise purified.
In this way, bell-metal (ghoṣa) as well as brass (kāṃsya) is purified by means of copper together with copper filings.

How many times are they purified? By seven sages through sprinklings; by the dust from its roots—that is, the powder of the *nirguṇḍī* root—through its applications; and by the casting of dust when lead, tin, copper, and iron have been melted.
Thus, these four are purified.

He describes the general purification and killing of all metals with the verse beginning "all," and so forth.
Every kind of metal is purified, becomes dead, and is then colored again.

By means of what? By means of *mākṣika-darada* (cinnabar from the Mākṣika mountain), that is, *tāpya-hiṅgula*, in such a way as to be "exceedingly" (*bhṛśam*) or "to the utmost" (*atyartham*). The "infusion" (*vāpa*) is the addition of *mākṣika-darada* once the metals have been melted; from that, all the metal becomes similar to an *indragopa* insect, resembling a red beetle.

Alternatively, copper wire (*śulba*) becomes similar to an earthworm (*suragopa*) by the application of *mākṣika* and *darada*; or, by the application of sulphur (*gandhaka*), it shall indeed become dead (*mṛta*)—this is the meaning.
START GRH 10.1 Now, the departure of the person (*sattva*) will be explained.
(The importance of the *sattva*:)

Vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, and the like do not combine even when purified, even without their *satva*, nor does mercury swallow them. (GRht 10.1) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* These minerals—vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, and so forth—even when individually purified, do not enter into a binary union (*dvandva*). Furthermore, mercury does not digest them. This is because they are heavy and difficult to process. However, when combined with *satva*, they become easily digestible and capable of entering into union. Thus, the meaning is that these [minerals] are not effective for medicinal purposes unless they are first liberated from their *satva*. Therefore, one should extract the *satva* from them. The method for this is as follows: one should take the aforementioned minerals and place them in a crucible (*puṭa*) smeared with a mixture of cow’s urine, cow dung, and cow’s milk. Then, having covered it with a lid, one should heat it in a fire until the *satva* is released. Once the *satva* has fallen out, one should collect it and purify it by heating it in a furnace (*bhastrā*) together with the juice of *arka* leaves. When it becomes white, it is purified. One should then place it in a *mūṣā* (crucible) smeared with a paste of *kāsīsa*, *gairika*, and *śilājatu*, and heat it over a fire of dried cow-dung cakes (*karīṣāgni*). By means of this process, the *satva* is extracted. Once the *satva* is obtained, one should grind it with the juice of *arka* leaves and place it in a *mūṣā* smeared with a paste of *kāsīsa*, *gairika*, and *śilājatu*. Then, having covered it with a lid, one should heat it in a fire until it melts. When it has melted, it is known as *rasabandha* (the binding of mercury). It should be used according to the prescribed dosage. Thus ends the tenth chapter on the extraction of *satva* from minerals. *End of commentary.*
He constantly bestowed happiness upon the pure and likewise misery upon the wicked; thus, he made himself the equal cause for both happiness and suffering.
Regarding the praise of the *sattva* of those substances known as "rasas," such as *vaikrānta* and others, he says: "*Vaikrāntam*" and so forth.
Vaikrānta, kānta, sasyaka, mākṣika, vimala, and the like do not combine even when purified, if they are of different classes.

Vaikrānta, the dust born from diamond-earth (vajrabhūmi), kānta, cumbaka, sasyaka, capala, mākṣika, tāpya, vimalā, raupyamākṣika, and so forth—along with sulphur and the others—are called "minor minerals" (uparasas); they do not "unite," meaning they do not attain a single unified state.
Wherein is the pair? In the union of both.
Furthermore, the mercury, the elixir, does not swallow even those [metals] that have been purified.
That which is called Nāganāsikā, Candrodaka, Amṛta, and Āptakāṭhinya,
as well as Rasavaikrāntaka— these bind the mercury by means of their own essence. (GRht 10.2)
Having obtained that stone which has various forms, produced from the peaks of mountain summits, and is the best among those found in flowing water— that stone is called *śailodaka*. 10.3.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the preeminence of vaikrānta with the words beginning "nāga," etc. GRhtCM_10.2-3:1.
Vaikrāntaka should be known as having such characteristics.
Of what kind was it? It was called "the nose of the serpent" (nāganāsikā); that is, its name or designation was the very nose of the serpents (nāgas), those who possess hoods.
Furthermore, what is its specific quality? It is the "water of the moon"—that is, the water or strength belonging to the moon—from which alone it is nectar.
The meaning is that it has attained a hardness that was previously obtained, such that this [body] has now arisen as soft.
Such a *rasavaikrānta*, known as *rasa-vaikrānta*, binds the mercury (*rasa*)—the *sūta*—which is *vaikrānta*.
By what? By one's own being and by one's own essence. // GRhtCM_10.2-3:7 //
He describes the varieties of vaikrānta with the words beginning "nānā" and so forth.

Vaikrānta, which was previously described, possesses various types of *saṃsthāna*; that is, its *saṃsthāna*—meaning its configuration (*vyañjana*), characteristic (*liṅga*), mark (*lakṣaṇa*), sign (*cihna*), or form (*ākṛti*)—is of many kinds and diverse types. According to the *Mādhavanidāna*, because it has white, black, red, and yellow colors, it is said to have "various types of *saṃsthāna*. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, it was produced on the peak of the mountain of the *nirjaras*—that is, the mountain (*śikharī*) of the gods (*nirjaras*), its summit (*śikhara*) or crest (*śṛṅga*)—where it arose. (GRhtCM_10.2-3:10) Why is it of various forms? Because at that time, during the rainy season when water flows wildly from the torrents (*dhārā*) of rain, having encountered the mountain-water—that is, the water associated with the rocks—it becomes excellent, like that very stone.
It is called *vaikrānta* because it occurs in various colors, due to the manifold nature of the water of the stone (*śilodaka*).
START GRHT 10.4–5 (Vaikrānta:
[the extraction of] the *sattva*)
Having added one-tenth part of the alkalis of svarjika, paṭu, ṭaṅkaṇa, and guñjikā, it should be forcefully blown with two bellows while well-bound with the hide of a buffalo.

That [substance] becomes hard, releases its essence in the form of sparks, and consists mostly of a mass of pearls; one should take it, having carefully avoided the glass-like [impurities]. (GRht 10.5) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* The term "that" refers to the aforementioned mercury (*rasa*). When mercury is heated by fire, it attains hardness and emits its essence in the form of sparks. This essence, which resembles a heap of pearls, should be collected after discarding the glass-like dross. One must avoid the glass-like substance and extract the pearl-like essence. The word "mostly" (*prāya*) is used because some impurities may still remain. One should collect that which has become hard and resembles a collection of pearls. The word "carefully" (*adhivarjya*) means that one should avoid the glass-like substance with great diligence. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Extraction of Mercury. Having done what? Having added the alkalis of *sarjikā*, *paṭu*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and *guñjikā* in the proportion of one-tenth; that is to say, having ground them and added the alkalis of *sarjikā*, salt (*lavaṇa*), *saubhāgya*, *raktikā*, and *yavakṣāra* to the *vaikrānta* in the division of one-tenth.
Once it has been heated, what would it become? To that he says: "That," and so forth.
The essence, appearing like a spark and resembling a glowing ember of fire, emits the vital principle (sattva).
Furthermore, that moisture becomes solidity; the meaning is that it becomes solid.
That substance, by its form, would be like a heap of pearls, resembling a mass of pearls; the meaning is that such a substance, having discarded and cast far away the glass, should be taken as pure.
A pair. (GRhtCM 10.4–5)
START GRht 10.6 (Vaikrānta:
the binding of mercury)
In this way, mercury and vaikrāntaka, when combined in a binary compound (dvandvānvita) in equal parts with gold,
yield a dense essence (ghanasatva); by means of that, the mercury attains fixation (bandha).
He explains the application of the essence (*sattva*) of *vaikrānta* with the verse beginning "rasa," and so forth.

That *sattva* of *vaikrāntaka*, when combined with an equal part of gold—that is, with an equal portion of *svarṇa*—and being accompanied by the medicinal herbs for dual-melting (*dvandvamelāpaka*), thus, by this procedure, it merges into the mercury;
such is the remainder [of the sense].

Furthermore, when that essence (satva) has been processed and refined together with dense essence (ghanasatva), which is the quintessence of clouds (abhrasāra), the mercury (rasa/sūta) attains a state of bondage—that is, it achieves fixation—through the union of both essences.
START GRht 10.7 (Minerals: *sattvapātana*)
The mass of all these minerals— such as diamond, mica, magnetite, iron pyrite, and copper ore—
when smelted with hard charcoal, causes their essence to fall out.
He states the procedure for the precipitation of the essence (sattvapātana) with the words beginning "vajra," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "with hard coals," because of the mention of "hard" and since *khadira* and other woods were mentioned previously, [the ore] is blown with two bellows. Among all the minerals such as *vajrābhra*,

*kānta*, *sasyaka*, *mākṣika*, and so forth— wherein the *abhra* designated as "diamond" (*vajra*) is *vajrābhra*, *kānta* is magnetite (*cumbaka*), *sasyaka* is *capalā*, and *mākṣika* is *svarṇamākṣika*— [it is processed].
All the metallic ores and all the secondary minerals—their mass causes the essence (sattva) to fall.
START GRht 10.8 (Honey: Essence:
Special Alchemical Potency)
Once the essence of honey (mākṣika-sattva) has been discarded, no other [substance] possesses the power to destroy the iron;
the essence does not fall until it is drawn out from within the bellows.
He speaks in praise of the essence of copper (*mākṣikasatva*) by virtue of its potency, beginning with the words "having abandoned," and so forth.
Apart from the essence of *mākṣika* and the core of *tāpya*, other *rasas* and *uparasas* possess no power or efficacy.
Of what nature is the power? It is "iron-slaying" (*lohaghnī*); the analysis of the compound is: that which slays iron (*loha*).

Furthermore, the substance (*sattva*) does not fall away as long as the bellows are not brought near or reached to the vicinity of the substance; therefore, the meaning is that there is no activation of the substance by a small fire.
Since the sattva fallen from *mākṣika* is red, soft, and equal to lead (*nāga*),
one should likewise strive with effort to bring about a state of softness even for *gandhāśman*. (GRht 10.9)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Having set aside the essence of copper pyrite (*mākṣika*), he speaks of the application of other essences, beginning with "red," etc. (GRhtCM 10.9:1).
Because such a substance— red, crimson, like lead, and equal to tin, soft and tender—

falls from *mākṣika* (vitriol) or emerges from *tāpya* (calamine), for that reason or by that method, one must with effort bring about the state of softness in *gandhāśman* (sulphur), so that even the sulphur becomes soft; this is the meaning.
START GRht 10.10 (Mākṣika:: Sattva:: Extraction):
Mākṣika [ore] should be well-enclosed with salt and sour substances, and then ground with acid according to the prescribed method.
When it is heated, it releases a morsel into an iron vessel, and it becomes a paste.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He describes the method for the essence of honey-ore (*mākṣika-sattva*) with the verse beginning "salt," etc.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_10.10:1): [Same as above]*

Mākṣika (pyrite) and tāpya (calamine), ground with salt and sour [juice]— the salt being primarily *saindhava* due to its preeminence and to accord with other texts— and with sour [juice] such as that of the *jambīra* fruit, and then, according to the prescribed method, roasted in fire with the aforementioned procedure using sour *jambīra* juice and so forth, it releases its essence (*sattva*); this is the ellipsis to be supplied from the connection with the preceding verse.
In this manner, the being who has fallen [into the womb] is to be grasped.
Even sulfur becomes soft by means of salt and sour [substances].
Furthermore, when heated in a hot iron vessel over a fire, it becomes a paste in an iron bowl; the meaning is that it takes the form of red-colored powder.
Indeed, when sattva is mixed with equal parts of tuttha and tāpyaja, it falls down.
Among those, the extraction of the essence (*satvapātana*) from abhra (mica), vaikrāntaka, kānta, and so forth, is like that of iron.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Regarding the phrase "tutthādi" and so on, it describes the extraction of the essence of tuttha and other such minerals.* *Commentary (GRhtCM 10.11:1): [Same as above]*

Tuttha is produced from *tuttha* and has a crest-like neck; therefore, it is equal to that which is born of heating (*tāpyaja*). This means that its extraction of essence (*satvapāta*) occurs according to the procedure for the essence of *mākṣika*.
"Completely mixed" means it has been thoroughly combined with the impurity (*tāpya*) and produced as equal in both color and softness; this is the meaning of "prepared."
A sentient being of such a kind falls into the state of a *tutthaka*.

Regarding "abhraka" and so forth: *abhraka* is well known; *vaikrānta* is *rasavaikrānta*; *kānta* is *cumbaka*, and so on. The meaning of "the essence (*tattva*) of these and others" in the context of the process of precipitating the leaf-essence (*patrasatvapātana*) is that it resembles iron, having the color of *muṇḍa* (raw iron). // GRhtCM_10.11:5 //
START GRht 10.12 (Svarṇamākṣika [?]; Extraction of the Essence [?])
Impregnated with the milk of Strīvajrī and impregnated with castor oil, it is blown [in the furnace] a hundred times; thus,
after three such cycles here, it becomes equal to copper and serves as a coloring agent for gold.
Furthermore, he states another method for gold-making (*mākṣika*) in the verse beginning with "strī" and so forth.

*Tāpya* (cinnabar) should be processed with the milk of a woman and a *vajrī*; "woman" means a female, and "*vajrī*" means *sehuṇḍa* (Euphorbia). One should process it with their milk and subject it to heating in a closed crucible (*gharmapuṭita*).
Furthermore, one should saturate it a hundred times, a hundred times, with castor oil.

Then, having been blown [in the furnace] three times, that golden *svarṇamākṣika* becomes its golden essence (*haima-sattva*), which is equal to copper in appearance and resembles copper; it is a coloring agent for mercury and also imparts its red color to gold.
START GRht 10.13 (Mākṣika and Rasaka: Extraction of the Essence; Precipitation)
Copper, having been processed with honey and castor oil that has been infused a hundred times with the juice of the plantain tree,
and having been subjected to three successive heatings (*trisantāpa*), releases its essence; and *rasaka* (calamine) does likewise through these same three heatings.
He states another method with the verse beginning "kadalī," and so forth.

Mākṣika mineral, having been heated and processed one hundred times with the juice of plantain (*kadalī*), and then thoroughly cooked together with honey and castor oil (*airaṇḍataila*), thus first saturated a hundred times with the juice of plantain and subsequently well-boiled with both honey and castor oil, releases its essence (*sattva*).
By means of what? By means of the three heats and the three types of blowing, performed three times.
In this way, both *rasaka* and *kharparaka* also release their essence (*satva*).
START GRht 10.14 (Minerals: *sattva*:: sublimation)

A bolus prepared from wool, borax, jaggery, lac, resin, and all the metallic minerals ground together with goat’s milk is indeed recommended for the process of extracting the essence (*sattva*). *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* Wool (*ūrṇā*) is the hair of a sheep; borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) is well known; jaggery (*guḍa*) is common; lac (*lākṣā*) is the resin of the *jatu* tree; resin (*sarjarasa*) is the exudation of the *śālmalī* tree. "All the metallic minerals" refers to iron and the others. These should be ground with goat’s milk and formed into a bolus. This is praised for the extraction of the essence.
