It is used as a flux (*saṃskāra*) for the purification of mercury. It should be applied to the crucible (*puṭa*) at the time of heating. It is said that this is the best among all fluxes. Thus ends the fourteenth verse.
Regarding the casting of the *satva*, he speaks of the *piṇḍī* (the ritual ball) in the verse beginning with "ūrṇā" and so forth.
Regarding "ūrṇā": *ūrṇā* is sheep's wool; *ṭaṅkaṇa* is borax; *saubhāgya* is sugar; *guḍa* is well-known as molasses; *pura* is bdellium; *lākṣā* is lac; *jatu* is shellac;

and *sarjarasa* is resin (*rāla*). With these—characterized by being all metallic ores or minor metals (*rasoparasa*) such as gold and the rest—ground together and then made into a ball with goat’s milk (*ajāpayas*), that ball is used in the process of extracting the essence (*sattvapātana*).
The Teacher is preeminent.
It certainly causes the essence (satva) of the ores, minerals, and secondary minerals to fall out.
START GRHT 10.15–17 (Minerals: *sattva*:: *pātana*)
Having carefully collected thirty palas of powdered *sattva-sambhāra*,
together with seven palas of *ṭaṅkaṇa* and three palas of *guñjā*.
Having mixed sesame powder, dregs, and fish— two parts each— with five *pala* of [the aforementioned substances],
one should form balls bound with wheat and saturate them repeatedly with the "five cows" (*gopañcaka*).
By means of the method of heating in a crucible with the intense fire of a bellows,
the essence of mercury (abhrasattva) falls down and likewise melts; in this same manner, all other metallic essences [behave].
He states another procedure, beginning with "cūrṇita" and so forth.

"Equal to the powdered essence": that which is powdered and ground is the *sattva*, the essential core; "equal to that" means equal to the *sattva* because of its purity—the remainder being the powder of metallic ores (*dhātu*), minerals (*rasa*), and secondary minerals (*uparasa*).
Having first collected such pure powder with care and devotion, one should add seven *palas* of borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*); the meaning is that one should combine it with seven *palas* of *saubhāgya*.

When thirty *pala* of purified powder have been prepared, seven *pala* of *saubhāgya* should be added; likewise, according to the procedure for *ṭaṅkaṇa*, one should further add three *pala* of *guñjā* and a quantity measuring three *pala* of *raktikā*. Thus it should be prepared.

With one *pala* each of sesame powder and dross—the powder being well-known as that of sesame, and the dross being the impurity of *muṇḍa* and other plants—with these two measured at one *pala* each, one should form a ball bound with wheat. This should be infused many times—that is, repeatedly—by means of the five products of a cow (*gopañcaka*), namely cow’s milk, clarified butter, curd, urine, and dung.
Having done what? Having stirred it with fish; that is to say, having mixed it by stirring with small aquatic creatures such as fish.

In a crucible or a retort, by means of the process of blowing and repeatedly lifting [the charge] with the fire of a bellows, that essence (*sattva*) falls out due to its prior connection with the *tāpya* (calamine) and other substances—this is the remainder of the sense.
Furthermore, the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*), the extract from mica, flows forth.
In the same way, by the aforementioned procedure, all the various essences fall for those not explicitly mentioned; this is the remainder of the sense.
START GRHT 11.1–2: Now, the extraction of the seed is commenced. (Gold pyrite:)
Just as the Gaṅgā, having taken up all rivers, enters the ocean and assumes its golden nature,
so too does [the mercury] enter the liquid [of the crucible], taking hold of it and assimilating the qualities of all metals.
That essence dissolves and merges into the crucible and turns into dross;
yet he was well-conducted, one who undertook noble deeds, wise, a revealer of true knowledge,
a knower of wealth and dharma, and a taker-away of the prosperity of his kinsmen.
First, he states the praise of gold, beginning with "having accepted," and so forth.

Having taken up all the qualities that are combined— that is, mixed— within all metals, within all minerals, the essence of gold and *svarṇamākṣika* enters into the mercury (*rasa*) in such a way that it becomes one with it, just as the Gaṅgā,
having accepted and embraced all rivers and streams, enters the ocean.
He states the section concerning the nature of the sentient being to be purified, beginning with "it decays," and so forth.

When that gold-like *tāpyasattva* (calamine essence) is mixed with *śulba* (copper), the *sattva* undergoes digestion (*jīryati*), meaning it attains the state of being assimilated (*jāraṇatvam āpnoti*) into the mercury (*rase*); this is the remainder of the sense.
When that being merges into the iron rod, it becomes dross, like the impurity of metal.
START GRh 11.2 (Suitable materials for the working of gold and silver)

In the processes of gold-making, that sattva should first be processed together with lead (trapu) for the purpose of gold; in the processes of silver-making, it should be processed with tin (tāra). This means one should carry out the extraction of the essence through the liquid medium in these operations.

Furthermore, one should cause [the mercury] to be processed together with tin (*trapu*) and lead (*vaṅga*) during the operations of transmutation (*tārakriyā*) and in silver-based works; the meaning is that lead and tin are recommended in all yellow and white operations.
START GRht 11.3 (The Preparation of a Seed)
Indeed, in the process of alchemy (*rasāyana*), solid mercury (*ghanasatva*) should be joined with sulfur in a binary compound (*dvaṃdvaka*),
having been processed with realgar, orpiment, yellow ochre, and vermilion, which have been infused with the application of the "red group" (*raktagaṇa*) of minerals.
He explains the application of the essence of mica with the words "the essence of clouds" (*ghanasatva*), and so forth.

Indeed—whether for emphasis or as a poetic ornament—the "essence of clouds" (ghanasattva), which is mica, and copper (tāmra) should be joined in pairs for the purpose of *rasāyana* (alchemy) to destroy old age and disease; that is, mica and copper should be combined. Furthermore, realgar (*girijatu*), honey-ore (*mākṣika*), red ochre (*gairika*), and vermilion (*darada*) should be processed by being soaked with the "falling" (*pāta*) of the "red group" (*raktagaṇa*)—meaning their infusion or application—and then heated in a closed crucible (*gharmapuṭita*).
Girija is *śilājatu*, and *mākṣika* is well known; *darada* is *hiṅgula*. It should be understood from the following verse that one should reduce these to the state of seed (*bīja*).
START GRht 11.4 (Gold:: Seed):
Soft copper that is beautiful and of dense essence, along with dead lead, sharp [iron], and gold.
One should leave a residue of seed by means of vermilion, mica, orpiment, and honey through sowing.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another procedure beginning with "mṛdula" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_11.4:1): [He states] another method starting with "mṛdula" etc.*

Soft copper known as Nepalese, iron of the *kānta* variety, the essence of mica (*ghanasattva*), again the essence of mica (*abhrasāra*), dead lead (*mṛtanāga*), tin (*sīsaka*), steel (*tīkṣṇaloha*), and gold (*kanaka* or *hema*)—these three are the "seeds" (*bīja*); and the triad beginning with copper (*śulba*) is also designated as "seed.

Through sowing (*vāpa*) with vermilion (*darada*), realgar (*śilā*), orpiment (*tāla*), and honey-ore (*mākṣika*)—vermilion being *hiṅgula*, realgar being *manohvā*, and orpiment being *haritāla*—by means of these [the process is performed].

Having performed the sowing, there is a casting [of the mixture] into fire-heated [substances]; therefore, one should leave a residue of the seed. The meaning is that one should leave a residue of both seeds—the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) and gold (*hema*). When this has been done, whatever remains is the "seed" (*bīja*).
START GRht 11.5 (Gold, Silver :: Seed):
Either dead lead or tin, or copper with a high proportion of essential essence, or gold;
All that very [substance] is blown [into a crucible] by means of a mountain [of ash] or by superior purificatory blowings.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method, beginning with "the dead lead" (mṛtaṃ nāgam).* *Commentary (GRhtCM_11.5:1): [He states] another procedure, beginning with "the dead lead," etc.*
Lead, tin, dead lead, dead tin, copper killed by the addition of red minerals,
or iron, or the essence of iron, silver, and gold— each of these, or all of them together,
should be smelted individually with mountain-resin (*śilājatu*) after excessive purification, through the addition of cinnabar, realgar, and yellow orpiment.
"One should leave a seed-remainder"—this is the connection with what precedes.
START GRht 11.6–7 (Gold: Seed [bīja]):
The red class, or the yellow, namely *mākṣika*, *rājāvarta*, and also *vimala*.
Or one may use any one of these: red ochre, realgar, earth, sulphur, or orpiment.
Only when it has been processed (*nirvyūḍha*) does the mercury (*rasa*) take up impurities such as redness (*rāga*) and so forth, and thereby undergoes bondage (*bandha*).
Just as a seed for a chain (*śṛṅkhalābīja*) is produced from dead metals, secondary minerals (*uparasa*), and so on, once they have been processed.

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [The commentary explains that just as base materials must first be purified and transmuted before they can serve as the basis for a higher product, so too the mercury must be processed to remove its impurities before it can be bound.]
The red group consists of pomegranate, *kiṃśuka*, and so forth; or the yellow group is as follows:
*kiṃśuka*, *karṇikāra*, and the two types of turmeric (*haridrā*);
this is declared to be the yellow category for the application of the King of Rasas.

Either honey (mākṣika), or pyrite (tāpya), or rājāvarta—rājāvarta being called *lājavarada* in the vernacular—or else pure silver pyrite (*tāramākṣika*); one of these, or all of them together, [is processed] with red ochre (*gairika*), realgar (*kunaṭī*), earth (*kṣiti*), sulphur (*gandhaka*), and "sky-goer" (*khaga*). Red ochre is well known; realgar is *manohvā*; earth is *sphaṭakī*; sulphur is well known; and "sky-goer" is *kāsīsa*. By means of these [the following is done].

When the mercury has been processed by these very aforementioned [substances], it takes on coloration (*rāga*) and so forth—where "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be understood to include *sāraṇa* (purification)—and it undergoes binding again; that is, it attains fixation once more through dead metals, minor minerals (*uparasa*), and the like. "Dead metals" refers to those metals which are ores, and "minor minerals" refers to sulfur and the like; by "and the like" (*ādya*), the primary juices (*rasa*) are also included. [The mercury becomes fixed] by those [substances] having been processed.
The meaning is that once the seed-syllable of the chain has been formed, it becomes increasingly more pleasing.
START GRHT 11.8 (The seed-mantra for the coloring and binding of mercury):
By means of iron rods, those called *advandva*, and those called *saṃkara*.
When processed with mercury and metals, it becomes suitable for the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Regarding the phrase "with mercury and metals": mercury refers to vaikrānta and others; metals refer to the well-known ores. With which [mercury and metals] is it processed? By those [mercury and metals] characterized as follows...*
"By all those called non-dual, having a single essence, or by mixtures (*saṃkara*); 'a mixture is a heap of refuse,' so says Amara.
When this has been accomplished, the meaning is that the seed is fit for the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*)."
This seed, sown in the red class [of mercury] by him who has performed the sowing,
merely by being processed through *cārita* and *jārita*, colors and binds the *sūta*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another specific injunction, beginning with "the seed" (*bījam*), etc. (GRhtCM 11.9:1).
One should sprinkle this perfected seed into the red group [of syllables].
Furthermore, it was one where a sowing had been made—that is, a sowing (vāpa) which had been performed—by that host of blood-drinkers.

Furthermore, that seed, having merely been processed by conduct (*cāritra*), and the mercury (*sūta*) which has been previously and subsequently processed, dyes it—that is, it causes it to attain color (*rāga*) and binds it.
START GRht 11.10 (bīja:: further processing):
But for all [the metals], [the purification] is performed by means of red oil, purified dead iron, mercury, and so forth.
Sow the seeds and perform the sprinkling with red oil.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "with red [oil]" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_11.10:1): [This refers to] that very point.*

"Raktasneha" refers to the group of red substances such as pomegranate (*dāḍima*), *kiṃśuka*, and so forth, and "sneha" refers to oils such as those from *kaṅguṇī* and others. Purified by these, the metals and the *rasas* and *uparasas* that have subsequently been killed—by means of these, perform the sowing (*vāpa*) of all the previously mentioned seeds; the word "in mercury" (*rase*) is understood as the remainder, or else "in blood" (*rakta*) meaning in a red-colored substance, or "in oil" (*snehe*) meaning in the category of oily substances. This is the twofold procedure for sprinkling (*niṣeka*). 11.10:2.
START GRHT 11.11 (Silver:
Seeds):
Tin and mica, mica and silver, white stone and sulphur, and white tin and mercury;
Copper, struck by white silver, becomes beautiful when the vanadium-impurity has been fully extracted.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
The seeds for the yellow process have been stated; now, he states the seeds for the white process beginning with "vaṅga" and so forth.*

"Vaṅga, raṅga, and abhra"—that is, tin (vaṅga), lead (raṅga), and mica (abhra), which is the sky (gagana); these [are used] for the sake of the seed-syllable (bīja)—this is the remainder [of the sense].

Furthermore, one should properly kill and reduce to ash tin and silver using "tāra-abhra"— where *abhra* is mica, *tāra* is silver, and *śailamala* is bitumen (*śilājatu*). Then, one should likewise kill and reduce to ash copper and mercury using "red gold" (*rakta-hema*) and "white silver" (*sita-tāra*), that is, by means of *tāpya* (cinnabar) and *mākṣika* (pyrite).
Furthermore, one should prepare that which has been processed with silver, tin, and mica.
The meaning is that all of this is to be employed in the operations involving mercury and the transmutation of metals (*tārakriyā*).
This procedure for the removal [of defects] has been revealed for the sake of pacifying all faults;
likewise, even for seeds, it is appropriate first to apply a thick essence.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
With the words "nirvāhaṇa" and so forth, he states that in the seed [mantra], the essence of mica (*abhrasatva*) is primary. GRhtCM_11.12:1.
For what purpose is this? It is for the pacification of all defects—that is to say, for the destruction of the entire collection of defects such as the [three] humors (dhātu) and so forth.

In this manner, according to the procedure for the sublimation of the minerals, one should perform the sublimation of the *bījas* into the liquid; in the sublimation of all *bījas*, the essence of mica (*abhrakasattva*) is to be sublimed first.
(START GRht 11.13: Crucible for *bījanirvāhaṇa*)

Having fashioned a crucible from the ashes of goat bones in the shape of a small bowl, with thick perforations for the insertion of leaves, and having applied a coating of borax, poison, and *guñjā* seeds; (GRht 11.13) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [The crucible] should be made from the ashes of goat bones, shaped like a small vessel (*mallaka*), provided with thick holes for the placement of [herbal] leaves, and smeared with a paste of borax, poison, and *guñjā* seeds.
He states the procedure for the removal [of the obstacle] in the verse beginning with "chāga" and so forth.
Having prepared a crucible of this kind, one should perform the extraction of the metal; this is the remainder of the sense.
"Of what nature? [It is] a crucible fashioned from goat-bone ashes; "goat" means *bast*, and it refers to that crucible which has been made or fashioned from the ashes of its bones.
Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is shaped like a water jar and resembles a cow's udder.
Furthermore, of what specific quality? Dense-holed, meaning possessing thick apertures.

Furthermore, "having a coating made of ṭaṅkaṇa, poison, and guñjā" means that which has a coating (*lepa*) made from those: *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), *viṣa* (poison), *guñjā* (the red berry, *raktikā*). *Note: This is a translation of the commentary on verse 11.13 of the *Garuḍapurāṇa*, Chapter on the Science of Horses (Aśvavaidyaka).*
The meaning is that such a crucible (mūṣā) should be employed for the process of smelting (dalayoga) and the joining of leaves (patramelana).
START GRHT 12.1 Now, the union of couples (*dvandvamelana*) will be explained.
(The motivation for *dvandvamelana*)
As long as the metals do not unite with one another among all beings as limbs and sub-limbs,
so long the mercury does not pervade the entire body through the application of dual union.
By the play of his speech, he indeed makes the world imitate nectar;
for the quality of being a man himself is like nectar when it rests upon a double-tongued serpent—thus there is no fault.
Now, he explains the method for the application of the pairs (dvandvayoga) with the words beginning with "yāvat" and so forth.
The word "yāvat" is used here in the sense of a limit.

Metals such as gold and others do not unite by way of being limbs of a serpent—that is, by way of becoming the body of a snake—because they are easily accessible; they do not attain the state of a single body.
In all sentient beings, within the essences of clouds and so forth, metals do not attain unity without a means due to the hardness of the sentient being.
Therefore, for that reason, the taste does not circulate throughout all the limbs.
By what means do metals unite with sentient beings through the application of pairs, such as mercury (*darada*) and so forth, or molasses, borax, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and so on?
START GRht 12.2 (Metals: Preparation for Dvandva):
Iron that has been sown with any one of the following—mākṣīka, rasaka, sasyaka, or darada—[is prepared].
It abandons its dense state and, when well-heated, merges with the *sattva*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He describes the procedure for the merging of the *sattva* with the words beginning with "mākṣika" and so forth.*
Metal refers to gold and the like.

Mākṣika, tāpya, rasaka, kharparika, sasyaka, capala, darada, and hiṅgula— by means of this quartet, or by any one of these, or by the aforementioned *rasa* or *uparasa*, [the substance] is infused (*vāpita*), well-blasted (*sudhmāta*), and blown with excellent technique (*śobhanayuktyā*); thus, it abandons its solid state and merges into the essence (*sattva*).
START GRht 12.3 (The Union of Pairs:
Preparation)
With jaggery, borax, lac, resin of the *sarja* tree, and *dhātakī*, ground together with breast milk,
it should be applied in combination for the purpose of rejuvenation (*rasāyana*).
He states another method, beginning with "guḍa" and so forth.

This iron, which has been subjected to the process of pairing (*dvaṃdvita*) and made into a compound (*dvaṃdvīkṛta*), when combined with mercury (*sattva*), should be employed in alchemy (*rasāyana*) for the destruction of old age and disease.
He explains by means of which dual unions (*dvandvamelāpaka*) it is "made dual" with the words beginning with *guḍa*, etc.

Having prepared these dual-unifying (dvandvamelāpaka) agents— namely, molasses (guḍa), the well-known resin *guggulu*, borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), *saubhāgya*, lac (*lākṣā*), *jatu*, and *sarjarasa* (resin)— together with *dhātakī* (the well-known flower), which has been ground and rubbed with *strīstanya* (female breast milk); // GRhtCM_12.3:4 //
START GRht 12.4 (The Union of Pairs):
With wool, borax, mountain-born lac, the juice from the ears, eye-secretion, indragopa insects, and crabs;
When ground with the milk of a woman, all [metals] indeed unite within the crucibles; for the metals, it is implied, become one with the essence (satva) within the crucibles.
By which of these? By wool and so forth.

With *ūrṇā* (wool), *pratīta* (well-known), *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), *saubhāgya* (alum), *girijatu* (bitumen), *śilājatu* (bitumen), the ear-wax and eye-secretion of a human, *indragopaka* (a specific type of insect), and *karkaṭaka* (crab)—of which Amara states: "The crab is *karkaṭaka*, and *kulīra* is also *karkaṭaka*"—with these [substances].
By what means? By those ground with the milk of a woman—that is, by a paste made with female breast-milk; thus, all three are "yogas for the union of couples. // GRhtCM_12.4:4 //
START GRht 12.5 (The binding of mercury by means of two parts each of *rasavaikrānta* and gold)
In this manner, mercury and vaikrāntaka, combined in a binary compound (dvandvānvita) in equal parts with gold,
are processed; by that means, the essence (satva) is extracted, and through it, the mercury attains fixation (bandha).
He states another method, beginning with "rasa" and so forth.
When prepared according to the method thus described, the mercury-vaikrāntaka, conjoined with its own pair—that is, accompanied by its respective pair—merges and abandons its separate state.
With what is it equal? With gold.

That essence of *rasavaikrānta*, having been processed together with gold, causes the mercury to undergo fixation (*bandha*) through that combination of the essence of *rasavaikrānta* and gold; it becomes bound. START GRht 12.6 (The Fusion of Pairs)
In all cases of dual affliction (*dvandva*), [the seed-mantra] is prescribed with *girija*, *tuttha*, *līlātaka*, *indragopa*, and so forth;
the seed-mantra should be prepared with the earwax of a buffalo and other such substances, along with *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), *ālaka*, and poisons.
Now, he states another specific rule, beginning with "praśastam" and so forth.
Such a seed is praised; where [is there] any duality at all?
Furthermore, having performed these [rites], the seed-syllable (bīja) would become auspicious.

By what [means]? By those beginning with *girijatu*, *lelītaka*, and *indragopa*. *Girijatu* is bitumen (*śilājatu*); *lelītaka* is sulfur (*gandhaka*); *indragopa* is the *surendragopa*, a specific type of insect. [The phrase] "by those beginning with these" refers to those for whom these are the first. (GRhtCM 12.6:4) Not only by these, but also by the ear-wax of a buffalo and so forth. "Ear-wax of a buffalo" is that for which it is the first; by the word "and so forth" (*ādya*), the impurities of the nose and eyes are also included. (GRhtCM 12.6:5)

Furthermore, with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *āla*, and *viṣa*—where *ṭaṅkaṇa* is *saubhāgya*, *āla* is *haritāla*, and *viṣa* is that which grows from a bulb—the connection is that a binary union (*dvandvamelāpa*) occurs when these are ground together. This is the further relationship [of the verse]. (GRhtCM 12.6:6) START GRht 12.7 (The Binary Union)
Even with these combined with honey, tāpyaka gold is fused with the star-cloud (tārābhra) by means of castor oil,
ṭaṅkaṇa, kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar, and indragopa insects.
He states another method with the words beginning "madhu" (honey), etc.
By means of these aforementioned formulations combined with honey—that is, mixed with *kṣaudra*—silver (*tārābhra*, the "sky" of silver) becomes unified.
Furthermore, this pair—tāpya gold and mākṣika gold—is also combined.

It does not only unite through the previously mentioned yogas; furthermore, it certainly unites in pairs when combined with these: castor oil (eraṇḍataila), borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar (śilā), and indragopa.

Castor oil is the fat of the enemy of wind (vātāri); ṭaṅkaṇa is saubhāgya; kaṅkuṣṭha is viraṅga; śilā is manohvā; and indragopa is a particular kind of insect. By making a pair with these along with honey, it necessarily unites.
START GRht 12.8 (The alchemical amalgamation of mercury and gold)
Having ground purified gold together with mercury and *abhra* (mica) in equal proportions,
one should prepare any one of the previously mentioned pairs [of substances] as a quarter-part.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the procedure for that [alchemical process] with the words "by the Sūta," and so forth. GRhtCM_12.8:1.

First, having ground pure gold together with mercury (rasa) and thoroughly rubbed it, one should then add an equal amount of mica (abhraka); having combined that mica with the gold, one should subsequently prepare any one of the previously mentioned "binary compounds" (dvandva) in a quarter-portion— that is, by the fourth part— such as the aforementioned binary compounds consisting of castor oil and so forth, or mica-bark and so forth.
And one should apply a pair [of practices] from among those others as well.
START GRHT 12.9-10 (The Melāpana of Gold and Abhra):
Having added purified mākṣika, twice the amount of the mercury, the uparasa, and the gold;
One should grind it with the juice of *kākamācī* and the root of *rambhā*.
"This prepared mass, consisting of gold and mica, melts in a diamond crucible.
He states another method beginning with "rasa" and so forth.

Among the *rasas* and *uparasas*, such as *vaikrānta* and sulfur, one should take pure, faultless *mākṣika* (sulphur ore) and give it twice the amount of gold—that is, having given gold doubled by the *mākṣika*.
This [mixture] of *rasa*, *uparasa*, and so forth, should be rubbed with the fresh juice (*svarasa*) of *kākamācī* (black nightshade); one should perform the rubbing.
And by "rambhākanda" is meant also by "kadalīkanda."
One should form this preceding medicinal paste into a ball in the shape of a cow-dung pellet.
By this procedure, golden mica and golden calamine are obtained.
Where? In the adamantine crucible.
Thus it is said: "Three parts of clay, two parts of hemp and lac, one part of burnt husks, stones, and the like,
and half a part of dross— having broken these into pieces, one should indeed prepare a diamond-crucible for the extraction of the essence."
Thus [it is said]. (GRhtCM 12.9:8)
Thus, the essences (*sattva*) of space and the other elements merge together with the sun, the moon, and the sharp [metal] (*tīkṣṇa*). (GRht 12.10)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Thus, by this method, together with the sun, moon, and sharp [metals]—the sun being copper (*tāmra*), the moon being silver (*rūpya*), and the sharp being a type of iron (*lohajāti*)—the essences (*sattva*) beginning with the sky (*gagana*), namely the quintessences of mica (*abhra*) and so forth, are combined.
This concludes the pair of verses.
START GRHT 12.11 (The procedure for the *saṅkarabīja*s):
"The procedure for the *saṅkarabīja*s," and so forth, by means of the union with the being of space (*gaganasattva*).
However, in all cases, another [substance] must necessarily be employed in conjunction with *mākṣika*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He states the section concerning the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) with the verse beginning "In the mixture," etc. *Commentary (GRhtCM 12.11:1):* [Same as above].
Even for those who possess the seeds of confusion, there must be an instruction regarding what is to be done; that is to say, an instruction on the purpose of action.

The aforementioned [passage] beginning with "thus" and so forth means that, furthermore, by means of the *sattva* of the sky (*gagana-sattva*), one should join another substance together with the *sattva* of mica (*abhraka-sattva*) through the application of *mākṣika*; the clarification is that *mākṣika* does not exist together with the *sattva* of mica.
First, the mouth of *kāntaloha* is the meeting point of all *sattvas*.
Honey combined with the previously mentioned paste, along with mercury, lead, and realgar; GRh 12.12.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, concerning the section on couples (*dvandva*), in the *Rasahṛdayatantra* composed by the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants who are supreme swans (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
"The beloved," and so forth.* GRhtCM_12.12:1

Lead (nāga) killed with honey, realgar (tāla), yellow orpiment (haritāla), mica (śilā), and blue vitriol (manohvā)— these, together with the previously mentioned paste, along with the paste of the mercury-group (rasa) and the secondary minerals (uparasa) and so forth,
should be applied to the surface of the magnetite (kānta). In the absence of the essence of mica (abhra-sattva), one should provide the essence of magnetite (kānta-sattva).
Or, in the absence of a beloved being, one should cause sharp iron to be given.
Thus. (GRhtCM 12.12:2)
Mākṣīka, kānta, and tīkṣṇa; tīkṣṇa, mākṣīka, and abhraka are the [minor] seeds (bīja).
Mākṣīka, kānta, śulba, tīkṣṇa, and abhraka are the great seeds (mahābīja).
In spring, the honey-bee indeed joyfully utters a sweet sound upon the honey;
even an excellent sound attains beauty when it accompanies the company of the virtuous—does it ever fail to reach its full charm? (GRhtCM 13.1)
Among the seeds of the *saṃkara* [mixture], he states those known as the "great seeds" with the words beginning with *mākṣika*, and so forth.

This triad is the great seed (*mahābīja*). What is this? It is *mākṣīka*, *kānta*, and *tīkṣṇa*; that is, *mākṣīka* (sulphide), *kānta* (magnetite), and *śulba* (copper); and *tīkṣṇa* (steel), *abhraka* (mica), *mākṣīka* (sulphide), *tāpya* (calamine), *kānta* (magnetite), *cumbaka* (lodestone), *śulba* (copper), *tīkṣṇa* (steel), and *abhraka* (mica)—the sky.
This triad is the seed, the great seed; each of these three groups is individually designated as "great."
There is a distinction here:
I shall now declare the ripening of the seed for the purpose of the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of mercury.
This sequence of the thread is purified by a seed that has been fully digested.
Thus. // GRhtCM_13.1:4 //
And each individual substance, by virtue of being a constituent part, is designated by the term "seed."
Mākṣīka, kānta-iron, and copper; copper, abhraka, and mākṣika;
kānta-iron, abhraka, and mākṣika; and tāpyaka, copper, and abhraka—this is the great seed (mahābīja).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "mākṣīka" and so forth. GRhtCM_13.2:1.
Mākṣīka, kānta, and śulba; mākṣīka is tāpya, kānta is cumbaka, and śulba is tāmra—this too is to be known as a great seed (mahābīja).

Furthermore, copper, mica, and vitriol; again, magnetite, mica, and vitriol; magnetite, loadstone, mica (gagana), and vitriol (mākṣika); likewise, iron pyrite, copper, and mica—this also should be known as a great seed (*mahābīja*).
Honey-processed sharp copper and sharp copper with mica constitute the "great seed" (mahābīja).
Honey-processed kāntaloha and gold, as well as gold-colored honey-processed ore, constitute the "great seed."
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "mākṣīka" and so forth. GRhtCM_13.3:1.
Mākṣīka, tīkṣṇa, and śulba; mākṣika is *tāpya*, tīkṣṇa is a type of *sāraloha* (cast iron), and śulba is copper.
Furthermore, *tīkṣṇa-śulbābhrakam* refers to *tīkṣṇa* (steel), *sāra* (essence), *śulba* (copper), and *abhraka* (mica); *gagana* means the sky.
Furthermore, *mākṣīkakāntakanakam* refers to *mākṣika* (sulphuride of iron), *tāpya* (cinnabar), *kānta* (magnetite), *kāntapāṣāṇa* (loadstone), and *kanaka* (gold).

Furthermore, *kanakāruṇamākṣika* consists of four components: *kanaka* (gold), *aruṇa* (copper), and *mākṣika* (golden pyrite). This quartet is the "great seed" (*mahābīja*), meaning the most excellent seed. Thus, each of these four is designated as a "great seed."
Honey, sharp [iron], silver, silver-copper,
and honey-silver; likewise, magnetite, copper-tin, copper-lead, and gold.
And he states that very point: "honey, copper, and silver.
(GRhtCM 13.4:1)
Mākṣika, tāpya, tīkṣṇa, sāra, tāra, and rūpya.
Furthermore, regarding "silver, copper, and pyrites": according to the aforementioned procedure, *tāra* is silver, *aruṇa* is copper, and *mākṣika* is *tāpya* (pyrite).
Furthermore, when the beloved is a kissing and pervasive locus, the copper, lead, gold, and pyrite that have been employed [are transformed]. // GRhtCM_13.4:4 //
"Api" means with certainty.

Copper, mica, pyrite, and gold—copper (*śulba*) being *tāmra*, mica (*abhra*) being *gagana*, pyrite (*tāpya*) being *svarṇamākṣika*, and gold (*kāñcana*) being *hema*—these four should be known as the "great seeds" (*mahābīja*).
The connection with the term "great seed" applies to each one individually; this is the clarification.
One should heat together magnetite, moonstone, mica, copper, and pyrite;
or else gold, mica, copper, and pyrite; or even gold, mica, copper, and pyrite. (GRht 13.5)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī): And he states that [mercury] as "to be heated by the moon-like lover" (kāntendusasyatāpya). GRhtCM_13.5:1.
Kānta, kāntapāṣāṇa, indu, tāra, sasyaka, capala, tāpya, and svarṇamākṣika.

Furthermore, *kānta*, *abhraka*, *tīkṣṇa*, and *mākṣika*; likewise, gold (*hema*), mica (*abhra*), copper (*śulba*), and *tāpya*; or again, gold (*hema*), mica (*abhra*), copper (*śulba*), and *mākṣika*—or alternatively, gold (*kanaka*), mica (*gagana*), copper (*śulba*), and *mākṣika* (which is *tāpya*)—these four together are to be known as the "great seed" (*mahābīja*).
And the meaning of the sound [of the word *bīja*] is that it is a designation for each individual substance.
Cinnabar, mica, copper, and iron filings, along with the seed of *saṅkara*, [weighing] sixty-four [units].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [This refers to the ingredients for the preparation of mercury.]
And he says that very thing in the verse beginning with "kāntā" and so forth.
Kānta, abhra, śulba, tāpya, kānta, cumbaka, abhraka, gagana, śulba, tāmra, and tāpya—mākṣika—is also known as the great seed (mahābīja).
If, among these great seeds, the seed of mixture were to be designated as a "seed" for each individual substance, then the meaning is that it would amount to sixty-four [seeds].
START GRh 13.7 (The Great Seed: Production)

Having first performed the prescribed combination for all the seeds, that seed which has been melted a hundred times in fire is indeed pure. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* This refers to the purification of mercury (*pārada*). "All the seeds" refers to the eight seeds such as mica (*abhraka*) and the rest. "Prescribed combination" means the aforementioned method of mixing with sulfur (*gandhaka*) and so forth. "Melted a hundred times in fire" means it has been processed by being repeatedly heated in fire until it can no longer be consumed by the flames; this is the purified seed. *Note: The term "bīja" here primarily denotes mercury, though in alchemical contexts it may refer to various mineral "seeds" used in transmutation.*
He states the method for the seed-syllables with the words "of all," and so forth.

First, at the outset, having performed the combination—the joining together in one—of all the seeds as described, namely the sixty-four substances possessing the aforementioned names; that which has been thus combined and melted in fire becomes the perfected seed (*bīja*) known as "hundred-fold purified" (*śatavāpya*), provided it is accomplished with effort. This is the meaning of the words.
START GRHT 13.8 (Cāraṇa, Garbhadruti, and Bāhyadruti are necessary for bandhana):
If the solid essence does not fall [into the crucible], or if the seeds do not melt within the womb [of the crucible].
And there is no conjunction with external liquefaction; how then is the mercury bound here?
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the causes for the binding of mercury with the words "na" and so forth.*

If the solid essence (*ghanasattva*), which is the core of mica (*abhrakasāra*), does not fall into or reach the interior of the womb (*garbha*)— that is, the interior of mercury (*rasodara*)— or if the seeds mentioned in this chapter, such as *mākṣika*, *kānta*, *śulba*, and so forth, do not liquefy, then there can be no external fluxion (*bāhyadruti*), nor the application (*yoga*) of that fluxion for the purpose of melting and blending with mercury. For that reason, how could mercury (*sūta*) [accomplish its purpose] in this process if this [fluxion] were absent?
It is bound and assumes solidity.
The intention is that the mercury (sūta) is invariably bound by means of both internal liquefaction (garbhadruti) and external liquefaction (bāhyadruti).
START GRht 14.1 (The production of gold: the preparation of mercury)
Furthermore, from that very same seed which has been consumed by the fire of samādhi, the transformation must be brought about;

for it is from that instrument (karaṇa) that gold is indeed produced. (GRht 14.1) *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* The word "furthermore" (*ca*) indicates an additional point. From that very same seed which has been burnt—that is, rendered devoid of its own nature—by the fire of samādhi, the transformation (*āvartana*) must be performed. That means [the transformation] must be accomplished by means of that very instrument from which gold is truly born. This is because the seed of mercury, when burnt by the fire of samādhi, becomes the cause of the production of gold. Therefore, one should perform the transformation by means of that very instrument. (GRht 14.1)
In autumn, the autumnal cloud rains; in the rainy season, the rain-cloud of the monsoon pours;
and in the springtime, the cuckoo, with its excellent speed, shines constantly.
He explains what arises from the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of the seed (*bīja*) with the words beginning "samādī" and so forth.

"Equal" means the same as the *sūta* (mercury); "more than equal" (*adhi*) means exceeding that by an immeasurable amount. The "matured seed" (*jīrṇa-bīja*) is the seed that has attained digestion; with that very same matured seed, the process of rotation (*āvarta*) must be performed. Thus, it is called "rotation. // GRhtCM_14.1:3 //
What is that? It is the process by which gold is indeed produced; it is the instrument of that process, the means of its production.
It is evident that when mercury has been matured through meditative concentration, it becomes gold by means of its application upon silver and other metals.

START Gṛhya-sūtra 14.2–9 (The seed of the *rasa*: production) 2. When the moon enters the asterism Puṣya, one should have the seeds of the *rasa* sown by a woman who has bathed after her courses. 3. Having performed the rites up to the pouring of water, he should place [the seeds] in a new vessel with a lid. 4. He should cover them with a cloth and keep them in a secret place until they sprout. 5. When they have sprouted, he should perform the rites up to the pouring of water. 6. He should offer a sacrifice to the herbs and to the *rasa*. 7. He should offer oblations of clarified butter with the verses addressed to Soma and Rudra. 8. He should give a cow as a sacrificial fee. 9. This is the production of the *rasa*.

Having caused [the ingredients] to flow into the vessel for the weapon with the foot of perfume, one should add the mercury; and having ground the medicinal herbs with their own juices, one should make pills. GRht_14.2 //
Having placed that pill on an iron plate and dried it in the shade,
one should cover it with a small iron dish and seal it very firmly.
One should coat [the vessel] with clay moistened with salt and make it very firm in order to block the smoke;
having placed well-compacted charcoal within, one should heat it with the fire of two bellows until it is smokeless.
This continues until the pill becomes red when blown; then, having removed the coals and ascertained that the crucible has become naturally cool— GRht_14.5.
Then, having repeatedly extracted [the mercury] from the crucible, the essence should be taken;
this king of dead mercury becomes like a ball when blown upon easily.
The mercury from *śikhigalatā* should be intensely heated with *kāca* and *ṭaṃkaṇa*;
then one should add tin three times in succession, and lead in very small quantities.
Thereafter, the seed-essence (rasabīja) should be joined with gold; it causes the binding of mercury.
He states the procedure for the killing of mercury, beginning with the words "having been melted," and so forth.
In the phrase "śastrapātre," the locative case is used in the sense of a proximate substratum (*aupaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*) with respect to the sharp metal vessel.

One should give the mercury (*sūtaka*) by means of the "fragrant foot," which is a division into one-fourth part of the fragrance; the remainder [of the instruction] is that it should be melted by fire once it has been placed upon the upper part of that vessel.
Furthermore, one should grind the medicinal herbs with their own fresh juices— just as described in other texts—
until the paste becomes like collyrium; thereafter, [one should add] the regulators such as *śatāvarī*, *kandukī*, *sudhā*, and so forth.
Thus. GRhtCM 14.2–7:4.
Having crushed and ground the ingredients beginning with *śatāvarī* with their own juices, one should form pills the size of jujube fruits (*badara*).
And he said that very thing, beginning with "having established," and so forth.

Having placed that aforementioned pill, dried in the shade, upon an iron plate or a surgical vessel, one should cover it again with a small iron bowl— that small iron bowl which is smaller than the previously mentioned iron plate— and seal it firmly and tightly,
as will be described hereafter. This is the implied meaning.
And he says that very thing, beginning with "Lavaṇa," and so forth.

One should coat that aforementioned small iron pan very firmly with clay moistened with salt— namely, clay mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*) or the like and sprinkled with water— for the purpose of blocking the smoke, so that no smoke should escape from the apparatus.

Furthermore, having placed very firm charcoal of *khadira* wood and other such trees, one should indeed blow the fire with the flame of two bellows—that is, with a dual fire—according to the connection with the following verse.
When what is present? When smoke is absent; when what is present? When taste is present, being devoid of the emission of smoke.
And he says that very thing, beginning with "tāvat" and so forth.

The aforementioned iron *śarāvikā*, smeared with the *sandhi* [cement], should be smelted for that duration until it becomes a *khoṭikā*—that is, one possessing a red luster and red radiance, having the very form of a *khoṭa*.
This is what is meant by *khoṭikā*.

Immediately after that, considering and knowing the bowl to be naturally cool and inherently cold, one should remove the coals and set them aside; having dug up the bowl, the essence is to be taken—this is the remainder [of the meaning], as connected to the following verse. He says this in the words beginning with "utkhanya" (having dug up).
Immediately after that, having repeatedly dug up and forcibly extracted the small iron bowl previously described, the mercury (rasa) or quicksilver (sūta) should be taken.
"Utkhanyotkhanya" (digging up again and again) is either due to its extreme hardness or is an intensive repetition (*vīpsā*) used out of great care.
From what crucible (kaṭorikā) should this king of dead mercury (mṛtasūtarāja) be known to have thus arisen? // GRhtCM_14.2-7:19 //
And being thus inflated by heat, it becomes like a ball within the *vajramūṣā* (adamant vessel); this is the remainder of the sense.

Glass is well-known; from that, borax (ṭaṅkaṇa) and saubhāgya [are obtained]. Then, the mercury, having been heated beyond its limits, becomes "of one taste" (ekarasa), which means it attains a state of equilibrium (samarasa).

The analysis of the compound *śikhigalatām* is "those which drip from the crest (*śikhin*) of the peacock (*śikhi*)," referring to the minerals that drip from the peacock's crest. When the essence (*rasa*) has thus been liquefied, one should add three parts of tin (*vaṅga*) and lead (*raṅga*). Then, after the addition of tin, one should gradually add lead (*nāga*) and antimony (*sīsaka*) by giving them in very small amounts.
And he says "that [he will explain] later," and so forth.
Subsequently, after the addition of three parts of lead, the mercury-seed—the great seed—should be joined with gold. What kind of great seed becomes when combined with gold?
And having also prepared a pill with mercury extracted from cinnabar and with regulating medicinal herbs, [one should administer it]. (GRht 14.8)
Having thus suppressed the fumes, the wise one should perform the killing of the mercury.

Furthermore, using *tālaka* (haritāla) which binds the mercury and bestows the binding of *pārada*, and by means of the previously mentioned *niyāmaka* herbs such as *śatāvarī* and others, one should form a pill; having formed it, one should suppress the fumes—that is, ensure that the fumes are restrained.

By a wise person, one who possesses intelligence and knows the essence of taste, the "killing" of the mercury (rasamāraṇa) should be performed according to this method; that is to say, the binding of mercury (pāradabandha) should be accomplished.
Alternatively, mercury may be perfected by means of stone or through the application of *mākṣika*.
Or else, by the obstruction of smoke from those two, it may arise as white in color.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth to state something further.*

Alternatively, by means of another method—having prepared it with *śilā* (realgar) and *manohvā* (calamine), or having effected a combination with *mākṣika* (pyrite) and *tāpya* (cinnabar)—the *sūta* (mercury) processed like the *tālaka* (orpiment) compound shall become white in color. By what means? By "smoke-obstruction" (*dhūmarodha*), or by an application of rock-salt (*saindhava*) and moist clay (*ārdrāmṛd*), or by both of these [realgar and pyrite] together; when processed like the *tālaka* compound, the *sūta* shall become white in color.
START GRhyasūtra 14.10 (Mercury: [the water] from a corpse;
medicinal use)

One should color the *khoṭa* with the powder of dead copper and *tāpya* (calamine) combined with *kānta* (iron); once it has been processed (*nirvyūḍha*) together with the essence of mica and gold, it is to be employed for the sake of alchemy (*rasāyana*). *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* The powder of dead copper and *tāpya*, joined with *kānta* iron, is used to color the *khoṭa*. When that [khoṭa] has been processed along with the essence of mica and gold, it is to be employed in the practice of alchemy.
And he says something else, beginning with "dead," and so forth.

The powder of dead copper and *tāpya*—that is, the powder of dead copper (*śulba*) and *tāpya*, which is gold-ore (*svarṇamākṣika*)—what is its specific quality? It is joined with *kānta* (magnetite), meaning it is mixed with lodestone. With that powder of dead copper and *tāpya* joined with *kānta*, one should color the previously prepared *khoṭa*.
Of what nature is it? It is joined with *ghanasattva* gold—that is, mixed with the gold of the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*).
Such a *khoṭa* as this is to be employed in alchemy for the destruction of old age and disease.
The mercury, rubbed with three times its weight of *rasa* combined with *parpaṭikā*,
and processed with the restraining divine herbs, is made into pills that have been dried in the shade. (GRht 14.11)
Having covered it within a *parpaṭikā* held in a crucible by means of a very firm and secret [sealing],
when blown with a bellows, the *khoṭa*— joined with gold— becomes a binder of mercury.
And he says something else, beginning with "by the powerful," and so forth.
One should grind the mercury (*rasa-sūta*) together with sulphur (*gandhaka*) three times its weight until it becomes very firm; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

By what kind of *balin*? It is joined with *parpaṭikā*; *parpaṭika* is understood here as iron-foil (*lohaparpaṭika*). Joined with that, meaning mixed with it, there are the *niyamaka* divine herbs mentioned in the ritual of preparation, such as *śatāvarī* and others.
From those, pills (*vaṭikā*) should be made and dried in the shade; "dried in the shade" means dried by means of shade and heat, rendered sapless; they should be prepared in such a manner.
And he says something else, beginning with "mūṣa" and so forth.

The *parpaṭikā* held in a crucible—that is, the aforementioned iron *parpaṭikā*—is placed inside [the crucible] and covered with a well-concealed and very firm alkali of radish and so forth (*mūlakādi-kṣāra-biḍa*).
When it is thus blown upon (heated), it becomes a *khoṭa*; that is, it attains the state of a *khoṭa*.
That cinnabar (khoṭa), when combined with gold—that is, mixed with gold—will cause the binding of mercury; the meaning is that it bestows the fixation of the mercury.
A pill made from *parpaṭikā* mixed with *bali*, rubbed and processed with *snuhī* and *arka*, [is used for] mercury (*māraṇa*) and *khoṭa*.
Thereafter, a pit should be made in the center, covered over with molten lead.
Having applied a fetter externally and placed it firmly inside a well-smeared crucible, the mercury,
when subjected to a *puṭa* and heated, dies and indeed becomes a solid bolus (*khoṭa*).
He states another method with the words beginning "balī" and so forth.

The aforementioned *parpaṭikā*— that is, iron-*parpaṭikā*— combined with *bali*, mixed with sulfur, and processed (*bhāvita*) with *snuhī* and *arka* (the meaning of "by the juice of these two" is that it is saturated with the milky sap of *snuhī* [Vajrī] and *arka* [Mandāra]); furthermore, having been rubbed and ground, when prepared in this manner, the *parpaṭikā* should be made into a pill (*guṭikā*) or bolus (*vaṭikā*), with the pill placed inside.
A pit should be made; that pit, having been filled with molten lead (sūta), should subsequently be covered over with a layer of clay—this is the intended meaning.
And he says "external" (*bāhya*) and so forth.

Externally, having placed a clamp (*nigaḍa*) over the pill inside the crucible (*sūtodaraguṭikā*), one should ensure that the interior of the well-lubricated crucible— referring to the medicinal herbs prescribed for the process of *sāraṇa*— is such that a firm clamp is applied and fixed within its belly; this is the sense.
The mercury, situated inside a pill within a crucible (mūṣodara), being subjected to a *puṭa* firing through the application of fire, dies; it attains the state of death (*pañcatva*).
When blown again, it becomes a *khoṭa*.
Thus, the indeclinable *eva* expresses the negation of anything else.
Thus, with realgar and mica, along with honey-juice and mercury combined with cinnabar and sulfur;
By means of the union of a crucible, it dies; thus the *khoṭa* is made stainless.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "evam" and so forth to state something else.*
In this way, when the *khoṭa* produced by the procedure of the iron-foil (*lohaparpaṭikā*) is heated with *tāla* and *śilā*, it becomes pure, that is, free from impurities.

Furthermore, by means of honey-liquors, *tāpya* (cinnabar), and *kharparika*, combined with *darada* (mercury) and *śikhin* (sulphur), or combined with *hiṅgula* and *śikhin*, acting as the instruments, it becomes pure; moreover, through the application of *puṭa* and contact with fire, when blown upon, it dies.
First, the characteristics of impurity were explained.
From mercury, when heated through combination with *kiṭṭaka* and *pura*, the dross is produced; and from that dross, the essence (*sattva*) is obtained.
The essence falls down and produces a vegetable-like sap; that [sap] also produces its own ash.
[Commentary, *Mugdhāvabodhinī*:
And he says that [it happens] through the conjunction with *kiṭṭa* and *pura*.]

The dross (*kiṭṭa*) is the impurity of iron; *guggulu* is the resin of the *guggulu* tree. From the combination of these two, when blown [into a furnace] with the previously mentioned forms of honey, mercury, and *darada*, there arises again a dross. From that dross, along with the mercury, the essence—the refined extract mixed with the quicksilver—falls out;
that essence produces, that is, generates, ash (*bhasma*).
The meaning is that even the essence of those ashes falls away.
START GRht 14.17:

By means of the combination of tin, mercury, sulfur, orpiment, and chalk, a fine medicinal tablet (*suparpaṭikā*) is produced through the process of *rañjana* [coloring] with smoke and without mercury.
It dyes the mineral cinnabar even without mercury.
(GRht 14.17) *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another method: "tin, mercury, sulphur, and cinnabar. (GRhtCM 14.17:1)

Tin (vaṅga), lead (trapu), mercury (rasa/sūta), and sulphur (gandhaka/bali)—this quartet, through its application with chalk (khaṭikā)—that is, by means of the pigment from the *citraka* plant—colors the aforementioned excellent *parpaṭikā*, namely the iron *parpaṭikā*, even without mercury; how much more so when combined with mercury and the essence of realgar (*tālasattva*)? This is the explicit meaning.
START GRHT 14.18 (Seed:
for coloring) Having thus prepared the seed from the *khoṭa*, it should be well-colored according to the procedure for coloring.
Having added three parts of mercury to gold, that is its excellent seed.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

He states the specific procedure for the great seeds and the [ordinary] seeds in the verse beginning with "evam" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_14.18:1): [He states the specific procedure for the great seeds and the seeds in the verse beginning with "evam" and so forth.]*
Having thus prepared the seed according to the prescribed method, one should perform the thorough coloring by means of the procedure for coloring.
To that product, three parts of mercury-essence (sūta) should be added; then, to that gold, three parts of the excellent seed (varabīja) should be added—this is the specific rule.
START GRH 15.1 (Cloud:: Sattva::
Melting)

I shall now describe the pure liquefaction derived from the essence of mica (*abhraka-sattva*), which is the support for the entire multitude of qualities; for it binds mercury when combined with it, and it merges with it easily. (GRHT 15.1)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:

Who would not fully experience the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through that Speech (*bhāratī*), which adorns the land of Bhārata and is a cluster of blossoms of bliss, as she always resides within the lotus of the face of the Victorious One? 15.1.1:1*
He speaks in praise of external liquefaction, beginning with the words "I shall speak," and so forth.

I am a poet; from the essence of the sky, which is the quintessence of the *abhraka* mineral, [I derive] "stainless liquefaction"—the analysis of the compound being that it is both stainless (*vimalā*) and a liquefaction (*druti*).

Of what nature is she? She is the support (*ādhārā*) of the entire multitude of qualities (*akhilaguṇagaṇa*). That is to say, she is the substratum of all those multitudes of qualities and clusters of attributes; the sense is that many qualities abide within her. She is the melting (*druti*) which has become *rasa*; she "binds" (*nibadhnāti*) the *rasa*—that is to say, she binds it with certainty.
Being of what nature? // GRhtCM_15.1:6 //

When it has been mixed equally and combined, the liquefaction (druti) occurs easily once again; for [otherwise], due to the difficulty of mixing with the leaf and other ingredients, it would be hard to combine.
START GRht 15.2 (Cloud: Sattva:
Melting)
The sky [substance] from *vajravallī*, ground with its own juice and combined with *sauvarcala* salt,
when thoroughly cooked in the sheaths of *nicula* leaves, becomes free of impurities and takes on the form of mercury (*rasa*).
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the procedure for liquefaction beginning with "of Vajravallī," etc. GRhtCM_15.2:1.
One should grind the sky—the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*)—together with *vajravallī* (its own juice), along with *sauvarcala* salt and *rucaka* salt; this is the remainder of the instruction.

What kind of sky? It is "cooked" by means of *nicula* leaf-pouches—that is, by saturations with the juice of reeds—and then "fired in a crucible. Having been thus cooked, it becomes "unstained," meaning free from contact and taking on the nature of mercury; this is the meaning of its becoming the form of *rasa*.
START GRht 15.3 (Clouds:: Essence::
Melting)
By merely sowing the powder of *kapitinduka* fruit drenched a hundred times in the juice of *ajajala*,
the quicksilver-like essence of mica (*abhrakasattva*) produced by heating becomes like mercury within the crucible.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states another method, beginning with "aja," etc. (GRhtCM_15.3:1).

The *drutajātarabhraka-sattva*—the essence of mica (*abhraka-sattva*), the quintessence of the sky—is melted in a crucible known as *vajra*; once liquefied, it becomes like mercury, meaning it attains the state of *pārada*. By what means? Merely by the addition of the powder of *kapitinduka*, which has been infused a hundred times with goat’s urine (*aja-jala*). "Goat" (*aja*) refers to a he-goat; its "water" (*jala*) is its urine.
Having been infused a hundred times (*śata-vāram*) and heated in a *gharma-puta* (steam-pot), merely by the addition of that *kapitinduka* powder, [the mercury is stabilized].
When the essence of the clouds has become liquefied, one should perform the sowing.
START GRht 15.4 (Cloud: Sattva:
Melting)
Just as the essence of mica remains quickly liquefied when its husk has been dissolved by a hundredfold decoction of its own juice and reduced to powder,
so too do all metals [behave].
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
The essence of abhraka (mica), through contact with fire, becomes liquefied; it remains in a liquid state. // GRhtCM_15.4:1 //
Of what nature is the *sattva*? It is that which has been "infused a hundred times with its own juice," and so forth.

By the infusion (*paribhāvita*) of the powder produced from the bulb of the *kañcukī* plant with its own juice—that is, its own liquid—the *sattva* remains liquefied; in the same way, all metals remain liquefied through the addition (*āvāpa*) of that powder produced from the bulb of the *kañcukī* plant which has been infused a hundred times.
START GRht 15.5 (Cloud: Sattva:
Melting)
The sky [is produced] by rubbing hair with oil; and when smeared with cow dung in a crucible made of *kuliśa* stone and heated well,
the essence (*sattva*) within it soon floats up, appearing like water.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says something else, beginning with "the sky," etc. // GRhtCM_15.5:1 //
The sky is the essence of clouds; "cikurataila" is well-known in the treatises as hair-oil.

Rubbed with that [oil] and smeared with cow-dung—meaning it has been rubbed and anointed with cow-dung—it is then well-blasted in a crucible made of adamant (vajra). The grammatical connection is that it becomes the form of water in a short time, after a brief period.
START GRht 15.6 (Cloud: Sattva: Fusion)
(General Rule) Here,
the liquefaction of mercury within a sattva is indeed to be known as this traditional method (sampradāya):
having first caused the sattva to fall [into the mercury], one should then add the additive (vāpa) to that liquefied substance.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the general procedure for the liquefaction of mica (*abhradruti*) with the verse beginning "gagana" and so forth. GRhtCM_15.6:1.

In this context, within this treatise, it should be supplied that when the *sattva* has become the essence of space (*gaganasāra*), the liquefaction of space (*gaganadruti*) occurs by means of its integration.
This, indeed, is to be known as the established tradition of mercury (sūta-rasa), which is certainly included within direct perception.

Furthermore, having first cast the essence of mica (*abhrasāra*) into the metal (*sattva*), once that *sattva* has been melted by fire into a liquid state, an infusion (*vāpa*) of the aforementioned medicinal herbs should be performed; this is the implied meaning.
(GRhtCM 15.6) [START GRht 15.7 (Gold:: Melting)]

Equal parts of the powder of the body of a cochineal insect (*suragopaka*) and the fruit of the *suradāli* should be administered; when cast into molten gold, it remains melted, appearing like the juice of that [insect]. *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* The powder of the body of a cochineal insect (*suragopaka*), which is red in color, and the fruit of the *suradāli* (a type of citron) should be taken in equal proportions. This mixture is to be applied to molten gold; once cast, the gold remains in a liquid state, resembling the color of the juice of those substances.
Now he describes the procedure for the liquefaction of gold, beginning with the phrase "the powder from the body of a *suragopaka*."

Having prepared a powder of *indragopa* (coccinella insects) mixed with equal parts of *suradālī* fruits and portions of *suragopa* (another type of insect) powder, it should be applied as a seed (*vāpa*). When [the metal] has been liquefied, this is to be cast on top; thus, when the seed is applied to gold, the gold remains liquefied. Of what nature is it?
It is "resembling mercury" (*rasaprakhya*), meaning it is like water. // GRhtCM_15.7:2 //
START GRht 15.8 (Gold:: Fusion):
Then, merely by the addition of the powder of *suradālī* processed with its own juice, [the base metal becomes gold].
Once it has become liquid, the gold remains so; it does not regain its hardness again.
// GRht 15.8 // *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "atha" and so forth to state something else.* // GRhtCM 15.8:1 //

Now, following the description of the *indragopa-devadālī* compound, gold—that is, mercury (*hema*)—when saturated with its own juice, remains dissolved immediately upon the mere addition of a sprinkling of powdered *suradālī*; that is to say, once it has melted, it stays in that state.
Furthermore, the gold does not regain its hardness or stability; this is the purpose for a long duration.
The ash of *suradālī* dissolved twenty-one times in cow’s urine and then dried; this is [the procedure for] the liquefaction of sharp iron (*tīkṣṇaloha*).
By means of sowing [the seed], one makes the *tīkṣṇa* (sharp metal) within the crucible resemble water.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now he describes the procedure for *tīkṣṇa*, beginning with the words "suradālī" and so forth.*

"Suradālī-bhasma-galitam": *suradālī* is *devadālī*; its ash is that produced by burning it. "By that galitam" (dissolved/saturated) means one should prepare cow's water—that is, the urine of a cow—having infused it twenty-one times (*trisaptakṛtvas*), i.e., twenty-one repetitions; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Then, the knower of ritual action (karmavid) makes the sharp essence situated within the crucible—designated as "vajra"—like water, that is, equal to water, by means of *vāpa*, which is to say, by its deposition. This is the remainder [of the sentence].
START GRHT 15.10 (The liquefaction of the essence of honey):
A *kāñcī* [alchemical vessel] smeared with tortoise shell, *śilājatu*, and the bones of a ewe, a deer, and a cow;
The crucible becomes like water; however, it should be given [as a vessel] when the mercury is in a liquid state.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now he describes the method for the liquefaction of honey-mercury (*mākṣika*), beginning with the words "kūrma" and so forth.*

Tortoise bone, *śilājatu* (bitumen), the ewe (*meṣī*), the female sheep (*meṣapatnī*), the deer (*mṛga*)—the spotted antelope—and the cow (*gauḥ*) are well-known; with their bones, whatever girdle (*kāñcī*) has been quenched becomes like water, namely *svarṇamākṣika*. For how long a duration? Always, eternally. Furthermore, when it is melted or liquefied, the casting (*vāpa*) should be performed; "casting" means the act of pouring in.
START GRht 15.11 (Cloud:: Fusion::
Alchemical Properties)
The flux of mica (abhrakadruti), which is non-specific and leaves no residue when applied in combination,
indeed binds the king of mercury, Āroṭa, through the application of a dual compound.
He states the scope for the common "flowing like a cloud" with the words beginning "abhradrutiḥ," etc.

Gaganadrava, which is undifferentiated and universal, when prepared according to the prescribed method, becomes stainless, intangible, and equal; when combined with mercury in equal parts and processed with the previous refinements, it binds the *āroṭa*—the mercury born of the tongue—which has been purified by prior treatments. By what means? Through the union of the pair, that is, by means of the medicinal herbs that effect the fusion of both.
The word "hi" (for/indeed) has its meaning [here] as "logical connection" (yukta). // GRhtCM_15.11:3 //
START GRHT 15.12 (Recipe for the *dvandvabandha* of *druti* and mercury): These *drutis* [are prepared] with black agallochum, navel-musk, garlic, white [substances], and asafoetida.

When warm, they are mixed with juice, having been crushed with the juices of the petals of the *strīkusuma* flower. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* He describes the mixing of the aforementioned substances with the words beginning "kṛṣṇa" (*GRhtCM_15.12:1*).
These *drutis*, having been rubbed in a mortar heated with hot husks, cow-dung, and the like, will combine with the mercury; one should proceed in this manner.
By means of what? By means of black agallochum (kṛṣṇāgaru) consecrated with the navel [of the earth].
Having prepared [the mixture] with black agallochum, musk, and camphor— not only with these alone— but furthermore with leek, white asafoetida, garlic, sugar, and asafoetida;

and again with the three substances consisting of the menstrual flow of a woman, the seeds of the *palāśa* tree, and juice— these three being in a copulative compound (*dvandva*) meaning "the menstrual flow of a woman, and the seeds of the *palāśa*, and the juice"— [the result is achieved] by these three applications, whether used separately or all combined together.
START Gṛhya-tantra 15.13 (Mercury: bound [by yoga] causes longevity)
Thus, the king of essences (rasarāja), when bound and consumed daily in a dose of only one guñjā,
produces a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas with just a single pala.
Thus, beginning with the words "iti" and so forth, he describes the majesty of the King of Flavors (rasarāja) who is bound [in this manner].

Thus, the mercury-king, the elixir (sūta), bound according to the previously mentioned method of sublimation, by means of a single *pala*—that is, sixteen *karṣas*—produces a lifespan of ten thousand *kalpas*. Why? Because of its daily consumption in the measure of a *guñjā*; that is, by the use of that mercury in the measure of a *raktikā* day after day, [it grants such a life] so that it may be eternal.
Now, when the mercury is properly digested according to the previously described sequence of boluses (*grāsa*),
these become the aforementioned "fluids" (*druti*) which bestow the fruits of the king of mercury.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

He states that the mercury, having been digested by means of the *grāsa* [ingestion] according to the prescribed method, becomes endowed with qualities, beginning with the words "Now," etc. (GRhtCM_15.14:1).

Then, immediately after the liquefaction (*druti*), the mercury (*rasa*, *sūta*) is digested according to the previously mentioned sequence of "swallowing" (*grāsa*), that is, the sequence of administering morsels (*kavala*) in accordance with the rules prescribed in the scriptures by means of *biḍa* and other fluxes; furthermore, these aforementioned liquefactions become givers of the fruit of the king of mercuries (*rasarāja*),
meaning that when employed in mercury, they shall be fruitful.
START GRht 15.15 (The piercing power [vedha-śakti] consisting of the digestion of mercury)

When well-digested, the mercury that pierces a hundred times becomes one that pierces a thousand with double [the quantity]; indeed, it gradually becomes one that pierces ten million through the doubling at each stage of the liquefaction process. (GRht 15.15) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī* [The mercury] which has been thoroughly digested is a "piercer of a hundred" (śatavedhī). With double [the amount], it is a "piercer of a thousand" (sahasravedhī). Indeed, by successively doubling the liquefaction, it becomes a "piercer of ten million" (koṭivedhī) through each step.
He says "well-digested" (*samajīrṇa*) to show that through digestion at an accelerated rate, the mercury acquires superior qualities.
Thus, it is that in which the flow [of time] has become equal, having reached a state of equilibrium and being fully matured.
When the mercury is liquefied, that liquefaction becomes twofold; by practicing this process gradually, one becomes a piercer of ten million (*koṭivedhin*), piercing with a ten-millionth part.
For it is evident that in the case of increase, the portion of the liquid metal would be greater. // GRhtCM_15.15:4 //
When sixteen or thirty-two morsels have been digested, or sixty-four,
then the mercury (rasendra) pierces the metal by means of observing the fumes.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the qualities resulting from the increase of the morsel (*grāsa*) with the words "sixteen," and so forth. GRhtCM_15.16:1.

When sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four morsels have been digested and have reached the state of assimilation (*jāraṇa*), then the sovereign mercury (*rasendra*), the elixir (*sūta*), pierces—that is, performs the transmutation (*vedha*)—of the metal known as a mineral (*dhātu*). Why? Because of the observation of smoke;
that is, the observation or sight of smoke.
Thus,
even if the mercury is colored and even if its seed has been processed, it remains devoid of *sāraṇā*.
It does not pervade the body, nor indeed does it reach even metals; furthermore, it attains a state of impotence.
The mind, which is directed by the intellect, should be employed by one of expansive self for the sake of performing actions that benefit others.
Like a flame, he attains a supreme splendor, having desisted even from slandering others.
The casting of gold and other substances into a crucible containing oil and a mechanical device, which increases the process of *vedha* (penetration) in the metal, is proclaimed as *sāraṇā*.
This is the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). 16.1.2.
Considering Sāraṇa to be preeminent, he spoke in praise, saying "Thus," and so forth.

Thus, according to the previously mentioned procedure, even if the mercury (rasendra), the alchemical elixir, is colored and possesses coloration, and even if it has "digested seeds" (jaritabīja)—meaning that the seeds have been processed within it—if it is devoid of *sāraṇā* (lacking the *sāraṇā* purification process which will be described later), it does not become pervasive;
it certainly will not be all-pervading within the body or in metal. Or rather, the mercury remains devoid of *sāraṇā*.
He becomes impotent and falls into a state of lack of vigor.
START GRH 16.2-5 (Sāraṇā-taila): [The ingredients are] frogs, fish, tortoises, sheep, leeches, snakes, pigs, and so forth.
Having combined these with the fat of one [animal], one should then cook the sāraṇā oil.
One should cook the oil of *jyotiṣmatī*, *vibhītaka*, *karañja*,
and bitter *tumbī* together with double the amount of red decoction and four times the amount of milk.
(Red Group):
This is the red group, consisting of pomegranate, palāśa, bandhūka flowers, and turmeric, together with madder;
and also mañjiṣṭhā, lac-dye, and sandalwood.
Coral, earth, snake-skin, feces, flies, crows, and locusts,
as well as the ear-wax of female buffaloes— these, in sequence, constitute the paste (kalka) by means of a sixteenth part (kalāṃśa).
Regarding the oil of fat for the purpose of attraction (*sāraṇa*), he says "maṇḍūka" and so forth.

The frog (*maṇḍūka*) is the *bheka*; the fish (*matsya*) is a specific type of aquatic creature; the tortoise (*kacchapa*) is well known as the *kamaṭha*; leeches (*jalaukā*) are well known; the snake (*ahi*) is the serpent;
the pig (*sūkara*) is the boar (*varāha*); and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), cows, buffaloes, elephants, camels, donkeys, crocodiles, crabs, and porpoises are also to be included.
Then, having separately mixed the fat (vasā) with each one among them individually, one should cook that very oil for the purpose of *sāraṇā* (merging), [using] fire; this is the implied meaning.
He describes a specific type of *sāraṇa* oil, beginning with the words "jyotiṣmatī" and so forth.

The oil of *jyotiṣmatī*, *vibhītaka*, *karañja*, and bitter *tumbī*— where *jyotiṣmatī* is the plant of that name, *kaṅguṇī* is the prickly nightshade, *vibhītaka* is the *kalidruma*, *karañja* is well known, and bitter *tumbī* is the gourd that is pungent— the oil of these [four] is one part; then, having added double that amount of red decoction,
which is the infusion of the "red group" (*raktagaṇa*), according to the previous connection.
One should cook it together with four times as much ghee and four times as much milk as there is oil; that is, one should perform the cooking in this manner.
Regarding the preparation of *sāraṇa* oil, he states the group of red substances beginning with "pomegranate" (*dāḍima*) and so forth.
Pomegranate is well known; *palāśa* is the *brahmavṛkṣa*; *bandhūkapuṣpa* is the flower that blooms at midday;
*rajanī* is turmeric. With these, together with *aruṇa*—that is, together with any substance that is reddish, such as the cotton flower and so forth.

What is the specific nature of this red group (*raktavarga*)? It is combined with *mañjiṣṭhā*, lac-resin, and sandalwood. *Mañjiṣṭhā* is well known; lac-resin is *alaktaka*; and sandalwood is red sandalwood (*raktacandana*). [Regarding the preparation of the paste for the *sāraṇa* oil, he says "coral" and so forth.]

Having added coral, *latāmaṇi*, earthworms, the dung of earthworms, and the excrement of flies, crows, and locusts— wherein "fly" refers to a specific type of insect, "crow" to a raven, and "locust" to a grasshopper (according to Hemacandra)— and furthermore, the earwax of female buffaloes, in the sequence of one-sixteenth part (*kalāṃśa*) as a paste (*kalka*) or additive (*prativāpa*), one should extract the aforementioned oil.
Having taken the mercury filtered through cloth from *Grṛtha* 16.6–8 (*Sāraṇa*), [place it] in a complete long crucible.
Thereafter, having melted it in hot oil, one should cast the seed-syllable into it evenly.
One should cover the mouth of the crucible with a cloth soaked in oil, stretched out and bound by two intertwined creepers; then, at that very moment, one should cast the seed [into it].
Mercury (sūta), when joined with seeds according to the method of sāraṇā in accordance with the flesh (piśita),
does not diminish and unites with the seeds; thus it indeed becomes bound.
He describes the ritual application of *siddhataila* (accomplished oil) with the words beginning "paṭa" and so forth.
Having taken that prepared oil, filtered through a cloth and purified by a strainer, thereafter—that is, after that—// GRhtCM_16.6-8:2 //
One should cast the mercury into hot oil or lukewarm *sāraṇa* oil within a full, long crucible shaped like a cow's udder.

Having done what? Having prepared—that is, having processed—the "great seed" (mahābīja), which is the seed that is equal, meaning its parts are in equal proportion, and which is equivalent to mercury (rasa). This is the meaning.
He describes the procedure for the *sāraṇayantra* with the words beginning "mūṣā" and so on.
Having simultaneously—that is, at one and the same time—cast the seed (*bīja*) inside the crucible (*mūṣā*), immediately thereafter one should seal the mouth of the crucible, that is, cover it.
"With what oil-soaked cloth? means with a garment moistened with *sāraṇa* oil.
By what kind of pair of creepers? By a pair of garments made of bark; it was strung together, stretched out, and spread wide, and it was bound and fastened by that.
"Not diminishing" means that it meets [its object] and is not exhausted.
It is to be known that when it is joined with the seeds, it is "bound" (baddha); the meaning is that when it has united with the seeds, it becomes bound.
It has also been indicated that [this] can be performed by means of describing colors such as yellow and so forth.
Similarly, the king of mercury (rasarāja) should be moistened with *sāraṇa*-oil in a deep crucible.
Having given twice as much gold as the mercury, one should then perform the re-purification (*pratisāraṇa*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

After the purification (*sāraṇā*) by means of the seed-mercury (*sūtabīja*), he describes the purification by means of gold, beginning with the words "tadvat" (in the same way), etc.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_16.9:1): [Same as above]*

In the same manner, according to the previous procedure, one should certainly prepare the king of mercury (rasarāja) in a deep crucible (*gabhīramūṣā*) or a long crucible (*dīrghamūṣā*), moistened with *sāraṇa*-oil and immersed in *sāraṇa*-oil; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Thereafter, having added gold (*kanaka*, *hema*) twice the amount of the mercury, one should re-process it—that is, perform the *sāraṇa*—as before.
One should cause the mercury, situated in light, to follow along by means of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) tripled with the *anusvāra*.
He states another method with the words "by the seed," and so forth.
One should cause the mercury (sūta), situated in the illuminator and placed in the crucible of illumination, to follow along and be refined by means of the triple seed.

A small amount of mercury (nāga) should be added during the three types of *sāraṇā*. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* START GRht 16.10 īṣannāgaṃ deyaṃ trividhāyāṃ sāraṇāyāṃ tu // GRht_16.10 // @------------------ *Comm.
Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
Having done what? Having given even a small amount of *nāga* (mercury), it should be processed in this manner during the three types of *sāraṇā*. Thus [it is said].
Having fashioned a long crucible with a channel attached to three parts of it, and having prepared that [apparatus] for the *sāraṇā* process;
In front of that [fire] is a manifest crucible, provided with holes and firmly smeared with clay.
Having cast mercury into that [vessel] which has been heated with *sāraṇa*-oil,
and having melted it together with an equal amount of gold, the king of mercury (*rasarāja*) merges when this is thrown in.
He describes the *sāraṇayantra* (the extraction apparatus) with the words beginning "having made," and so forth.

First, having made a long crucible, and then having made it with a channel attached at one-third [of its length]— meaning that a channel is attached at one-third of it— one should place [the substance] in the channel at the front of the machine, that is to say, inside the crucible at the front.
A crucible that is well-smeared with very firm clay, yet possesses openings and perforations, should be made as an "open crucible" (*prakaṭamūṣā*); this constitutes the apparatus.

Having poured mercury mixed with *sāraṇa* oil into that crucible, and immediately thereafter having melted and drained an equal amount of gold, when it is cast into that very heated crucible, the mercury mingles and attains oneness.
