Having fashioned a long tube six finger-breadths in length, resembling the flower of the *dhūrta* plant; this is the *sāraṇāyantra*.
The crucible should indeed be fixed at the bottom and smeared with clay.

Another subtle tube, seven finger-breadths long and very firm, should be made; it must be constructed so that it enters [the previous one] in the middle, and its opening must likewise be firmly secured.
Into that [crucible] was cast lead, combined with sāraṇa oil and its mouth blocked by madana;
thereafter, having melted the gold with a very large golden crucible.
Having inserted it into the middle of that [tube], one should make the tip of the tube face downwards;
the mercury, pressed by the weight [of the vessel] from above within, flows out— of this there is no doubt.
He describes another yantra with the words "having made," and so forth.

As before, one should make a tube six finger-breadths long, resembling the *dhūrta* flower or the *dhattūra* flower; this is the explicit instruction for its placement in the position of the previous tube.
The crucible should also be attached below; it should be made firmly joined to the lower part of the tube.
And that [image] is to be plastered with soft, fine clay.

Furthermore, another subtle tube (*nālikā*) seven finger-breadths in length and seven finger-breadths in circumference should be made very firm and of a pleasingly hard texture, such that it enters into the middle of the six-finger-long tube; it should be fashioned accordingly.

Of what nature is it? It is "dṛḍhamukhā," meaning that which has a firm mouth (*mukha*). When such a machine has been perfected, the mercury (*sūta*) mixed with *sāraṇa* oil should be cast into it and its mouth must be blocked by *madana* (lac).
That is, its mouth is blocked—that is, sealed—by *madana*, which is lac (*sikthaka*).

Thereafter, following that, having melted gold by means of a crucible made of gold—that is, a crucible which is gold itself—one should cast [the mercury] therein; this is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having inserted the tip of a tube—a tube seven finger-breadths long—into the middle of that vessel and turned it downward, one should then press it upward with a weight. When this has been done, the mercury flows and mingles with the gold; of this there is no doubt, meaning it is certain.
Having fashioned a firm and smooth crucible eight finger-breadths in size, resembling the flower of the *dhūrta* plant; this is the *sāraṇāyantra*.
Furthermore, another [tube], being of medium size, should be made with a hole and seven finger-breadths in length.
Having brought about cessation and having added the mercury mixed with oil,
one should place it in a smokeless fire of one *karṣa* weight, having ensured that the crucible is well-sealed.
*GRht_16.18* *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):*
He describes another method for the mechanical device, beginning with the words "having made," and so forth.

Having prepared a crucible (*mūṣā*) eight fingers in length, resembling the *dhūrta* flower and similar to a golden blossom, firm, hard, smooth, and polished— one should likewise make a second, separate crucible seven fingers in length, provided with a hole, which must be inserted and placed within the middle of the first; such is the apparatus consisting of two crucibles.
Success! GRhtCM_16.17-18:2.

And regarding that, he says: having poured into the previously mentioned crucible—which has been inserted within and measures seven finger-breadths—molten metal mixed with oil, that is, combined with *sāraṇa* oil, and having ensured it is sealed so that no smoke escapes, one should place the crucible in a fire of one *karṣa* weight; furthermore, having done what? Having made it well-jointed, meaning having sealed the joint, one should cause it to flow as before; this is the meaning.
A tube measuring one *vitasti* in length should also be made; at its front end, two crucibles (*mūṣā*) should be fixed very firmly.
One [hand] should be placed palm-upward on the body, free of gaps, with any openings sealed.
Having first added the *sūta* (mercury) mixed with *sāraṇa-taila* and placed it upon the ground,
one should then cover the seed within that crucible which is positioned face upwards.
Having recognized it as pure, one should then place that seed within the aperture;
the seed falls upon the mercury and binds it without a doubt.
(GRht 16.21) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
He states the procedure for other instruments: [they] are to be made in crucibles.

The intended meaning is that those two [tubes] should be made very firm, being of such a kind that their stalks (*nalikā*) are located directly in front of that [aperture] and measure one span (*vitasti*) in length.
The meaning is that between those two, one crucible should be made convex (upturned) and the other concave.

What is the nature of the "upturned" [mold]? It is "without gaps" (*niśchidrā*), meaning without cracks; it is "sealed against gaps," meaning that in which body—the mold-body—any gap has been closed. Thus.

And I have previously stated that, having first placed that [substance] together with *sāraṇataila* into the aforementioned crucible and set it upon the ground, one should enclose the seed—the "great seed"—within that aforementioned vessel which is lying face-up, melt it, and then add [the other ingredients]; such is the meaning.

Immediately after that, having recognized the seed as clear, stainless, and liquid in form, one should place it within the aperture; the intended meaning is that one should cast it into the interior of the aperture. By casting it into the interior of the aperture, when the seed falls upon the mercury (rasa), it binds the mercury without doubt. After the casting of the seed into the interior of the aperture, the meaning is that the aperture becomes non-porous (acchidra).
START GRHT 16.22–23 (Sāraṇā [6]):
And that [vessel] is a light-crucible (prakāśamūṣā) which should be made inverted and set at a depth of half a finger-breadth.
A tube should be prepared according to the prescribed method, with the mercury above and the seed-substance below.
Having sealed the crucible according to the prescribed method and heated it in the furnace, one should recognize when the seed has been liquefied;
then, having turned it back, one binds the king of mercury.
"Setyādi" (and so forth). GRhtCM 16.22–23:1.

Furthermore, that tube measuring one *vitasti* should be made as a transparent crucible; it should be well-seated at half a finger-breadth, inserted into the interior of the crucible, and positioned inverted with its opening facing downward.

The tube—the conduit—of that transparent crucible should be fashioned according to the rule, following the tradition of the *Śāstravārtika*, so that the mercury (*sūta*) is above and the seed (*bīja*) is below; such is the meaning of the passage beginning with "the crucible" (*mūṣām*).
Having sealed the crucible and removed the opening according to the prescribed method, that crucible is to be heated in a *koṣṭhīyantra* furnace.
Once it is known that the seed has been liquefied into a liquid form, and having turned it over— that is, having performed the inversion of the seed within the crucible—
one then binds the seed, which is the king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*).
START GRht 16.24:
Alternatively, mercury processed by the method of *sāraṇā* may be employed in a *ḍamaruyantra*.
The lord of mercury flows [as desired] when one knows the skill for that procedure according to the rule.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now he describes another apparatus, beginning with "athavā" (or else).* *Commentary (GRhtCM_16.24:1): [Same as above]*

When the mercury (sūta) has been applied according to the prescribed method of sublimation (*sāraṇa*) in the *ḍamaruka* apparatus—a vessel suitable for the aforementioned process of precipitation—it flows and unites with the seed (*bīja*).
START GRht 16.25 (the piercing power resulting from jāraṇā after sāraṇā)
Thereafter, one should digest that processed mercury by means of the method of "swallowing" (grāsa). Furthermore,
the mercury processed again in this way penetrates copper in the proportion of ten million to one.
Having done what was the mercury employed? Having understood its skill in action—that is, having understood its proficiency in the work of mercury.
START GRht 16.26:
Through the application of the *krāmaṇa* and *avasā* [mantras] according to the prescribed rule, the mercury (*sūta*) indeed flows.
Since the seed [of the mantra] is extremely light due to its fickleness, it must therefore be made into a spark.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "krāmaṇa" etc., in order to strengthen what was stated previously.*

By means of the application of those substances beginning with the fat of frogs and others—prepared according to the procedure prescribed in the ritual—the mercury (*sūta*) undergoes *sāraṇā* (the process of flowing).

Furthermore, even when joined with the seed (*bīja*), the mercury must be made stable and non-diffusive, because of its fickleness and extreme lightness; "fickleness" being its instability and "extreme lightness" being its excessive buoyancy. For that reason, it should be rendered steady and free from leakage.
START GRhyasūtra 16.27 (Sāraṇa and Krāmaṇa:
with lead, etc.)
The mercury flows easily and does not burn the mouth or the hands and feet;
by means of the application of *phaṇi* [a type of mineral] along with honey and golden *gerika*, the mercury moves forward.
(GRht 16.27) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
He states the previously mentioned qualities beginning with "it flows," and so forth.
When the charioteer proceeds according to the previous instructions, the chariot, being guided, does not burn the face, nor does it burn the hands, feet, or any other division of the limbs.
Furthermore, through the application of *phaṇi* and by means of the union with *nāga*, it transmutes together with *mākṣika* and *hemagairika*, as well as with *tāpya* and *svarṇagairika*.
START GRht 16.28 (druti, sāraṇā):
Through the application of the essence of honey (*mākṣīkasattva*) and the application of *phaṇi*, it flows rapidly like a serpent.
And while the gold flows, the fluxing agent (sūta) is transmuted by the prescribed method.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He describes the process of easy transmutation (sāraṇa) with the words beginning "mākṣika" and so forth.*

Gold, through its union with *mākṣika* essence, with *phaṇi*, and with *nāga*, melts quickly; once the gold has melted, it is transmuted according to the prescribed method by means of *sāraṇa-taila* and other such substances, and thus the process of *sāraṇā* is performed.
Therefore, the mercury that imparts its properties, having been processed with a light seed-mantra (*bīja*), is prepared for *vedha*.
When thoroughly processed by *sāraṇā* and well-bound within the crucible (*mūṣā*), it becomes a *samāvarta*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* By means of *sāraṇā*, he states the qualities of mercury, beginning with "therefore" (*tasmāt*). *Commentary (GRhtCM_16.29:1):* [As stated above].
Therefore, for that reason, the *sūta* (alchemist) should be one who provides the substances; this is the remainder [of the sentence], meaning he is the maker of the substances.

Having been set in motion by a seed that is not small—that is, by a great seed of no insignificant magnitude—and having been evenly set in motion (*samasārita*), it becomes bound; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the crucible, there should be a complete melting—that is, liquefaction—due to the blowing of the fire; this is the remainder [of the sense].
START GRH 16.30:
Regarding the process of *anusāraṇā* (following along):
that which is to be followed (*sārya*) is one that meets with a seed of equal quality after its course has been set in motion by the following [seed].
Having drawn it back with double [the force], that same [substance] is to be drawn along with triple [the force].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the sequence of drawing [the mercury] in the verse beginning with "sari" and so forth.*
The analysis of the compound is: "one whose thread has been spun and wound," meaning that which is both spun (*sārita*) and wound (*vartita*).

The sequence of *sāraṇā* (merging) is shown as follows: that which merges with one of equal seed and equal great-seed is *sārya*; that which merges with one of double [the size] is *pratisārya*; and that which merges with one of triple [the size] is *anusārya*.
START GRht 16.31 (sāraṇa [piercing] potency)

Having understood the relative strength and weakness [of the substances], one should first perform a hundredfold piercing (*śatavedhī*), then a thousandfold piercing (*sahasravedhī*), and finally an application of ten-thousandfold piercing (*ayutavedhī*) according to the prescribed method.
(GRht 16.31) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* [The text explains that the process involves sequential saturation and transference of potency.]
He states the qualities of the sequence of recollection with the words beginning "hundred," and so forth.
The intention is that whatever is to be pierced, when it has been made level by being pierced, shall become a hundred-piercer (śatavedhī).
Furthermore, the mercury which has been processed again by means of double the amount of seed (bīja) shall become a thousandfold penetrator (sahasravedhī).
Furthermore, when processed with the seed-mantra of the three qualities and infused ten thousand times, he becomes a piercer of ten thousand; this is the explicit meaning.
"According to the rule" means by the method already described.
Having understood the relative strength and weakness and having considered the deficiency or excess—this is to be supplemented by the phrase "it is joined with the proper method."
When the breath is drawn out in accordance with the count, it becomes equal and clear; when subsequently drawn back,
it becomes a piercer of a hundred thousand targets, and when drawn back again, a piercer of ten million.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the distinction of anusārita from sārita and pratisārita with the words beginning "anv... (GRhtCM_16.32:1).

Furthermore, if the mercury (sūta), which has been purified by primary refinements (saṃskāra) and made clear, should become equal to that which has been driven (anusārita)—meaning it is driven by the seed of the three qualities (triguṇabīja) and thus becomes identical to it—it would be a piercer of a hundred thousand (lakṣavedhī).
Likewise, if the mercury is driven back (pratisārita) and driven by an equal [agent], it would be a piercer of ten thousand (ayutavedhī).
Thus, when one's own will increases to the point of utter transparency, even the Creator undergoes increase; this is the secret.
When pierced by ten million [breaths], the vital breath (sūta) moves following the seed-syllable;
when turned back and followed, the vital breath pierces ten times ten million.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Likewise, he states that there is a preponderance of qualities due to the presence of the subsequent [element], beginning with "ten million" (*koṭi*), and so forth. GRhtCM_16.33:1.

Having abandoned the method of consumption, that mercury (*sūta*) which is processed with equal proportions of seed-mantras pierces the minerals numbering in the millions; this is the implied meaning.
It should be understood that in the case of mercury processed according to the aforementioned method of extraction (*sārita*), a tenfold increase in potency occurs in all instances.
In the same way, having first drawn back [the breath] to the lotus, one should then follow it through the piercing of the *kharva* [channel];
thus, by means of the application of *sāraṇā*, one performs the piercing as desired according to the prescribed method.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific detail beginning with "pratīti" and so forth. GRhtCM_16.34:1.
The mercury, having been processed by being drawn back and then driven for one cycle with double the seed, pierces a number of petals equal to that of a lotus (sixteen).

Furthermore, when processed with a seed three times its weight and processed for one day, the mercury becomes a "dwarf-penetrator" (*kharvavedhī*); the intention is that it effects a penetration into a substance of "dwarf" (one thousand) units of measure.

By the aforementioned method, according to the tradition of the *Vārtikas* by those learned in the scriptures, through the application of processing (*sāraṇā*), it performs a penetration as desired; that is to say, according to one's wish.
When the cord is drawn out according to the measurement, it pierces [the target] at the number of *nikharva*;
when drawn back, however, it pierces a *padma*, and when drawn out in accordance with its own measure, it pierces a *śaṅkha*.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states another distinction with the words beginning "anvi" (and so forth). GRhtCM_16.35:1.
When the mercury is processed with the seed-mantra according to the method of the first three-fold dose, it pierces lead numbering one hundred million (nikharva);
however, when processed again according to the method of the first six-fold dose, the mercury pierces lead numbering one billion (padma).

Furthermore, when the mercury (sūta) has been processed again according to the method of consuming nine-fold qualities and has been infused with the seed-mantra (bīja), it pierces the number of conch shells (śaṅkhasaṃkhyā).
One should pierce the double amount of the substance, and having added lead, one should cause it to flow slowly.
Until all the divine gold is fully revealed.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, concerning extraction (*sāraṇā*), in the *Rasahṛdayatantra* composed by the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpāda, the teacher of the wandering mendicants who are supreme swans (*paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states a further distinction beginning with "vidhyet" (one should pierce).* GRhtCM_16.36:1
Having given gold and refined metal (hema), one should cause it to be smelted gradually and gently until it becomes divine and excellent gold; this is the implied meaning.
Furthermore, the intention is that one should open up the entire nāga in its entirety, making it complete without exception.

Furthermore, one should pierce that gold with twice its own amount of base metal; or, when the base metal has been processed by *sūtaka*, it should pierce the gold—meaning that the base metal, such as copper and so forth, which was originally counted in the hundreds, thousands, and so on, shall pierce [the gold] to a quantity double that number. This is the secret.

Thus, even if the procedure for sāraṇa has been performed and the king of elixirs (sūtarāja) is powerful, it remains wrapped within the metal due to the application of the process; lacking the *krāmaṇa* [transmigration] rite, it does not enter [the metal]. (GRht 17.1)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:* Well-refined, situated within the mouth, clear, and meaningful for one's welfare;

likewise, when examined and purified, the words of the Immortal (the Veda) become free from defects. 17.1.1.1 GRhtCM_17.1:1: Susanskṛtā mukhāntasthā viśadāśca hitārthakāḥ / Tathā parocitāḥ pūtā bhavantyamarajā giraḥ // 1 // The speech of the Immortal (Amarajā)—that is, the Vedic words—become pure (pūtāḥ) when they are well-refined (susanskṛtāḥ), situated within the mouth (mukhāntasthāḥ), clear (viśadāḥ), meaningful for one's welfare (hitārthakāḥ), and likewise thoroughly examined (parocitāḥ). Thus, they become free from defects. 17.1.1.1 (Note: The term *amarajāḥ* is interpreted as "born of the Immortal" or "Vedic," referring to the speech of the gods or the eternal Word.)
Now, he speaks the praise of the transference [of consciousness], beginning with "iti" and so forth.

The procedure for *sāraṇā* (mercurial amalgamation) performed according to the described method—[performed] upon that very king of elixirs (*sūtarāja*)—is such that the king of elixirs becomes powerful; this is the implied meaning.
Why? Because of the application of action, that is, because of the performance of what is to be done.
The intention is that the ritual act should be as powerful as the nature of the rite being performed.
Even such [a substance], if devoid of *krāmaṇa*—that is, lacking the process of penetration—does not enter the metal; it does not effect entry into the interior of the metal.
Therefore, having merely wrapped around or enveloped the metal ore, it remains outside, imparting its color only to the exterior.
Just as food or a substance enters the bodily constituents (dhātus) through appropriate processing,
so too does the king of mercury enter into metals by means of the application of transmuting agents (krāmaṇa).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the similarity between the body and metals in the verse beginning with "annam" (food), etc. (GRhtCM_17.2:1).
The word "yathā" signifies similarity.

Food such as wheat and other substances, or medicinal drugs, together with a liquid vehicle such as water, permeates— that is, pervades— the seven bodily constituents (dhātus) beginning with flesh; likewise, by means of this "permeation-yoga" (krāmaṇayoga) which will be described hereafter, the King of Mercury (sūtarāja) enters into iron, silver, and so forth, meaning it pierces both their exterior and interior.
START GRHT 17.3–5 (Krāmaṇayoga 1):
With lovely poisons, mercury, cinnabar, red oil, indragopikā insects, and so forth;
This is the most excellent method for causing movement; it should always be employed in both smearing and casting.
(Transference Yoga 2) Realgar, honey, poison, human blood,
crow excrement, the ear-wax of buffaloes, and women’s milk— these produce power for the purpose of transference. GRht 17.4.
(3) The Transmuting Yoga: Great blood combined with borax, realgar, asafoetida, and bhūmilatā—
this is declared to be the transmuting [agent], which should always be employed as an ointment or a powder.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the method for transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) beginning with "the beloved poison" (*kāntaviṣa*), etc. (GRhtCM 17.3–5).

Kānta (magnet), cumbaka, poison born from a bulb (*kandaja-viṣa*), the thirteen bulb-poisons such as *kālakūṭa* and others, *darada* (cinnabar) and *hiṅgula*—and furthermore, with the red substances such as red oil and *indragopa* (the cochineal insect): "red" refers to the group of red minerals, "oil" refers to that of *kaṅguṇī* and other plants, and *indragopa* is a specific type of living creature; these and others are suitable for the process of transference (*krāmaṇa*). And that [is as follows]: GRhtCM_17.3–5:2: [The text continues with the preparation of the mercury.]
This is the most excellent and supreme *krāmaṇa*; by means of this, the *sūta* (mercury) "steps" (*krāmati*) or enters into metals—this is its pervasion (*vyāpti*). That is what is called *krāmaṇa*.
The meaning is that this should be applied both to the ointment and to the casting [of the powder].
START GRhyasūtra 17.6 (Krāmaṇayoga [4]: for the production of gold/silver)
An elephant slain by a stone, or tin purified by means of pure *tālaka*—
when these are drunk sequentially, white [and then yellow], this is declared to be the *krāmaṇa* [transference].
And he says something else, beginning with "By means of stone," and so forth.

Lead (nāga) killed—that is, destroyed—by realgar (śilā) and orpiment (manohvā), and again tin (vaṅga) killed by pure, defect-free antimony (tāla), should be applied sequentially and in due order: lead for yellow work (gold) and tin for white work (silver). This process of transmutation (krāmaṇa) has been fully declared and correctly revealed; thus, lead is to be employed for yellow work and tin for white work.
This is the meaning.
START GRHT 17.7 (krāmaṇa):
Copper killed with cinnabar, or lead killed by the prescribed method, is sharp [as a poison].
This transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) has been described; it may also be performed with honey upon the lovely face [of the mercury].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He speaks of another method as well, beginning with "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*), and so forth.*

Tīkṣṇa (steel) killed and reduced to ash with cinnabar (*darada*) and vermilion (*hiṅgula*), or copper (*śulba*) killed with *tāpya* (calamine) and *svarṇamākṣika* (golden pyrite) according to the procedure for the group of enemies;

this too is said to be a *krāmaṇa* (transmuting agent). Or else, that which has "the face of *kānta*"—*kānta* being a type of iron mentioned at the beginning of the text—is that which has that as its primary [ingredient]; it should be employed after being killed with *mākṣikas* (pyrites). This is the remainder [of the meaning].
There is no transmuting agent (*krāmaṇa*) whatsoever other than the essence of honey and lead (*mākṣikasattva* and *nāga*). Indeed,
this [agent] becomes fruitful in the procedure for the perfection of the petals and the perfection of the mercury.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific injunction beginning with "the essence of honey" (*mākṣikasattva*) and so forth. GRhtCM_17.8:1.
The essence of honey (mākṣikasattva), the core of tāpya (tāpyasāra), and lead (nāga)—apart from these, there is nothing else that acts as a *krāmaṇa*; such is the meaning of "not a *krāmaṇa*."
The word "khalu" is used here in the sense of inquiry.
When the ritual has been accomplished and brought to completion by means of the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), that ritual becomes fruitful.
START GRHT 18.1 (The Greatness of the Piercing):
Indeed, by means of this recollection and the transference, one who is joined [to the practice] according to rule enters.
In the absence of the process of piercing (*vedha*), mercury does not manifest its own qualities.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Indeed, when mercury is cast into a substance mixed with a penetrating medicine (*vyavāyi-bhaiṣajya*), [it manifests its qualities].*
"That which is called *vedha* by the knowers of that [science] is remembered as being of many kinds"—this is the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). 18.1.1.
He states the section concerning the consecration of transference with the words beginning "by this," and so forth.

When the process of *krāmaṇa* (transference) has been performed together with this aforementioned *sāraṇā*, the mercury enters and transmits itself; furthermore, when the procedure of *vedha* (penetration) is performed, it should be understood that the mercury manifests its own qualities.
(Hemakṛṣṭi, GRHT 18.2)
Mercury, cinnabar, silver, sulphur, realgar, and rājavartaka,
along with purified (vimala) copper killed by the puṭa-process, when drawn out into silver— this is the extraction of gold.
He states the procedure for piercing [the mercury] in the verse beginning with "rasa," etc.

Rasa is mercury; darada is cinnabar (hiṅgula); tāpya is pyrites (mākṣika); gandhaka is well known as sulphur; manaḥśilā is realgar; manohvā is orpiment; rājavartaka is rājāvarta; vimala is silver pyrites (raupyamākṣika)—here the dvandva compound is treated as a singular unit. Puṭamṛtaśulba means copper that has been killed by the puṭapāka process applied to the substances beginning with mercury.
Copper of this kind, when processed with silver, is "hemakṛṣṭi"; the meaning is that it is the production of gold.
START GRHT 18.3 (The Method/Process of a Hundredfold [Alloying]):
Ninety-eight parts shall be the base metal, and there shall be even one part of gold.
One part of the *sūta* (mercury) [is added]; this is known as the "hundredth-part" (*śatāṃśa*) procedure.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the method of piercing (*vedha*) beginning with "ninety-eight," etc.*

This is the procedure for the hundredth-part penetration (*śatāṃśavedha*) beginning with mercury and cinnabar (*darada*). How so? Here, in the hundredth part, there are ninety-eight parts of *tāra* (silver), while the portion of gold (*kanaka*) here is only one. Furthermore, there is one part of the mercury (*sūta*) mixed with cinnabar and other substances;
thus, all [these] constitute the hundredth part, and the penetration is by means of that hundredth part.
START GRH 18.4 (The Rule for the Hundredth Part [2]) Here,
forty-nine parts belong to the star and likewise to the cord.
One part of gold and one part of mercury [are used for] the piercing.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says another thing, beginning with "forty-nine," etc.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_18.4:1): [He says another thing, beginning with "forty-nine," etc.]*
Forty-nine parts of silver (tāra) and likewise forty-nine parts of copper (śulva) should be prepared;
furthermore, one part of gold (kanaka or hema) and one part of mercury (sūta) should be used for the piercing— this too is the method for the hundredth-part [piercing].
In this way, the thousand-piercer and the ten-million-piercer are employed.

Having ascertained the strength or weakness of the mercury (sūta) by means of the seed for digestion (jāraṇabīja), according to the previously stated rule—thus [it is said] in the verse beginning with "evam" etc. (Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī).
In this way, by the principle of piercing with a hundredth part, through a division of tenfold increase, it becomes a piercer of a thousand.

And thus, by virtue of the seed used in the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*), the sense is that whatever seed has been digested to what degree of quality, by that degree it shall become a "piercer of ten million" (*koṭivedhī*).
The intended meaning is: having understood that very strength or weakness—the deficiency or excess—of it by means of that same seed for digestion (*jāraṇabīja*).
First, having applied a counter-additive (*prativāpa*) through impregnation with the bile of lac, fish, and so forth, [one should proceed] with the *kuntavedha* (piercing with a spear).
In silver, or in copper, or likewise in silver-ore, or in [metal] extracted from ore.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific procedure for piercing with the words "having given," etc.* *Commentary (GRhtCM_18.6:1)*: He states the specific procedure for piercing with the words "having given," etc.

First, initially, by means of the impregnation (*bhāvanā*) with lac and the bile of fish and so forth—lac being well-known, and the biles of fish and so forth being those derived from fish, buffalo, peacock, and boar—one should perform the addition (*prativāpa*) by casting it into the melted [silver] or into copper; or else, having performed the addition in the crucible (*kṛṣṭi*) for the making of gold, one should employ it. This is the remainder [of the sense].

Thereafter, when [the mercury] has been softened by that [substance], it is pierced by means of the *kuntavedha* (spear-piercing) using a paste made from its own powder or even with the solidified juice (*piṇḍitarasa*),
once that mercury has become extremely liquefied (*atividruta*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states "tadanu" and so forth specifically for this reason. GRhtCM_18.7:1.

Thereafter, following the saturation with lac, fish-bile, and so forth, once that paste of lac and other ingredients has been rubbed with *krāmaṇa*, mercury, *mṛdita*, *kānta*, copper, *darada*, red oil, *indragopa*, and the like, then—
this is the remainder of the sense— one should perform the transmutation (*vedha*) using that paste, or even its powder, as well as the mercury made into a ball (*piṇḍitarasa*).
The meaning is: when the water-form has flowed away into either the *tāra* or the *śulba*.
START GRht 18.8 (krāmaṇa):
One should cover it with a cloth moistened with that oil, or else with meat-mince or ashes.
Indeed, the substance to be pierced according to the prescribed rule is for the purpose of the transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) by the king of essences (*rasarāja*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific detail beginning with "that," etc.*

The substance to be pierced (*vedhya*) is that which is suitable for piercing, intended for the transmutation (*krāmaṇa*) by the king of essences (*rasarāja*). For the purpose of causing the essence to enter, one should cover or conceal it with a cloth moistened with *sāraṇa*-oil—that is, a cloth moistened with *sāraṇa*-oil—or one should cover it with some kind of minced meat (*palala*) or with ashes; this is the meaning.
Thus, the process of transmuting (*vedha*) and so forth for the mercury that has been processed as described in GRHT 18.9—the ritual of *krāmaṇa*—has been explained.
He states the specific details in the passage beginning with "iti" and so forth. (GRHTCM 18.8:1)

The process of *krāmaṇa*—the transference of the mercury that has been processed (*sārita*) according to the prescribed method of *sāraṇā*, such as by means of *vedha* and so forth—is declared to be the ritual of *krāmaṇa* as taught in the instructions for *vedha*.
START GRhyasūtra 18.9 (The Piercing with Paste / Dyeing the Petals)

One whose seed (bīja) has been digested by a quarter (pāda) or more [of the mercury] is joined with a leaf-application (patralepa); the intention is that from this, the coloring of the leaf (patrarañjana) occurs.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

"One whose seed has been digested by a quarter or more" means one in whom the seed has been digested by a quarter, a half-quarter, or an equal or lesser amount; he is joined with a leaf-application, and thus the coloring of the leaf will take place—this is the intended meaning.*
START GRht 18.10 (pattrarañjana [2] by means of anointment)

A leaf of tāra (silver) or ariṣṭa (copper), etc., which has been rubbed with sour substances and the like and is thus highly purified, is then smeared with mercury; having been coated with a *krāmaṇa* (penetrating agent), it is then rested within crucibles (*puṭa*).
— *Mugdhāvabodhinī Commentary* —
One should take gold that is extremely pure, stainless, rubbed with sour substances and the like, and white in color according to the term *tārāriṣṭa*. Then,

having smeared it with mercury and subsequently coated it with the *krāmaṇa* paste, once the application is made, one should place it within the crucibles (*puṭa*) and let it rest in the fire of blue lotuses (*utpalāgni*).
This is the procedure for coloring the leaves.
START GRht 18.11 (Further processing of the *pattras*; the *varṇapuṭa*)
Having mixed half of that leaf with the finest gold and then encased it, this "color-encasement" (varṇapuṭa) should then be applied using earth from a field, a bird’s nest, and red clay.
*GRht_18.11* *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī*
Now he states the procedure for gold-making, beginning with the words "with half," and so forth.
It should be understood that "colored with half" means colored with a half-division, starting from the petals.
Having mixed that petal with superior gold—the finest of metals—and colored its leaf, one should fold it so that it adheres.
Furthermore, having prepared the earth with "sharp red clay"— where "earth" (kṣiti) refers to crystal, "sky-goer" (khaga) to yellow iron sulfate,

"sharp" (paṭu) to rock salt, "red clay" (raktamṛt) to red ochre, and these are combined as a dual compound in the singular— the leaf should be smeared on top with this mixture of earth and the other substances; the remainder [of the procedure] is that it should be placed in a crucible made of "forest-stones" (vanopala).
Take the powder of *bhūpati* and *vartaka*, which has been repeatedly saturated with the juice of *śirīṣa* flowers.
It immediately turns [the base metal] into red, white, or golden [mercury] by means of an eightieth part [of the additive].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
This describes the method for producing colors, beginning with the words "bhūpati" and so forth.* *Commentary (GRhtCM): [Same as above]*
One should repeatedly—that is, many times—impregnate the powder of *bhūpativartaka* (minium) and the dust of *rājāvarta* with the juice of *śirīṣa* flowers; this is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"It has been processed by heating," [this is] the remainder of the statement for one who knows the ritual procedure.
Mercury,
antimony, vimala, tāpya, salt, mica, realgar, and lead;
Gold becomes white when treated with a mixture of coral, *kaṅkuṣṭha*, *ṭaṅkaṇa*, and red ochre.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "rasa" and so forth to state another method.*

Mercury (rasa), lead (sūta), cinnabar (darada or hiṅgula), vimala, a type of pyrites (tāpyabheda), rock salt (paṭu or saindhava), realgar (śilā), orpiment (manohvā), the well-known merchant’s substance (mākṣika), the king (rājāvarta), coral (pravāla or vidruma), kaṅkuṣṭha, viraṅga, borax (ṭaṅkaṇa or saubhāgya),
and the well-known red ochre (gairika)— white metal, when treated with an after-powder (prativāpita) of these, becomes gold; this is to be supplied as the conclusion.
START GRht 18.14 (The coloring of gold):
It was moistened by the juice of *bījapūra* fruits from the whirlpools of the Tāpī river and its kings.
By means of *puṭapāka* (sealed heating), one makes the gold resemble vermilion.
*Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* Furthermore, he says "becoming heated," and so forth. *Commentary: GRhtCM 18.14:1*

One should treat *mākṣikasattva* (copper vitriol essence) originating from *tāpī*, and *rājāvartaka* (king’s-turning stone)—these two—by grinding them with the juice of *bījapūra* and the juice of *mātuluṅga*. From the combination of these two, through the process of *puṭapāka* (sealed-pot firing) according to the fire-protocol, one produces gold; whether it be the previously mentioned gold or gold of inferior color, it becomes like vermilion (*sindūra*).
The compound *sindūravannibhā yasya* means "he whose [complexion] resembles the color of vermilion."
START GRht 18.15 (Silver: Improvement of Colour):
One should process tin, mica, white vitriol, or realgar with white [substances].
Indeed, by adding one-tenth part of silver, it brings about an excellence of the silver.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Now, he states the procedure for the [purification of] the syllable *tāra* (silver) with the verse beginning "vaṅga" and so forth.*
Regarding "vaṅga-abhra": *vaṅga* is tin, *abhra* is white mica; furthermore, one should process white *mākṣika*, *vimala*, *śaila*, or white *śilājatu* with silver (*sita-tāra*).

Furthermore, by means of a tenth part of this collection of medicinal substances— having set aside a tenth portion from the *tāra* (silver)— one certainly effects an excellence of the *tāra*, meaning that one transforms it from an inferior color into a superior one; such is the intended meaning.

The *nāga* wind produces softness; the sun produces that redness and yellowishness; and the *tīkṣṇa* fire produces the cloudiness of the glass as well as its immediate destruction. (Physical results) GRht 18.16.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: He states a specific detail regarding the *tāra* with the words "nāga" and so forth. GRhtCM_18.16:1.
Lead, when refined in silver, produces softness and delicacy.
Furthermore, when copper has been processed by fire, it again attains that softness and a redness resembling the color of blood.
Furthermore, when it is sharp and refined with borax, it produces that redness and yellowness.
Furthermore, the connection is that glass, which is well-known in the world, undergoes blackish destruction; thus it is "carried out" (nirvyūḍha) in the *tārā* [verse].
START GRht 18.17 (Gold: Improvement):
When soaked in a mixture of honey and *karañja* oil, and then smelted, [the gold] becomes equal to the reddish hue of refined gold.
At every step one obtains ten, and indeed up to ten million [gold pieces].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific quality of the gold with the verse beginning "kanakāruṇa" and so forth.*
Gold, copper, and iron—each in equal parts—and *mākṣika* (sulphur ore); this group should be soaked in *karañja* oil and then smelted.
Furthermore, with each successive falling—that is, when it is repeatedly cast—the increase of tenfold excellence is perceived; the word "blown" (*dhmāta*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
For "hi" means certainly.
For how long a time does one obtain the number of ten million?
And this [mercury], having been thoroughly liquefied, should be sprinkled many times with *kaṅguṇī* oil.
It pierces gold with a hundredth part [of its weight] by means of the addition of honey-ash (*mākṣīkara*).
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific detail beginning with "sa" and so forth.*

This compound, saturated with *karañja* oil and repeatedly sprinkled many times with *kaṅguṇī* oil until it is thoroughly dissolved, must again be subjected to the addition of honey and borax; and gold prepared in this manner pierces white gold by a hundredth part— that is, by a division of one hundred.
START GRht 18.19:
Gold [is prepared] by being struck with mercury and sulphur, and then struck ten parts by yellow khaga.
It pierces gold and, when thoroughly rubbed and processed within it, makes that [gold] very firm.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific detail beginning with "śulba" (copper), etc.* *Commentary (GRhtCM 18.19:1): [Same as above]*

One should thoroughly grind this collection of medicinal substances—namely, mercury and sulphur (rasagandha) struck by copper (śulbahata), that which has reached a state of dissolution (pañcatva) when struck by it, and yellow vitriol (pītakāsīsa) consumed by the bird (khaga)—until it becomes very firm. Then, having been processed (nirvyūḍha), it pierces [the base metal] with a tenth part [of its weight] and turns white gold into gold; this is the specific result.
Having consumed gold that has been well-smelted and made equal to mercury by means of *vedha*, one should then apply a coating of sun and moon (*arkacandra*).
The mercury, when fully digested, transforms copper into gold by means of even a hundredth part [of its own weight].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says "rasaka" and so forth to state another point.*

Immediately thereafter, one should smelt gold together with an equal amount of *rasaka* using a coating of mercury and sulfur; furthermore, by consuming this medicine, it becomes gold. Moreover, the essence of *mākṣika* (copper pyrite) that has been digested along with gold pierces [the base metal] by a hundredth part of its weight—this is the meaning.
Eight times the amount of dead copper, smeared with silver in a *mūkamūṣā* crucible, [is used for] the *gr̥h* process (piercing; silver = gold).
When that [mercury] has been digested for one-sixteenth part [of its duration], it pierces silver with half of a hundred [parts].
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says another [point] beginning with "eightfold," etc.*

Copper that has been killed eight times along with the group of enemies— that copper which has been digested by sixteen parts of silver and fifty parts of gold— pierces [the base metal], meaning it turns it into gold.
START GRht 18.22 (piercing: the tenth part [of silver] = gold)
Having covered two golden elephants with a stone and then heated them,
mercury that has been digested by sulphur in a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*) shall effect a tenfold penetration (*vedha*) into silver.
Furthermore, he says "āvṛtya" and so forth.

Having encased two golden elephants (kanakakariṇau) with equal quantities of gold and lead (nāga), and having processed them by melting with realgar (manaḥśilā), they are then subsequently subjected to the swinging apparatus (dolāyantra).
The mercury that has digested sulphur (gandhakajīrṇa) after consuming the two golden elephants shall be a ten-part penetrator (daśāṃśavedhī) for silver;
the meaning is that it penetrates [the base metal] by a tenth part.
START GRht 18.23 (piercing with a hundredth part;
bronze = gold)

Six metals killed by mercury (ripunihataloha), aged for four months while stored in grain, and combined with sulfur and alcohol, pierce a bell-metal vessel by a hundredth part [of its thickness]. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* The six metals are copper, tin, lead, iron, brass, and bronze. "Killed" means they have been rendered malleable through the process of sublimation (*svedana*) and other operations. "Aged" refers to having been kept for four months. "Stored in grain" means placed within a heap of rice or similar grain. "Combined with sulfur and alcohol" means mixed with these two substances. "Bell-metal" (*ghoṣa*) refers to a specific type of metal alloy. "By a hundredth part" means that the mixture penetrates a layer of the metal equal to one-hundredth of its total thickness. This is a method for piercing metal plates.
And he says something else, beginning with "slain by the enemy," and so forth.
"Six metals struck by enemies": those six metals—namely gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, and iron—which have been struck or killed by enemies, that is, by groups of adversaries;
when the mercury has been processed (*jīrṇa*) for four months while staying in a granary, that is, kept in a storehouse of grain.

Of what nature is it? It is *dhānyasthita* (situated in grain), combined and mixed with *purasurā* (guggulu resin and wine) in a hundredth part; it pierces bell-metal (*ghoṣa*), that is to say, it turns it into gold. Now I shall correctly describe the seed that has been digested in *samarasa*.
O wise ones, listen to the procedure for the liquefaction and solidification [of mercury], which is now being revealed.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific detail with the words "I shall speak," and so forth.*
"O wise ones, listen attentively to the truth being revealed by me"—this is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Therefore, I, who am named Govinda, shall now speak—that is, I shall declare—what that seed is which, having undergone complete digestion (*jāraṇa*) within the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), has become properly matured and yields an equal result.

Furthermore, I shall describe the procedure for the immobilization of flour and so forth—that procedure whose first part is the immobilization of flour—as well as that which is known as *pāṭa*, *khoṭa*, and *jalaukā*.
START GRHT 18.25–40 (vedha; ghoṣākṛṣṭa = gold):
With rājāvartaka, vimala, yellow clouds (pītābhra), gandhatāpya, and rasaka;
And one should prepare a paste of lead combined with antimony, green vitriol, realgar, and red ochre.
Purify the lead by means of the juices of *ahimāra* in a sealed crucible (*puṭita*) until it becomes "non-revivable" (*nirutthaka*).
Thereafter, place within its center copper, sulfur, salt, and *kaṅkuṣṭha*.
Meditate upon all that one hundred times, and with the juice of ripe arka leaves,
one should wash the powder into the lead wire drawn by sound a hundred times.
Indeed, with that same thread-measure, one should take pure mercury, iron, and the essence of mica,
as well as the essence of red ochre and realgar, borax, lead, and steel.
Having formed a binary compound with these, one should color copper by sowing *mākṣika*;
thereafter, one should sprinkle it twenty times with the liquid that has been strained.
Having prepared a mixture of the juices of *nirguṇḍī*, *kākamācī*, and *kanyā*,
one should quench that [mixture] into gold seven times according to the prescribed ritual.
One should dye that excellent seed twenty-four times;
indeed, by that same procedure, even the processed honey becomes twenty-four times [more potent].
That seed, having first been processed in the king of juices (rasarāja) until it is merely light,
should indeed be placed in a crucible and ten times its weight of sulfur should be burned [with it].

Alternatively, having placed the mercury in the center of a very firm sand-crucible with a crucible-mold fourteen finger-breadths deep, it is covered by means of the application of a very light *puṭa*.
With that, a paste should be made from the best seed by adding one-quarter part [of other ingredients];
having placed the paste in the middle of a crucible measuring nine finger-breadths in size.
It should be covered on all sides with *nirguṇḍī*, *kākamācī*, *gojihvā*, *dugdhikā*, and *raktā*, along with *gṛhakanyā*, honey, and lumps of rock salt (*saindhava*).
The process of heating in a closed crucible (puṭayoga) should be performed until firmness is attained;
[using] six times the amount of sulphur, orpiment, potassium carbonate, green vitriol, salt, and alkali.
Having heated that [substance], an equal amount of it should be added externally;
then, having combined it with six times and again six times [the previous amount], one should place the resulting paste into a *kacchapa* machine.
It should be subjected to sweating by means of the *puṭa* process for three days, lasting up to three *ghaṭikās*.
Then, having carefully extracted it and ground it, one should make it into a fine powder.
Then, having extracted the tripled naga with an equal amount of seed,
a purification (pratisāraṇā) must be performed using the processed mercury combined with the seed.
And following that sequence, where the seed-syllable is threefold,

one should apply the previously mentioned "dead serpent" (mṛtanāga) above it, increased a hundredfold. By means of that, when the copper is drawn by the sound (ghoṣa), there is penetration (vedha) with seven hundred [applications].
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: Now he speaks of lead (*nāga*), beginning with "rājāvartaka... etc. (GRhtCM_18.25–40.1).

Rājāvartaka is well-known; vimala is white vitriol; yellow abhra is of yellow color; gandha is sulphur; tāpya is gold-mākṣika; rasaka is kharparika. Furthermore, combined with these: kāṅkṣī (known in the world as kāhī or kāsīsa), yellow kāsīsa, śilā (manohvā), and darada (hiṅgula)—with these it is endowed, that is, mixed together.
The meaning is that one should make it into a nāga.
And he says that very thing with the words beginning "ahī" and so forth.
One should combine the previously mentioned medicinal ingredients with lead (nāga), and then subject it to *puṭapāka* using the juices of *ahimāra* and the sap of *karavīra*.
Kill the lead and the tin so completely that they cannot rise again, so that they may never arise once more.

Thereafter, following that, one should mix together all of the following for that serpent [alchemical preparation]: *śulba* (copper), *gandha* (sulphur), the well-known *lavaṇa* (salt), *saindhava* (rock salt), *kaṅkuṣṭha*, and *viraṅga*. This is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
(This is the *kṣepavedha*).
This is the process of transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), which even prior to this [stage] is performed with honey, cinnabar, sulphur, and mica,
as well as with *rājāvarta*, *vimala*, coral, *kaṅkuṣṭha*, *tuttha*, and poison.
With lovely red ochre, borax, earth, creepers, blood, cochineal insects, and juices;
with the ear-wax of female buffaloes, dead iron, and the excrement of a crow.
Having combined together the excrement of a pigeon, the milk of a woman,
and this paste for causing movement, one should process it a hundred times with the red and yellow groups of substances.
It should be processed seven times with *kaṅgu* oil and the bile of the *krauñcī* bird;
then one should cook the paste (*piṣṭi*) of *sārita* with this medicinal powder (*kalka*) in a pot.
Indeed, as long as she remains impassioned, one should lead the nāga out;
for that duration, one should cast the "throw" in all instances, such as during the drawing-in and so forth.

For in this way, the king of mercury (rasarāja), having become "pierced to the limit" (koṭivedhī) and having been transmuted (krāmita), bestows an increase of virility and so forth, and then grants enjoyments.

*Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:* In this manner, the sovereign mercury, once it has attained the state of being "pierced to the limit" and has been transmuted, acts as a provider of the exaltation of manhood and other qualities, and subsequently grants worldly enjoyments.
He states the method of transference with the words "transference," and so forth.
"Even previously" means it was also stated in the preceding chapter; "it was said" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Furthermore, the ellipsis to be supplied here is: "one should produce this quality of transference (*krāmaṇa*) which is about to be described."
How did he say that? [He said: "Honey," and so forth.
With *mākṣika*, *tāpya*, *darada*, *hiṅgula*, well-known *gandhaka*, *śilā*, and *manohvā*.
Furthermore, "rājāvartaka," and so forth. (GRhtCM 18.41–46:6)

With *rājāvartaka* (known in common parlance as *lājavarada*), pure white *ākṣika*, coral (*pravāla*), *vidruma*, *kaṅkuṣṭha*, *viraṅga*, *tutthaka*, *śikhigrīva*, poison (*viṣa*), and that which is produced from the bulbous roots of *saktuka* and other such plants—
with these [one should proceed].

"Kānta" and so forth: *kānta* is magnetite; *cumbaka* is well-known as red ochre (*gairika*); *ṭaṅkaṇa* is borax (*saubhāgya*); *bhūmilatā* is the earth-creeper (*bhūnāga*); *rudhira* is the cochineal insect (*śakragopa*); *rasa* is poison. Here, from the "repeated" poison, double the amount [of poison] is used. With these [substances]. (GRhtCM_18.41-46:8)

Furthermore, there are the ear-wax of the female buffaloes and the impurities of the ears of the wives of the enemies of horses; together with these, there is dead iron—that is, iron that has been consumed—and the excrement, or dung, of the crow.

The excrement of a pigeon (*pārāvata*) is the same as the droppings of a dove (*kapota*); "female milk" (*strīpayas*) is the milk of a woman (*nārīkṣīra*). Having placed all these items—from honey (*mākṣika*) up to female milk—on one side and mixed them together, one should then saturate this *krāmaṇa*-paste one hundred times with substances belonging to the red and yellow groups, such as *kiṃśuka*, *haridrā*, and so forth; this follows from the connection with the subsequent verse.
He states the procedure for the paste of *sāraṇā* in the verse beginning with "bhāvyam" and so forth.

The previously mentioned *sāraṇā* paste should be processed (*bhāvya*) seven times in *kaṅguṇī* oil and seven times in *jyotiṣmatī* oil; thereafter, seven applications of *krauñcī* bile should be administered.

Furthermore, one should cook the processed mercury-paste—that is, the paste of the seed of mercury (*rasendra-bīja*) that has been processed—with this medicinal powder in a crucible; the cooking should be performed with fire.
He states the cooking of the *sāraṇa* paste with the words beginning "as long as," and so forth.

One should cook the paste combined with the previous *kalka* for some time until it becomes red and enters the *nāga*; thus there will be the destruction of the *nāga*. When it has entered the *nāga*, one should remove it from the fire and then, in the sequence of adding [reagents] such as the *sāraṇā*, one should add [the ingredients] to the whole [mixture].
The intention is that it bestows enjoyments beginning with virility and ending with the power of traveling through the sky.
Abhra, mākṣika, and gold, combined with nāga and processed according to the prescribed method; START GRht 18.47-48 (silver = gold).
The powder should be prepared from the divine herbs and then subjected to the puṭa process.
Having extracted the lead (nāga) from the burnt sulphur of six qualities by means of mica (śilā),
the extraction of gold (hemākṛṣṭi) into the silver (tāra) shall be achieved when combined with a sixteenth part.
He states another method for the pulverization [of mercury] in the verse beginning with "abhrakam" (mica), etc.

Abhraka is well-known; mākṣika is tāpya; kanaka is gold (hema); "joined with nāga" means joined or accompanied by nāga, which is lead (sīsaka). All of this, when combined with mercury (sūta), should be made into a paste (piṣṭi) according to the prescribed method and instruction, through the application of divine herbs;
the paste should then be subjected to the puṭa process.
Tārā explains the extraction of gold with the words beginning with "six," and so forth.

In the aforementioned *piṣṭī*, one should perform the roasting of sixfold sulfur; then, having added sixfold *śilā* (mica), one should extract the lead (*nāga*) and discard the tin (*sīsaka*). When that prepared *piṣṭī* is mixed with silver (*tāra*) in a sixteenfold proportion, it becomes an extraction of gold (*hemākṛṣṭi*), resulting in the recovery of gold.
Since gold exists inherently within metals such as copper and lead, the term "extraction" (*ākṛṣṭi*) is appropriate.
Copper struck with honey-gold and struck with realgar, when combined with an equal portion of lead, [becomes silver].
One should cook it, wrapped in leaves, together with rock salt and the juice of *jambīra* fruits in a pot.
That powder, combined with ghee, madhuka, and ṭaṅkaṇa, should be placed secretly in a crucible (*guptamūṣā*).
When it is processed three times in silver, there shall be a divine extraction of gold.
He states the procedure for slaying the *nāgas* with the words beginning "mākṣika" and so forth.
Copper that has been killed— that is, processed— by *mākṣika* (sulphur), and lead that has been killed— that is, processed— by *manaḥśilā* (realgar),

both of these should be made in equal parts (*tulyāṃśa*). Then, having combined both with *saindhava* (rock salt) and treated them by means of *puṭa*-firing with the juice of *jambīra* (citron), one should cook them over a fire once they have been thoroughly saturated.
"Where? means "in a pot," that is to say, in an earthen vessel.
Copper multiplied by lead and sharp copper [multiplied] by cinnabar in equal parts [yields] gold.
Having combined these, one should seal them and cook them with mother’s milk alone.
It should be arranged in three layers upon *tāra* (silver), resembling the eye of a cat;
it is then smeared with mercury and enclosed (*puṭita*) with a quantity equal to half a part of gold.
Regarding the extraction of gold from nāga and tāra, he says "śulva" and so forth.
The remainder is that one should make the mercury killed by sulphur equal in parts—that is, in equal portions.
The meaning of the verse is: having combined and mixed both together, one should cook them in a *puṭa* using mother’s milk—that is, human breast milk.
He states the procedure for the extraction of gold, beginning with the words "tāre" and so forth.

The previously mentioned powder made from copper or iron, when processed three times in silver (*tāra*) and properly smelted, will turn that silver into something resembling a cat’s eye, like the eye of an *otū* (a type of wild cat).
With a measure of half a part of gold, and with milk as the liquid, it should be equal to the amount of silver—neither less nor more.
Thereafter, lead smeared with mercury mixed with one-fourth part [of sulfur] should indeed be subjected to *puṭa* firing.
Having placed it in a crucible, it should be firmly heated according to the prescribed method.
One should form a smooth pill with *śilājatu* that has been processed and infused with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*,
and it should be repeatedly crushed and heated until it reaches a state from which it cannot be revived.

That [mercury] should be processed until it becomes beautifully yellow; when mixed with an equal measure of gold, it shall become pure gold. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* Tāra means silver. It should be understood that this applies to all types of mercury.
