He speaks again of the procedure for the *nāga* [substance] in the verse beginning with "liptam" (smeared), etc.
In such a way that it becomes threefold, one should place lead (nāga), which is tin (sīsaka),
in a crucible (kharparaka)— that is, in a fragment of an earthen vessel— and having heated it strongly according to the prescribed method based on the instruction of a master of mercury,
one should, while it is joined with fire, reduce it to a state of being killed; this is the meaning of the sentence.
And he says that very thing in the verse beginning with "nirguṇḍī" and so forth.
The finely ground powder of processed *nāga* (lead), prepared according to the most excellent method, should be rolled into a pill with *śilā* (realgar).

Having been saturated and sealed within a *puṭa* using the juice of *nirguṇḍī*, and having been fully impregnated, one should subsequently subject it to heating in a *gharma-puṭa* and then to firing in a fire-pit (*vahnipuṭa*).

Furthermore, the meaning is that one should continue to crush, fold, knead, and cook it until it reaches a state where it has lost its original form and attained a consistency like that of a cold porridge.
And he says that very thing in the passage beginning with "tāre" and so forth.
One should repeatedly process that powder of *tanniruttanāga* until, when drunk, the mercury becomes yellow; it should be processed for as many times as it takes to achieve that state.
Furthermore, the meaning is that when combined with an equal portion of gold—that is, an amount equal to the measure of the [other] metal—it shall all become beautiful and pleasing gold.
Having made *tāpya* (cinnabar) and *aṅguli* (red arsenic) into a powder and having placed it inside [the crucible], [one should proceed].
A secret crucible for silver should be prepared, then subjected to heating in a closed crucible (puṭa) and subsequently blown with a bellows.
When combined with gold according to the prescribed method, it indeed becomes equal in measure to the gold.
He states the procedure for *tāpya* (bitumen) and so forth: "The *tāpya*... and so on.

Having made a powder of *aṅgulisaṃjña* (copper sulfate), *tāpya* (calamine), and *svarṇamākṣika* (pyrite), and having placed that powder inside—that is, in the middle—of a *guptamūṣā* (blind crucible) made of *śulba* (copper), one should [heat] it there in a tube (*nala*); this is the intended meaning.
That crucible should be sealed and blown with a blowpipe; such is the prescribed method.
And he says this with the words beginning "by gold," and so forth.
Having prepared that refined honey-powder together with gold;
When the mercury has been processed starting from the foot-stage, one should lick the leaves of *hemakṛṣṭī*. (GRht 18.57)
Then, having smeared it with the *krāmaṇa* compound according to the ritual procedure and placed it upon an equal [substance] below,
one should subsequently blow it in a crucible together with gold and process it by smelting.

The *yantra* cooked in a crucible (*haṇḍyā*) and then subjected to *puṭapāka* (sealed-furnace heating) using the five-fold clay (*pañcamṛdā*): one should lick the leaves of *hemakṛṣṭī* (refined gold) and the leaves of *kaluṣakanaka* (impure gold) upon that mercury which has been digested by a quarter-part or similar amount, or for a period of days equal to a quarter or half [of the mercury’s weight], according to the subsequent verse which states that one should smear them with the application of *krāmaṇa*.
And he says that very thing with the words beginning "krāmaṇa" (GRhtCM 18.57–58).

Then, immediately after the application of the liquid paste, one should smear [the crucible] with the "application for transference" (krāmaṇayoga) described in the passage beginning with "kunaṭī, mākṣika, viṣa," and so on; having placed [the substance] at the bottom such that it is equal in quantity to the lower part, one should cause it to be blown [with fire] inside the crucible.
Furthermore, one should subsequently melt it together with gold (*hema*, *kanaka*) and blow upon it to refine it.
I shall now describe the procedure for the medicinal application (*ālepa*) and how the mercury (*sūta*) indeed moves through the leaves.
In brief, by whatever method the king of elixirs is colored, [that is the process].
Having smeared a cloth with lac and anointed it with oil,
one should then powder it over with sulphur and realgar according to the prescribed ritual.
Having added mercury heated over that, along with powdered sulphur and mica,
one should subsequently prepare a wick, placing it in an even iron vessel.
Having lit the lamp and then added a small amount of oil, one should perform the cooking for half a watch; thereafter, it should be cooled upon one's own body.
Then one should take the earth extracted from the crucible and smear it with that [mercury];
having smeared it with the *krāmaṇa* formulations and enclosed it in a *puṭa*, it is then smelted in gold.
And he says "that [is] the yantra," and so forth.
Alternatively, having fashioned a crucible (*yantra*) from the "five earths"—namely, ant-hill soil, red ochre, chalk, rock salt, and brick—one should cook it in a pot or vessel.
Furthermore, "cooked by *puṭa*" means it should be cooked using the *gajapuṭa* (elephant-crucible) method or similar techniques.

I shall describe the procedure for smearing (*lepanavidhi*): how the smear is to be applied upon the leaves; furthermore, how it permeates the leaves and manifests its own qualities; and finally, by what procedure it bestows coloration (*rañjana*) and tint (*rāga*). Briefly, in summary, I shall describe that method by which the King of Mercury (*sūtarāja*) becomes of such a nature through this ritual (*vidhi*) or performance (*vidhāna*). // GRhtCM_18.59-63:4 //
Now he describes the procedure for dyeing by means of an application, beginning with the words "having prepared a cloth of lac" (alaktakavastra), and so forth.

First, regarding "ālaktaka" cloth: that cloth which is dyed with lac is called *ālaktaka*. Subsequently, it should be smeared with oil, such as the oil of *kaṅguṇī* and other seeds. Upon that cloth smeared with oil, one should perform the dusting (*avacūrṇana*) with the powder of the medicinal herbs to be described later. Having dusted the oil-smeared cloth with sulphur and mica (*gandhaka-śilā*), [one should place] upon it...
It shows that [the gift] must be given.

Again, having placed [the mercury] boiled over sulphur stone powder, and again having placed sulphur stone powder upon the excellent mercury (sūtavara), that is, upon the king of mercury (sūtarāja); thereafter, immediately following that procedure, a wick (varti) should be made. That wick, having been placed in an iron vessel (āyasa)—that is, a metal vessel—that is level and even, should be worked upon there.
He shows another method with the words "a lamp," and so forth.

Then, after placing the wick upon the vessel, one should awaken—that is, ignite—the lamp; thereafter, by adding oil little by little and repeatedly, one should carry out the cooking for as long as it takes to reach half of a *yāma*, which is a watch [of three hours].
This is the remainder [of the instruction].

Immediately after that, the oil that has fallen [upon the body] should be made cool on one's own limb; that is, it should be made so that it becomes cool by itself upon the limb—the body—in its liquid state, according to its own nature. Regarding this, he says: "One should take," and so forth.
Then, immediately after the performance of the cooling rite.
And one who knows the ritual (*karmavit*) should take the soil that has been ploughed; this is the remainder [of the sentence].

Immediately thereafter, that copper ore, having been smeared with that leaf and then treated with transmuting agents (*krāmaṇa-yoga*), should be smelted in gold (*hema*) to produce pure gold (*suvarṇa*).
Alternatively, [one may proceed] with cinnabar, realgar, sulphur, pyrite, and mercury processed with lead.
And with *kaṅkuṣṭha* and coral ground together in *kaṅguṇī* oil.
The mercury, having been joined and rubbed in an iron mortar according to the prescribed method,
should be steamed for three days using a bamboo tube within a dolāyantra.
Having smeared the leaf with these black substances according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should administer the *nāga* (mercury) openly, little by little, in gradual succession.

For gold indeed becomes divine, inexhaustible, and fit for the gods; likewise, when processed by smelting, all crucibles indeed become [fit for that purpose]. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [This verse explains that] just as gold attains a state worthy of the deities through refinement, so too do all crucibles become suitable for their intended use once they have been thoroughly processed by smelting.
He states another method, beginning with "Alternatively," and so forth.

Cinnabar (darada), vermilion (hiṅgula), realgar (śilā), orpiment (manohvā), alum (āla), yellow orpiment (haritāla), sulphur (gandhaka), refined copper pyrite (mākṣika), and dead lead (mṛtanāga)—with these [the preparation is made].
Furthermore, with those accompanied by kaṅkuṣṭha and coral—namely, kaṅkuṣṭha, viraṅga, and coral (vidruma)—together with those two.

Furthermore, mercury (sūta) should be combined with these [substances]—Kaṅguṇī oil, Jyotiṣmatī oil, and powders made from grinding [the herbs]—in the middle [of the mixture], as indicated by the connection to the following verse.
And he says that very thing with the words "In the middle," and so forth.
Having prepared the medicinal substances as previously described, the mercury (sūta) should be joined with them inside the medicine in the center.
Having crushed it again and inserted it into a hollow bamboo tube, one should subject it to sweating for three days using a swinging apparatus (*dolāyantra*); this is the meaning.
And he says that very thing in the passage beginning with "having smeared," and so forth.
These medicinal herbs, having been heated, are combined with those aforementioned black salts according to the previously described procedure for the extraction of mercury (*sūtaka*).
Having smeared the leaf, one should gradually add a small amount—very little—of lead (*nāga*) so that it becomes manifest once more;
thus gold (*kanaka*) is produced. This is the connection with the following verse.
When this has been done, it becomes divine, excellent, and fit for the gods—an inexhaustible and imperishable gold suitable for Indra and the other deities.
This point is logical.

Thus, when the mercury has been processed (*jārita*) and the work of processing has been performed, it is certain that all crucibles (*haṇḍikā*), all metals and so forth, and everything along with their progeny shall indeed be [transformed]; this is the meaning.
START GRht 18.68 (The relationship between *bīja* and gold)

When [the mercury] has been fully digested, it is "seedless" (*nirbīja*); with one-sixteenth part, one-fourth, or one-eighth of the foot-addition (*pādayoga*), and with an equal amount of gold—GRht 18.68.

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [This refers to the process where, once the mercury is completely processed, it is rendered seedless; then, by adding one-sixteenth, one-fourth, or one-eighth of the "foot-addition," along with an equal quantity of gold...]
He states the distinction with the words "seedless," and so forth.

Just as it is seedless when fully digested, it yields fruit by one-quarter; likewise, when half-digested, it yields fruit by a sixteenth part. Furthermore, when half of that is digested, it yields fruit by a quarter of that quarter; and when a quarter of that is digested, it yields fruit by a quarter of that quarter—this should be stated in all cases.
And gold that has been worn down for an equal length of time yields its full fruit.
START GRHT 18.69 (Tārākṛṣṭi):
I shall describe the extraction of mercury (*tārākṛṣṭi*): dead tin (*mṛtavaṅga*) in equal parts with thallium (*tālaka*).
Then, when heated and blown upon, the copper assumes the luster of silver.
[Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:
After the extraction of gold, I, the poet, shall speak of the extraction of silver. I declare that dead tin—that is, tin that has been killed by means of *tālaka* (orpiment)—[is to be used].
Then, when that copper—equal in parts—is blown while suspended so as to be wide, it bears the luster of silver; the meaning is that it attains the brilliance of silver.
Thereafter, the nāga should be added to the open crucibles until it becomes stainless;
when blown according to the prescribed method, it becomes perfectly pure and free from ripples.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "paścāt" (afterwards), etc. GRhtCM_18.70:1.
Afterwards, following the application of tin and copper, lead (nāga) should be added until it becomes stainless, that is, free from impurities;
furthermore, one should cause it to be blown with the prescribed method until it is stainless, brilliant, and waveless—that is, devoid of the ripples of lead. This is the meaning.

Having applied a piercing with *tāla*, *śilā*, and *sarjikā*— either individually or combined— with *saindhava* salt and substances beneficial for the eyes, one should again apply it to the copper (*śulba*). (GRhT 18.71)
In the process of piercing, there should be sprinkling with cow-dung cake, buffalo-whey, the milk of *snuhī*, and ghee, each mixed respectively with jaggery,
milk, and honey.
He states the distinction [between them] with the words beginning "tāla" and so forth.

Tāla is yellow orpiment (haritāla), śilā is realgar, and manohvā is cinnabar; sarjikā is well-known. With these, along with rock salt (saindhava)—that is, with these substances beneficial for the eyes—one should apply the process of transmutation (vedha) to copper (śulva), either individually or collectively. Thus ends verse 18.71–72.2.
He describes the consecrations for the *tāravedha* [piercing by means of stars] starting with the words "chagaṇa" and so forth.
Cow-dung produced from the forest, buffalo buttermilk (mahiṣyāḥ), this buffalo [buttermilk] together with the milk of the *snuhī* plant (*sehuṇḍa*),

and further combined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), molasses, milk, and honey— all these being mixed together, the sprinkling (*niṣeka*) should be performed gradually during the process of transmutation (*vedhakarma*).
START GRht 18.73 (Tārakṛṣṭī;
copper =) silver)
Kāñcī, brāhmī, kuṭila, and tālaka, combined in equal parts and smelted,
pierce base metal (śulba); by means of this, the divine extraction of silver (tāra) occurs.
He explains the attraction of the stars with the verse beginning "kāñcī" and so forth.
Kāñcī, gold-ore (svarṇamākṣika), brāhmī, somāhvā, kuṭila, lead (sīsa), and the well-known tālaka—

when these are combined in equal proportions and smelted, and when copper is subsequently treated with this group of substances beginning with kāñcī, there will be a divine and enchanting extraction of silver.
Thus, having smeared the drawn-out mercury with the processed *sārita* [mercury], the attraction of the stars (*tārākṛṣṭi*) is accomplished.
One makes it clear by applying a stainless ointment, such as that derived from the decayed parts of the feet and so forth.
Thus, when the pierced [gem] has been mixed, then it becomes equal to the Mother (mātṛkā);
with the cutting, striking, and rubbing, it becomes a "star-petal" (tāradala) and is free from defects.
He speaks of the attraction of the stars with the words "Thus," and so forth.
Thus, having been smeared by means of the procedure described above—performed through the act of *sāraṇā* (rubbing)—and having been pierced, it becomes the extraction of mercury (*tārākṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, this "star-attracting" [practice] makes the mercury (*tāra*) stainless and free from impurities; or else, it refers to that which is "worn by the foot" (*pādajīrṇa*), where "foot" means a quarter-part, and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), one should understand the inclusion of a half-part—that is, the specific application of the ointment—as stated in the passage beginning with "thus," and so forth.

Thus, by the previously mentioned procedure, when [the substances] are mixed, combined, pierced, and arranged in sequence, becoming equal in proportion to the *mātṛkā*, it becomes a silver leaf with the quality of the *tāra* metal; that silver leaf becomes free from defects through cutting, hammering, and rubbing on a touchstone— where "cutting" means breaking into pieces, "hammering" means striking with a heavy blow, and "rubbing" means testing upon a stone— as well as through heating.

Thus, having understood the procedure for piercing according to the instructions of the scriptures from the teacher’s oral teaching, it should be performed by one who is skilled in ritual action and proficient in its execution.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

In this manner—that is, by this method—one who knows the injunctions of the scripture (*śāstravidhijña*) is so called because he knows the procedure of the scripture; by such a skilled agent, who is proficient in ritual action (*karmanipuṇa*) and expert in consecration (*saṃskārapravīṇa*), there is the "instruction of the Guru" (*gurūpadeśa*). The Guru is defined by the characteristics mentioned at the beginning of the book, and his instruction [is what follows].
The meaning is that, having understood the method of piercing (*vedha*), it should be performed.
Thus, in the procedure for the King of Mercury (rasarāja), the method of transmutation (vedha) has been explained incidentally.
Now, I shall describe the formulations for the elixir of longevity (rasāyana), even those already mentioned.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: Now he states the procedure for consumption, beginning with "iti" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.1:1.

In the procedure for the king of mercury—the performance of the operations of mercury—the method of transmutation (vedha) has been explained incidentally by way of context, but not according to my own independent wisdom.

Now, I shall describe—which means I shall speak of—certain formulations, that is, collections of substances, for the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*) which destroys old age and disease, both those already mentioned and, by the word "also" (*api*), those previously experienced. (19.2–4) [The Process of Becoming a Field (Purification of the Body)]*gr̥hītvā navanītākhyam auṣadhaṃ tu rasāyanam / mardayitvā yathānyāyaṃ bhakṣayed rasabandhanam // tasyaiva ca tathā yuktyā kuryād āvartanaṃ punaḥ / evaṃ hi saptavārāṇi kuryāt kāyakṣayaṃ prati // tataḥ saṃjāyate dehaḥ kṣetrabhūtaḥ sunirmalaḥ / yogyaḥ sarvarasāyanānāṃ sarvavyādhivivarjitaḥ // Having taken the medicinal substance known as *navanīta*, which is an elixir (*rasāyana*), one should grind it according to the prescribed rule and consume it to bind the mercury. Furthermore, by the same method, one should perform the process of *āvartana* (reversion) upon that very substance seven times; thus, for the sake of the emaciation of the body, one should act in this manner. Then the body becomes purified like a field, fit for all elixirs, and freed from all diseases.
In the beginning, one should drink ghee mixed with rock salt every morning for three days;
thereafter, one should employ a decoction derived from *ketakī* for three days.
The body should be fomented according to the prescribed method by the master of the medical arts;
one should then administer a purifying decoction of *kaṭurohiṇī*.
Thereafter, when the entire [substance] has been expelled at the end of the phlegm-stage following the pure stage,
one should administer a diet of barley-gruel mixed with ghee for three days.
He speaks of the purification of the body, beginning with the words "In the beginning," and so forth.
First, for three days, one should drink ghee (ājya) mixed with rock salt every morning at dawn.

He describes another combination: after that, following the ghee and rock salt, one should employ a decoction born from the body of the *ketakī*—that is, produced from the root of the *ketakī*, according to the maxim that "even when not explicitly stated, the root is prescribed. This should be used for three days.
He states another method with the words beginning "by means of the injunction" (vidhinā), etc.

Then, according to the prescribed method of sudation, the body—the physical frame—must be fomented, that is, made to perspire, by the master of the laboratory who is conversant with the tradition of alchemical mercury.

What else? One should subsequently apply a properly prepared decoction of *kaṭurohiṇī* (gentian), which is bitter, for the purpose of purification immediately after sudation; this is the intended meaning.
He states another method with the words "That," and so forth.

Thereafter, following the administration of kaṭukarohiṇī, once the body has been purified and the upward movement [of the humors] has occurred, and when the interior has been cleansed of phlegm— that is, when it has been purged so as to reach the end of the phlegm— one should employ a diet of barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) with ghee for a duration of three days.
Furthermore, I shall again describe the application of the drink for the sake of the welfare of the entire world:
having drunk this powder, equal in measure to warm water, during the first watch of the night. (GRht 19.5)

One should administer for three days a powder composed of *pathyā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *dhātrī*, black pepper (*marica*), *vacā*, jaggery (*guḍa*), *viḍaṅga*, turmeric (*rajanī*), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and long pepper (*pippalī*).
By this means, one whose body is purified and who has overcome the power of the defects of association becomes pure by drinking barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) mixed with milk.
He states another method with the words "again," and so forth.

"Furthermore" (*punarapi*) means that after the application of the *pathyā* [remedy], I shall again describe the application of the drink. For what purpose? For the sake of benefiting the entire world—that is, for the sake of bringing about the welfare of all transmigrating beings. Having drunk this powder to be described, beginning with *pathyā*, together with hot water—meaning with boiled water—within the first watch (*prathamayāma*), that is, within the first period of three hours, one becomes pure of body; this is according to the connection with the following verse.
Regarding the powder for purification, he says "pathyā" and so forth.

One should employ for three days the powder of these medicinal substances: *pathyā* (harītakī), *saindhava* salt, the well-known *dhātrī* (āmalaka), *marīca* (black pepper), *ūṣaṇa*, *vacā*, the pungent-smelling *ugragandhā*, well-known jaggery (*guḍa*), *viḍaṅga* (the worm-killer), *rajanī* (haridrā), as well as *śuṇṭhī* (nāgara) and *pippalī* (māgadhī). One should apply the powder of these herbs for three days.
It should be understood as being equal to warm water.
"By this," and so forth.

Having purified his body by means of this purgative to be described—such as the barley-gruel (yāvaka) and other such substances—he becomes one whose strength has overcome the defects of contact (*saṃsargadoṣa*).
Those defects which exist within the interior of the body due to contact are the "defects of contact"; he is one by whom these have been abandoned, that is, conquered.
Having avoided the fault of association, he is strong and endowed with power; for when faults cease, virtues necessarily arise.
Having done what, does one become free from fault? The meaning is: by drinking this water—namely, warm water mixed with barley gruel and lac—one becomes pure.

If a man should employ an elixir (*rasāyana*) without having first prepared his body as a fit field, the essence does not take effect; that essence becomes a cause of disorders throughout all his limbs. (GRht 19.8)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the fault in not performing purification with the verse beginning "akṛta," etc. (GRhtCM 19.8:1).

If a man applies an elixir (*rasāyana*)—a medicine that destroys old age and disease—to a body in which the process of "field-making" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*) has not been performed, his vital essence (*rasa*) does not circulate;
it does not manifest its own qualities. In that case, does it produce defects in all the limbs? [The answer is: in the six limbs, such as the arms and feet.
It would cause a transformation.

Thus, one who is pure and has attained strength— having made his own body a field for cultivation— should duly perform the practice of *rasāyana* using rice-gruel, barley-meal, beans, and meat-broth. (GRht 19.9)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
[The author] states "Thus," etc., to indicate that this constitutes the section on elixirs (*rasāyana*). GRhtCM_19.9:1.

One who has become pure through the previously described procedure and has attained strength—that wise man, having made his own body a "field" (having transformed his non-field body into a field)—should duly practice *rasāyana*. (GRhtCM 19.9:2)
By means of which [herbs], having gained strength, he [consumed] śāli rice, that which is called barley-gruel (yāvaka), and mung beans.
Having churned together the oils of *surasa* and *taru*, clarified butter, honey, the juice of *dhātrī*,
and milk, and having drunk it, a man becomes purified in his internal organs and cleansed of intervening impurities. (GRht 19.10)
In one month, O Medhā, it bestows beauty; in two months, it pacifies the entire collection of humors (*doṣa*);
and after three months, one becomes possessed of great splendor, with a divine body and a delicious [complexion].
He states another method, beginning with "surataru" and so forth.
"Internally purified" (*antaritaśuddha*) means one whose internal state is pure; the meaning is that he is free from diseases of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*) and the like.

Having churned and drunk these medicinal herbs, he becomes "one with a purified interior" (*viśuddhakoṣṭha*). "Purified" (*viśuddha*) means free from impurities (*mala*); "interior" (*koṣṭha*) refers to the stomach (*udara*); thus, he becomes one who possesses such a [purified] state.

Regarding the phrase "those [substances], such as the oil of the celestial tree" (*suratarutaileti*): the "celestial tree" (*surataru*) is a divine tree; "its oil" (*tattaila*) means the oil produced by its pressing, that is, oil.

*Ghṛta* is clarified butter (*ājya*); *madhu* is honey (*kṣaudra*); *dhātrī-rasa* is the juice of the *āmalaka* fruit; *payaḥ* is milk. Having "churned all these together" means having combined them into one.
He describes the benefit of consuming this medicine through a monthly progression, beginning with the words "by a month," and so forth.
By consuming this medicine for one month—that is, for a duration of one month—beauty and intelligence arise;
by two months—that is, for a duration of two months—it pacifies and brings to rest the entire collection of humors (doṣas), the multitude of diseases;

and furthermore, by three months—that is, for a duration of three months—one shall possess a divine body like that of an immortal, endowed with great splendor and radiance from one's own ordinary physical frame. This is the meaning.
Equal parts of *suradāru* oil, clarified butter (*ājya*), and the decoction of *triphalā*,
when drunk, bring about the pacification of eye disorders within seven days. (GRhT 19.12)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states another yoga, beginning with "suradāru" (deodar), etc. GRhtCM_19.12:1.
Devadāru oil (suradārutaila), clarified butter (ājya), and the juice of triphalā combined with the liquid juice of triphalā— these, taken in equal parts and drunk for seven days,
bring about the pacification and cessation of eye disorders arising in the eyes.

Having drunk the oil of *surataru* with ghee and having eaten *śāli* rice with milk once the previous meal has been digested, one indeed removes skin diseases such as *kuṣṭha*, chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*), and other ailments. (GRht 19.13)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states another yoga, beginning with "the oil of the celestial tree" (*suratarutaila*), and so forth. GRhtCM_19.13:1.

Having drunk both of these— devadāru oil with ghee and clarified butter— and having eaten śāli rice with milk (the intention being sixty-day rice), this should be understood as the procedure for daily consumption at the end of the day once the previous meal has been digested, during the two "heroic" periods.
Furthermore, it removes—that is, drives far away—such diseases as chronic catarrh (pīnasa) and others that coexist with skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

The juice of *amaradāru* (devadāru), when combined with ghee, cures diseases arising from *pitta*; when combined with oil, it cures diseases arising from *vāta*; and when combined with jaggery or honey, it destroys those born of *kapha*. (GRhT 19.14)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states another yoga beginning with "accompanied by ghee," etc. GRhtCM_19.14:1.
The juice of *amaradāru* (deodar), or water from a *devadāru* tree mixed with clarified butter, when combined with ghee, removes and destroys diseases caused by *pitta*.
Furthermore, the juice of *devadāru* mixed with oil—that is, combined with oil—destroys diseases arising from wind (*vāta*).
Furthermore, the juice of *devadāru* taken together with jaggery or with honey (*kṣaudra*) destroys diseases arising from wind (*vāta*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the sentence is that the juice of *devadāru*, when combined with jaggery (*guḍa*) or with honey (*kṣaudra*), destroys diseases born of phlegm (*kapha*).
One should consume rice cooked with milk, avoiding sour gruel and leafy vegetables;
the portions should be two, four, or six palas, corresponding respectively to the lowest, middling, and highest doses. (GRHṬ 19.15)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Regarding the elixir (*rasāyana*), he states what is to be eaten and what is not to be eaten, beginning with "varjita" and so forth. (GRhtCM 19.15:1)
One should eat śāli-rice with milk, avoiding sour gruel (kāñjika), avoiding vegetables such as sauvīra or vāstūka, and so forth;
furthermore, as for the quantity of the śāli-rice, it should be two, four, or six palas.

The meaning here is that the inferior, middling, and superior doses—measuring two, four, and six *pala*s respectively—should be administered according to the weak, moderate, and strong physical constitutions.
Thereafter, one should consume mercury (sūtaka) purified by precipitation (pātana), along with *āroṭa*.

[The processes of] sweating (*svedana*), fainting (*mūrchā*), reviving (*utthāpana*), precipitation (*pātana*), and confinement (*rodha*), as well as the restrictive regimen (*niyama*), [are required]. (GRht 19.16)

The mercury should be subjected to the process of falling (pātana) together with mica according to the prescribed rule until it becomes stable; alternatively, the mercury may be subjected to the process of falling together with pyrite according to the ritual procedure.
Thus, the *āroṭa* mercury is first employed for the purpose of "field-making" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*).
Next, he describes the formulation of the mercury with the words beginning with "that" (*tat*), and so forth.

Thereafter, immediately following the administration of the beneficial regimen, one should consume—that is, eat—the *sūtaka* (mercurial preparation) purified by *pātana*, which is indeed the common *āroṭa* itself.

Furthermore, regarding "sweating, fainting, raising, and the falls, as well as the suppression"— this is a *dvandva* compound meaning sweating (*svedana*), fainting (*mūrchā*), raising (*utthāpana*), the falls (*pātanāni*), and suppression (*nirodha*). Even though these exist and even though there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), the meaning is that [the mercury] becomes *āroṭa* through the falling (*pātana*).
In this context, he states the method of causing [the substance] to fall, beginning with the words "abhraka" and so forth.
The *sūta* (mercury), combined with *abhra* (mica) and joined with *gagana* (iron), should be subjected to the process of *pātana* (precipitation).
By what procedure? By means of the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), the yantra, and so forth.
Furthermore, this continues until he becomes stable.
Alternatively, according to another procedure, this lead (sūta) together with sulfur (mākṣika) should be subjected to the process of falling (pātana) by means of this method until it becomes stable.
Regarding the alchemical elixir (*rasāyana*), he describes the procedure for *āroṭa* and other substances in mercury (*sūta*) with the words beginning "iti" and so forth.

*Āroṭa* is that which has been prepared through the previously mentioned process of *pātana* (precipitation) by means of its upward, downward, and transverse movement; it is first employed in *rasāyana* for the destruction of old age and disease.
Thus.
Alternatively, having turned mercury into ash by means of a *kalka* application produced from mercury and other substances;
Alternatively, having reduced it to ashes, it may be bound [to the body] by means of a medicinal paste (*kalka*). (GRht 19.18)
One should first employ mercury combined with honey, mica, iron powder, harītakī, vibhītaka, viḍaṅga, ghee,
and honey for the purpose of "field-making" (kṣetrīkaraṇa).
There are two kinds of ash: that which rises upward and that which remains on the ground. According to the distinction of color, it is of six types:
white ash, yellow ash, green ash, red ash, black ash, and variegated ash. Having prepared these six types, they are first employed for the consecration of the sacred field (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*).
He states the formulation of the elixir (*rasayoga*) beginning with "mākṣika" and so forth.

The meaning of the sentence is that one should employ the mercury combined with these— mākṣika (sulphur), tāpya (cinnabar), śilājatu (bitumen), well-known iron powder, the dust of killed muṇḍaloha (iron), pathyā (harītakī), akṣa (vibhītaka), viḍaṅga (kṛmighna), ghee (ājya), and honey (kṣaudra)— for the purpose of transforming the body into a field (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*).

Having consumed mercury (sūta) reduced to a paste (kalkīkṛta), combined with thick, beautiful honey, clarified butter, and so forth, one shall attain immortality; this is the primary method for transforming the body into a sacred field (kṣetrīkaraṇa). (GRht 19.20)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Having consumed the mercury (*sūta*) reduced to a paste according to the procedure thus described, one shall attain immortality and divinity. GRhtCM_19.20:1 //

Thus, what is "combined with thick, lovely honey, ghee, and so forth"? "Thick" (ghana) refers to mica (abhraka); "lovely" (kānta) refers to a type of iron; "honey" (madhu) is nectar; "ghee" (ghṛta) is clarified butter; and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), sugar (sitā) is to be understood. Being combined with these and made into a paste (kalkīkṛta), this is the primary "field-making" (kṣetrīkaraṇa)—that by which one becomes a field.
Thus ends the ritual of the Āroṭaka.
Then, having repeatedly processed black or yellow *ghana* that has the luster of fire,
it should be sprinkled with fragrant cow’s milk; once freed from the defects of the mountain, it may be employed for alchemy (*rasāyana*).
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: Now follows the preparation of leaf-abhraka (patrābhra). GRhtCM_19.21:1.
One should repeatedly— many times— not once, purify that black or dark-colored thick cloud-like substance, or yellow or yellow-colored thick substance,

which has the luster of fire or the brilliance of a flame, by sprinkling it with fragrant milk; having thus purified it so that the defects arising from the mountain (mahīdhara) have departed— that is, the defects born of the mountain have been removed— that thick substance is fit for alchemy (rasāyana).
It should be employed for the purpose of bringing about the destruction of old age and disease.

Even without moonlight, one who consumes one *pala* daily of pure *viḍaṅga*, *triphalā*, clarified butter, and honey, while following the prescribed method and subsisting on milk, [attains purity]. (GRht 19.22)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the application of mica with the words "devoid of luster" (*niścandrika*), etc. (GRhtCM_19.22:1).

One should consume daily, according to the prescribed method for purifying the body, one *pala* of this thick preparation—which, though devoid of moonlight, is pure; and though lacking the light of the moon, is faultless—blended with *viḍaṅga*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), clarified butter, and honey, combined with *kṛmighna*, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*, along with ghee and honey. Having eaten all of it, one should subsist on milk alone, or eat *śāli* rice with milk.
The meaning is that one should practice accordingly.
One who eats *vyoma* (mica) combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *viḍaṅga*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), honey, and *śilājatu*,
along with milk-rice, lives for a hundred years. (GRhT 19.23)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the verse beginning with "trikaṭuka," etc. GRhtCM_19.23:1.

One should consume *vyomābhraka* (mica) combined with *trikaṭu*, *viḍaṅga*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), honey, and *śilājatu*; or again, one should eat it mixed with *pippalī*, black pepper, ginger, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, honey, and *śilājatu*. Afterward, one should eat wholesome food consisting of rice with milk.
When this has been done, a living being lives for a hundred years; "jantu," "janyu," and "śarīrin" are synonyms for a living being, according to Amara.
Thus ends the procedure for leaf-processed abhraka.
"START GRht 19.24" and so forth—other such applications involving *kāñjika* (sour gruel) have been proclaimed many times.
Indeed, those applications of leaf-processed *abhraka* (mica) that lack a [proper] formulation (*niryuktika*) should be avoided. GRht 19.24. @------------------
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Showing the successive stages of abhraka, he says "iti" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.24:1.

"Thus, beginning with these"—meaning those previously mentioned formulations (yogas) and others like them, which are combined with *kāñjika* (sour gruel or fermented rice water)—these other formulations prepared with *kāñjika* (*aranāla*) are frequently proclaimed and described in other texts such as the *Rasāvatāra*. These "leaf-and-abhraka formulations" are "devoid of logic" (*niryuktika*); that is, they are derived from the suffix *-ika* in the sense of being "without logic," meaning they are unfit for use.
Those formulations of mica (*abhraka*) with *patra* that have been proclaimed according to the prescribed method for the purpose of elixirs (*rasāyana*)—
if taught by those who do not know the properties of substances— result in old age and death.

*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī: Since the combination of leaf and abhraka [mica] performed without the prescribed method leads to a transformation [of the mercury], he says "yaḥ" (he who), etc. (GRhtCM 19.25:1).

By those men who are ignorant of the qualities of substances— that is, by those whose knowledge of the properties of substances such as mica (*abhra*) and the like is deficient— the preparations of leaf-mica (*patrābhra*) for the purpose of rejuvenation (*rasāyana*) have been proclaimed according to the general injunction; yet by those very same people, old age and death have been taught—
old age being grey hair and death being disease.
The dense [food] brings about the pacification of his digestive fire, which has not yet attained its natural state;
even without the fire, he perishes, overwhelmed by various hosts of diseases.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

He states the reason for the instruction on aging and death with the words "aprāpta" and so forth: "In such a way that worldly existence is not attained, [this] is the dense [instruction] of this author. 19.26:1.
Even without digestive fire, a person perishes; that is, he meets with destruction.
In what state? Being overcome—that is, conquered—by various hosts of diseases, by numerous collections of ailments; such is the meaning of the sentence.

Even though the essence of mica (*abhrasattva*) is present within wood and even within a mass of clouds in the sky, he says that this *abhrasattva*, the condensed essence (*ghanasāra*), does not perform its own function—its proper task—in that manner, nor does fire (*vahni*). (GRhtCM 19.26:4)

Just as ghee situated within wood does not perform its own function, nor does it do so while remaining in milk, yet like a snake [hidden] in a hole or wealth [buried] underground, once it has emerged and become separate, it performs its own function; such is the intended meaning.
START GRH 19.27:
Among those who practice *rasāyana*, the essence of *abhra* is proclaimed here as the supreme edible substance.
The sky is of three kinds and is inedible: glass, dross, and leaf-dust.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Regarding what is edible and inedible, he speaks of the cloud with the words "of the cloud," and so forth.*

In this world, for those practitioners of elixirs who desire the destruction of old age and disease, the essence of mica (abhrakasattva) is proclaimed as the supreme, most excellent food fit for consumption for the purpose of transforming the body into a field [of immortality].
Furthermore, the sky-like cloud is threefold and of three kinds: that which is not to be eaten and that which is not to be consumed.

What is that? It means there are three kinds: glass (kāca), which is the form of colored glass; dross (kiṭṭa), which is the form of impurity; and leaf-dust (pattrarajaḥ), which is common cloud-powder.
First, having rubbed [the powder] with the juice of triphalā and dense iron filings,
one should make it resemble collyrium by exposing it to the rays of the sun while covered with a cloth. (GRht 19.28)
Having thus made it smooth, like various beautiful powders of metal,
one should repeatedly process that very mass of iron with *bhṛṅga*.
This nectar, mixed with *triphalā*, ghee, and honey, having been kept for a month in grain,
is placed within a pair of metal caskets and consecrated with mantras.
Having extracted that [knowledge] within a month and understood its power, one should employ it;
for without the beloved there is the sky, and likewise, without the sky there is the beloved.
It destroys cataracts, films, opacities, darkness, tumors, tinnitus, and pain; it also cures hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, splenic enlargement, and graying hair.
Acting thus, the wise man should eat milk products as his primary food,
along with meat from wild animals, mung beans, ghee, milk, and *śāli* rice, while observing celibacy.
Now he explains the alchemical process for dense sattva-iron, beginning with the words "In the beginning," and so forth.

First, at the outset, one should take thick iron dust— that is, dense mica-essence and iron filings, specifically the powder of magnetite— and rub it with the juices of the three myrobalans (harītakī, vibhītaka, and āmalaka) through repeated heating and cooling (puṭapāka). Once thoroughly rubbed until it resembles collyrium, equal to *sauvīrāñjana*, one should cover it with a cloth shielded from the rays of the sun by means of a concealing garment.
The meaning is that it should be worn in the presence of the rays of the sun.
"Thus," and so forth. (GRhtCM 19.28–33:3)

In this manner, having made [the substance] smooth and resembling collyrium, and likewise having prepared a mass of iron— meaning iron such as *muṇḍa* and other types— as well as a mass of mica-ore (*abhra-sattva*), these two together should be made equal to the powder of various magnetic metals; that is,
having made them equal to the powder of the various kinds of different species of magnetite (*ayaskānta*), [one should process them] many times, repeatedly, with *bhṛṅga*.
"One should accomplish" means "one should cultivate."
And he states that [formula] beginning with "triphalā" and so forth.

This nectar, which is like the essence of ambrosia (*sudhā*), has been repeatedly processed with *bhṛṅgarāja* and is as pleasing as pure mercury; it is not merely "not dead" (immortal), for it is truly immortal.

One should mix it with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*)—namely, *harītakī*, *vibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*—along with ghee and honey, and place it inside some kind of grain for one month. It should be prepared there in a quantity of one *māṣa*; this is the explicit instruction.
Of what specific qualities is it, and how is it fully worshipped with mantras?
Likewise, the mantra is as follows:
"Homage to Śivā, whose locks of hair are adorned with garlands of mandāra flowers, who has a crest marked by a garland of skulls, who wears divine garments; and homage to Śiva, who is naked."
By such [verses] as these. // GRhtCM_19.28-33:8 //
And that he stated with the words "by a month," and so forth.

Having extracted [the substance] from the grain in a period of one month—that is, with a measure of one month—and having brought it outside, one should employ it again after ascertaining its strength;
that is, one should give it to the consumer. Now, he shows the specific distinction: "without *kānta*" means one should employ it having prepared *abhraka-sattva* alone;
and furthermore, "without *gagana*" means one should employ *kānta* alone, having accomplished it according to the previously mentioned procedure. This is the meaning.
He states the result [of this] with the words "grossness," and so forth.

It destroys obesity (which is the disease of excessive fat), eye diseases such as *paṭala*, *kāca*, and *timira*, *arbuda* (a specific type of tumor), *granthi* (a glandular swelling), the well-known ringing in the ears (*karṇanāda*), and the eight kinds of colic (*śūla*). It also destroys hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*) born in the rectum, fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), urinary disorders (*meha*), splenic diseases (*plīhādi*), and so forth—where "fistula-in-ano" refers to a rectal ulcer and "urinary disorder" refers to *prameha*; it also destroys disorders of the reproductive seed (*bījavikāra*) and splenic enlargement (*plīharoga*). These are the diseases that it cures.
The meaning is that it destroys both graying hair and old age.
"He states what is beneficial" and so forth. (GRhtCM_19.28-33:13)

A wise person, while consuming this prepared medicinal preparation, should eat food in which cow's milk (*gorasa*) and whey (*mastu*) predominate—where *gorasa* means cow's milk and *mastu* means the whey of curds—and he should further consume meat from arid lands (*jāṅgala*), mung beans (*mudga*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and milk (*payaḥ*). *Jāṅgala* refers to that which comes from a region with little water and sparse trees; *mudga* is a well-known specific type of grain; *ājya* is ghee; and *payaḥ* is either milk or water. He should consume that which consists of mung beans, ghee, and milk.
Furthermore, one should eat boiled rice of the *śāli* variety.
The meaning is that all of this must be performed through celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Thus ends the activity of the cloud of sentient beings.
When mercury (satva) has been digested by the solid [metal], when it has been digested by the magnetite (kānta), and when it has been equally digested by the sharp [metal],
it becomes the supreme "field-maker" (kṣetrīkaraṇa); furthermore, even the *āroṭa* [mercury] may be employed.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Now, demonstrating the superiority of the matured mercury (*jīrṇarasa*), he says "ghanādi" and so forth. (GRhtCM_19.34:1)
It is that in which there is a dense mass of beings, as large as a tree, that has decayed.
"Kāntajīrṇa" means one who has become emaciated to the extent of his own stature.
Furthermore, that elixir in which the sharpness has become even and digested is of such a kind.
The meaning is that "making into a field" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*) is primary everywhere.
That which is bound, having become a *khoṭa*, and being repeatedly smelted, goes to destruction;
that *khoṭa* is to be known as a "bond" (*bandha*), which quickly removes all diseases.
Thus it is stated in another treatise.
Gold killed by mercury that is beloved by *ghanasattva*, combined with the juice of *śatāvarī* and licked with ghee and honey, destroys death and old age within a year. (GRhT 19.35)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Ghanasattva is the essence of mica; kānta is that which arises from magnetite; sūta is mercury; there is a singular form [for the compound] due to the dvandva-samāsa.

Likewise, mṛta-hema is gold that has reached the state of being reduced to ash, and kanaka is [ordinary] gold. This quartet, combined with the juice of śatāvarī and processed by the liquid of śatamūlī—

Furthermore, when licked with ghee and honey—that is, tasted together with ghee and honey—it destroys death, disease, and old age after a year; the meaning is that it eradicates them within the span of one year.
Having first undertaken one of these yogas for the purpose of making it one's field of practice,
one should apply oneself to it for a year or a half-year in order to achieve the highest good.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states the specific distinction [of these] with the words "of these," and so forth. GRhtCM_19.36:1.

Among these aforementioned yogas, having practiced one yoga from the very beginning, it should be applied for a year— that is, for a duration of one year— or for an *ayana*, meaning up to six months, among those who enjoy [the practice], for the sake of attaining *niḥśreyasa*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*), that is, for its accomplishment. This is the implied sense.
"Mukti, kaivalya, nirvāṇa, śreyas, niḥśreyasa, and amṛta" are synonyms, according to Amarasimha.
With abhraka, sasyaka, mākṣika, rasaka, darada, vimala, vajra, girija, and tuttha;
with vaikrānta, kānta, tīkṣṇa, hāṭaka, tāra, āra, and tāmra; GRht 19.37.
Whether combined or separate, taken two, three, or four at a time according to availability,
the "digested" (*jīrṇa*) mercury, when thus "slain," is praised by the wise for the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Pointing out many [other] distinctions, he says "abhraka" and so forth.
Abhraka is well-known; sasyaka is capala; mākṣika is tāpya; rasaka is kharpara; darada is hiṅgula; vimala is white mākṣika; vajraka is hīraka; and girijatu is śilājatu—with these.

Furthermore, regarding "vaikrānta" and so forth: *vaikrānta* is the powder produced from diamond-earth (*vajrabhūmi*); *kānta* is a type of iron; and *tīkṣṇa* is the essence [of steel]. And with these...
By means of gold (*hāṭaka*), silver (*tāra*), copper (*tāmra*), and so forth— where "gold" is *hema*, "silver" is *rūpya*, "copper" is *āra* (royal brass), and "copper" is *śulba*—
by these aforementioned substances from mica (*abhraka*) up to copper, whether all combined together, or separately, or individually according to availability (*yathālābha*)—
meaning not exceeding what is obtainable— it occurs; that is, by two, three, or four such substances starting with mica, [the metal] is digested and killed.

That in which there is the killing (*hati*) of digested mica (*jīrṇābhra*) and so forth by the lord of mercury (*rasendra*) is thus described; it is praised for alchemy (*rasāyana*), meaning for the destruction of old age and disease, by those who know the essential points of the science of mercury.
The meaning is that mica and the other substances are said to be excellent.
A pair. (GRhtCM 19.37–38:5)
Mercury struck by diamonds and other such gems is called *hatasūta*; another variety is named *śṛṅkhalābaddha*. These are used for the preparation of medicinal elixirs (*dehaloha*).
By their power, the pervasion [of the mercury] occurs with great speed; this is certain.
Thus, in another treatise. (GRhtCM 19.37–38:6)
Indeed, mercury bound with poisonous snakes and mica, when consumed, causes leprosy and other diseases; however,
when mercury is bound with secondary minerals (uparasa), the limbs burst [with pain] upon its consumption.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Showing the contemptible method, he says "viṣa" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.39:1.

The mercury bound with poison, lead, and tin— where "poison" refers to *saktuka* and the like, "lead" (*nāga*) is antimony, and "tin" (*vaṅga*) is tin— if this [mercury] is bound by these and consumed, it certainly destroys leprosy, fever, consumption, and other ailments. However,

when the mercury is bound with secondary minerals (*uparasa*), that is, bound with the eight secondary minerals such as sulfur (*gandha*) and so forth, if that mercury is consumed, the limbs of the consumer— the hands, feet, and so on— will burst apart.
For mercury that has been processed and digested with *ghanasattva*, *kāntaloha*, *kāñcī*, *bhāskara*, and *tīkṣṇa*, the dose is one *guñjā*; the maximum dose is one *māṣaka*.
Two *guñjā* [of mercury] pierce a hundred [times]; likewise, one *guñjā* pierces a thousand;
half a *guñjā* belongs to that which pierces a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*); and from the mercury that pierces ten million (*koṭi*), [the dose is] a *siddhārtha*.
Regarding the dosage of the processed mercury (*jīrṇarasa*), he says "ghanā" and so forth.

"By these [processes], it has first been 'eaten' (consumed) and then digested; that is, it has undergone *jāraṇā* (digestion). Of that mercury (*sūta*), the dose for consumption is one *guñjā*, just as a *guñjā* is defined:
"Three mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*) make one barleycorn (*yava*); three barleycorns make one *guñjā*.

"The dosage for others is different; the dosage for one who has digested the elixir is as follows: ten *guñjās* were declared by Brahmā in ancient times to be one *māṣaka*, and a *māṣaka* is equal to one *māṣa*."
By which of these? By those possessing the essence of mica, the lovely essence of iron, the sun-like sharpness of magnetite, and the refined essence of copper. Thus.
Now, he states the measurement according to the specific piercing, beginning with "one hundred" and so forth.

The dose of mercury that pierces a hundred [times] should be known as the measure of one *guñjā*; likewise, by that same method, the dose of mercury that pierces a thousand [times] is also just one *guñjā*. Furthermore, from mercury that pierces a hundred thousand [times], it is half a *raktikā*, and from mercury that pierces ten million [times], it is a *siddhārtha*, the measure of a mustard seed.
That in which penetration occurs by a hundredth part is "hundred-piercing" (śatavedhin); [it refers to] that which is hundred-piercing.
Thus it should be understood in all cases.
A man devoted to recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of deities should wear a beautiful gem set in gold, along with various medicinal pills. (GRht 19.42)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):

Japa is the recitation of [mantras] such as Aghora; homa is the fire-oblation performed with a tenth part of that [number]; devatārcana is the worship of the deities—Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Ravi, Śiva, and Caṇḍī. A man devoted to these [practices], following such a rule, would he not wear mercury combined with gold? That is, mercury which has been joined—that is, mixed—with gold—is [like] the kāntamaṇi.
It is both lovely and a gem, thus it is a "lovely gem" (kāntamaṇi), meaning a gem known as "lovely"; furthermore, there are various pills, meaning those which are both various and pills.

For rice, however, the meal should consist of flour-based food with clarified butter and the broth of mung beans and meat; likewise, foods made from barley and wheat, cow’s milk, and especially whey. (GRht 19.43)
For drinking, water that is not alkaline and whatever sweet substances are auspicious are recommended;
one should drink with a mouth gladdened by the fragrance of the four spices (*cāturjātaka*) and camphor.
Next, he speaks of wholesome foods, beginning with "of rice," and so forth.
The food produced from flour refers to rice, sixty-day rice, and the like, as well as that food which is produced from flour-cakes.
Ājya is clarified butter (ghṛta).

With what? Together with green gram (*mudga*) meat soups—wherein green gram is well-known and meats are specifically to be eaten—and cow’s milk is also to be eaten; furthermore, *mastu* (whey) derived from cow’s milk is specifically to be eaten. For drinking, non-alkaline water—that is, sweet water—is to be used. Moreover, whatever sweet substances are not explicitly mentioned here are praised as excellent. Furthermore, one should consume the substance such that the mouth is gladdened by the fragrance of the four spices (*caturjātaka*) and camphor.

The drink to be consumed consists of the "fourfold" (caturjātaka)—namely, cinnamon-bark, cardamom, eaglewood, and nāgakesara—as well as camphor, which is *ghanasāra*; the meaning is that his mouth was perfumed, being delighted by the fragrance and scent of these.
Conversation with a young woman should be carried out, as should the massaging of her limbs;
by the mere touch of her, the *sūtaka* (mercury) courses through the body.
This distinction is derived from another text.
At the start [of the regimen], at 19.45 muhūrtas,
the drinking of wine, sour gruel, oil, or curd is not desired with the meat-broth.
A wise person should not apply mustard oil as an ointment to the body during the practice of *rasāyana*.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the unwholesome [factors] beginning with "liquor," etc. (GRhtCM_19.45:1).

Regarding the passage beginning with "madyāranāla": *madya* is liquor (*surā*), and *āranāla* is fermented gruel (*kāñjika*); drinking these two is not desired nor is it recommended. *Taila* is sesame oil, and *dadhi* is a product of milk; drinking these two as well is not recommended. One should not perform anointing or massaging of the body with pungent oil, such as mustard oil (*sarṣapataila*).
The wise one [is so called] in the context of *rasāyana*; that is the meaning.
Burnt, undercooked, not sweet, and hot milk is forbidden; likewise, meat that has lost its essence,
and fruits or roots that have turned stale are never prescribed as food here.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
A burnt substance is not desired for alchemy (*rasāyana*), nor is an uncooked one; nor are those that are non-sweet—namely pungent, bitter, astringent, sour, and salty;
nor is that which is hot, i.e., heated by fire. Furthermore, meat that is spoiled or censured is not desired, as is meat that has been kept overnight (*paryuṣita*).
In this *rasāyana*, such fruits and roots that have been combined (*saṃdhānīkṛta*) are not specified as being edible; rather, it is stated:
"The *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the *karkaṭī*, the *kaliṅga*, the *kāravellaka*, the *kusumbhikā*, the *karkoṭī*, the *kadalī*, and the *kākamācikā*."
"One who consumes meat should indeed avoid these eight words beginning with the letter *ka*," so it is stated in another text.
Now, fasting (laṅghana) should not be performed, nor indeed should one eat before three hours (yāma) have passed;
having thus removed these prohibitions, the wise person should apply themselves to the king of essences (rasarāja).

*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī): In this elixir, fasting is not to be practiced; furthermore, the meaning is that one must not eat for half a watch—that is, within the middle of a watch. GRhtCM_19.47:1*
Free from anxiety and anger, one should perform a bath with pleasant water;
thus one shall not drive away the planetary fevers, rākṣasas, bhūtas, or the Mātṛ-devīs.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the passage beginning with "varjita" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.48:1.

"Free from anxiety and anger" means that by whom anxiety (*cintā*) and anger (*kopa*)—these two "anxiety-anger"—have been abandoned, being such, he should perform his bath with "pleasure-water," that is, pleasantly warm water.

One should not expel *grahas*, *rākṣasas*, or *bhūtas*. *Grahās* are those who seize, such as *piśācas* and the like; *jvara* is the king of diseases; *rākṣasas* are flesh-eaters; and *bhūtas* are beings born of the divine class. One should not expel these, nor should one displace them from their own places.
Furthermore, one should not cause the goddesses of the Mothers—the Seven Mothers, Dakṣiṇī, and the others—to be eradicated.
Dissolved in the Supreme Brahman, with a tranquil mind and having attained equanimity,
he comforted the three aims of life, conquered the [six] flavors, and was completely satisfied by the bliss of aesthetic rapture.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states "in the Supreme," etc., as the reason for the cessation of anxiety and anger. GRhtCM_19.49:1.

The practitioner of *rasāyana*, absorbed in the supreme Brahman which is the nature of consciousness, shall attain identity with it; his mind shall become tranquil, his thoughts withdrawn from sense objects, and he shall reach a state of equanimity. Free from enmity toward both his own son and his enemy, and having conquered the three aims of life—dharma, artha, and kāma—he shall be completely satisfied with the bliss of *rasa* and filled with joy.
This is the meaning.
That fool who, disregarding the injunctions of the scriptures, engages in the practice of mercury according to his own whims,
will certainly suffer from indigestion due to that contrary conduct. (GRht 19.50)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Showing the necessity of destiny, he says "yaḥ" and so forth. (GRhtCM 19.50:1)

That man who, having abandoned the injunctions of the scriptures, engages in mercury (rasa) according to his own whims with an unrestrained mind, is a fool devoid of knowledge; due to that man’s contrary conduct, a severe indigestion arises, which is known as *rasājīrṇa*.
In this case, when indigestion occurs, there arises sleepiness, laziness, fever, darkness of vision,
a burning sensation, pain in the region of the navel, a slight dullness, loss of appetite, and a breaking pain in the limbs.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the symptoms of the indigestion of mercury (rasājīrṇa) with the words "sambhavati" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.51:1.
In this context of alchemy (*rasāyana*), when indigestion occurs or arises, then these symptoms will manifest.
Excessive sleep, lassitude, looseness of the limbs, fever (which is well known), darkness (fainting), burning sensation, heat,
slight pain in the region of the navel and the bladder, numbness of the mouth, loss of appetite, lack of desire for food, breaking pain, and aching of the limbs—
these are the symptoms that occur when there is indigestion of the *rasa* (nutrient fluid). This is the meaning.
Having understood this [condition] to be indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), the wise man should abandon the elixir (*rasāyana*) for three days and employ this following method to conceal it. (GRht 19.52)
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the remedy even for indigestion in the verse beginning with "having known," etc. (GRhtCM 19.52:1).

Having thus recognized indigestion by its characteristics, such as excessive sleep and so forth, a wise person should abandon the *rasāyana* for three days and practice *yoga* in order to conceal— that is, to destroy— this indigestion.
One should drink the decoction of the root of *karkoṭī* for three days with rock salt (*sindhu*),
or with black salt (*sauvarcala*) and cow’s urine, in the event of indigestion caused by meat. (GRht 19.53)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the verse beginning with "karkoṭī" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.53:1.

One should drink the juice of the root of *karkoṭī*—that is, the juice from the root of the *karkoṭī* creeper—for three days; or else one should drink its decoction together with *sindhunā*, that is, with rock salt (*saindhava*). Or, for the digestion of mercury (*rasājīrṇa*), one should drink that decoction mixed with cow’s urine (*gojala*). Alternatively, one should drink it for three days after adding a sprinkling (*prativāpa*) of black salt (*sauvarcala*) into the *karkoṭī* juice.
The meaning is "everywhere."
Having ground the *mātuluṅgī* fruit, one who drinks its juice with ginger and rock salt in the morning,
or drinks it boiled with cow’s urine, properly cures indigestion caused by meat.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He says something else, beginning with "having ground," etc. (GRhtCM_19.54:1).

This is the root-fiber (*jaṭā*) of *mātuluṅga*; it is called *mātuluṅgī*. That man who grinds it and drinks its juice in the morning, along with ginger and rock salt (*saindhava*), or who drinks its decoction (*kaṣāya*) boiled with cow’s urine, is protected from indigestion of the juices (*rasājīrṇa*); the meaning is that it does not destroy him.
If, by some means, mercury has been consumed that is defiled by serpents or other impurities due to ignorance,
one should drink cow’s urine along with the roots of *kaṭukā* and *āravallī* in order to counteract it.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
He states the method for consuming mercury combined with [the substances of] the Nāgas and so forth, beginning with "In some way... (katham api) etc. (GRhtCM_19.55:1).

Furthermore, because mercury (rasa) may be tainted by lead (nāga) and other impurities, and if such mercury—containing lead and tin—is somehow consumed through ignorance, then for the purpose of counteracting that lead- and tin-tainted mercury, one should drink this medicinal preparation consisting of cow’s urine (gojala), *kaṭukā*, and the root-fiber (*śiphā*) or root-tangle (*jaṭā*) of the *kāravallī* creeper.
*Gojala* means cow’s urine; *kaṭutiktā* refers to the bitter *kaṭukā*; and the *śiphā* of the *kāravallī* creeper is its fibrous root. One should drink this medicine.
By that, the defects such as those of *nāgavaṅga* and so forth are destroyed.
If indigestion occurs, one should indeed consume any one of these— *śarapuṅkhā*, *asuradālī*, *paṭola*, *bimbī*, or *kākamācī*— prepared as a decoction. (GRht 19.56)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states that very point in the verse beginning with "śarapuṅkha" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.56:1.

Among these medicinal herbs, whichever one is mentioned—that is, declared—and boiled—that is, decocted—one should certainly consume that during indigestion; the sense is that by this means, indigestion is destroyed.

What are those herbs? They are *śarapuṅkhā*, which is well-known; *suradālī* (also called *devadālī*); *paṭola*, whose name is familiar; *bimbī*; *golā*; and *kākamācī*, which is well-known—this is the meaning. START GRht 19.57
Excessive intake of very sour, salty, and pungent tastes causes the flow of digestive fluids (*rasasaṃsrāva*) and results in fever;
likewise, the gastric fire (*jaṭharavahni*) is destroyed by excessively sweet foods and by eating constantly.
And he says that very thing in the verse beginning with "atyamla" and so forth.

Excessively sour substances such as *cukra* and the like, excessively salty substances such as alkalis (*kṣāra*) and the like, and excessively pungent substances such as *nimba* and *kaṭukī* and so forth—by these, a "digestive fire" (*jara*) arises which causes digestion (*jaraṇa*); it is called *jara* because it digests (*jarati*). Furthermore, by the constant consumption of sweet substances such as sugarcane juice and the like, the digestive fire of the stomach (*jaṭharavahni*), that is, the fire of the internal cavity (*koṣṭhāgni*), perishes; the intention is that its substratum perishes.

Furthermore, that fool who constantly practices such a dietary regimen (samāhāra) will find his digestive fire destroyed; indeed, the nutrient essence (rasa) does not circulate, and disease will arise. (GRht 19.58)
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
He states its specific characteristics in the verse beginning with "ya" and so forth. GRhtCM_19.58:1.

Furthermore, if a foolish and ignorant person constantly and continuously consumes very sour, salty, and pungent food immediately after indigestion, his digestive fire (agni) in the stomach is destroyed; the nutrient essence (rasa) does not circulate, and it does not manifest its own qualities.
To the question "What would then happen?", he says: the meaning is that there would be disease.
But he who, by virtue of enduring great fire, is a master of the mercury that pierces hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands [of times],
attains success through this practice by means of the application of alchemical operations with effort.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Through this aforementioned procedure, that mercury which, by effort, becomes capable of penetrating a hundred thousand lakhs [of times] will be perfected. GRhtCM_19.59:1.
Whether it pierces a hundred thousand, a lakh, ten million, or even a hundred million or a billion targets,
one should consume the ground powder with its juice along with *balī*; thus one becomes a bestower of success.
*Commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī:
Now, he states the definition according to the subsequent rule, beginning with "one hundred," etc. (GRhtCM_19.60:1).
The mercury that pierces through a hundred thousand lakhs [of targets].

One should consume the mercury (rasa) ground together with *bali*—that is, together with sulfur (*gandhaka*). Starting from one hundred, the number should be understood to increase tenfold in succession through one thousand, ten thousand, a million, ten million, and a hundred million.
When prepared in this manner, the mercury becomes a bestower of success (*siddhi*), meaning it produces the qualities as described.
Then, indeed, the practitioner traverses [the earth] and begets sons who resemble the offspring of gods;
his desire for women becomes steady, and he is freed from wrinkles and graying hair. (GRht 19.61)
The intellect, strength, power, and lifespan increase for one who practices alchemy;
having attained divine intellect, his divine qualities continue to flourish.
Thus perfected by the elixir, free from suffering, old age, and death, and endowed with virtues,
he constantly travels through all the worlds by means of moving through the sky.
He is a donor in the three worlds; he is also a creator here like the lotus-born Brahmā;
he may be a sustainer like Viṣṇu, and he becomes a destroyer like Rudra.
Praising the previous injunction, he says "he strides," and so forth.

Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, the *sūta* (vital essence) moves forward and manifests its own qualities; while the *sūta* is moving, it produces sons who possess a luster like that of divine embryos—those whose radiance (*ābhā*) is like that of divine embryos. Furthermore, he in whom desire (*kāma*), longing for pleasure (*raty-abhilāṣa*), or passion (*madana*) remains always steady and stable among women, and who is moreover freed from wrinkles and grey hair—the *valīs* being... [wrinkles]... and the *palitas* being grey hairs.

"He is freed from and devoid of gray hairs (*palitāni*); *vali* is the skin wrinkled by old age" (Amara). "Grayness of the hair" (*palitam*)—such a man becomes; this is the ellipsis (*iti śeṣaḥ*).
