He asks again, "What else might it be? and says, beginning with "intellect" (*buddhi*).

For a person who has attained *rasāyana*, the intellect increases and strength increases along with *āyus*, that is, the duration of life. Furthermore, for the practitioner of *rasāyana* who has attained divine intellect— meaning that, according to the context, divine qualities such as *medhā* (retentive memory) and so forth increase and become manifest.
And he says that very thing with the words "In this way," and so forth.

In this manner, a person who has attained perfection through *rasa*—where *rasa* refers to mercury (*pārada*) that is perfectly perfected (*saṃsiddha*), or one who is perfected by means of *rasa*—becomes free from old age and death; the meaning is that he is devoid of decrepitude and disease.
Furthermore, he becomes endowed with qualities (*guṇavān*), such as intelligence and other faculties.
Furthermore, by means of moving through the sky—that is, traveling through the atmosphere—he constantly wanders throughout all the worlds, meaning across all the realms of existence.
The intention is that the donor becomes preeminent over all in the three worlds—of heaven, earth, and the netherworld (pātāla).
That person also becomes a creator, a progenitor, within these three worlds—here in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld (pātāla).
Who was he like? Like the lotus-born Brahmā.
Furthermore, the husband becomes like Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the triad.
Furthermore, he becomes a destroyer like Rudra; the meaning is that he may act as the triad of Brahmā and the others in the processes of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
START GRHT 19.65–66 (Amarasundarī-guṭikā):
Take equal parts of kānta-loha, sattva of abhra, gold, silver, and copper; this is the count.
The bound [substance] with equal parts of mercury, when smelted, forms a ball (gola) which becomes a khoṭa.
The pill named Amarasuṇdarī, which has its exterior smeared with mercury and is placed in the mouth as a weapon-warder, indeed destroys diseases residing within the body.
He describes the procedure for the *amarasundarī* pill and its qualities, beginning with the words "kānta" and so forth.
The beloved, the magnet, the cloud, and the pair.

The essence of mica (abhrakasattva) is well known; gold (hema), kanaka, and silver (tāra) constitute a single unit because they form a dvandva compound. Then there is copper (arka). The number or calculation of these—starting with kānta and the others—is to be understood as being in equal parts, that is, in equal proportions.

Furthermore, one should smelt [the mixture] with an equal portion of mercury, such that the amount of sulfur is equal to the amount of mercury; the remaining part of the process is to do so in a blind crucible (andhamūṣā).
Once it has been prepared, having been smeared with the liquid mentioned for the purpose of killing—namely, mercury—over a bound ball (golaka) on the exterior, one should heat it.
When prepared in this manner, the solidified mass becomes a globular pill known as *piṣṭistambha*.
That sword-shield situated within the mouth—that is, located inside the face—will be present; and when this has entered the mouth, a blow from swords and other weapons does not strike the body.
This pill should be known by its name as the *amarasundarī-guṭikā*.
This [medicine], whether situated within the body or applied to another part of the face or elsewhere, destroys and eradicates diseases located in the body.
The meaning is that even though the measure is not explicitly stated, it should be understood as being five niṣkas.
Thus [ends the description of] the Amarasundarī pill.
When combined with either gold or silver and heated, it attains a state of unity; and when not diminished and compacted, molasses produces long and brilliant pills.
When ground with effort, that powder acts like a cloth; it does not release its impurity, yet being odorless, it dissolves in an instant—this is considered mercury known as "bound" (baddha).
Thus it is stated in another treatise.
START GRHT 19.67–72 (The Life-Reviving Pill): That aforementioned mercury which, exceeding one hundred thousand [parts], penetrates the metals;
When bound by the application of *sāraṇā* and placed in the mouth [of the crucible], one should digest the gem.
Combined with equal parts of mercury, magnetite,
copper, and iron, and joined with the essence of mica, this pill is named *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī* (the Rejuvenator of the Dead).
Whether in a cluster of flowers, on a crown, or as a necklace or earring made of gold,
it [destroys] the mass of constant sufferings born of death, fear, grief, disease, poison, weapons, and old age.
He upon whose body this pill named *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī* has been placed is most worthy of worship by asuras, yakṣas, and kinnaras, as well as by the masters of accomplished yogins.
Having washed it and then cast the pill into water for two *ghaṭikās*, that [pill],
when placed in the mouth of a corpse, brings him back to life.
Then that very same water, when accompanied by wholesome diet, a healthy person drinks;
he thereby attains a divine, very firm body, free from death and old age.
(GRht 19.72) *Commentary: Mugdhāvabodhinī:*
He describes the procedure for the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī* pill and its qualities, beginning with the words "ya" and so forth.

When the aforementioned mercury (sūta), which transfixes metals such as silver and others beyond a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) up to ten million (*koṭi*), a billion (*arbuda*), and so forth, has been bound and placed in a *prakāśamukha* apparatus with its opening facing upward, one should digest gems such as diamonds (*vajra*) and the like using the processes of *sāraṇā* and *sāraṇataila*.

Furthermore, mercury should be joined with equal parts of lead and an equal portion of tin; it should also be joined with the essences of *suraloha*, magnetite (*ayaskānta*), and *tāpya* (cinnabar). With these—namely, gold (*kanaka*), magnetite (*kāntaloha*), the essence of *mākṣika* (sulphide ore), and the essence of mica (*abhrakasattva*)—there arises a pill named *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī*. Furthermore, this [pill] is placed there in the crucible (*mūṣā*).
It should be made with gold.
Furthermore, for one to whom this pill is constantly placed upon a cluster of flowers, or on a crown or diadem, or on a necklace or an ear—

where "necklace and ear" (*kaṇṭhasūtrakarṇa*) refers to that [ornament] or on a limb such as a hand or foot— their accumulation of sufferings consisting of the fear of death, grief, disease, weapons, old age, and constant affliction is destroyed; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
He in whose hands this [mudrā] is placed and established in these locations becomes most worthy of worship by asuras,

yakṣas, and kinnaras— the asuras being the Daityas, the yakṣas being a class of divine beings, and the kinnaras being those with horse-like faces; he becomes their most worshipful, meaning most exceptionally worthy of honor.

Most worthy of worship by the lords of accomplished yogis—where *siddhas* are specific deities and *yogīndras* are [masters] such as Nāgārjuna and others—thereafter, having cast the "life-restoring" pill (*mṛtajīvanī*) into water and washed it for two *ghaṭikās*, that very water used for washing the pill becomes clear and stainless; when placed in the mouth of a deceased person, it effects his rising and awakening. As for the man: he is the person who performs this.

Endowed with wholesome regimen—that is, engaged in the consumption of beneficial substances—that person attains a divine body, a celestial form. Furthermore, what kind of divine body? It is free from death and old age, devoid of disease and graying hair, and exceedingly firm like a diamond (*vajra*). The size of the pill and the method of its preparation are as described previously; this is the meaning.
Thus ends the pill that restores the dead to life.
START GRHT 19.73–74 (Vajriṇī-guṭikā): Take mercury, mica,
and lotus, along with gold and silver, joined together in pairs as appropriate.
The excellent seed, well-digested and joined with the thunderbolt, is the Vajriṇī pill.
Once this has entered the cavity of the mouth, it produces strength equal to that of a young elephant;
its body likewise becomes impenetrable and is liberated from death, old age, and disease.
He describes the procedure for the *vajriṇī* pill and its qualities, beginning with the words "kānta" and so forth.

*Kānta* and *ghana*—the essence of these two is *kāntaghanasattva*. *Kāntasattva* is [magnetite], *ghanasattva* is *abhrakasāra* (mica), and *kamala* is copper. Furthermore, *hema* is gold, and *tāra* is silver, as before. That which has been made into a pair (*dvandva*) by whatever method—that pair is the "excellent seed" (*bījavara*).

The task is accomplished once it is fully digested. Of what nature is it? It is the "excellent seed" (*bījavara*), joined with diamond (*vajra*), that is, joined with a *hīraka* (adamant). This pill is named *Vajriṇī*. Furthermore, when this *Vajriṇī* pill has entered the cavity of the mouth—that is, having reached the interior of the mouth—it produces a strength equal to nine *nāgas*, meaning nine elephants; it bestows upon his body a strength equivalent to those.

The meaning is that the body— the physical form— of one who holds a pill in the mouth is "unbreakable," meaning it is difficult to break, and furthermore, it is liberated from death, old age, and disease.
Thus ends the Vajriṇī pill.
START GRHT 19.75–76 (Khecarīguṭikā):
When the mercury has been subjected to fuming and observation, and when it has been infused with the five great jewels and processed;
By means of the seed-syllable applied with honey and magnetite within the being of space.
The pill known as Khecarī falls into the mouth the very moment it is cast;
one becomes most worthy of worship by the hosts of gods, asuras, and siddhas, as well as by Indra and the others.
He describes the procedure for the *khecarī-guṭikā* (the pill of the sky-farer) and its qualities, beginning with the words "dhūma" and so forth.

In the mercury (*rasa*) known as *dhūmāvalokita* and *dhūmavedhin*, which has been processed with the five great jewels (*pañcamahāratna*), namely the five types of great jewels beginning with diamond (*vajra*), as follows: "Diamond, pearl, ruby, sapphire, and emerald— these should be known as the five kinds of great jewels."
Thus. GRhtCM_19.75-76:2.

Furthermore, when the mercury—the essence of the sky—is processed with the seed-mantra (bīja) joined by *mākṣika* and *kānta*, and combined with *tāpya* and *cumbaka*, it becomes a pill known as *khecarī*.

As soon as that mercury in the form of a pill is cast into the mouth and falls therein, one becomes most worthy of worship by Indra and the others—the hosts of gods, asuras, and siddhas. "Indra" refers to Maghavat; "and the others" refers to those [deities] beginning with him. "Gods" are the immortals; "asuras" are the Daityas; "siddhas" are a specific class of deities. By these, meaning by their hosts or assemblies, one becomes exceedingly venerable—this is the meaning.
Thus ends the pill known as Khecarī.
Those men who have witnessed the infinitely varied discourse on mercury— divided into the categories of liquid, globules, and paste—
as it was mastered by the foremost adepts, are victorious.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Indicating the infinity of the discourse on mercury (*rasa*), he says "rasa... and so forth. GRhtCM_19.77:1.
The "discourse on taste" has infinite qualities; he who possesses such infinite qualities is thus described.
They are infinite and immeasurable.
By what means is the discourse on alchemy (rasavāda) infinite? Because liquids, globules, and pastes are each infinite, the discourse on alchemy is also infinite.
Of what nature is it? It is fashioned and composed by the preeminent Siddhas, such as Nityanātha and others.
Those men by whom this alchemy was seen by the great Siddhas conquer and abide in supreme excellence.

Victorious is that illustrious Madana, lord of the Kirātas and master of aesthetic flavor (rasācārya), whose greatness of virtue was born from his birth in the Haihaya lineage and his descent from the moon dynasty.

To him descended of its own accord the science of alchemy (*rasavidyā*), which is the support of all auspiciousness and the cause of the supreme welfare of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) from of old. *Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):* [The science] which is the abode of every blessing and the cause of the highest beatitude for the Supreme Lord [Śiva], first descended of its own accord upon him.
Now, he describes the lineage of the author of the work, beginning with the words "In the lineage of the Moon," and so forth.
The illustrious King Madana, known by that name, triumphs; he exists in a state of supreme excellence.
Of what nature was the lord of the Kirātas? The Kirātas are the Bhillas; he is their master.
Furthermore, what were his specific qualities? He was one whose greatness of virtues was produced by his birth in the Haihaya clan, which itself originated in the Lunar dynasty (*śītāṃśuvaṃśa*).
That is to say, he was so described because the greatness of his virtues was generated by his arising—his birth—within that very lineage of the Haihayas, which had its origin in the Lunar dynasty.
Furthermore, what further qualification does Madana have? He is the *rasācārya*, meaning the progenitor of the science of *rasa*.
Now, he describes the praise of the qualities of the one who causes this [stūpa] to be made, beginning with the words "yasya" and so forth.
The science of alchemy (rasavidyā) descended and manifested itself as the very nature of the patron named Śrīmadana.
Of what nature is this science of rasa? It is the support of all auspiciousness; that is, it is that in which all those auspicious things—meaning those of excellent form—have their support or refuge.

This science of alchemy (rasavidyā) makes the body free from old age and death; and since the body is the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, it is rightly said to be the basis of all auspiciousness. Furthermore, the science of alchemy is the supreme and most excellent cause for the highest good, which is liberation.
By this very science of alchemy, the supreme state of Brahmā, the Parameṣṭhin, first attained in the past that which is the highest good, characterized by freedom from old age and death.
Therefore, having received great honor from the Kirāta king, the mendicant Govinda, devoted to the practice of alchemy (*rasakarma*), composed this treatise (*tantra*) titled *Rasahṛdaya*.
*Commentary (Mugdhāvabodhinī):
Indicating the greatness of his own name, the author says "Therefore," and so forth. (GRhtCM_19.80:1)
The meaning is that he has composed, that is, produced, this treatise on the science of alchemy (rasatantra).
What are the specific characteristics of this tantra called *Rasahṛdaya*, and what having done [to it], [did he say] "from that," and so forth? // GRhtCM_19.80:3 //
